There is another text of this name that is much shorter and is framed as a dialogue between Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. This Vārāhī Tantra consists of 4,631 verses. Another complete manuscript is deposited in...
the library of Sampūrṇānanda Sanskrit University in Vārāṇasī.
Vārāhī is one of the eight Mothers (mātṛkā). Although tantras bearing the names of the other Mothers have not [been found],...
Having recovered it, Lakṣmīdhara quotes a verse in his commentary on the *Saundaryalaharī* which lists them as a standard group of Tantras.
This *Vārāhītantra* associates itself with Kāmarūpa, where it...

It may possibly have been redacted. The colophons state that it belongs to the Dakṣiṇāmnāya. It draws extensively from other Tantras but also contains much original material. Indeed, it is a veritable...
A compendium of Śākta ritual procedures. It is quoted in several texts, including the *Mantramahārṇava*, the *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava*, and the *Āgamakalpalatā*.
the *Saubhāgyabhāskara*, the *Tārārahasyavṛtti*, the *Āgamatattvavilāsa*, the *Sarvollāsatantra*, the Bengali *Tantrasāra*,
and Lakṣmīdhara’s commentary on the *Saundaryalaharī*. It is also...
It is quoted in the *Puraścaryārṇava*, attributed to the Nepalese king Pratāpasiṃhaśāha. This work is known to have been completed in 1775 CE, thereby establishing the *terminus ante quem*.
Regarding the date of the *Vārāhītantra*: incidentally, this fact demonstrates that the aforementioned texts must all be later. Practically all colophons follow the following simple format:
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Śrīvārāhītantra*, within the *Nirvāṇapada* of the *Dakṣiṇāmnāya*, in the descent of the Great Most Secret Tantra.

Oṃ, homage to the Goddess Śrī Sundarī Kālikā Vārāhī; homage!
In Kāmarūpa, the great pīṭha situated upon heaps of severed heads and trunks,
crowded with various hosts and a multitude of diverse yoginīs.
Having separately taken up their respective mounts as was fitting,
the hero Pracaṇḍa, seated upon a boar, stood positioned in their midst.
Having paid homage with devotion, Guhyakālī asked:
"O Lord, how is one joined with the nectar? What would be the most excellent state everywhere?"
O Lord, tell me of that wondrous and marvelous tantra known as Vārāhī, which purifies the impure and describes the path of meditative absorption.
Having paid homage to her who is proclaimed as the bestower of the four aims of human life through mere remembrance,
he spoke again with eyes wide open in wonder.
The illustrious Caṇḍabhairava said:
Listen, Kālī; I shall speak, having taken up the mind that is well-guarded.
Formerly, in the middle of the Kṛta Yuga, she was renowned throughout the three worlds.
The Cat-Rākṣasa has been described as holding a goad and a spear in his hands;
he oppresses the entire world and possesses great strength in battle and victory.
The goddess Vārāhī, who is auspicious and fair-faced, is her worshipper;
when she is brought under control as a servant, Kālī is intent upon her command.
Sometimes the deity, though merely a name, takes refuge [in the mind];
trembling, with limbs shaking from great fear, one remains with the breath suspended.
The Goddess said:
Where are the guardians of the directions, gates, and paths stationed within the house?
O Bhairava, having thus slain the heroes, by whom were they crushed?
"Tell the truth, O mighty-armed one, O you whose banner is a monkey, O possessor of great strength!
O Goddess, what lore was obtained by you for the purpose of killing the cat?"
Pracaṇḍa said:
Listen, O Goddess of beautiful hips; I shall speak to you with the underlying reasons.
Formerly, when Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Jānakī had gone to dwell in the forest...
For the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa, Janakī was born from a human being among the gods;
after some time had passed, she was there in a secluded part of the forest.
When the demon was captured and taken away by Śītā, he went to the city of Laṅkā;
yet he did not see Vedeḥī, and this is the lamentation of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Wandering through all places in the forest and upon the mountains, both stationary and moving,
they may, by the conjunction of destiny, obtain the Great Goddess.
O Śailarṣabha, in the presence of the Lord of Monkeys and his host at the site of Ṛkṣamukha,
before Rāmacandra, ask the monkey about what has been forgotten.
"Who are you, O weeping human? What is this sorrow that has come upon you? Speak quickly; tell me all of it, and give me your garment as a sign."
Pracaṇḍā said:
I, the Goddess, have not spoken of the wondrous nature of the Rāmāyaṇa,
which is like a golden necklace set with pearls and gems that has been woven and adorned.
Vasiṣṭha said:
The various texts composed by Vasiṣṭha speak differently;
yet, through the discharge of Rāma’s arrow, Vālī’s life was taken and he passed away.
And the monkey Rāma conversed with Sugrīva;
through mutual assistance, they increased their affection for one another.
Having risen, he should announce their names before Sugrīva:
"O Lord of monkeys, listen to Vālin’s sons and the rest, who are enduring great sorrow."
In every place and in all four directions, searching for where Jānakī might be alive,
he saw her, spoke with her, and having seen her, quickly returned here.
Having thus heard from the mouth of Vālin concerning the strength, heroism, and prowess [of Rāmacandra],
and having offered salutations, she [acknowledged] the proper path for all those beginning with Rāmacandra.
Taking Rāma’s signet ring and uttering a piercing cry,
the beloved of the monkeys went to Laṅkā and was seen in the four directions.
O monkey, having paid homage to them with great secrecy and due preparation, let Vaidehī be seen in their Aśoka grove, which is well-adorned.
Mayinī fell into the full water-pot while her waist was bound;
Janakī likewise engaged in conversation with them as they adorned their dwellings.
Having offered salutations and prostrations, the great monkey rose up again;
having reached the presence of Rāma, he bowed and paid his respects.
Having heard this at length from the mouth of Rāmacandra, who was adorned by his attendants,
[Sugrīva], together with the hosts of Sugrīva and others among the descendants of Raghu, [acted accordingly].
Possessing the strength, heroism, and majesty of a single army with its four divisions,
he went everywhere to the battle and then took refuge at the gate of Laṅkā.
Accompanied by his armies and resounding with the roar of a terrible battle,
he went forth to obtain the hearing of that sound.
The cat with sharp fangs and the elephant with its trunk— these two fought together,
charging directly toward one another amidst a multitude of troops.
Seizing their anger and directed toward Hanumān,
they took up iron mallets and struck him down as if he were falling.
"Just as one situated upon wood, stone, or rock [is unharmed] by a fallen rākṣasa,
so too this cat, having seen [the danger], remembers it and becomes overcome with fear."
Vārāhī, Mātā, Mātaṅgī, Saṃkaṣṭā, and Antarā; and also:
The cat said:
O Great Goddess, you have arrived, bearing a trident and a skull-bowl;
you are the Goddess who delivers from distress, Vārāhī, the remover of fear.
Having heard this, the world-pervading Mother, the Sovereign of the Three Worlds,
was indeed quickly found at the entrance by him who bore the sword and the trident.
"Hūṃ! Hūṃ! Hūṃ!"—by this sound of *hūṃ*, he devours the army along with its forces;
all are swallowed and crushed, yet they spare Hanumān and Rāma.
"O Rāmacandra, look! He has fainted and been struck down.
O you who are foremost among the strong, behold him; this one of great power has been forgotten."
Having performed the propitiation of Lord Rāma, the sage Durvāsas, O pearl among sages, spoke these words:
"O Lord of Lords, you who are devoted to the swift arrival [of the Lord], be gracious."
O Agnitejas, you who possess the bow-tipped arrow of mantras,
you have come as the Teacher of the World for the protection of Śrī Rāmacandra.
O tiger among sages, one who desires meditative absorption hears a signal sound;
at that moment, one should quickly recollect the great mantra Vāyuvega and proceed with haste.
They ran toward the tip of Laṅkā, and there the monkey encountered them face-to-face;
seeing the monkey, the army of the bird-eaters (vultures) cried out, "O twice-born one, where are you going?"
The monkey said:
Listen, O Brahmin, to this great account of the Lord himself:
while Ghasmara was devouring them, Sugrīva, Lakṣmaṇa, and all the others were swallowed up.
"O great brahmin, having remained fearless, I quickly remembered her; what shall I do now that she has arrived with her army?"
Durvāsas said:
Seeing the Lord of the Raghus thus surrounded, as if sprinkling him with nectar-water,
he stood weeping, having taken hold of the sage’s feet and bowed down.
Seeing the compassion of the Sage, she placed her two arms behind his back;
rising up, she kissed his face, O Great King, and they did not weep.
O best of brahmin sages, having placed his left thigh upon Rāma, the monkey established his right thigh; thus was the Vārāhī mantra-queen recited by him.
The bow of the mantra-arrow and the mantra of the moon-arrow bestow excellent accomplishment;
having quickly cast that aside before the Goddess, the sage [proceeded].
Having composed this hymn of praise, the lord of sages should perform the recitation of the mantra;
for this Śrī Mantravārāhī, Durvāsas is likewise the seer (ṛṣi).
The meter is Anuṣṭubh, the great goddess Vārāhī is remembered as the deity,
and the application (viniyoga) is proclaimed to be the destruction of all wicked enemies.
Having first uttered the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], one should then pronounce the Māyā-bīja;
thereafter, one should utter the Lakṣmī-bīja, and after that, one should extract the Khphreṃ-bīja.
Then follows Vārāhī with the dative case-ending (ṅe), ending with the fire-born wife (svāhā); this is the mantra.

I bow to Vārāhikā, who causes the destruction of worldly existence, whose abode is the seat of the fourfold offerings, who has the excellent face of a sow, who is intent on wandering through the nose,
who is seated upon a buffalo throne,
whose limbs are the abode of the *hūṃ* syllable at her seat, who is adorned with a girdle, and who is full of majesty.
I pay homage.
May she who destroys the enemy, the fierce Asura; who is seated upon the king of beasts (a lion); who is as white as a conch, the moon, and the *kunda* flower;
whose eyes are as long as lotuses; who holds a noose, a goad, and a rosary; who is worshipped by sages and gods; protect me forever—she whose garment is the western quarter.
They were adorned.
Oṃ hrīṃ glūṃ ḷṃ vrīṃ svāhā.
Thus, O Kālī, I have told you this supreme Vārāhī mantra;
the entire account of its origin has been related. What else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Śrīvārāhītantra*, within the *Nirvāṇapada* of the *Dakṣiṇāmnāya*, in the introduction to the most secret of great tantras.
The Goddess said:
I bow to the Śrīkrama, which is joined with the four seats (pīṭhas), endowed with the sixfold method, and accompanied by the Vālakrama.
I bow to the venerable Goddess Śrīdevī, who bestows eternal bliss upon the Goddess, who is the adversary of the Śrīkrama mounted upon the seat of the Yoginīs.
I bow down to the glorious Guru, who carries one across to the further shore of saṃsāra, who is the unsurpassed ultimate goal, and who knows the distinction between the higher and the lower.
I bow to the venerable Guru, who performs the threefold piercing— namely, the individual (āṇava), the cosmic (sāṃbhava), and that of power (śākta)— for the disciple.

I bow to the venerable Guru, by whose power there exists extremely intense ignorance regarding both the perceptible and the imperceptible, within this initiation that pierces through [all] capacities.
I bow to the glorious Guru, who bestows liberation from the bonds of karma acquired through births since beginningless time, by means of the power of the fire of knowledge.
I bow to the glorious Guru, who, having pervaded the heart-lotus with the rays of his wisdom, awakens it and is eternally compassionate toward all the world.

I bow down to the glorious Guru, who is endowed with wisdom and discernment, who bestows the eight supernatural powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā), and who is completely free from attachment and aversion.
The Goddess said:
"Worldly and otherworldly affairs are always known by the gurus;
what kind of beings are these gurus? O Lord, you ought to show us favor."
Whatever teachers there may be wandering upon this earth,
I truly desire to hear their characteristics according to reality.
O Sadāśiva, tell me also the characteristics of disciples, as well as initiation, the conduct of the observances (samaya), and liberation.
Īśvara said:
Excellent, excellent! O noble lady, since you have asked out of a desire to grasp the truth, listen to all this exactly in its proper sequence.
Those teachers who are indeed characterized by dress and hypocrisy are merely instructors;
however, those who are true teachers are not at all characterized by dress and hypocrisy.
Slander, cruelty, deceit, petty actions, possessiveness,
excessive egoism and pride, crookedness, or likewise wealth— these are [the obstacles].
Excessive anger, arrogance, deceit, reviling others,
thirst for wealth, delusion, roguery, and likewise curiosity;
Those who harm others, are devoid of morality, and are not engaged in conventional practice— those who possess such qualities as these are despised as mere bearers of the name.
Because of that, there were others who were hypocrites, and no true worship took place upon the earth;
they were greedy for the property of their gurus, and the yoginīs were consumers of wealth.
One who desires the wife of a hero and those who deceive their own place of worship are undoubtedly liable for penance; they wander according to the desire of their [future] womb.
One who transgresses the command of the Guru does not return from hell—
not out of fear, nor through greed for wealth, nor out of delusion, nor from a longing for sense objects.
Someone else, acting unjustly for the sake of his own personal gain, performs the initiation ritual (dīkṣā-vidhi) devoid of [proper] qualities and bereft of the emergence of virtues.
But he who, having not received it himself, bestows the Śrīkrama,
is always such a one for the venerable Guru who lives by the Command (ājñā).
Whether giving [initiation] or even merely questioning [the disciple], one may go to the Raurava hell;
such a disciple of a teacher devoid of qualities does not transcend saṃsāra and the like.
Just as one who has boarded a wrecked ship does not go elsewhere,
so too do those teachers who are hypocrites toward the noble family and are possessed by a delight in suffering.
I shall describe the six qualities that one should avoid; listen, O lotus-faced one!
They are: possessing intense command, being accomplished in piercing [the centers], and being observers of the guru’s command.
Endowed with both knowledge and discernment, they are confident in the scriptures of the *Tulā*;
perfected in the qualities of meditative absorption, they are constant worshippers of the *Śrīkrama*.
Free from delusion, free from conceptual proliferation, eternal, without possessions, beyond accomplishment,
devoid of ego, free from craving, and free from dualistic thought.
Ever patient, contented, truthful, and with senses conquered;
intent upon his own welfare, pure, and compassionate toward all living beings.
With a peaceful mind, virtuous conduct, and firm vows, he has renounced the pairs of opposites;
he is neither lustful toward women nor cruel, and is entirely free from mean actions.
Free from hypocrisy and deceit, devoid of anger and greed,
fully satisfied by divine knowledge and bliss, he is upright, virtuous, and a true enlightener.
Such is the teacher described; having seen him, the disciple should diligently perform three circumambulations and offer a prostration like a staff.
One who is endowed with devotion at all times, having performed [practice] in accordance with their own nature despite afflictions,
attains the perfection of the goal through the acquisition of grace.
The Goddess said:
O Śrīnātha, by your grace, the characteristics of the Ācārya have been understood;
O Lord Śaṅkara, grant your favor regarding the characteristics of the disciple.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Excellent, O blessed lady, you have asked about the supreme characteristics of a disciple;
I shall describe them in brief—listen, O lotus-faced one.
He is sought after for the examination of minerals, mines, and fields; for mantras, tantras, and alchemy;
for poisons, planetary afflictions, mercury, and the like; and for debate.
Independent of anything else, he is one for whom the accomplishment of his goal depends [on himself];
his soul is terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, and he yearns for the path to liberation.
Free from deceit, wise, peaceful, and devoid of hypocrisy or frivolity;
devoted to another deity, seeking his command, and speaking kindly.
Free from the vice of anger, from slander, and from false humility; noble and discerning, he is devoted to the nature of what is to be cultivated and intent upon forbearance.
One should offer one's body, life-breath, and wealth to the true gurus—
those who are affectionate toward their devotees— with action, mind, and speech.
One who is free from stinginess, who examines the inner self,
and who desires the principle of Śiva— such a person is a disciple who is a lamp for the lineage.
Having thus diligently examined the disciple for such qualities,
the preceptor, possessing the vision of the intensely powerful Command, should always initiate him.
Otherwise, a guru who initiates a disciple devoid of virtues will always become a defiler of the lineage, whether he is the one bestowing the initiation or the one receiving it.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, by your grace I have understood the characteristics of a disciple;
O Supreme Lord, tell me now the procedure for his initiation.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Excellent, O Goddess, that you have asked about initiation according to the ritual procedure,
as well as the wheel of stars (tārācakra), the wheel of zodiac signs (rāśicakra), and likewise the wheel of names (nāmacakra).
If that root-mantra of the Guru is present here, one should not contemplate another wheel;
mantras exceeding twenty syllables are proclaimed to be *mālāmantras*.
One should not examine the success (siddhi) and other qualities of a neuter mantra;
nor, O Pārvatī, should one examine those of a single-syllable mantra or a Rāla mantra.
One should not purify the Vedic mantra by means of *siddhi* and so forth;
for Vaiṣṇavas, there is purification through *tāra*, and for Śiva, purification through the *koṣṭha*.
In the Traipura system, the purity of the zodiac signs is considered, while in the Gopāla system, the *akaḍama* is prescribed.
Now I shall explain the *vargacakra*, which is in accordance with the Jyotirāgama.
For the purpose of purifying the mantras, one should first prepare eight squares preceded by the initial letter of the name, and then write the eight classes of consonants therein.
Birds, cats, lions, elephants, snakes, mice, and horses,
as well as rams— these, in order, are the eight classes beginning with 'A' (Akārādi) and are situated within their respective groups.
One should always understand that the relationship between the seeker and the teacher is based on affection by birth;
whereas there is enmity between birds and cats, and enmity between dogs and birds.
The enmity between birds and serpents, the hostility between elephants and lions,
and the animosity between rams and dogs— one should consider these through the logic of their underlying affection.
Having thus understood the excellent wheel, one should take up the supreme mantra;
[otherwise] there will be enmity with cats, dogs, jackals, and birds.
A cat [is defeated] by a dog or a mouse; a lion always [by a mouse];
a dog by two birds; and a serpent by a donkey or a mouse.
The rat has friendship with the two snakes;
the deer with the elephant; likewise, there is friendship between the serpent and the lion, as well as between the elephant and the ram.
It should be understood as distinct from the worldly [calendar] through its application in ritual practice;
the commencement of mantras in the month of Caitra bestows all human goals.
In Vaiśākha there will be the acquisition of jewels; in Jyeṣṭha, however, death will occur.
In Āṣāḍha there will be the loss of kinsmen, while in Śrāvaṇa one's purpose will be fulfilled.
In Bhādrapada, wisdom shall perish; in Āśvina, there will be an accumulation of jewels.
In Kārttika, there will be the accomplishment of mantras; and it shall be the same in Mārgaśīrṣa.
In Pauṣa there shall be affliction from enemies; in Māgha, the increase of wisdom;
in Phālguna, all desires shall be fulfilled; one should avoid the intercalary month (mala-māsa).
On Sunday there will be wealth; on Monday, indeed, there will be peace;
on Tuesday, it destroys longevity—one should therefore avoid initiation on that day.
One attains the beauty of Mercury, while with Jupiter there will be wisdom;
one attains the good fortune of Venus, but with Saturn there is loss of fame.
Initiation performed on the first lunar day (pratipad) is considered to cause the destruction of knowledge;
on the second day, knowledge arises, and on the third day, one becomes pure.
On the fourth day there shall be loss of mind; on the fifth, the increase of intellect;
on the sixth, the destruction of knowledge; and on the seventh day, one obtains happiness.
On the eighth day, there would be loss of intellect; on the ninth, the destruction of the person;
on the tenth, royal fortune; and on the eleventh, one becomes pure.
On the twelfth day there shall be all success; on the thirteenth, poverty;
on the fourteenth, birth as an animal; and at the end of the month, one becomes a worm.

At the end of the fortnight, there shall be an increase in unrighteousness; one should avoid Vedic study during the thundering of clouds at twilight, during a clap of thunder, an earthquake, or the falling of meteors.
One should avoid these and other days mentioned in the Śruti;
if one dies under Aśvinī, one attains happiness, but under Bharaṇī, death is certain.
If it occurs on Kārttikā, one will suffer misery; if on Rohiṇī, one becomes a sinner;
on Mṛgaśīrṣa there is the attainment of happiness, while on Ārdrā death is certain.
Under Punarvasu one shall be wealthy; under Puṣya there is the destruction of enemies;
under Āśleṣā death occurs; and under Maghā there is liberation from suffering.
In *Sauṃdarya* one attains *Pūrvaphalgunī*, of this there is no doubt;
in *Jñāna* one attains *Uttaraphalgunī*, and in *Hasta* there shall be wealth.
Under Citrā there shall be an increase in knowledge; under Svātī, the destruction of enemies;
under Viśākhā, happiness; and under Anurādhā, the prosperity of kinsmen.
In Jyeṣṭhā there shall be the destruction of enemies; in Mūlā there is the increase of fame;
and Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā are bestowers of renown.
Under Śravaṇā one will be miserable; under Dhaniṣṭhā there is poverty;
under Śatabhiṣā there will be intelligence; and under Pūrvabhādrapadā one will be happy.
There is happiness under Uttara-bhādrapadā, and under Revatī there is the increase of fame; then follow the auspicious Siddhi and Āyuṣmān, after which comes the Dhruva yoga.
Prīti, Saubhāgya, and Yoga, followed by Vṛddhiyoga,
and likewise Harṣaṇa— these yogas bring happiness in all tantras.
One should undertake another yoga that yields contrary results:
Vava, Vālava, Taitila, and Vanija immediately following that.
O noble lady, that is declared in all the tantras as the *karaṇāna*.
Now I shall proclaim the auspicious time for initiation (*dīkṣālagna*) as established in the Vārāhī Tantra.
The Guru should always bestow initiation during the zodiacal signs of Taurus, Leo, Virgo, Sagittarius, or Pisces, provided that the moon and the stars are favorable.
In a stable ascendant, the auspicious and mobile mantras of Viṣṇu or Śiva are recommended;
however, for the mantras of Śakti, an ascendant situated in its own natural sign (svabhāva) is praised.
I shall proclaim the places for initiation as taught by Bhairava; one should reveal them in a cowshed, in the house of a guru, in a place where divine embers remain, or in a forest.
Likewise, at a sacred bathing place, in a garden, on a riverbank, in one's own hermitage,
near the dhātrī and bilva trees, on a mountain peak, and in a cave;
Everything performed at the Gaṅgā becomes multiplied ten million-fold;
likewise, the consumption of sacrificial food, vegetables, and the like, as well as the prescribed fruit and milk, yield the same result.
The root is barley-gruel produced from barley; these are not to be consumed by the practitioner of mantras.
When the practitioner of mantras has performed the initiation, he should indeed observe a fast.
The Lord is always angry with him, and a curse falls upon his head;
therefore, one should not eat while fasting, for such fasting would take away one's prosperity.
O Śāṅkarī, one should eat his food along with sacrificial food (haviṣya).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the extraction of the mantra; listen, O beloved.
One should utter the mantra: "Tāraḥ namo bhagavate varāhāya rūpam uccaret | bhūpatitvaṃ me dehi," and thus cause the wife to bestow [the fruit] at the end in the fire-house.
This Vārāha Mantra, consisting of thirty-three syllables, has been declared:
*Oṃ pārthive ca pṛthivītalavāriṇi vāyumā*.
*Tatolini ca tāruṇyaṃ kuru yugmaṃ ca dhaṃcadhaṃ svāhā*— this mantra of Pārthivī is remembered as consisting of twenty-nine syllables.

Oṃ hrīṃ namaśca vārāhi ghore svapnaṃ visargayuk | Ṭhadvayaṃ vahnijāyānto mantraḥ pañcadaśākṣaraḥ || Oṃ hrīṃ namo vārāhi ghore svapnaṃ visargaḥ | Ṭha-ṭha Svāhā. This fifteen-syllable mantra ends with the fire-born wife (Svāhā).
Then one should meditate upon her who is dark as a rain-cloud, with three eyes and elevated breasts;
she has the face of a boar, the crescent moon upon her brow, and the earth uplifted by her tusks.
She holds a sword and a kuśa grass blade in her two right hands, and a shield and a noose in her two left;
she is mounted upon a horse, has the face of a boar, and is adorned with various ornaments.
May she who dwells upon the pericarp of a red lotus, seated upon a corpse-throne,
possessing a dark-blue luster and wearing a shimmering garland of severed heads, protect me with her hands.
She holds the gesture of fearlessness, a pestle, and likewise a fruit as her excellent attribute;
she has the face of a boar, high-set breasts, three eyes, and is clad in red garments.
Having meditated thus, O Maheśānī, one should sprinkle the disciple on the head with the flower-conch consecration and the proof of the balance.
The drawing of the lines for the royal mandala and initiation are recorded as being fivefold:
the hundred-fold hand of the disciple, the flower, and the head-bowl held by oneself.
By the power of knowledge, one ascends; the initiation consists of the sprinkling of flowers.
The water from the conch held in the hand is itself to be made to ascend to the crown of the head.
Then one should perform the consecration and likewise the consecration with a conch;
immediately thereafter, one should initiate the disciple who has been weighed on a scale.
Lightness arises from the cutting off of karma; it is known as the perception of balance.
Having drawn an eight-petalled lotus, one should draw a vajra-maṇḍala on the outside.
In the midst of that, the Yoginī should place the disciple provided with the ritual substances;
having worshipped the assembly of Yoginīs with perfumes, flowers, garlands, and so forth.
The consecration of the teacher is the powder mandala;
thus, this fourfold initiation has been declared by me in the *Apsu-tantra*.
Then, from the *mūlādhāra*, the teacher should, by means of the *haṃsa* [mantra], join the seed-syllable with the Supreme Self in the station of the *puṣkara* via the path of Brahmā.
O lady of excellent limbs, I shall describe the initiation by piercing (vedhadīkṣā) in brief:
the first is said to be the individual (āṇava), while the second is that of power (śākta).
O Goddess, the third [category], the *sāṃbhava*, is explained as having a threefold division;
by means of any mantra whatsoever, through the procedure of *stobha* upon the sacrificial blade (*parśu*).
The arising of qualities over time is declared to be the lineage of the individual soul (āṇava-vaṃśa),
through the transference of powers such as those of the earrings and so forth onto the body of the disciple.
The arising of qualities at that very moment is proclaimed as pertaining to Śakti;
it consists of the visual, the tactile, the verbal, and likewise the mental.
Thus, compassion toward a disciple who is devoted and affectionate has been described as having four modes, even by a mere glance.
The piercing that produces qualities immediately becomes visible through the touching of the staff,
the neck, the seat, the vessel, and so forth.
Or even from the touching of the limbs,
the piercing by touch is said to occur when the disciple is always known to possess a mind equal to that of the guru.
Whatever word the Creator utters becomes a verbal command,
whether it extends for hundreds of yojanas or even two, three, or five hundred.
When one who serves from afar with true devotion and the triple purity acts thus,
the Guru, recognizing that devotion, remembers him out of compassion.
That very attainment of qualities is called "piercing" (vedha).
Thus, by means of this procedure for initiation, one who desires the initiation of a disciple [should proceed].
All the requisites for initiation should be brought into the presence of the Guru:
fragrant unadorned flowers, incense, lamps, and sacrificial oblation (caru).
It was provided with various kinds of food and drink, garments, gold, camphor,
flowers, betel, ornaments, and cotton cloths.
Having then offered everything that is available to the Guru,
one should worship the assembly of Yoginīs with a single-pointed and concentrated mind.
Thereafter, one should offer one's own body to the venerable gurus;
otherwise, even if one is destitute of wealth, one will be intent on causing distress to the guru.
Having performed prostration with the staff-like body,
he who is devoted to devotion should offer his person— whether wealthy or poor— with the triple purity.
The teacher should look upon the disciplined disciple with compassion;
by the mere sight of that compassion, the disciple falls to the ground.
Because it quickly expresses a reality that is inexpressible and endowed with gnosis,
there arise bliss, emission, trembling, sleep, and the fifth, which is the surging wave.
O Goddess of the Gods, for one who knows that reality, five states are proclaimed:
the departure from the ground, the possession, and the various forms of binding the mudrās.
The supernormal cognition of hearing from afar, proficiency in all languages, the manifestation of non-existent objects through yoga, intoxication by flavors, and likewise singing and laughing.
Accompanied by song and instrumental music, it initiates play according to one's own desire;
even before that, a hundred qualities arise from the emergence of the qualities.
Through a thousand dissolutions of that, a hundred thousand arises when it has dissolved;
in that very state occurs dissolution through the power of the intense Command in song.
The supreme state, free from old age and death, is attained;
thus, by performing the ritual of initiation according to the prescribed rules, the guru brings about the exhaustion of karma.
And when all the qualities have been attained, one should then bestow the Śrīkrama.
Thus ends the second chapter of the Great Secret, in the section on Nirvāṇa within the Dakṣiṇāmnāya of the Śrī Vārāhī Tantra. || 2 ||
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, having understood the sequence of the initiation rite through your grace,
O Supreme Lord, tell me truly of the conduct required of a disciple.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
You have asked exactly what should be asked regarding the characteristics of a disciple’s conduct;
O Goddess of the Gods, listen now to all of that in due order.
For one who has exhausted their own karma over many previous lifetimes,
that supreme accomplishment shall arise for the disciple through initiation alone.
For one who possesses the bondage of karma from previous births,
the Guru’s compassion does not prevail as long as that karma is not released.
If one has obtained the compassion of the Guru, no pure conduct is required;
if there were accomplishment [otherwise], it would not exist. Therefore, conduct should be based on speech.
In the morning, one should prepare a sacred maṇḍala with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings;
then, following the instructions of the guru, one should perform prostrations like a staff.
Having first worshipped the book containing the instruction on reality in a secluded, solitary place, listen to the Śrīkulāgama.
Having heard the meaning of the scriptural instructions and having applied oneself with diligence, one should perform everything that he commands, like a servant, even if it involves hardship.
Whether he is illustrious, dressed in the garb of another form of austerity, or even one who follows the sequence of the scriptures,
he must not omit the prostration that is the punishment for affliction in the presence of the Guru.
Excessive laughter, yawning, stretching the limbs in playfulness,
loud noise, blazing fire, bodily transformation, and cleaning the teeth [should be avoided].
If one desires success, one should not perform the washing of the teacher's feet, nor adornment, nor musical performance while looking at the guru.
The seat of the gurus, the neck-ornament, the yoga-staff, the two sandals,
the rosary, the bed, the loincloth, and the garment;
One who possesses devotion should not touch with his feet, nor step over, the water used for washing the alms-bowl, nor the various implements used for one another.
Having offered perfumes, flowers, betel, and various kinds of food and seating to the guru, one should afterwards receive [the initiation] according to the prescribed procedure.
Having acted thus, the disciple who is free from afflictions and possesses unwavering devotion receives the fourfold consecration through the compassion of the guru.
Having received the command from the Guru, he should set it in motion for the disciple;
then, desiring constant accomplishment, he may wander through the world according to his own will.

One should accept alms-food for the sake of sustaining the body, a garment to ward off cold from the neck, and an alms-bowl for the purpose of eating; these alone constitute one's personal possession.
The lord of yogis should always dwell at the foot of a tree, in a cremation ground, on a mountain peak, within a cave, in an empty temple, or even in a cow-pen.
Friend and foe, pleasure and pain, the desirable and the undesirable, the auspicious and the inauspicious; likewise, honor and dishonor, as well as blame and praise.
The yogi who desires the attainment of the goal should regard a skull-bowl, gold, and a vessel of bell-metal or iron as equal.
In some places a Bhaṭṭa, in some a Caṭṭa, and in some a renunciant man—
a yogin bearing a pure form— is indeed cooked upon the surface of the earth.
One should always worship with devotion the Guru, this [Goddess], the Tradition (Āmnāya), the Kula scripture, the Mantra, Madirā, and the Eldest (Jyeṣṭhā).
One who desires liberation should not harbor unpleasantness, agitation, laziness, disobedience, possessiveness, lust for another's wife, or arrogance.
One should conceal the mantras, mudrās, and rosaries, as well as the assembly of yoginīs, the potency of yoga, the vaṭa tree, the sacred seat (pīṭha), and the substances of accomplishment.
One should destroy passion, hatred, egoism, malice, hypocrisy, deceit, anger, greed, and delusion; one should cause these to be slain.
One should not disparage the conventional conduct of others, nor the assembly of maidens and yoginīs, nor the substances of accomplishment, nor their sacred seats, nor those who dwell within them.
The Yoginī spoke the secret scripture, the conduct of the Siddhas that has come down through the lineage in succession, which had never been seen or heard before.
The wrestling match of Mallakurjaṭa, the naked woman with breasts flapping as she runs,
and the game of everyone taking turns at seizing the rules— all these proceed as play.
A Kulayogin should not look upon a light, a dance, a master of illusion, hunting, a battle between heroes, a maiden, a female organ, or anything secret.

One should not feel disgust toward an old person, one afflicted by leprosy, one who is limb-deficient, raw meat, the diseased, a corpse, one's own excrement, urine, or a foul state; likewise, one should not feel disgust toward a river.
One should never uproot trees, creepers, vines, grass, or other stationary beings;
one should not split them, nor cut them, nor cause them pain.

Whatever little there may be— perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as the substance for the Yoginī— if it is obtained by whatever means requested, with that one worships the worthy and capable [deity].
If these are unavailable, the yogi, devoted to the purity of being,
should worship the sandals of the Guru with the flower of constant remembrance.
Deceit, disputatious assemblies, envy, and association with the vulgar;
as well as nooses, iron, wood, and heaps of clay—one should not employ these as causes for attaining success.
One should sleep in a solitary place and should not cause physical pain;
one should avoid excessive eating, loud laughter, and base actions.
One should not desire various scriptures nor recall unwholesome objects;
therefore, one should avoid what has been acquired, for by this one becomes a master of the senses.
Wherever it pleases, there one should go;
one who desires unimpeded success must act according to the mind's inclination.
He who constantly practices according to this conduct and path attains various kinds of supernatural powers (siddhis) that far surpass those of ordinary wanderers.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, through your compassion, I have understood the supreme conduct;
now I wish to know about Nirvana—please explain that which is both transcendent and immanent.
The Lord said:
O lady of beautiful hips, you have asked well regarding the immutable state of Nirvana; O lotus-faced one, listen as I explain that supreme and inferior reality (tattva).
By always practicing correctly according to the path of right conduct,
all the Gaṇas arise, as does the intense command of the Proclaimer.
The reality that is eternally arisen and undivided resides in the navel, heart, throat, mouth, the tip of the nose, the center of the eyes, and the ears.
The sound of the ocean is the visible form; the small and large bells are equal.
One should utter the reality that resonates like the thundering of clouds in every way.
Whether walking or standing, sitting or even lying down; whether waking or sleeping, or during the opening and closing of the eyes—whether in a state of purity or impurity.
Whether in a moment or half a moment, he is always free from setting;
just as his rising is, so too does he exist continuously.
In this body, which is the source of eternal bliss, there is neither sleep, nor thirst, nor hunger;
neither delusion, nor hatred, nor passion, nor even mental reflection.
Neither does he experience lack of pleasure, nor cold, nor the sensation of heat;
nor does he hear singing, laughter, dancing, or the playing of musical instruments.
Running, jumping, and engaging in idle chatter according to one's own whim—
such and other such disorders arise in whatever manner they may.
"In such and such a way, one should not be afraid; one plays upon the surface of the earth.
Thus is the conduct of one who is intoxicated by supreme bliss.
O Supreme Person, upon seeing this, all the wise do not laugh;
it is like a fool regarding the paths of the scriptures, or like a young maiden regarding sexual pleasure.
Thus indeed, the most wicked ones mock the path of yoga;
to the wise, worldly conduct appears as the behavior of a madman.
Even by worldly people, that knowledge is viewed as if it were madness;
in the world, they always regard it as a mere play, neither censuring nor praising it.
By means of those whose sole form is the name Śiva, who are the nature of supreme bliss,
the supreme state has been brought forth as the Self residing within the body.
The messenger, intent on yoga, should know all comings and goings;
having realized this reality of the self, one should dissolve it into the supreme reality.
One who constantly observes that state attains imperishable perfection;
there is neither bathing, nor recitation, nor fire-offering, nor meditation, nor concentration.
There is no mudrā, nor indeed any destruction [of breath], no suṣumnā, nor piṅgalā; there is no kumbhaka at all, nor the procedure for pūraka.
Neither the lunar day, nor the constellation, nor fasting, vows, and so forth—
all that is for the sake of worldly existence and is not a cause for the destruction of karma.
Having abandoned that which resembles the manifold world of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), one should practice in the state free from proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
The entire world, being in a state of liberation, is not at all afflicted by delusion.
Freed from the delusion of desire, liberation becomes one's very nature;
there is neither intellect, nor mind, nor even the five senses.
Neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air, nor space; neither the mind, nor the atoms, nor a sentient being, nor that which is to be attained, nor an impeller.
It is neither distant nor near, neither effect nor cause;
it has not undergone decay or increase, and it does not differentiate between colors or non-colors.
Thus, the supreme, imperishable state is described as being liberated;
it is like oil within sesame seeds, or like fire within wood.
Just as gold exists within stone and ghee within milk,
so too does the all-pervading reality abide within every body.
Those of deluded mind do not know the supreme, subtle, and stainless [reality];
otherwise, the sixfold system of logic and the study of the scriptures are pursued in a contrary manner.
The meaning of the Vedic path is one way, the teaching of the Gama is another;
the worldly path is one way, and the ultimate path is another.
Therefore, the yogi should abandon delusion and practice the state free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa),
which is liberated from the thirty-six principles and devoid of the five pentads.
It is beyond the loss of the moon's digits, devoid of the end of the sixteen, and not at all surpassed by anything else; it is the supreme state within the end of the twelve.
The soul of all, omnipresent, eternal, omniscient, facing in all directions,
unbroken, uninterrupted, immeasurable, and unassailable.
Partless, stainless, peaceful, established in the state beyond ritual conduct,
infinite, imperishable, subtle, transcending form, both supreme and non-supreme.
Thus, having attained the eight supernatural powers through the nature of Śiva, you shall rejoice;
[these include] the power of hearing from afar and the power of seeing from afar.
Free from shadow, possessing the true nature, and capable of entering the bodies of others, one’s form shall be eternally at will; thus does accomplishment proceed.
He himself is the Guru, he himself is the disciple; he himself is Śakti, he himself is Śiva.
He himself is the subtle, he himself is the gross; he himself is indeed both the transcendent and the immanent.
When the mandalas have been prepared for all [the deities], one should perform the propitiation;
if one desires the highest accomplishment, one should not leave a mandala empty.
If, out of greed, one makes a circle empty for the Guru,
there shall be a violation of the mantra for him, and the Yoginīs will revile his mother.
If one fails to obtain the ritual materials and other necessities, one should offer even one's own body.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Great Secret, in the *Nirvāṇapada* of the *Dakṣiṇāmnāya* within the *Śrīvārāhītantra*.
Bhairava said:
And the initiate [should be consecrated] in an auspicious region, during the auspicious rising of Jupiter or Venus,
at a favorable ascendant situated in a house of increase (upacaya), and free from the aspect of malefic planets.
In an auspicious month, on a day free from inauspicious red [planets],
and joined by favorable planets and other factors, one should undertake the *puraścaraṇa*.
Initiation and the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) are recommended in the months of Kārttika, Citta, Vaiśākha, Māgha, Mārgaśīrṣa, Phālguna, and Śrāvaṇa.
That rite of *puraścaraṇa* should be performed on a Sunday, Thursday, Monday, or Wednesday during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
when the moon and the stars are favorable.
Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Ārdrā, Dhaniṣṭhā, the three Uttaras,
Puṣya, Śatabhiṣā, and Hastā are [auspicious] for the rite of preparatory service (puraścaraṇa).
The full moon day, the fifth, the second, the seventh,
as well as the thirteenth and the tenth, are praised for all ritual acts.
During the eclipse of one of the two moons at a sacred ford (sattīrtha), or during the two-thread (tantu-dvaya) and the parvan days,
one performing the *puraścaraṇa* rite need not observe the restrictions regarding months, fasting, and so forth.
The commencement of mantras and other rites during Aries bestows wealth and grain;
in Taurus, there is the arrival of death; and in Gemini, it is the destroyer of speech.
In Cancer there shall be the attainment of all perfections; in Leo, the destruction of intelligence;
in Virgo, constant prosperity; and in Libra, the accomplishment of all goals.
In Scorpio there shall be gain of gold; Sagittarius is the destroyer of knowledge;
Capricorn is said to bestow sons; and Aquarius brings about the abundance of wealth.
In Pisces, it always bestows suffering; let it not be thus, for such is the fruit of the Rāśi.
When the Moon and the stars are favorable, during the bright fortnight on an auspicious day—
One should commence the *puraścaraṇa* while Hari is asleep; one should not perform it anew during the [ordinary] sleep.
Having gone to an auspicious constellation and so forth, one should perform the consecration of the ground (*bhūmiparigraha*).
Likewise, for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) of this particular mantra,
I myself take possession of this ground, so that this mantra may be perfected.
Even within a city or similar place, one may traverse a distance of one *krośa*, or even two *krośas*, for the purpose of obtaining food and other necessities for one's livelihood.

One should drive into the ground at the cardinal and intermediate points of the site stakes made from milky trees and consecrated with weapon-mantras (astramantra), and one should worship the Weapon-deity (astra) within them.
The wise one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) before them with perfumes and other offerings;
thereafter, he should duly worship Kṣetrapāla and the others there according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship the Lord of Obstacles named Kṣetraśaṃvāstu,
offer oblations to the guardians of the directions, and then enter the field.
Those who are fierce, whose deeds are fierce, and who dwell in fierce abodes—
the Mothers of foremost form and those who are the lords of the hosts— [all these I salute].
And those others who have become obstacles, dwelling in the cardinal and intermediate directions—
may you all, with joyful minds, accept this bali offering.
Having bathed in the morning, being self-restrained, one should recite the Gāyatrī a thousand times;
first, for the sake of expiating known and unknown sins.
Hrīṃ! We know Brahmāyaṇī; we meditate upon the four-petaled one; may that Goddess inspire us.

We know the Great Goddess; we meditate on her who is dear to Gaurī; may that Ugra-Śiva inspire us. We know Kaumārī; we meditate on her who is accompanied by Viṃdu; may that Goddess inspire us. We know the Power of Viṣṇu;
we meditate on her whose face is fierce.
May that Kālī inspire us.

We know Vārāhī, we meditate upon the Fierce-faced One; may Kālī inspire us. We know Indrāṇī, we meditate upon Indra’s Power; may Śakra inspire us. We know Guhyakālī, we meditate upon the Hidden Power; may Kālī inspire us. We know Mahālakṣmī, we meditate upon the Great Power; may Śrī inspire us.
May it impel us forward.
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Aparājitā,
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Bhīmā, and Kālī— these are likewise the eight [Aṣṭakās].
Diviyoginī, Mahāyoginī, Siddhiyoginī, Gaṇeśvarī, Sākiṇī,
Kālarātrī, Ūrdhvakeśī, and Niśācarī.
Gambhīrāghoṣaṇī, Sthūlā, Pavanāṅgī, Ulīnitā, Bhīṣaṇā, Mahānandā, and likewise Jvālāmukhī.
Piśācī, Hastinī, Yakṣiṇī, Dhūrjatī,
Viṣabhakṣā, Sarvasiddhi, Stuti, and likewise Icchā.
HŪM! O Kālī, Bhāsvārī, Dīrghā, Dhūmrākṣī, grant us favor, O Beloved!
And likewise, O Mātaṅgī, Kākadr̥ṣṭī, and Tripurāntakī!
The Rākṣasīs were of terrible roar, red-eyed, and possessing universal forms;
they were fearsome, fierce, and hideous, devouring the limbs of men and their flesh.
Vīrabhadra, Mahākālī, Kaṅkālī, Vikṛtānanā, Krodharā,
Bhīmabhadra, Vāyuvegā, and Bhayānanā.
Brahmā, Vaiṣṇavī, Raudrī, Carcikā, Īśvarī,
as well as Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, and the fourfold Śivadūtī.
O Goddess, always accept this offering for the great fire;
however, one should not perform the Śākta initiation when the sun is eclipsed.
I would certainly not perform [the rites] for the Vaiṣṇavas during an eclipse of the moon,
nor during other auspicious conjunctions, nor during eclipses of the moon or the sun.
At the time of a solar eclipse, however, that [result] occurs even if it is not otherwise.
If the Guru, out of compassion, grants [the initiation] after having summoned the disciple,
then no consideration whatsoever need be made regarding the auspicious moment (lagna) and so forth.
Without a doubt, all the planets and all the lunar mansions are auspicious on that day when the preceptor is pleased and speaks with words of favor.
At the great pilgrimage site of Grahaṇa, there is no restriction regarding the time;
likewise at Gayā, Bhāskarakṣetra, Virajā, and Candraparvata.
O Pārvatī, one should not receive initiation at these holy sites: at Vaṭula, at Mataṅga, and likewise in the hermitages of maidens.
If Venus is eclipsed, or if it is old (past its prime), or if Jupiter and the Sun should be together,
then no fault exists provided they are in Aries, Scorpio, or Leo.
I shall explain the *kālamālā*, as stated in the *Vārāhītantra*:
"The index finger, middle finger, ring finger, and little finger, in this order."
The three fingers [of the hand] have three joints each, while the middle finger has one joint;
one should designate two joints of the middle finger as the Meru.
Beginning from the ring finger and the middle finger,
and starting from the little finger up to the base of the index finger, one should perform the recitation across the ten joints.
Beginning from the root of the ring finger and proceeding through the little finger and so forth,
up to the index and middle fingers, one should perform the recitation over the eight joints.
The ring finger [measures] three joints, the little finger three joints, and the middle finger three joints; [the thumb measures] the joint at the base of the index finger.
One who joins the tips of the index finger and the middle finger in that manner is indeed a doer of evil;
[the sequence] begins from the ring finger and the middle finger, and likewise from the little finger.
One should perform the recitation over the ten joints from the base of the index finger to its tip;
the two joints of the mind and the illusion [syllables] should be repeated in succession by rotation.
One should take three knots on the middle finger and one on the index finger;
this is declared to be the Śaktimālā, which illuminates all tantras.
Beginning from the base of the ring finger and proceeding in a clockwise direction up to the base of the middle finger,
one should recite [the mantra] during the eight auspicious joints.
Starting from the ring finger and proceeding in order through the little finger and so on,
up to the base of the index finger, the two joints of each finger are proclaimed to be the "grains" (kala) of the rosary.
If the fingers are slightly bent at the tips and the palms are somewhat contracted,
and if the recitation flows through the gaps created by the separation of the fingers;
Whatever is recited while the fingers are curled at the tips, or while crossing over Mount Meru, or while the joints of the fingers are pressed together— all that becomes fruitless.
If a person performs recitation while transgressing the rules of counting, the Rākṣasas seize that recitation; therefore, a wise person should always count.
Placing the hand upon the heart and holding it crosswise at the distance of a few finger-breadths,
or covering it, one should always perform the recitation with both hands equalized, using the right hand.
The garland [of phonemes] is formed by the letters of the Mātṛkā, arranged in successive order along with Meru, together with the bindus;
these eight groups of letters are proclaimed as the eight vargas.

Listen now to these [beads] for the external sacrifice: rosaries made from lotus seeds and the like, as well as those known by the numbers of *rudrākṣas* and lotuses, O Son, and those made of *jīvaka* and pearls.
A rosary for a householder may be made of crystal, precious gems, gold, coral,
silver, or the roots of *kuśa* grass.
Counting on the fingers yields one; with knots, it becomes eightfold;
with putrajīva beads, tenfold; and with conch shells, a thousandfold.
One [set] made of coral and precious gems is known as ten thousand;
that bound with crystal is proclaimed [to be] one hundred thousand, and with pearls it is said to be a lakh.
With five-seeded [beads], ten lakhs [of repetitions] are required; with golden beads, it is said to be ten million (koṭi).
With knots of kuśa grass, it is one hundred million; with rudrākṣa beads, it is infinite.
A rosary fashioned from all types of seeds bestows the fruit of liberation upon men;
a rosary fashioned from lotus seeds is considered a destroyer of enemies.
A garland made of knots of *kuśa* grass destroys all sins;
fashioned with the fruits of the *putrajīva*, it brings about the abundance of sons.
By means of garlands of *nirmita* (created) *arūpya* (formless) gems, one bestows desired results while reciting;
a garland fashioned from coral bestows abundant wealth.
One may make a garland from gold, jewels, crystal, or fashioned from conch-shell, or indeed from coral; however, one should avoid using *putrajīva* seeds.
O Nīlasarasvatī, rosaries made of lotus seeds, rudrākṣa, and especially bhadrākṣa, as well as those made of great conch shells, are to be known [as suitable].
A rosary fashioned from human forehead bone fragments,
or a garland made of great conch shells, is dear to Tārā and Jyeṣṭhā for the purpose of recitation.
O Goddess, between the ear and the eye, she is celebrated as Mahāśaṅkhā;
indeed, Raktacandanamālā bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
A garland of *tulasī* is recommended for the worship of Viṣṇu; an elephant tusk for Gaṇeśvara;
and for the recitation of the *Tripurā* mantra, *rudrākṣa* beads and red sandalwood are praised.
They should be uniform in shape, neither too thick nor too thin,
free from defects such as insects, and indeed neither decayed nor brand new.
A garland consisting of fifty beads is prescribed for all ritual acts;
it is proclaimed as the sequence of letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'.
O best of sages, one should visualize Mount Meru as the mouth there;
by means of this, the recitation of all vidyās bestows all prosperity.
In the ritual of Dhūmāvatī, a garland made of *dhuttūra* flowers from a cremation ground is to be known [as required];
a garland strung with human finger-bones grants all desires.
O beloved, one should never wear a garment that is ill-fitting or even stained with blood; it must always be guarded with great effort, as a mother protects her paramour.
One should always perform the recitation (japa) with the hand, but never that which is performed for specific desires (kāmya).
O beautiful one, one may even perform the recitation for desires with the hand in the absence of a rosary.
The procedure for my rosary of beads is here described:
with twenty-five beads there is liberation, and with thirty beads for the attainment of wealth.
With twenty-seven *sarvartha* [mantras], with fifteen for *abhicāra*,
and with fifty-four, the accomplishment of one's purpose shall occur.
The wise have declared that success is achieved with one hundred and eight [offerings] for all purposes; however,
for the sake of specific desires, a woolen blanket is required, and a red woolen blanket is the most excellent.
Success in knowledge is attained on a black antelope skin; liberation on a tiger skin;
and success in mantra on a seat of kuśa grass. In this matter, there is no need for deliberation regarding what should or should not be done.
On a seat made of earth, there arises suffering; on one made of wood, misfortune;
on a seat of bamboo, one becomes poor; and on a stone seat, there is the affliction of disease.
Eating grass causes loss of reputation; a flickering mind causes the failure of the rosary recitation; and using cloth as a seat indeed causes the failure of austerity.
O Goddess, a seat of human skin is for the accomplishment of the mantra of Vārāhī;
O Pārvatī, the great rosary and the great vessel are for the mantra of Mālā.
The goddess Vajravārāhī is difficult even for the thirty gods to attain;
this is the practice of the great garland of mantras consisting of the ten purificatory rites.
Now I shall speak; listen, O lotus-faced one!
These mantras are proclaimed to be corrupted by defects such as being cut or otherwise flawed.
If these are cultivated constantly, they do not fail to yield fruit;
therefore, I shall describe ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) for the destruction of their defects.
The practitioner should divide the triangle into seven equal parts,
starting from the northeast corner and likewise proceeding from the southeast corner.
There are forty-nine deities;
in all those [spaces], one should place the letters of the alphabet in sequence, starting from Īśāna and ending with Vāruṇa, beginning with the mantra of the eastern direction.
Having worshipped the Goddess here, one should extract all the mantras;
they call this "generation" (janana), and thereafter one is not released from the lamp (dīpa).
One should recite the mantra one thousand times, encapsulated by the *haṃsa* mantra;
this is called "illumination" (*dīpana*), and now "awakening" (*bodhana*) is described.
The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra encapsulated by the *varman* (hūṃ) joined with the *ariha* (kṣa);
this awakening is said to be performed five thousand times.
The wise practitioner should recite the mantra, encased by the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one thousand times;
this is called "striking" (*tāḍana*), and now the "consecration" (*abhiṣeka*) is described.
The practitioner of mantras should recite the mantra "vāk haṃsa praṇava" one thousand times over the water;
then, reciting this mantra, he should consecrate [the disciple] with those auspicious waters.
The practitioner of mantra should recite one thousand times the encapsulated (saṃpuṭa) mantra "tāvān srausāt," ending with the syllable vaṣaṭ; this indeed is the purification (vimalīkaraṇa).
The wise practitioner should recite the mantra "svadhā śikhā puṭam" one thousand times;
this is declared to be the "life-giving" rite when performed with water mixed with milk and clarified butter.
The mantra is known as *tarpaṇa* when it is a libation, and as *saṃpuṭa* when encapsulated by the *māyā* syllable;
when recited five thousand times, that is called *gopana*.

The libation with honey is prescribed for the Vaiṣṇava mantra, that with water containing moonstones for the Śaiva mantra, and that with ghee for the mantras of the other [deities]; thus it has been correctly declared by the masters of mantras.
One should recite the mantra with the white *caṃ* and the favoring *indu* as its two envelopes;
this is declared by those expert in the science of mantras to be "nourishment" (*āpyāyana*).
The ten consecrations (saṃskāras) have been fully declared; these are the mantra-syllables enjoined in the Tantra:
"O Garland! O Garland! O Great Garland! You whose nature is all reality!"
"The fourfold aims have been entrusted to you; therefore, grant me success.
Having prepared the rosary with its seed-syllables and so forth, one should worship it with red flowers."
Then, one should worship with this mantra: Vāgbhava, Lakṣmī, the rosary beginning with the letter 'A', and the syllable 'Ṅe' ending with the letter of the heart.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Having consecrated it seven times with this mantra, one should cast it into the furrow.
Then, having invoked the Blessed Lady together with her retinue by means of the mantras for invocation and so forth,
and having worshipped her with the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra), one should repeat the root mantra while recollecting the third seed-syllable; then,
having rendered [the offering] nectar-like by means of the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā), veiled it with the armor-mantra (kavaca), and covered it with the great mudrā (mahāmudrā).
The goddess Mālī, meditating on Rūpītā, should perform the visualization of the bindu; the mantra for that is as follows:
oṃ hrīṃ svāhā | oṃ hūṃ svāhā || oṃ phaṭ svāhā || oṃ strīṃ svāhā || oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ svāhā || oṃ hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā || With this, one should perform the ten [recitations] and the application of the *bindu*.
Having offered incense and other offerings with musk, agarwood, and camphor, and having removed it from the cauldron, one should consecrate it with these mantras.

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ mahāvajriṇi mahāghorarūpe karkaśa mahāsthimaṇḍale praviśa sarvasiddhiṃ prayaccha oṃ hūṃ hrīṃ svāhā | mahākapālini mahāghorarūpe svāhā || Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Having worshipped with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), one performs the kindling (*uddīpana*) with the seed-syllable of pride (*darpa*).

Having performed the sixteen-fold service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) and worshipped [the deity], one should kindle [the fire] with the *mātṛkā* mantra, encircle it with the syllable *hūṃ*, and offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*). It is as follows: *oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hūṃ oṃ phaṭ hūṃ oṃ oṃ hūṃ svāhā*. *Oṃ hūṃ*, O Great Yoginī, Savior of the Three Worlds, [you who possess] the great conch and bone...
"Reside, reside in the midst of the garland; grant, grant all accomplishments! Accept, accept the offerings of wine and meat;

cause [them] to be accepted! Hrīṃ Strīṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! Having offered the bali-oblation with the aforementioned substances and having dismissed the Goddess, one should wear the garland in a secluded place.
Having performed the ritual worship one thousand and eight times with devotion, one should recite [the mantra] every day; this is known as the daily recitation (*nitya-japa*).
Then, from the *mūlādhāra*, the teacher should join the seed-syllable with the *paramātman* at the station of the heart by means of the *haṃsa* through the path of Brahmā.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Great Secret, in the Dakṣiṇāmnāya-Nirvāṇapada of the venerable Vārāhī Tantra. || 4 ||
Bhairava said:
Having received the command of the guru, a person with a purified inner heart should then perform the preliminary rites (puraskriyā) with the desire for the attainment of mantra-siddhi.
O Goddess, just as one devoid of life is incapable of performing any action, [so too is he].
Even a mantra devoid of purashcharana is proclaimed to be effective in that same way.
Therefore, at the outset, the wise man should perform it himself or have it performed by a guru;
or, in the absence of a guru, he should have it performed by a brahmin who is devoted to the welfare of all living beings.
First, for the purpose of honoring a friend who is affectionate, knowledgeable in mantras, and endowed with various virtues, the rules for bathing are now described.
A field of merit, the bank of a river, the summit of a mountain cave,
sacred sites, and the confluence of rivers are places that lead to purification.
Solitary gardens, the foot of a bilva tree,
the head of a mountain, a grove of tulasī, a cow-pen, a place devoid of bulls, and a temple of Śiva.
The root of the aśvattha and malakī trees, the middle of the water at a cow-pen,
a temple, the shore of the ocean, and one's own home.
One should know that the merit is a hundredfold at home, it becomes a hundred-thousandfold in a cow-pen, a crore-fold in a temple, and infinite in the presence of Śiva.
In a secluded, pure place, free from barbarians, wicked beasts, hunters, and thorns,
devoid of censure, and filled with devotion.
O beloved of asceticism, one should dwell in one's own country, in a righteous land, where food is abundant, free from calamity, and inhabited by delightful devotees.
In the presence of one's gurus, or in a place where the mind is concentrated,
or likewise in any one of these locations, one should take refuge and begin the recitation.
In whatever village the practitioner of mantra recites, there he should visualize the Tortoise;
likewise on a mountain, by a riverbank, in a sacred forest, or on the shore of a river.
If one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), one should meditate upon the Tortoise (Kūrma) there;
whether in a village, a kingdom, or a house, one should likewise meditate upon Him.
A practitioner who has completed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) should consider what is fit and unfit to eat;
otherwise, through the fault of improper eating, the loss of spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) occurs.
Curd, milk, cow's ghee, sugarcane juice, jaggery-free molasses,
sesame seeds, white lentils, and tubers excluding onions and garlic.
The coconut fruit, the plantain, and likewise the lavalī;
the mango, the āmalaka, the jackfruit, and the harītakī.
Alternatively, other types of sacrificial food (haviṣya) are considered praiseworthy by the wise;
or one may eat sacrificial food, or even vegetables and barley-gruel (yāvaka).
Wherever water, roots, or fruit are found,
as well as seeds, stalk-vegetables, peas, and likewise nakas;
During the vow, one should abandon the kadamba, the coconut, and the kushmanda gourd;
one should also avoid honey, alkaline substances, salt, and oil.
Betel leaf, a bell-metal vessel, eating during the day,
as well as grapes, salt, meat, and eating garlic— these [are forbidden].
Black gram, pigeon pea, lentils, kodrava, and chickpeas;
crookedness, shaving, excessive bodily adornment, and eating food that has not been offered.
One should avoid unpremeditated actions such as massaging and the like;
one should bathe with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or with soap-nut (malaka) alone.
One should perform bathing with mantra-infused waters, as well as mental recitation and feeding [of the deity],
and worship the deity at the three junctions of the day according to the prescribed rules.
If one recites while having unwashed hands, or being naked, or even with a cloth wrapped around one's head,
it is said to be fruitless for as long as that [impurity] remains.
Since one whose limbs are nourished by another accumulates merit through the Dharma,
there is no doubt that half of the fruit belongs to the giver of food and half to the doer.
Therefore, a wise person who knows the scriptures should avoid the food of others with every effort during the time of *puraścaraṇa* and in all ritual acts.
The tongue is burnt by the food of others, the hands are burnt by receiving gifts, and the mind is burnt by the wives of others; O fair-faced one, how can there be success?
For those who are endowed with Vedic conduct, pure, prosperous, virtuous,
born of noble lineage and station, and for the twice-born who subsist on alms;
Whenever the sound "durite" occurs, one should utter the *praṇava*;
before the word "hare," one should perform the *prāṇāyāma*.
One who speaks excessively should place the limbs of the mantra upon the body and then recite it;
likewise, one should do so after sneezing, after touching something untouchable, or even upon touching sacred places.
While these and other such [impurities] are being bestowed, one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* rite;
for he who performs an action joined with the discharge of feces, urine, or similar things [is affected].
O Dear One, all [acts] such as recitation and worship would become impure for one who is unclean,
whose hair and so forth are disheveled, and who is possessed of foul breath.
Whoever should recite [this] a hundred times, the deities stationed for protection will swiftly [act]:
they shall destroy laziness, sleep, sneezing, spitting, and fear.

One should avoid touching a low-caste person and suppressing anger during the time of recitation; one should proceed according to the prescribed rule in this manner, neither too slowly nor too hurriedly.
One should perform the recitation (japa) the stated number of times for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa);
one should contemplate with the intellect the oneness of the deity, the guru, and the mantra.
With a single-minded focus on the recitation, from the morning until midday,
one should perform day and night that same number of recitations which was undertaken.
If one should perform [the recitation] with deficiency or excess, that man would fall from his vow;
therefore, it should be recited day by day according to the number with which it was commenced.
One must not perform [the recitation] with deficiency or excess; one should always recite until it is completed. Ritual acts that are deficient or excessive never bear fruit.
Furthermore, those other rites performed according to the prescribed rule indeed bear fruit:
sleeping on the ground, celibacy, silence, and service to the teacher.
Daily worship, daily charity, praise and chanting of the deity's names,
occasional ritual offerings, and faith in both the Guru and the Deity.
These twelve qualities residing in a Japanese person grant success in mantra;
[namely: women, Śūdras, those who have violated their vows, atheists, and speaking impure words.
One should avoid speaking falsehoods with the tongue; yet, even when speaking the truth, one should remain silent during japa, homa, worship, and other such rites.
Otherwise, all contentment becomes utterly meaningless;
for one who always wears clean garments lies upon a bed of withered kusha grass.
Every day, one should sleep alone and fearlessly upon the bed in the *jāla* [cave].
One should avoid false speech and crooked words.
One should avoid listening to singing and instrumental music, watching dances,
excessive application of perfumes and ointments, and even the wearing of flowers.
One should abandon bathing with dry powder or water, as well as other forms of worship;
one should not recite the mantra while wearing only a single garment, whether one is highly dressed or of humble lineage.
One should cease the recitation upon seeing, speaking with, or hearing the name of outcasts (patitas);
likewise, one should abandon the recitation when sneezing, passing wind, yawning, or crossing over a yoke.
Likewise, upon attaining that [state], one should perform the six-limbed *prāṇāyāma* and then complete the remainder of the recitation, or else do so at the sight of the sun and other [luminaries].
Withdrawal of the mind, purity, silence, reflection on the meaning of the mantra,
freedom from distraction, and lack of despondency are the causes for the successful accomplishment of japa.
One who wears a turban, one wearing a bodice, one who is naked, one with disheveled hair, one surrounded by women,
one whose hands lack the purificatory thread (*pavitra*), or one who is impure— such a person should never recite the mantra while lying down.
Whether fasting or lying down, walking or even eating,
having folded his hands, or even with his head covered;
One who is distracted by anxiety, whose mind is agitated, who is angry, deluded, or afflicted by hunger,
does not achieve victory when reciting within a temple of Śiva, on a street, or in the interior of a house.
One should not recite while wearing shoes, with feet covered, or while situated on a vehicle or a bed;
nor should one recite with the feet outstretched or while seated in the utkaṭāsana posture.
Upon seeing a cat, a cock, a crane, a dog, a Śūdra, a monkey, or a donkey, one should properly recite the *campaka* mantra; having touched them, bathing is prescribed.
Whether impure or pure, whether walking, standing, sleeping,
or sitting, the wise person who takes refuge solely in mantra should always act with the mind alone.
There is no fault in mental recitation at all times and in all places;
the twice-born man devoted to recitation is most excellent, for through recitation he obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
He becomes the recipient of the great fruits of all sacrifices;
the deity, being constantly heard through recitation, is ever-pleased.
When pleased, they bestow vast desires and eternal liberation;
likewise, the yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and other such beings, as well as the terrifying grahas and serpents.
Those who recite [the mantra] are pursued on all sides by serpents, terrified with fear;
for as long as there are ritual sacrifices and established ascetic penances.
All those [other sacrifices] are said to be worth but a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation;
this greatness of the vocal sacrifice of recitation has thus been proclaimed.
Therefore, the whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is said to be a hundred times more effective than that, and the mental recitation (mānasa) a thousand times more so.
Mental recitation is for one desiring spiritual perfection (siddhi), while the whispered recitation is for those desiring nourishment (puṣṭi).
For killing, verbal recitation is indeed praised;
one should bathe at Śeṣavana according to one's capacity, otherwise twice or once.
One should recite the mantra at the three junctions of the day; that shall be equal to worship. Worship may be performed once [a day], but one should not recite the mantra without performing worship.
Either worship may take place at the end of the recitation, or one should recite the mantra at the end of the worship;
beginning at the time of dawn, one should recite until midday.

Having withdrawn the mind from sense objects and with the intellect focused on the meaning of the mantra, one should recite it neither too quickly nor too slowly; thus one becomes like a string of pearls.
Japa is the repetition of syllables; it is mental when performed with sand or woolen threads, consisting of a sequence of letters, vowels, and words, recited mentally.
One should utter [the mantra] while keeping it directed toward its meaning; that is known as mental recitation (mānasajapa).
One whose mind is absorbed in the deity should move the tongue and lips only slightly.
That which can be heard slightly by others is known as whispered recitation (upāṃśu-japa);
that which one utters the mantra with the voice is known as vocal recitation (vācika-japa).
That which is within the range of one's own ears but is mental is known as *japa*; that which is audible to one's own ears alone is proclaimed as *upāṃśu*.
The recitation known as *japa* is said by people to be of three kinds;
the whispered (*upāṃśu*) is ten times superior to the loud (*uccaiḥ*) recitation.
Recitation with the tongue is said to be a hundredfold [more effective] than [mental recitation], while that performed mentally is considered a thousandfold.
Loud recitation is declared to be the lowest; whispered recitation is remembered as middling.
O Goddess, the supreme mental recitation has been described as being of three kinds:
one that is too short causes disease, and one that is too long causes emaciation of the body.
One should recite [the mantra] joined with the syllables and the imperishable, like a string of pearls;
whoever should remember the hymn with the mind or recite the mantra with speech.
Both become fruitless, like water in a broken vessel;
mantras that remain in a state of mere animal-nature consist only of the forms of letters.
Those who have practiced the meditation on the *sauṣumna* attain sovereignty;
one should contemplate the syllables of the mantra as they are proclaimed during the ritual distribution (*vichaktau*).
Having revealed that very [nature] in the supreme sky, which is nourished by the supreme nectar, one should manifest one's own being through worship, fire-offerings, and other rites.
If Śiva is in one place, Śakti in another, and Māruta in yet another,
O lady of beautiful hips, one does not attain success even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Birth-impurity (sūtaka) occurs at the beginning, and death-impurity (mṛtasūtaka) at the end;
a mantra joined with both types of impurity does not attain perfection.
Having removed that [impurity] from the mantra through the intellect of the Guru's power,
that mantra— though joined with the two types of birth-impurity (sūtaka)— bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis).
O Supreme Goddess, having placed the seed-syllable of Brahmā at the beginning and end of the mantra,
one should recite the mantra seven times for liberation from the two types of birth-impurity (sūtaka).
If the meaning of the mantra, the consciousness of the mantra, and the yonimudrā are not explained,
then even by reciting it a hundred million times, accomplishment (siddhi) will not arise for him.
O Dear One, those mantras whose seed-syllables are lost will not yield fruit;
however, mantras endowed with consciousness are said to grant all accomplishments.
Mantras are said to be devoid of consciousness; they are merely letters. They do not yield fruit even through millions or tens of millions of recitations.
Whatever form first arises through the utterance of the mantra,
that is the fruit obtained by reciting it a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand times, or ten million times.
O Kuleśvarī, there is the breaking of the knot in the heart, the growth of all limbs,
bliss, horripilation, and the possession of the body.
The speech of Gaṅgā arises instantaneously; there is no doubt in this matter.
Even when [the mantra] is uttered just once, it is thus encapsulated by the consciousness of the mantra.
Where a sign is perceived, that is called "succession" (pāraṃparya).
One should recite for exactly one month the *bhūtalipi* mantra as a "sandwich" (*saṃpuṭa*).
Gradually, by reciting it a thousand times, his mantra becomes perfected.
The five short vowels, the conjunct consonants, and the letters *vyoma* (ha), *agni* (ra), *yela* (ya), and *dharā* (la) [constitute the seed-syllable].

The final letter of each group, followed by the first, second, fourth, and middle letters respectively, constitute the five groups of consonants; at the end of these are the vowels, along with the anusvāra (m) and visarga (ḥ).
This is declared to be the Bhūta-tvipi mantra consisting of forty-two syllables;
having first performed the recitation (japa) in this manner, one should offer it in the form of radiant energy (tejas).
