Having visualized that [the deity] in the right hand of the Lord, together with kusha grass, flowers, and water,
is endowed with fruit, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should perform three [prostrations] at the beginning of the recitation and three at the end;
having thus completed the recitation, one should [worship] with scents, unbroken rice grains, and water with kuśa grass.
The wise practitioner should conclude the recitation by placing it in the left hand of the Goddess;
at the end of the daily recitation, the mantra-master should perform a fire oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth of that number.
O beloved, one should perform libations and ablutions, and recite the mantra ten times that number;
every day, one should feed Brahmins to pacify any deficiency or excess.
Otherwise, when all [the offerings] are complete, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites;
if there should be a deficiency or a breakage, the recitation (japa) shall be double that number.
In the absence of fire-offerings (homa), recitation (japa) should be performed; it is prescribed as four times the number of the homas for Brahmins, and six times for Kṣatriyas.
This is the rule for these women of the Vaiśya class, who are eight in number; and whatever Śūdra woman has resorted to a particular caste, she shall follow the rule pertaining to that caste.
For a Śūdra who is the servant of a Brāhmaṇa, as well as for his wife, the recitation (japa) is equal [to the standard];
for Brāhmaṇas who are unable to perform the fire-sacrifice (homa), the recitation is double.

But for the other castes, [he becomes one] endowed with the three qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth through the utterance of the *praṇava*, through fire-offerings (*homa*), and through the worship of the *śālagrāma* stone.
By approaching a Brāhmaṇa woman, even a Śūdra falls into the state of a Caṇḍāla;
however, the great eight-syllable mantra is for both women and Śūdras, while the seven-syllable one is as well.
Any mantra that begins with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) is not recommended for women or Śūdras;
however, for whatever limb [of the ritual] may be deficient, the recitation (*japa*) must be performed twice that number of times.
It should be performed with devotion for the sake of accomplishing the ancillaries (aṅgas), even if one lacks the capacity for them;
for one who is devoid of these ancillaries shall not attain that which is distinguished by them.
If one is capable of performing the fire sacrifice (homa), the worship (pūjā), or the libation (tarpaṇa),
one should simply recite [the mantra] that many times and need not perform the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa).
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru with food, clothing, and other such gifts;
by the mere satisfaction of the guru, the accomplishment of the mantra (mantrasiddhi) will certainly occur.
O Kuleśvarī, by the perfect accomplishment of a single mantra through the worship of its five limbs,
all mantras become accomplished through His grace.
Those who know the tantras say that all this has its root in the Guru;
therefore, having gone [to him], one should always pay homage to the Guru, even if he resides in the same village.
The Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman; therefore, one should worship him at the beginning.
At the conclusion of that, the best of practitioners should perform a great worship.
One should also adorn the Suvāsinī and the Kumārī with ornaments;
then, together with one's kinsmen, one should eat sweet food prepared in great abundance.
Thus, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra shall accomplish all desired objects;
or alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is prescribed by another method.
During an eclipse of either the sun or the moon, one who is pure, having fasted while facing east,
should stand waist-deep in the water of a river flowing toward the ocean.
With a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra from the time of touching [the water] until liberation;
or else, having bathed in sacred water, being pure and having previously fasted.
With a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra from the time of its reception until its liberation;
or else, there is another method for the procedure of *puraścaraṇa*.

Having bathed with the pollen [of the flowers] during the conjunction of the moon and sun, one with a restrained mind and undistracted intellect should recite the mantra from the moment of touch until liberation.
Having seen [the deity] and bathed with a firm resolve, one should perform the recitation (japa) ending with liberation;
for every hundred recitations there should be ten oblations (homa), and likewise, for each oblation there should be a libation (tarpaṇa).
By acting in this way, the supreme accomplishment of the mantra arises;
therefore, a pure man should perform sacrifices and other rites at the conclusion of an eclipse.
By reciting the mantra in this way, success will surely be attained; of this there is no doubt.
A person should not abandon the recitation out of faith, devotion, or compliance with others.
He becomes an offender against the deity and leads his seven ancestors to the nether regions;
therefore, the practitioner of mantras, being composed, should perform the fire-oblation according to the procedure prescribed in the Kalpa.
Alternatively, one should perform the fire-offerings (*homa*) and other rites with a tenth part of that;
subsequently, one should perform the fire-offerings and so forth in sequence with a tenth part [of the preceding].
At the conclusion of that, one should perform a grand worship and feed the Brahmins;
thereafter, for the sake of the mantra's success, one should fully honor and satisfy the Guru.
In this way, the accomplishment of the mantra will occur and the deity will be pleased;
[this is achieved through] recitation, fire-offerings, libations, consecration, and the feeding of Brahmins.
In this world, the worship of the five limbs is called *puraścaraṇa*.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Great Secret, in the Dakṣiṇāmnāya section of the Nirvāṇapada within the Vārāhī Tantra.
Bhairava said:
I shall explain the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), which brings auspiciousness to practitioners;
without this consecration, a practitioner cannot attain complete awakening.
One does not attain the status of a teacher nor the state of the virtuous ones if one is not composed;
therefore, the Guru, having instructed his beloved disciple, should consecrate him.
Having fashioned a vast wheel within an exceedingly beautiful pavilion,
one should place a jar filled with a khārī of water in the center of the wheel.
Having duly placed other jars there, provided with cloth and gold, upon the petals, one should invoke the eight deities therein.
Having worshipped the presiding deity in the center and the other deities of the enclosure,
one should perform the consecration for the disciple under his birth constellation as previously described.
Having worshipped with various offerings, one should perform a thousand oblations of clarified butter;
the Guru should then consecrate the disciple, while Rāmā herself pronounces the benediction.
The full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) is that which bestows the status of a teacher;
this full consecration shall grant the desired accomplishments of the practitioner.
Two *pala*s are considered a *prasṛti*; a *kuḍava* is twice that;
four *kuḍavas* make a *prastha*, and likewise, four *prasthas* make an *āḍhaka*. These are the measures for *guggulu*.
Four *droṇas* make one *kuṃbha*, and twice that amount is traditionally known as a *pūrṇābhiṣeka*;
however, if a Kaulika dies while lacking this full consecration, [he suffers].
He attains the state of a Piśāca until the dissolution of all beings;
likewise, [he who practices] sitting at sacred fords (tīrtha), renunciation (saṃnyāsa), and the observance of vows [attains the same].
One should entirely avoid fasting and shaving the head;
therefore, in the case of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), there is no shaving on the head.
The Kāmarūpas, Caṃpākas, those born in Nepāla, the Saindhakas, Vāgas, Gāndhāras, and Pauṇḍrakas— all these are the lowest of the low.
The husband of heroic Kaulikas should perform the initiation;
in the Kālikāgama, there is no fault in the husband bestowing the initiation.
O Pārvatī, just as that auspicious [power] was previously given by Śiva to Gaurī—
whether as a daughter or as a wife— the same applies here as well.
If they have no daughter, then a wife of a hero (vīrabhāryā) is proclaimed [as a substitute];
likewise, a śrāddha performed by one who is uninitiated, or a śrāddha for one who is uninitiated.
Having seized their fathers, he falls into a most terrible hell;
there is no doubt that this continues for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras.
An Ācārya who is unable to accept many gifts should bring forth disciples;
he should not perform the duties of a Guru under his own name, and his wife should bear the name of his mother.
O King, having performed various rites with a skilled counselor and by offering a great sacrifice,
the queen expanded her dominion over the entire region.
On the left-hand path, one should offer the bali-oblation at the four directions of the maṇḍala;
at the station of Brahmā, however, there is Vetāla, for whom the bali consists of a ram and liquor.
In the place of Viṣṇu, a goat sacrifice is prescribed for Bhairavī;
however, Bhairava, in the place of Śiva, desires a buffalo sacrifice.
In that context, liquor made from molasses, honey, and flour are considered *surā* in their respective order;
fish and meat mixed with intoxicants are offered as oblations (*vali*) to the spirits (*bhūtas*).

To the ancestors, an offering of meat with liquor; to the yakṣas, a cock and honey. For the serpent [deities], there is the offering of an *aduṇḍu* fruit; these offerings are made on the left-hand path.
Grass, twigs, wood, stones, as well as earthenware,
a bamboo seat, a cloth, or simply the bare ground as a seat.
The third worship of the skull (kapālārcā) is said to consist of eleven syllables:
*māyā* (hrl-lekha), *strī* (hrīḥ), *hūṃ*, *svarga* (phaṭ), followed by *kapālāya* and *sarvāpadam*.
"Obeisance to the Goddess Kapālā"— this is declared to be the fourth mantra,
consisting of fifty-six syllables, for the worship of Kapāla.
Then, one should worship the solar orb within that skull;
this nine-syllable mantra ends with "namaḥ sūryamaṇḍalāya."
In the worship of the solar mandala, the mantra is considered to be "nṛkapāle manu" (O skull-bowl, [accept] the oblation),
followed by the pair of kūrca-mantras and the two words "mahākāla prasīda" (O Mahākāla, be gracious).
The sixteen-syllable mantra is formed by the pair of *lajjā* (the seed syllables of the Goddess of Modesty) joined with the consort of Fire (*svāhā*).
[It is addressed to the deity] who possesses the luster of ten million fires of time, has four arms, and three eyes.
The God stands in the midst of eight cremation grounds, adorned by eight skull-bearers,
and is accompanied by five corpses, as well as a trident and a hand-drum.
Holding a sword and a skull-bowl in his left and right hands respectively,
he is the beautiful god adorned with the ashes of the cremation ground.
Kālikā, seated upon his heart, wears a garland of various severed heads;
she caresses him as he is intent on passion, devoted to a terrible kiss.
Surrounded by vultures, jackals, and packs of howling dogs,
she dwells in her abode within the cremation ground, enriched with the beauty of her mass of matted locks.
All-empty, adorned with a shaven head, with a serene countenance, and auspicious.
O Lord of the three worlds, Sovereign of the universe, you are Maheśvara; O inconceivable one, you who have manifested from the belly of millions of cosmic eggs!
Since you were meditated upon by me, a person of small intellect, with a body possessing two arms and so forth, please forgive my hundredfold transgressions.
O Śiva, you who are the very essence of the sun, moon, fire, Īśa, Gaṇeśa, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, Śakti, Mṛtyu, Yoga, and the Naga;
when meditated upon within the sphere of my soul and worshipped, please forgive those hundreds of my transgressions.
Neither the Vedas, nor the sages, nor even Sarasvatī herself know you, O dull-witted one, according to the manner in which I have described you.
Yet, meditated upon by me as such, you have become the perpetrator of this offense; I have now experienced this suffering, and here I am, come to you for refuge.
I perform meditation with my mind, for I contemplate this form of yours, O Infinite One, which consists of the syllables of mantra;
that which the Vedas proclaim as your very form is attained through recitation, and not through external acts such as worship and the like.
O Śivā, from the wrist down to below the toes of the feet, the Goddess should wash her face;
this shall be the Hero’s Bath (vīrasnāna).
Likewise, bathing is not for me, nor do I possess a body, nor indeed does sin exist for me.
What is bathing? To whom does bathing belong? For one who has bathed, the meal has already been taken.
One should always bathe with divine waters; in their absence, as prescribed by the water [mantra]:
the syllable *ha* is the form of Śiva, and the syllable *u* is the destroyer of sins.
The vowel *ī* is proclaimed as Māyā because of its nature as the form of desire;
the bindu is Vajrasattva, and likewise the half-moon is Rocanā.
The letter *re* is the Lord of Jewels (*Ratnādhipa*), and the letter *ha* is joined with nectar (*amṛta*).
The letter *ū* is the accomplishment of the clouds (*meghasiddhi*); having known these as the nature of the five Jinas.
Likewise, [he propitiated] the goddess Śmaśānabhairavī,
Ugratārā, Ucciṣṭabhairavī, Caṇḍī, Tārā, and Tripurasundarī.
The goddess Vajravārāhikā is known to have a vetāla as her vehicle;
she is [invoked] by the fourth seed-syllable adorned with the sixth vowel.
This Agnivetālavīja destroys fear everywhere;
for whoever worships this mantra, there shall be no fear of spirits or the sun.
Two-armed, with a yellow face and red eyes, he is terrifying;
he holds a drum in his right hand and a vessel of blood in his left.
Then, with a mouth formidable with fangs and emaciated veins clearly visible,
he bore long matted locks and likewise a terrifying body.
Mohinī said:
O Maheśvara, I do not know the Vīrakavaca for the sādhana;
O Lord, how should I perform the mantra-ritual, since you are my sovereign Master?
The illustrious Ānandadeva said:
O Mahākāla, hear the armor-mantra of Pārvatī, who is the embodiment of the Great Time.
Of this Śrīvetāla-kavaca, the seer is Śrīvīravetāla, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, the deity is Bhūtanātha,
the power is Ḍākinī-Śākinī, and the application is for the attainment of the mantra for all purposes.
O Vīradhvaja, with the left hand [holding] a vessel and the right hand holding a bowl,
one should daily feed that deity, O beloved, who delights in wine and meat.
And having heard this armor (kavaca) from the wise one who possesses the form of Mahākāla and the nature of Time, that best of practitioners who recites it—
Oṃ Hsauṃ! May the Revealer of the Supreme Brahman protect the heads;
may Bhairavī protect the forehead, and may the Single Syllable protect the nose.
May Viśālākṣī protect my throat; may Kālī protect my heart.
May Phreṃ protect my two arms, and may Huṃ protect the center of my navel.
May Mahāvīra protect the abdomen; may the Great Treasure (Mahānidhi) protect the genitals;
may Vighnarāja protect the *mūlādhāra*; and may Mālika protect the middle of the feet.
Protect, protect, O Great Hero! May the toes of your feet protect me.
Oṃ hsauṃ, O Great Hero, O Vetāla, grant success in all undertakings!
Hearing the name-mantra in this world burns away all enemies.
Haṃ haṃ haṃ! He who blazes with a terrifying form and crests of fire—homage to Vīranātha!
Saṃ saṃ saṃ! O crusher of enemies, adorned with serpents upon serpents—protect me, O Vīranātha!
Śrīṃ Śrīṃ Śrīṃ! I bow to the one in the form of Time (*kālarūpa*), who brings about the destruction of obstacles;
Vaṃ Vaṃ Vaṃ! He is named Vetāla, the sixth among the six Bhairavas of the mounts.
Oṃ oṃ oṃ, the Heroic Roar, the destroyer of poison and venom, the one who dwells upon the earth, the purifier;
Phrīṃ Phrīṃ Phrīṃ, the speed of the wind, go, go, that which is uttered as Sound, Hūṃ, the Eye of Time!
Kaṃ kaṃ kaṃ! O Kālakūṭa, brought forth by the hoods of serpents as ornaments, foremost of all!
Taṃ taṃ taṃ! With the sound of striking, *paṭa paṭa*, it falls; it strikes, it strikes away evil!

Ghaṃ ghaṃ ghaṃ! O Vīranātha, you who laugh with the sounds of song and instrumental music, ghu ghu ru ghu ghura! Paṃ paṃ paṃ! O Vīranātha, protector of us who enjoy human blood, you who hold a vessel in your hand!

Listen: if one should practice the heroic sādhana (vīrasādhana) without knowing this armor-mantra (kavaca), the procedure for worship is stated as follows, having performed the seasonal offerings (kālopacāra).
I am the hero among heroes, contented, yellow-hued and terrifying;
O Goddess, [I am] the savior, the slayer, as well as the one who causes expulsion and delusion.
The practitioner, possessing the fourfold knowledge, should bestow the state [of initiation] upon the Śakti in a place of light,
in the essence of tranquility, or amidst water or within a forest.
One should write the mantra of Kālakukkuṭavīra, which is terrifying to the greedy,
upon a Bhoja leaf with devotion at the base of the right arm.
When the hero of the tips of tongues of all the poets who are heroes among scholars has arrived,
the wise man should certainly bestow his heroic prowess of past deeds upon that certainty.
Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ! We know the Great Hero Vetāla; we meditate upon him who has Bhairava as his seat; may that Hero inspire us.
One should worship a banner, a flagstaff, or cloth that has been blown down;
likewise, one should worship [the deity] elsewhere, such as at the feet, even if [the image] has been destroyed or fallen.
One should worship Mahādevī with a red silken garment;
one should indeed offer yellow and blue silken garments to Keśava.
One should offer a red blanket to Śiva, the Supreme Self,
and present a multicolored divine garment to all the gods.
Whether it be reduced to powder, ground, or even drawn out by burning,
or through contact with liquids, or even in the state of being milked from a cow;
Fragrance is said to be of five kinds, which bestows pleasure upon the gods:
scented powder, scented leaves, incense powder, and likewise *sumanas* flowers.
Where there are powders of excellent fragrant substances,
those which are produced from fragrance are known as the first type of scent.
The fragrance of ground Malaya sandalwood and Śarala resin cannot be matched by Meru;
nor can even the paste of agallochum and other such substances equal it.
Then, this second [type] known as *pṛṣṭagandha* is proclaimed;
it consists of *devadāru*, *guru*, *brahmadāru*, *sāra*, and *candana*.
And that essence which is extracted from the burnt priyodīna by means of heating is called "smell" (gandha) when it has been refined by the heat in the third stage.
The juice of fragrant oleanders, sweet-scented jasmine, sesame,
and so forth, which is obtained by being squeezed out for him;
The fragrance arising from *samasya* is considered to be the "all-pervading fragrance" (*sarvagandha*),
as well as that produced from musk (*mṛganābhi*) and that produced from *tagara*.
Fragrance is said to be the food of the elephants dwelling in heaven, bestowing delight;
it consists of camphor, sandalwood, and the like, prepared by being cooked and rubbed.
The Candrabhāgā and other rivers are likewise contained within the essence of the ripened flavor;
however, the Gandharāra is worshipped everywhere at the beginning of the Samarman and other rites.
When musk is ground into a powder through such a process,
then everywhere and in every case, the fragrance becomes fivefold.
Beyond the qualities such as touch, there is another supreme, pleasing fragrance;
the detailed classification of fragrance is said to include *kālīpaka* and so forth.
One becomes established in all five ways in an instant.
That which is sandalwood from the Malaya mountains is considered a Vasu for both the gods and the ancestors.
Whether it be sandalwood, agaru, or even camphor, Viṣṇu is pleased by them all; yet among all varieties of fragrances, that which is produced from me (musk) is most highly praised.
Therefore, with every effort, the gods should always use sandalwood paste mixed with camphor,
along with full measures of *guru* and *karpūra*.
O Bhairava, this fragrance, made from equal parts of saffron, agallochum, musk, and camphor, is pleasing to Vaiṣṇavī and to Kāmākhyā.
Through the pleasure of Tripurā, as well as through the two-fold Śambhu, the deities are said to be the deities; by worshipping with fragrance, the practitioner attains success.
To the god who possesses eightfold power and always bestows all accomplishments, one does not obtain desires through fragrance; rather, fragrance always bestows the Dharma.
Fragrance is the accomplisher of all objects; fragrance is established as liberation from scent.
O sons, Vetāla and Bhairava, this fragrance has been described to you.
The practitioner should not take old or soiled reeds, musical instruments, or clothing,
nor anything already used, for the purpose of making wicks.
One should always preserve the very root for the increase of prosperity;
one should not acquire new cloth born of anger or cloth born of grief for the purpose of making wicks.
O Bhairava, lamp-trees made of gold and other precious materials should be fashioned;
lamps should be offered, but never those made of clay.
The entire earth, along with its inhabitants, endured two things:
the blow of his foot and likewise the heat of the lamp.
O Goddess Vaiṣṇavī, you have made this person a widow; you do not take [the life of] a person,
nor does the practitioner apply collyrium to his eyes for the purpose of joining him with an earthen vessel.
One does not obtain the fruit of worship when [the offering] is made with collyrium in an earthen vessel;
however, incense bestows the four aims of life, fulfills desires, and delights the eyes.
Therefore, a man should devoutly offer this gateway to the gods—
either *āmikṣā*, supreme rice-pudding, or curd mixed with sugar—
as an offering to Mahādevī, which yields the merit of a horse sacrifice (*vājimedha*).
Well-prepared with radish, venison, and meat in an iron vessel.
One who offers side dishes combined with fragrant scents shall attain the world of the goddesses.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Great Secret, in the *Nirvāṇapada* of the *Dakṣiṇāmnāya* within the illustrious *Vārāhitantra*.
Bhairava said:
O Caṇḍikā, how does the great siddhi of the vetālas and so forth come to be?
Tell me that, O Queen of the Gods, if you have affection for me.
The illustrious Bhairavī said:
"O Lord, you are held in my hand; fulfill my command.
Having thus addressed the Vetāla, wherever he might be released, [he should follow him].
The land, the river, Gayā, the mountain, Gaṅgā, Narmadā, Puṣkara, Vārāṇasī, Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, and Jaṃbukeśvara.
Keḍāra, Vāmapāda, Puḍava, the one called Puṣkara,
Someśvara, Mahāraṇya, and likewise Marakaṇṭhaka.
The region where the Kālindī river, the Jala, the Vindhya mountains, and the abode of Guha are located—
this land created by Brahmā is called Brahmāvarta.
In whatever region a particular custom has been handed down through successive tradition for the castes and the intermediate classes, that is always declared to be appropriate.
Kurukṣetra, the Matsyas, the Pāñcālas, and the Śūrasenakas—
this is indeed the land of the Brahmarṣis, which follows immediately after Brahmāvarta.
The Matsyas, Cirāgas, Pāñcālas, Kānyakubjas, and Śūrasenikas;
and that which lies between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, as far as Vinaśana.
The region between Pratyag and Prayāga is declared to be Madhyadeśa;
it extends from the eastern ocean to the western ocean.
The wise know that region between those two very mountains to be Āryāvarta,
where the black antelope roams by its own nature.
O best of the twice-born, he who is born in a land of Mlecchas within a region fit for sacrifice should be known as a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra.
They worship Mahādeva through sacrifices, gifts, and meditative absorptions;
through vows, fasts, and observances; and through fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations.
O Goddess, for them indeed union (sāyujya) and proximity (sāmīpya) are extremely difficult to attain;
yet, by my grace, they come to possess the same world (salokatā) and the same form (sārūpya).
Bathed and filled with joy and delight, [the assembly consisted of] Brahmins, Kshatriyas, kings, Vaishyas,
Shudras endowed with devotion, Mlecchas, and other human beings.
Taking a vessel of udumbara wood filled with water, the wise man, with a joyful countenance,
should undertake the fast, whatever vow he intends to perform.
Having bathed and rinsed his mouth with a concentrated mind before eating his morning meal,
he should offer it to the Sun and the deities and then observe his vow.
Forgiveness, truthfulness, compassion, charity, purity, restraint of the senses,
worship of the gods, fire-sacrifice, contentment, and avoidance of theft.
This common duty exists in ten ways across all vows:
if the breaking of a vow should occur through anger, negligence, or greed, [one must perform the prescribed expiation].
One should not eat for three days, or else undergo the shaving of the head;
nor should one drink water repeatedly or chew betel leaf.
Fasting is destroyed by sleeping during the day and by sexual intercourse; however,
in times of extreme distress, fasting is not destroyed even by drinking water.
Having consumed sugarcane, the bow, milk, roots, betel leaf, and the great medicinal herb (mahauṣadha), one should indeed perform the rites of bathing, giving gifts, and so forth.

A woman in her menses, a caṇḍāla, one who has committed a great sin (mahāpātakin), a woman who has recently given birth, an outcast (patita), one who is impure from eating, and a washerman or similar [low-caste person].
If one hears the sound of these [recitations] while in the midst of observing vows, being the most excellent of men,
one should indeed recite the Mother of the Vedas one thousand and eight times.
One who is devoid of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) is perpetually impure and unworthy for all ritual acts;
whatever else he may perform, he does not enjoy its fruit.
Upon the downward emission of wind, laughing, speaking with a lowered face,
touching a cat or a mouse, being reviled, or when anger arises;
Performing all these ritual acts amidst these signs,
one should touch iron during bathing, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), libations (tarpaṇa), and so forth, as well as recitation (japa), fire-offerings (homa), and the worship of the gods.
The observance of fasting is not to be performed in the evening, except for the *saṃkāhuti* offerings;
likewise, this applies when there is a pregnant woman, one who has recently given birth, a maiden, or a sick person.
When she is pure, then she should have it performed by another, just as she herself [would];
the wife should perform the vow for her husband, and the husband should perform the vow for his wife.
If one lacks the capacity, no violation of the vow occurs through the husband;
likewise, even for one who has maintained the sacred fires, fasting is possible according to his own ability.
One may have it performed by one's son, or one may have it performed by another Brāhmaṇa;
both should observe the fast, and they shall obtain a hundredfold merit.
And regarding a woman who, having fasted, partakes of food offered to the Goddess,
Bhairava declared that her merit is a hundredfold.
There is no substitute for a rite performed for a specific desire (kāmya), nor for those that are obligatory (nitya) or occasional (naimittika).
However, some authorities maintain that even in the case of a rite for a specific desire, a substitute is permissible after the commencement of the ritual.

There is no substitute for this [person] in the mantras, nor in the duties toward the master, the gods, or the sacred fire; there is no such thing in regard to place or time, except for the crossing [of obstacles] by means of the fire-mind.
Among substances fit for oblation, barley is the foremost, followed by rice;
one should avoid mung beans, kodrava, cow's meat, and the like, even when all other options are unavailable.
Rice, barley, mung beans, peas, water,
milk, śyāmāka, nīvāra, wheat, and so forth, are prescribed for vows.
One should avoid the *kūṣmāṇḍa*, the *alābu*, the *vārtāka*, the *pālakya*, and the *jyotsnikā*. One should also avoid eating *caru*, *saktu*, arrows, grief, curd, clarified butter, and honey.
Śyāmāka, śāli, nīvāra, pāvaka,
and root-rice are beneficial as sacrificial offerings (haviṣya), for the observance of eating only at night (vratana), and for fire-rituals and similar practices.
Having abandoned honey and meat, other things beneficial for the vow have been declared:
ṣaṣṭika rice, kālaśāka, and radish, provided they are not of the *kemu* variety.
Garlic, rock salt, sea salt, cow's curd,
cow's clarified butter, milk that is not the essence of the udders, breadfruit, tamarind, and myrobalan.
Long pepper, cumin, citron, and *kaṭiṅkiṇī*;
plantain, *lavalī*, and *dhātrī* fruits, along with jaggery and sugarcane products.
Gold, silver, pearl, lapis lazuli, and coral—these are declared to be the five jewels; I shall now describe the remaining substances.
Gold, sapphire, ruby, and pearl—
those who are learned in the treatises on gems know these to be the five precious jewels.
In the absence of all these gems, one should employ gold everywhere;
likewise pearl, silver, lapis lazuli, and ruby.
Puṣparāga, gomeda, nīla, gāruḍamata,
and pravāla— these nine great jewels are indeed both combined and separate.
The Aśvattha, the Udumbara, the Plakṣa, the Cūta, and the Nyagrodha shoots are declared to be the five-fold bhaṅgas, which are auspicious for all ritual acts.
Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass—
this is declared to be the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), which is purifying and cleanses the body.
Taking cow urine with the Gāyatrī mantra, cow dung with "gandhadvārām," milk with "āpyāyasva," and curd with "dadhikrāvṇo."
"Tejosi śukram" for the clarified butter (ājya), and "Devasya tvā" for the water with kuśa grass;
that which is joined with these five is called *pañcagavya*.
The five nectars (pañcāmṛta) are curd, milk, sugar, honey, and ghee;
as well as sweet, sour, salty, astringent, and bitter.
And pungent—thus, O Goddess, the sixfold group of tastes has been described.
[In this preparation,] there are two parts of musk and four of sandalwood.
Three parts of saffron and one part of camphor should be equalized;
[along with] costus, patchouli, the two types of turmeric, mūrvā, śailēya, and sandalwood.
Vacā, campaka, and musta—these ten are known as the "all-herbs" (sarvauṣadhyaḥ).
Also, sugarcane, tṛṇarāja, niṣpāva, jāti, and dhānyaka.
Like a modification [of milk], cow's milk, safflower, and saffron,
as well as salt as the eighth— this is called the "Eightfold Auspiciousness" (saubhāgyāṣṭaka).
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, curd, unbroken rice, sesame seeds,
as well as barley and siddhārthaka— this is proclaimed as the eightfold arghya.
One should indeed cause five-colored powders to be prepared for the sake of the mandala;
the white [powder] is made from rice flour or from the flour of parched grain.
Red [pigments] arise from flowers, vermilion, red chalk, and the like;
yellow [pigments] likewise consist of liquid orpiment and that produced from turmeric.
Dūrvā grass, kura, bālaka, mango sprouts, the two types of haridrā, white mustard, peacock feathers, and snake skins;
These nine medicinal herbs known as *kautuka* are remembered as follows:
from an elephant, a horse, a carriage-track, an anthill, a confluence of rivers, a cow-pen, and a herd of cattle.
Having brought the clay, one should quickly cast it into the jars,
as well as gold, silver, copper, and likewise brass.
Iron, lead, and the seven metals are thus proclaimed; likewise, barley, wheat, grains, sesame, and kaṅgu.
Śyāmāka and canaka are declared to be the seven grains:
rice, barley, wheat, millet, and sesame.
Priyaṅgu, kovidāra, koradūṣa, satīnaka, black gram, mung bean, lentils, niṣpāva, and kulattha; these are the pulses.
Āḍhakī and caṇaka constitute the seventeenth group;
likewise, barley, wheat, grains, sesame, aṅku, and kulattha.
Black gram, mung beans, lentils, parched rice, black mustard,
Gavedhuka grass, wild rice, Adhaki beans, and Gatinaka.
Chickpeas and cīnaka grains—these indeed are the eighteen types of grain;
as well as those with roots, leaves, pungent fruits, and those that grow from stalks.
Bark, flowers, and mushrooms—these are recorded as the ten types of vegetables.
[The vessels] made of gold, silver, copper, or clay should be endowed with the proper characteristics.
In processions, weddings, consecrations, and the ritual bathing of the jar-mouthed image,
the height [of the pedestal] should be five fingers, while its width should be sixteen fingers.

The base should be twelve finger-breadths wide and the face should be eight finger-breadths; O Dear One, for images of deities where the material is not specified, that same [wood] should be used in the prescribed number.
It may be made of gold, silver, copper, wood, or likewise of clay; it may be fashioned from the mind, from lacquer, or from plaster, according to one's own means and circumstances.
They should be made by those free from pride, starting from the size of an unripe *āmāṣa* fruit up to the limit of a *palāśa* leaf;
they are traditionally prescribed as being no smaller than the joint of the thumb and extending up to one span (*vitasti*).
Starting from the joint of the thumb, or indeed starting from the feet up to the forehead, an image should be made for the home; anything larger than that is not recommended by the wise.
In the worship of the homa-graha and others, there should be one hundred and eight [offerings];
alternatively, twenty-eight may be prescribed according to one's capacity.
When the object as described is not available, that which resembles it is to be grasped;
just as wheat [is accepted] in place of barley, or rice in place of paddy.
When no specific substance is prescribed for oblations, clarified butter (ājya) is ordained;
as for the mantra and the deity, Prajāpati is the established rule.
O best of men, the root mantra (mūlamantra) is proclaimed to be the deity’s own name, preceded by the syllable Om, followed by "namaḥ," and ending in the dative case.
In the absence of curd, milk should be used; likewise, in the absence of honey, jaggery.
O Dear One, one may substitute milk or curd for ghee.
In all oblations of clarified butter (ājya-homa), that which is extracted from a cow should be used;
in its absence, however, that of a buffalo, a goat, or even a sheep may be used.
If that is unavailable, there should be oil; if that is unavailable, there should be *jātila*.
One who does not offer [this] into the great fire becomes poor indeed.
Therefore, one should offer oblations only when the fire is well-kindled, and never when it is not kindled;
for this [oblation] is prescribed as being the measure of a karṣa, while milk is remembered as being the measure of a śukti.
The virtuous have declared that the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) should be taken in the measure of a śukti;
honey and milk are said to be equal to that, and clarified butter in the measure of a mouthful.

The curd should be the measure of a handful; the parched grains (lāja) should be equal to a fistful; the flattened grains (pṛthuka) should be of that same measure, and the roasted flour (saktu) should likewise be of that kind.
Half a *pala* is the measure for jaggery (*guḍa*), and sugar (*śarkarā*) is likewise;
half a mouthful is the measure for molasses (*matsyaṇḍikā*), and sugarcane is measured by the size of a joint.
One may offer a leaf and a flower, as well as incense and other such items;
the Mother’s linga is fourfold, while the jackfruit is prepared in ten ways.
The coconut is divided into eight parts, the plantain fruit into four;
the wood-apple fruit is made into three, and the kapittha is cut into two pieces.
Rice, mung beans, black gram, and barley should each be measured by a handful;
rice grains should be half that amount, and kodrava grain should be equal to a handful.
There should be one *śukti* of salt and twenty-one *marīca* peppers;
the oblation of clarified butter is one *karṣa*, and that of milk is likewise sweet.
An oblation of curd is the measure of a śukti; that of milk-rice is a prasṛti;
and for roots and fruits, it is three pieces according to their own size.
Only a mouthful of other grains should be offered as oblations;
however, unbroken barley (akṣata) is prescribed, and in its absence, rice (vrīhi) is traditionally taught.
In the absence of those, however, one may use wheat; but not sugar, sesame, or barley.
Or else, when other substances are available for certain [specific] purposes.
For in all respects, O Bharadvāja, this is to be accepted according to the sage’s doctrine;
by means of all valid cognition, there are five subtle elements and five [gross] ones.
The measurement for sugarcanes is one joint; for creepers, it is two finger-breadths.
[One should worship] the Moon from the face, and [the deities] from saffron, musk, and yakṣakardama.
One should offer these substances—sesame, guggulu, and jujube seeds—with the *sruva* ladle;
however, solid oblations (*havis*) should be offered with the hand.
The liquids are said to be full in the *sruva* ladle; the solids, such as rice, barley, wheat, *priyaṅgu*, sesame, and *śāli* rice, should be of equal measure with their tips intact.
The rice grains of others should be offered in their own natural form;
[one should offer them] to a Brahmin who is a child-initiated Agnihotrin, handsome and endowed with good qualities.
Having honored him together with his wife and adorned them with ornaments,
the twice-born man, having placed the family priest as the foremost, as well as the others likewise;
They invited those endowed with the twenty-four qualities, together with their wives;
they were dressed in unwashed garments, yet concealed by them, wearing garlands and adorned with pure ornaments.
A pair of garments, as well as a turban, earrings, a neck ornament,
a finger-ring, and an ornament for the wrist.
And having first assigned all these items at the commencement of the religious rites,
the officiating priest (purohita) should cause them to be presented to the sacrificial priests (ṛtvij).
One should give all the aforementioned ornaments, together with a turban and clothing,
as well as a garment for the practitioner of this rite.
Having honored the officiating priests with the honey-mixture (madhuparka), one should have them perform the ritual;
if one has them perform the ritual without honoring them, one is not honored at all due to that transgression.
Twenty-five officiating priests (ṛtvij) should be appointed who are capable of handling gold;
one should honor them all equally, and there should not be a double portion for the preceptor (ācārya).
One should draw a line extending toward the northeast and mark nineteen divisions;
the crescent moon consists of three squares, while the corner chains consist of five squares each.
The pond is twenty-four paces [in area], the embankment twenty paces;
in the center, with sixteen squares, an eight-petaled lotus is prescribed.
One should fill the white [area] with black creepers and dark stalks;
the auspicious pond is reddish-brown and black, and the enclosure is yellow in color.
The lotus has white petals on the outside and a yellow pericarp within; it is encircled by a rim and possesses the qualities of rajas and tamas both externally and internally.
In the center of that, one should place the gods, beginning with Brahmā, as well as the Suras and Asuras;
twenty-four lines should be drawn extending from east to south.
In the corners, there should be chains; on the sides, five rows of squares are to be drawn with nine squares each, while the short chains consist of four squares.
Then, with six short steps one should perform the *vṛtti*, and with eight steps the *apada*;
having made the *liṅgas*, there should be ponds (*vāpīs*) at intervals of thirteen steps.
Therefore, the wise man should not construct two doorways or a pedestal;
its base shall consist of five padas, and the doorways likewise.
In the center, one should draw an eighty-one-square grid, which is called the lotus and the svastika;
one should fill the chains with black color and the creepers with yellow.
One should fill the small chains with red lac and the creepers with yellow; the lingas should be black in color, or alternatively, the ponds should be white.
That pedestal at its sides is neither yellow nor does it fill the door;
in the center there should be red chains, and one should fill the creeper with blue.
One should fashion auspicious [lotuses] with yellow joints and yellow lotus-receptacles;
the petals may be white in color or variegated.
Three lines should be drawn on the outside, white, red, and white in sequence;
eighteen lines are thus declared, from which the four liṅgas arise.
The corner-moon is white and consists of three squares; the black chains consist of three squares each;
the creeper is blue and consists of four squares; and the auspicious [lotus] is red and consists of four squares.
On the side of Mahārudra is Bhadrapārśva; with eighteen black squares on the side of Śiva, there is Vāṇa on the right, who is red in color.
Likewise, one square should be yellow, or it may be auspiciously situated in the middle;
one should then form three squares for drinking at the head of the chain.
From the shoulders of the *liṅgas*, there are twenty chambers with red leaves;
the perimeter is said to consist of sixteen squares of yellow color.
Subsequently, with nine steps, one should fashion a red lotus with its pericarp;
one should then arrange twenty-six lines toward the east and north.
There are one thousand two hundred and twenty-five squares;
the rhombus is said to occupy six squares at each corner, and the chain occupies six squares.
The *padāvallī* consists of thirteen [syllables], while the *bhadra* is formed by four [sets of] three syllables;
the *vāpī* has thirteen syllables, and the *liṅga* is traditionally said to consist of eighteen.
In the row of the three *liṅgas*, there are fourteen squares for the ornamentation;
in their well-formed row, however, there are exactly seventeen squares.
The worship-row (pūjā-pakti) should be understood as arranged all around;
within the row between the worship-rows, there are eighty-two squares in number.
That should be known as the *paridhi*, situated between the two mandalas; in the intermediate squares between the *paridhis*, one should draw the auspicious *bhadra* from the center.
A specific distinction should be understood here: the *śṛṅkhalā* consists of six feet;
the *vallī* has thirteen feet; and the *bhadra* has nine feet.
The pond consists of twenty-five squares; with sixteen parts [forming the lotus], there is a square in the center, and the petals are provided with a pericarp and filaments.
The qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas are the colors; having fallen from the mandala, one should fashion three enclosures (paridhis) there and cause doors to be made.
The Śṛṅkhalā is proclaimed as black like the moon on the seventh day, while the Vallī is blue;
the Bhadra is to be known as belonging to Varuṇa, and the Vāpī is white in color.
The lingas on the sides shall be twelve and black in color;
the perimeter (paridhi) shall be yellow, and the lotus shall be five colors.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the section on Nirvāṇa within the illustrious Vārāhī Tantra. || 7 ||
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, who bestows grace upon devotees,
how may a person attain the purifying bliss that results from all calamities being overcome?
The Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme armor known as Āpaduddhāraṇa, which is more secret than the secret and most wonderful.
O Goddess, having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and meditated upon Kālikā,
Indra was formerly liberated from his bonds by Indrajit.
Bhairava is its seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī its meter (chandas), and the Lord the deity;
Kālikā is its application (viniyoga) for the warding off of all calamities.
Oṃ, may Kālikā protect my head; may she who begins with *krīṃ* and is joined with *ṅe* protect [my face]. May Caṇḍikā protect my forehead, and may Parāmbikā protect my throat.
May Cāmuṇḍā protect the heart; may Maṅgalacaṇḍikā protect the navel;
may Ugracaṇḍā protect the head; and may Pracaṇḍā protect the pair of feet.
Bhairavī, Tvaritā, Durgā, Cāmuṇḍā, Caṇḍanāsikā,
Jayadurgā, Viśālākṣī, Bhadrakālī, and Kapālinī.
May Śivadūtī, Tārā, Kālī, Śivā, Svāhā, Jayantī, Maṅgalā, and Svadhā always protect me in the ten directions.
Yoginī, Yoganindā, Chinnamastā, and Ḍākinī—
[these are to be worshipped] at the royal gate, in water, in a forest, in union, and during times of distress or planetary affliction.
And upon the falling of the king’s sword, and in the terrors of the prison-house and the like—
may the Supreme One always protect me everywhere from these calamities through his battles.
And this armor, O Goddess, which has the nature of Brahman, has been told;
it is named "The Deliverer from Calamity," the warder-off of all misfortunes.
O Goddess, because of its retention, you have become free from all calamities in this very moment.
Having offered a handful of flowers to the Goddess, one should recite the armor-mantra (kavaca) once.
Truth destroys all calamities at that very moment; there is no doubt in this.
By reciting it three times, having destroyed all misfortunes through truth, [one attains liberation].
Having become beloved by all, one shall attain all sovereignty,
even while standing in the midst of molten iron, firmly bound by neck-chains.
Having worshipped the Goddess in one's heart and recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times,
one who is otherwise incapable of being slain by swords and other weapons will certainly be released from bondage.
If one who is pure should study the *lakṣa* having obtained it from the mouth of the Guru,
then Kālī, being thoroughly pleased, will manifest herself before him.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who are proficient in all the Āgamas;
now I wish to hear about the mudrās and their characteristics.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the characteristics of the mudrās:
having brought the two hands together facing each other, with the fingers of both slightly bent.
The *mukulī* (bud) is thus described; it is like a lotus in full bloom. The previously mentioned *mukulīyā* has its fingers extended at the tip.
One should display the Vyokeśa mudrā, the Mukula mudrā, and the Padma mudrā;
in these, the two thumbs are joined together and encircled by one's own fingers.
Having joined the two hands facing upwards, one should make them harsh;
likewise, having bent the two index fingers and the two little fingers.
With the nails facing downward, place them in the middle of the hand;
having raised the four fingers, join the two thumbs together at the back.
When two [fingers] are not fixed [in place], it is proclaimed as the Sky Mudrā (vyomamudrā);
by this, the deity is satisfied and shall always remain present before one.

One should place the two thumbs [within the palms]; this mudrā is considered the āvāhanī (invocation). Alternatively, by interlacing [the fingers] and placing them [together], this mudrā is likewise known as the āvāhanī.
If this [mudrā] is turned face downwards, it is known as the *sthāpanī* (establishing) mudrā;
if raised upwards, it should perform the act of uplifting, and if facing forward, it becomes the *saṃmukhīkaraṇī* (making present) mudrā.
With the fingers extended and the two hands joined together with their palms facing each other, one should place them upon one's own heart; this is the mudrā known as Prārthanā (Entreaty).
Thus, in the worship of all the gods, one should display six [mudrās]:
one should raise the right thumb and bind it with the left thumb.
One should encircle [the base] with the left thumb and the right fingers;
this is declared to be the Liṅga-mudrā, which brings about the presence of Śiva.
One desiring prosperity should apply it to the head; one desiring sovereignty, to the eyes; one desiring freedom from hunger, to the mouth; and one seeking the pacification of disease, to the neck.
One who desires all things should [place it] at the heart; one seeking knowledge, in the circle of the navel;
one desiring sovereignty, in the secret place; and one desiring a kingdom, at the feet.
The mudrās for invocation, installation, bringing into proximity, as well as perfect restraint, and likewise for making [the deity] face-to-face.
Likewise, there is the *saṃkalīkaraṇa* and the *mahāmudrā*;
as well as the conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, *kaustubha* jewel, and the *gāruḍa* [mudrās].
One should display the Śrīvatsa, the Vanamālā, and the Yonimudrā;
with these seventeen mudrās, the wise practitioner [should perform the rite].
O Dear One, this very mudrā is for the rite of worshipping the deity during the invocation;
furthermore, when turned face downwards, it is recommended for the act of installation.
O Dear One, the two fists formed by joining the raised thumbs at the heart are the Sannidhīkaraṇī mudrā in the ritual of deity worship.
The *saṃnirodhinī* mudrā consists of the two thumbs placed within [the fists];
the *karaṇī* mudrā is considered to be formed by two upward-facing fists brought face-to-face.
The placement of the limbs upon the limbs themselves constitutes the *sakala* (complete) mudrā;
it is formed by the two hands spread out with the thumbs joined to one another.
This is declared to be Mahāmudrā, which balances the deficient and the excessive;
the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger [are joined], with the thumb at their tips.
With the bases of the two thumbs concealed and the fingers folded into a bud-like shape with both hands, this mudrā named Śaṅkha is used for the worship of the gods.
O Dear One, there should be a mutual face-to-face touch with a reversal of positions, but one should not wrap [the hands] around;
rather, the fingers should be diligently formed into a circle.
This is declared to be the Cakra-mudrā; after that follows the Gadā-mudrā;
then, with the hands joined facing one another and interlocked, it is known as the Kaustubha-mudrā.
The two little fingers are joined together and facing one another;
likewise, the left index finger is placed between the middle and ring fingers.
The left ring finger joined with the index finger, beautified by the middle finger,
with the two thumbs bent in alternation, is the mudrā characterized as the Kaustubha.

O Sage, when the tips of both hands are joined with the little fingers, ring fingers, middle fingers, and index fingers [touching], this is the Śrīvatsa mudrā; thereafter, the Vanamālā [mudrā] should be formed.
With the little finger, ring finger, and middle finger held in a fist,
the index fingers raised high and rotated— the gods are [invoked] by these two index fingers.
The Yonimudrā is fully described as resting upon two shining [fingers];
the two ring fingers are positioned at the end of the middle finger drawn by the index finger.
The worship of the syllable *yaṃ* situated on the middle part of the thumb is praised;
it consists of thirty-eight, sixteen, ten, or five types of offerings (*upacāra*).
Having analyzed those [questions], I shall explain them; and what is done by means of these?

[The response is: the water for honoring (arghya), the water for washing the feet (pādya) and so forth, the water for sipping (ācamana), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and the ritual touching (upaspṛśa).
Bathing, collyrium application, clothing, sipping water (ācamana), and the sacred thread; then again sipping water, followed by ornaments and looking into a mirror.
Then, in sequence: perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings;
followed by water for drinking, water for rinsing the mouth, and thereafter water for the hands and a garment.
Betel-leaf, unguents, and the repeated offering of flowers;
likewise, song, instrumental music, dance, hymns of praise, and circumambulation.
The offering of a handful of flowers and prostrations are declared to be thirty-eight;
[the remaining items are] the seat, welcome, the arghya water, the pādya water, and the water for sipping (ācamanīya).
The honey-mixture, the seat, the bath, garments, ornaments,
fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, food, and the offering of water for satisfaction.

There is no need for garlands or ointments, nor for prostrations or the dismissal of guests; likewise, there is no requirement for the water-offering, the foot-water, the water for sipping, or even the honey-mixture.
Fragrance and the rest are not [the primary] sleep-inducers; rather, they are designated as such by way of metaphorical usage. The sequence is as follows:
fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, and the offering of food is recorded as the fifth.
Then one should offer scented oil to the image of the God;
furthermore, [the herbs] pūrvā, viṣṇukrāntā, śyāmāka, and padma [should be offered].
The four components of the water for the feet have been briefly described;
camphor, agaru, and flowers are the substances for the water for sipping.
Siddhārtha, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), dūrvā grass, sesame seeds,
the five fragrances, fruit, and flowers— this is said to be the eightfold arghya.
During bathing, dressing, and eating, one should offer water for sipping;
likewise, the goddess Rajani, Shirisha, and Lakshmana.
Mahābhadrā, tips of kuśa grass, and unguents are said here to be for the anointing; likewise, unbroken rice, perfumes, and flowers—these three are for the bathing vessel.
Only pure, washed, and auspicious grains of rice should be offered;
likewise, O beloved, one should also place a jasmine flower in the vessel of the mind.
Lavaṅga, kaṅkola, and the prescribed water for sipping (ācamanīya) should be added to those [other substances];
in the absence of these materials, one should add them while recollecting them.
One should not perform a daily bath for images, cloth paintings, or yantras;
one should do so on every day, or whenever they become soiled with impurities.
One should not worship Viṣṇu with unbroken grains (akṣata), nor the Lord of the Gaṇas with Tulasī;
one should not propitiate the Goddess with Dūrvā grass, nor the Sun with Bilva leaves.
One should never employ the *mahābhiṣeka* (great consecration) with a conch shell anywhere;
indeed, it is prescribed as commendable everywhere except for the worship of Śiva and Sūrya.
The Mandāra and Pārijāta flowers bestow subjugation and good fortune;
when yellow in color, they are beneficial at all times, and are especially intended for the rite of immobilization (staṃbhanam).
The *kharjūrapuṣpa* and *jātī*, as well as the *kunda*, bestow prosperity;
the *bandhūka* grants liberation and good fortune, and the *japā* is dear to Tripurā, O beloved.
The *utpala* brings increase of wealth, while the *padma* is indeed for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*). The *punnāga* brings all prosperity, whereas the *vabhrūka* causes the loss of wealth.
One should avoid *kahlāra*, *hlāda*, *siddhi*, and *ketakī*;
furthermore, *mallikā* should be known as fruitless and a giver of suffering.
The Campakā is for the fulfillment of desires, while Trisaṃdhyā grants liberation from suffering;
Droṇa bestows liberation, and Sevantī grants all perfections.
The *sephālikā* brings victory; the *karṇikā* bestows growth;
the *kumuda* grants joy; and the *sudarśana* bestows wealth.
Kuruṇṭha brings success and good fortune; blue substances bring away [misfortune];
damana brings all prosperity; and the bilva leaf is dear to the Supreme Goddess.
In the worship of the Cakra, one should avoid flowers that are scentless or have an overpowering fragrance,
as well as the black Aparājitā, Mṛtyu, and Sutamālī.
The name Mallikā always brings about misfortune, bestows suffering, and grants death; it likewise causes disease, poverty, and loss accompanied by distress.
There is great fear of worms and the great terror of royal punishment;
O Maheśānī, one should worship Śivā with Hibiscus flowers as before.
Within just one month, the practitioner of the Vāgbhava mantra destroys even the sins accumulated over a hundred lifetimes; through the grace of Tripurā, he attains good fortune.
O Maheśānī, a person worshipping with large white flowers shall destroy all sin; he should perform this worship for the duration of one month.
The wise one should burn away all his sins; he shall bring the three worlds under his control by worshipping with bilva leaves, water-born flowers, and with truth.
O Supreme Goddess, as before, for one month with a tranquil mind,
the practitioner of mantra shall become prosperous and shall always destroy all evil.
One should worship for the duration of one month with Mallikā, Mālatī, Jātī, Kunda, Śatapatraka, and very cool white lotuses.
Among the flowers gathered from the Kulācala mountains, the *palāśa* is said to be the best;
the *aśoka* removes sorrow and is supremely pleasing to the Goddess.

Having offered salutations, one should recite the mantra according to its characteristics, for it bestows accomplishment. O child, I shall speak of those mantras which grant accomplishment in the Kali age; listen to them in truth.
Though much has been said at great length, I shall now briefly describe that which is auspicious among all powers and difficult to attain even in the worlds of Viṣṇu.
Without Śakti there can be no accomplishment, nor does Aśakti become propitious.
Therefore, the wise man should perform worship with those who are empowered and endowed with Śakti.
By worshipping with the flowers that are the sense objects, one becomes identical with That in that very moment;
non-violence is the supreme flower, and the restraint of the senses is a flower.
Compassion is the flower, the Dharma is the flower, and wisdom is the fifth flower;
musk, saffron, camphor, the lotus, and the lineage [are likewise].
The letter Ka is indeed Kaulika, which brings about delight for the deity.
The illustrious Pārvatī said:
O Lord, O Creator, for which specific flowers do you have a longing? Tell me, please, what auspicious flowers I should gather.
The Lord said:
O Goddess, that curiosity of yours which you have expressed to me,
I shall indeed relate with diligence for the benefit of the worlds.
Having bathed on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha,
one should burn guggulu incense and likewise offer flowers and a seat.
Having been uplifted to the world of Brahmā, they too attain the supreme goal;
so it is for that man who, during the month of Śrāvaṇa, observes eating only once a day.
One who worships with *karavīra* flowers shall obtain the fruit of a thousand cows;
likewise, one who worships with *apāmārga* in the month of Bhādrapada.
He travels in a celestial chariot joined with swan-banners,
he who worships with *arka* flowers during the month of Āśvina.
He travels by means of a celestial chariot adorned with a peacock banner;
one should bathe him with milk during the month of Kārttika.
Having worshipped Śiva with *arcaya* flowers while beholding Him as the stainless one,
he worships Him again in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa with *vaka* flowers.
Having transcended the three worlds, he goes there as a teacher;
indeed, one should worship him with *dhuttūra* flowers during the month of Pauṣa.
O Goddess, by worshipping with *tuṣa* grains during the month of Soma, one attains the supreme state;
O Goddess, one should worship Hara with *bilva* fruits during the months of Māgha and Phālguna.
He travels in a celestial chariot joined with the sun, the moon, and the hair;
one should bathe him with scented water during the month of Phālguna.
By worshipping with *droṇa* flowers, one obtains half of Indra’s throne;
and then, in the month of Caitra, one should worship Śaṅkara with dance and song.
One should worship with *droṇa* flowers; if available, many varieties of gold [should be offered]. In the month of Vaiśākha, one should always bathe [the deity] with ghee.
One should worship with white mandāra flowers and obtain the fruit of an aśvamedha sacrifice;
thereafter, in the month of Jyeṣṭha, a person should constantly bathe the [image] that has been purified by fire.

Worship him with lotus flowers; he too shall go to the supreme state—he who is endowed with austerity, virtue, and excellence, a worthy recipient of the Veda, and one who has reached the further shore.
Having given ten gold pieces, O Hare, one becomes a giver of flowers;
likewise, *mālatī*, *mallikā*, *yūthikā*, and *atimuktaka* [yield the same fruit].
Pāṭalā, kaṇavīra, jayā, pāvitī,
kubjaka, tagara, keṭakī, lodhra, and campaka;
With *punnāga*, *nāga*, and *vakula* flowers, with *padma*, *utpala*, and *jāti* flowers,
and with these and other praiseworthy blossoms, a person [should worship] Acyuta.
By worshipping with even a single white or non-white *kanavīra* flower, one obtains the fruit of [giving] ten measures of gold for each.
Having worshipped Hari and Hara, your ascetic penance shall not be in vain;
likewise, *mālatī*, *mallikā*, *jāti*, and *yūthikā* are auspicious flowers.
Pāṭalā, kaṇavīra, jayā, apāmārga,
as well as karkaṭu, kuṃbha, tara, karṇikāra, and kuruṇṭhaka.
The campaka, vātaka, kunda, vāṇa, varvara, mallikā,
aśoka, tilaka, campaka, and likewise the vātacūṣaka.
O Keśava, the śamī flower is an auspicious variety for worship;
likewise, lotuses grown in water, as well as red and blue utpala lilies, are suitable.
O beloved, white lotuses are always dear to Kṛṣṇa;
those flowers should be offered to Viṣṇu, the radiant Lord Viṣṇu.
Likewise, by offering a single *droṇa* of flowers to Mādhava,
one obtains the same fruit as that which is gained by giving ten gold pieces.
In this way, O beloved, the fruit resulting from a specific flower should be known as even greater; listen now to how this applies even to another city.
One *khadira* flower is superior to thousands of *droṇa* flowers;
one *samī* flower is superior to thousands of *khadira* flowers.
A single bilva leaf is superior to a thousand śamī flowers;
a single bakula flower is superior to a thousand bilva leaves.
Indeed, the *nandyāvarta* is superior to a thousand *vakapuṣpa* flowers;
and indeed, the *kanavīra* is superior to a thousand *nandyāvarta* flowers.
Indeed, a single campaka flower is superior to a thousand kanavīra flowers;
and a single aśoka flower is the most excellent, being superior to a thousand campaka flowers.
They worship thousands of flowers with the *kubjaka* as the supreme flower;
thousands of *kubjaka* flowers at the three junctions of the day constitute the supreme offering.
Four thousand times three daily offerings of kunda flowers are especially distinguished.
Thousands of kunda flowers, thousands of śatapatra flowers, and the most excellent mallikā flower.
(34a) Among thousands of *mallikā* flowers, the *jāti* flower is superior;
among all species of flowers, this *jāti* flower is the most excellent.
Listen to the meritorious fruit of him who, with devotion and according to the prescribed rite, offers a thousand jasmine flowers to Viṣṇu at the beautiful Sālā.
For thousands of crores of kalpas and hundreds of crores of kalpas,
the wise one shall dwell in the city of Viṣṇu, possessing prowess equal to that of Viṣṇu.
Whatever fruit is prescribed by the rules for the remaining varieties of flowers,
one is honored in the world of Viṣṇu in accordance with that fruit.
"According to rule" means from a tree possessing the characteristics described by Puṣpa;
the leaves and flowers as well must be those that bring pleasure to Hari.
I shall speak; listen, O Goddess, as I speak before you:
the leaves of the apāmārga are meritorious, and so too those of the bhṛṅgarāja.
Therefore, the khadira leaf is excellent; therefore, the śamī leaf is excellent;
yet even compared to the bilva leaf, the tulasī leaf is supreme for Hari.
One should worship Hari with whatever leaves of these plants are available;
thus liberated from all sins, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
The lotus, the *kaṇavīra*, the two types of *tulasī*, the *ajātī*, the *keṭakī*, the *nāgakeśara*, the *yāvaṃtī*, the *kahnāra*, and the *campaka* and *utpala*.
The river-spiral, the jasmine vine, the mallikā and the non-mallikā,
as well as the kunda, mandāraka, saugandhika, and kesara.
Kuraṇṭha, śoka, lajjā, bilva, munipuṣpaka,
patra, āmalaka, karṇikāra, and palāśa.
One should offer these and other flowers as they are available— indeed,
all fragrant flowers, whether growing on land or in water.
And those very same flowers are highly praised and most beloved, O Greatly Dear One,
which are endowed with gold and possessed of both flavor and fragrance.
The vāṇa, campaka, and śoka; the kara and likewise the yūthikā;
the pāribhadra, pāṭalā, vakula, and giriśālinī.
Kanaka, jambūvana-ja, prītaka, and tagara—
these flowers are indeed recommended for the worship of Acyuta.
Those who worship Mālatī, Tulasī, Padma, Ketakī, and Munipuṣpaka,
O Lord of the World, go to the abode of Hari.
O Daityas, he who worships with kadamba flowers remains pleased for twenty thousand years and three hundred years.
Just as Mādhava becomes delighted upon reaching his lotus-abode,
so too does Keśava experience joy upon seeing the kadamba flower.
O Goddess of gods, if Hari is worshipped even once with a kadamba flower as a matter of sport,
for seven births the [divine powers] will not be far from him throughout the year.
The wise man who places a heap of kadamba flowers upon the head of Keśava shall obtain the merit of giving a thousand cows.
He who worships Viṣṇu with a garland of *mālatī* flowers during the month of Kārttika obtains the supreme fruit of giving away a hundred tawny cows.
O Lord whose banner is Garuḍa, he who worships with jasmine flowers in the springtime with supreme devotion shall burn away the sins accumulated in the three ways.
O Lord of Gods, when the month of Madhava arrives, even by means of self-restraint,
one obtains the fruit equal to the gift of a hundred tawny cows through worship at Lalita.
When the Garuḍa-bannered Lord Madhusūdana is worshipped with even a single Ketakī leaf, he becomes well-pleased for a thousand years.
O best of sages, even Indra, the lord of the gods, cannot create a flower-petal as beautiful as the garland made of *munipuṣpa* flowers that those people who worship Janārdana offer.
Furthermore, the yogi who worships the Garuḍa-bannered Lord with Pāṭala flowers in the spring with supreme devotion shall become liberated and like Viṣṇu himself.
Those who worship the Lord of the World with abundant *aśoka* flowers shall become free from sorrow as long as the moon and sun endure.
O best of Brahmins, by worshipping the Lord of Waters with white and black oleanders,
a human being becomes a Brahmin for four yugas.
O Keśava,
those fortunate ones who always worship with the blossoms of the mango tree partake in the fruit of giving ten million cows.
The man who offers *durvā* sprouts at the time of worship obtains a hundredfold merit when the worship is properly performed.
O beloved, he who worships the God, the enemy of the asuras,
with nearby leaves has crossed over the most terrible path of Yama.
O Lord of Devas, those who worship Varṣākāra with flowers born of the campaka tree are not fish; they are no longer subject to rebirth within saṃsāra.
O divine sage, those people who worship Janārdana with a *kuṃbhī* flower obtain, O beloved, the fruit of [giving] a supreme quantity of gold.
The Garuda-bannered Lord, the Destroyer of Death, destroys the sins accumulated over ten million lifetimes for those who worship the golden Ketakī flower.
O Lord of the World, he who offers two saffron-red lotuses and two fragrant *śatapatrikā* flowers shall dwell for a long time on the White Island (*Śvetadvīpa*).
O beloved, whatever fruit is obtained from all flowers and even from a single flower petal,
that is attained by worshipping Keśava with even a single leaf of tulasī.
The auspicious Tulasī has been seen, questioned, meditated upon, praised, saluted, and lauded; she has been planted, watered, and constantly worshipped.
O beloved, as long as the planted tulasī spreads its roots, for that many thousands of yugas it extends one’s merit.
O dweller of the earth, the Tulasī planted by men flourishes;
it uplifts their lineage—those who have passed away, those who are present, and those who are yet to come.
They shall dwell in the abode of Hari for a hundred thousand kalpas;
one should not drink or take red sandalwood or red flowers.
I shall not speak of one who does not worship Him with bilva leaves and their blossoms;
nor shall I worship Viṣṇu with flowers, leaves, or fruits that are withered.
Having bathed, one should use unsoiled, non-stale, and unsolicited black pigments; likewise, one should avoid ketaki flowers, even if they are fragrant, as well as other such items.
The flowers of the mandāra, arka, dhuttūra, śālmalī,
and kāpuṣpaka are forbidden for the worship of Viṣṇu, as is the flower of the vaibhītaka.
The goddesses are pleased by flowers, and the gods are established through flowers;
what more need be said? The praise of the flower is beyond all weariness.
The supreme light is considered the flower; it does not take pleasure in [ordinary] flowers.
The flower is the means for achieving the three goals of life (trivarga), and the flower bestows prosperity, heaven, and liberation.
Brahmā dwells at the root of the flower, Keśava in its center,
Mahādeva at its tip, and all the gods reside upon its petals.
White flowers belong to the gods, while fragrant incense belongs to Durgā;
that which is rough and red is proclaimed for the Rākṣasas.

Even if a flower has been plucked from a plant that is not yet trembling [with life], or has been made to bloom by another means—that flower shall belong to the ancestors; this I tell you truly, O Goddess.
If even a single flower worth ten gold pieces is offered without fragrance,
O Mahādeva, a garland of a hundred thousand flowers will please you.
O best of the twice-born, the procedure for even scentless flowers is well known;
now hear the fruit of that [offering] with beautiful, pungent, and fragrant [scents].
By offering even a single flower at lingas or images,
a person shall not go to an evil rebirth for eighty koṭis of kalpas.
He whose tree’s flowers, leaves, and fruits are dedicated to Mahādeva, he too shall go to the supreme goal.
Śiva himself, standing before one who has personally gathered flowers and worships with devotion,
accepts them directly and constantly out of affection.
The fruit for each individual loose flower is ten suvarṇas;
when flowers are joined together to form a garland, the fruit is held to be double.
Five *kṛṣṇala*s make one *māṣa*, and sixteen of those make a *suvarṇa*.
Having worshipped Maheśvara here even with five flowers, [one attains the fruit].
A man who duly worships with eight flowers sacred to Śiva obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
Does one not go to the abode of Śiva by means of thousands of cities?
There is no fault in using flowers for the daily worship of the deity, whether they are purchased or stolen.
O Supreme Goddess, whatever effort is exerted by a seeker shall become entirely fruitless,
unless it is directed toward You, in whom such love as this for maidens resides.
Even among the most excellent there is none such as that found even among those born in the villages.
The illustrious Umā said:
You ought to explain all that you have described regarding worship, adoration,
and the ritual procedure for flowers.
The illustrious Lord said:
O daughter of Himavat, it is true that among the glorious flowers, there are those which do not shine for me; I shall describe them to you in detail.
Kanavīra, uduṃbara, arka, and likewise unmattaka;
pāṭalī, bṛhatī, and likewise girikarṇikā.
One should offer aśoka, śamī, kuraṇṭaka, mandāra, aparājitā,
śatapuṣpā, and other flowers such as kubjaka and śikhinī.
Apāmārga, as well as lotus, jasmine flower along with the red lotus, campaka, śīlatapana, and likewise nāgakeśara.
The punnāga, the kikirāsa, and likewise the auspicious droṇapuṣpa;
as well as the śiṃśapā, the udumbara, and similarly the jayā and mallī.
The flowers of the sacrificial tree, as well as the auspicious bilva leaf,
the blossoms of the kusuṃbha flower, and likewise those of saffron.
Blue lotuses, saffron, and likewise red water-lilies,
as well as all fragrant flowers growing on land and in water.
I shall receive upon my head, O Goddess, that which you bestow upon me with devotion.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the section on Nirvāṇa within the Dakṣiṇāmnāya of the glorious Vārāhī Tantra.
Bhairava said:
In this world, there is nothing equal to evil, nor is there anything superior to the dharma of compassion;
there is no god higher than Rudra, and no flower more precious than the golden lotus.
A person who worships Viṣṇu with garlands and fragrant perfumes,
especially at the altar, enjoys infinite fruit.
Having fashioned a linga from pieces of bilva leaves, one should worship it;
being liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
The man who worships the Liṅga even once with Dhattūra flowers attains the fruit of a hundred thousand cows and reaches the supreme state.
Whoever worships the Liṅga with devotion using Bṛhatī flowers obtains the fruit of giving ten thousand cows and shall go to Śiva.
Mallikā, nyagrodha, padma, jāti, punnāga, campaka, aśoka, caitra, mandāra, karṇikāra, and cukā.
[One should offer] Kaṇavīra, Arka, Mandāra, Śamī, Tagara, Keśara,
as well as those produced from Kuśa, Yamā, Mārga, Kumuda, Kadamba, and Droṇa.
Listen with one-pointed mind: whatever merit a man obtains by worshipping Śiva with flowers according to his means, he attains that same merit from the Sun.
With celestial palaces shining like ten million suns, fulfilling all desires,
adorned with garlands of flowers, and resounding with the sounds of song and instrumental music.
In the expanse of the sky, he moved at will amidst the sounds of musical instruments and sweet songs,
surrounded by the daughters of Rudra and the nine deities who are difficult to attain.
Fanned by chowries and praised by gods and asuras,
he proceeds to a divine city, or wherever it may please him.
Those who, having worshipped Śiva with flowers from trees, ponds, and water or land-growing plants,
sprinkle [him] with devotion, are glorified in the world of Śiva.
Whoever should create a very dense floral mandala upon Śiva,
adorned with Mandāra flowers hanging down as far as the pedestal;
Adorned with the most wonderful Great Vehicles and divine flowers,
he dwells happily in the City of Śiva, possessing the splendor of all various flowers.
He who, during the auspicious festival occasions, makes his house auspicious, filled with many forms and radiant with various flowers, like a white water-lily;
Surrounded by a thousand [attendants], he enjoyed the pleasures of divine women in the Puṣpaka chariot, endowed with delight in sport.
At the proper time, he rejoices imperishably, his mind unassailable by the teachings;
wherever Śiva and others are seen in all the worlds, there he goes.
O Goddess, by offering an *ivuka* fruit just once, one obtains the merit of a thousand cows;
by [offering it] for a fortnight, one becomes a yogi, and by [doing so] for a month, one goes to heaven.
For two months one obtains the supreme fruit of a sacrifice;
for three months, they attain the unsurpassed world of Brahmā.
Through four [months] one attains success, and through five, the perfection of yoga;
within six months, a person goes to the world of Rudra, without a doubt.
Assuming the form of Rudra, with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament,
he set out on a bull-vehicle like a second wielder of the trident.
The bilva leaf, the samī leaf, the leaf of bhṛṅgarāja,
the leaf of āṭarūṣa, and the leaf of śiṃśuka and colika.
The leaf of the *tamāla* tree, O Lord, which is the source of purity;
and the white and black leaves of the *unmatta*, and the leaf of the *kesara*.
The leaf of the Gaṅgāpattrī, the leaf of the Kahlāra,
the leaf of the Jalakahlārikā, and the leaf where the Marūvaka grows.
The *śatapatra* is always prescribed, as are the *gandhādyāvuka* leaves,
the leaves of the *duṃvarikā*, and the leaves of the village disciple (*grāmaśiṣya*).
The leaves of the Droṇa, Apāmārga, and Khadira—
whichever leaves are used for the worship of Śiva, with those same [leaves] and their flowers, it should always be performed.
O Śāla, Aśoka, and Durvā grass, with ancient offerings and through constant devotion, Sadāśiva is always worshipped by practitioners.
Whether on a leaf or a flower, a fruit that faces downward is not desired;
it is declared to be a giver of suffering, and one should report it exactly as it was found.
Offering flowers with the face turned downward is lost; according to the prescribed rite, golden *kadaṃba* flowers should be offered to Śaṅkara at night.
Flowers that remain fresh during the day [are suitable], as is the *mallikā* at midnight; the *jātī* remains fresh for one watch, and the *kaṇavīra* throughout both day and night.
Flowers should be offered at night; this is the ocean of the *toṭanāṃtroṭa* [tradition].
A *liṅga* worshipped with *apāmārga*—this fruit has been declared by me.
Now hear of the fruit that belongs even to one who worships with desire:
the God is a bestower of boons when worshipped with *cūka*, and a giver of wealth when worshipped with *kanavīra*.
One attains prosperity through *arka* flowers, but through *dhuttūraka* one attains the world of cows;
however, he who worships the supreme *liṅga* with blue lotuses shall experience divine enjoyment.

With red lotuses one shall obtain a kingdom, and with white lotuses (puṇḍarīka) one shall become a universal monarch; with campaka flowers one obtains all desires, as does one with punnāga and nāgakeśara flowers.
One obtains desired objects through garlands of *kesara* flowers;
likewise, he who worships with *puṣpaka* flowers attains the perfection of mantras.
O Supreme Goddess, one should likewise worship with white flowers;
he who worships with perfumes and flowers attains all desires.
One who worships the Supreme Lord with *kubjika* flowers obtains abundant gain, and *vāruṇī* brings good fortune; one who desires a daughter should worship Him with *jātī* flowers.
Within six months, he undoubtedly obtains an excellent daughter;
this is true for one who, desiring knowledge, worships Maheśvara with *mallikā* flowers.
A pure man who desires a son should worship with kunda flowers; he thereby obtains supreme knowledge that destroys the fear of saṃsāra.
One obtains many sons, wealth, and long life; through *kuśa* grass and flowers, one attains health, and through *aśoka* flowers, union with beloved ones.
One should know that a dense cluster of *karṇikāra* flowers brings subjugation (*vaśya*), while *droṇa* flowers bring nourishment;
one who is constant in his vows should always worship the *liṅga* with *kadaṃba* flowers.
One who desires to bring enemies under control should always cause [this] to be offered;
