the diseases of one who worships with "atimuktaka" flowers shall perish.
By means of a *sindhuvāra* flower, one bound is released from bondage;
those flowers which are dark-colored like a black antelope horn are honored for their fragrance.
One should offer those [red flowers] to the God of gods for the destruction of enemies;
yellow flowers, however, are for the purpose of flowers and for victory.
He who gives [these] constantly shall obtain his desires;
however, one should employ water-born flowers for the purpose of subjugation.
Those very [leaves] which are blue and red are indeed for subjugation;
the bilva fruit is the source of all desires and the liberator of the poor.
There is nothing superior to the bilva leaf by which Śaṅkara is pleased;
for the sake of victory, one established in religious observance should employ the damanaka plant.
The enemy is conquered by him who worships the Bull-bannered Lord;
Aruvaka brings happiness, while Jaṃbuḍa grants all desires.
Tiraka bestows wealth, Odhana desires cattle, Vaca is of noble lineage, Saukhya grants happiness, Aśva is likewise, Tagara is a servant, and Kiṅkarāṭa fulfills all desires.

Health is indeed obtained from the bandhūka tree; it is remembered that one receives fruit from the phalinī; from the śāla and priyaka trees one gains what is dear, and from the kiṃśuka tree one attains long life.
One desiring elephants and cattle should worship Śiva with *kuṭaja* flowers;
one should offer camphor and *damana* for the destruction of enemies.
Enemies perish quickly through the worship of the God of gods;
likewise, the *śyāmā* flower constantly bestows health, as does the *javā* flower.
O God of gods, Maheśvara, for the sake of bringing the Kurus under one's control, one should always worship the Liṅga by applying Dveṣikā and Yūthikā.
One should worship the Ketakī Liṅga when enraged for the destruction of enemies;
O Goddess, the Vyāghrī is proclaimed as the bestower of all desires.
Likewise, Jyotsnākarī here always grants desires;
by worshipping her with incense, the gods increase one's strength and lifespan.
The *jhiṇṭhikā* always bestows happiness, as do the *apsarā* and the *campaka*;
likewise, the *triṃbhaka* and the horse-colored [flower] are for the purpose of destroying disease.
One who desires victory should worship with Jayantī; for one desiring white [results], with Girikarṇikā;
and he who worships with Nimba flowers for the sake of causing hatred or subjugation, [shall succeed].
Bheṇḍī should be employed for attraction, and by ādamatī, victory shall be attained;
ṛṣipuṣpa and rudrajaṭī destroy all calamities.
That which is called *sanapuṣpa* and likewise *kokilākṣa*—
all that which is white brings great misfortune, while all that is yellow brings evil.
O beloved, one should offer leaves, flowers, fruits, water, and even grass to Kṛṣṇa and to the God of gods for the purpose of exorcism.
If one offers [these] daily when available, one shall not fall into an evil rebirth;
likewise, ketakī, atiyukta, kunda, yūthī, and padāntikā.
One should avoid the flowers of the śirīṣa, sarja, and bandhūka; likewise, one should avoid the leaf and flower of the vākucī, which originates from the king of trees (the karaja).
One should avoid vaibhītaka flowers and leaves;
likewise, the *japā*, *kunda*, *śirīṣa*, *yūthikā*, and *mālatī*.
Śaṅkara is never to be worshipped with *keṭakī* or *bhavapuṣpa* flowers;
nor with *sarja*, *bandhūka*, *kunda*, *yūthī*, or *madantikā*.
The *keṭakī*, the *jāti* flower, the white *aparājitā*,
the withered lotus, the red and white [lotuses], as well as the *bhaṇḍika* flowers.
Having worshipped with gold, aguru, akṣa, and the vaibhītaka flower, as well as with these other flowers, O man, one should always worship.
In the Avīci hell, the sinner dwells for five divine eons; of this there is no doubt.
[One who consumes] the wood-apple, the Keṭakī flower, or the Māṃdinī with its wood and leaves [is reborn there].
One should avoid the nimba flower, the karañja, the dhātakī flower, the śirīṣa, the guñjā flower, and the atimukta.
However, O beloved Puṣpaka, out of supreme devotion, that which is forbidden—
even if it be auspicious, whether water-born or endowed with fruit and flowers— must not be offered.
One should offer everything with devotion; one shall never encounter anything inauspicious. Worship may always be performed with all flowers, even those not prescribed by rule.
Devotion to all the gods must be practiced, for it is the cause of prosperity;
[one should avoid] those places which are strewn with thorns and those which are defiled.
One should avoid from afar those things that have been left overnight here.
A seat that has been washed with water and is naturally clean, or one where fine powder has settled of its own accord—
these flowers, they say, require no ritual action when used in the worship of all the gods.
O twice-born one, some indeed gather flowers after having bathed and performed their rites;
the deities do not accept those, for they turn to ashes like wood.

One should never offer to a woman incense that is pungent-smelling or odorless, nor one that is purchased, nor one that is proclaimed to be fruitless, nor one worn above the head by a deity, nor one used for bathing.
One should avoid hair and other things that are dirty, touched by the ground, or defiled; one should also avoid flowers that have been stale when performing the worship of the deities.
One should worship the God with flowers that have been plucked,
as well as those that have fallen naturally upon the ground, and those that have blossomed spontaneously.
One should never worship with flowers that have been carried on the back of an animal, or those covered with clothes, or those lacking three parts.
One should avoid flowers that have fallen to the ground, with the exception of *śephālī* and *vakula*;
likewise, one should discard those with black spots, as well as *campaka* and *padmaka*.
The leaf of the *bilva*, the *khadira*, as well as the *dhātrī*, the *darada*, and the *tamāla*— when torn or broken, it is not defiled.
Regarding *turasya*, *agastya*, and *bilva* fruits, it is held that there is no such thing as "stale. However, one should avoid stale flowers; they are excluded from worship.
The water of the Ganges is never to be discarded, nor is a tulasī leaf;
tulasī is always pure, as are the leaves of the bilva tree.
Indeed, for water-born flowers and for the bilva leaf, the impurity lasts for one day; however, for other [flowers], it lasts for five days.
A wise person should offer a wolf to Rudra for seven nights;
it should be given day after day, leaving over a portion each time to be offered again and again.
After seven nights have passed, it becomes unfit for offering;
likewise, a dry lotus and a *māsalaka* remain fit for three days.
One may eat grains and vegetables fit for consumption for a single day after purification;
there is no fault if they are kept in a house that has been sprinkled and is free from impurities.
The *kuñcaka*, the white lotus, the red lotus, the great blue water-lily (*mahotpala*),
the pale lotus, the blue lotus, and the white night-lily (*kairava*).
Tagara, kiṅkilāta, vahula, bṛhatī, śamī,
karavīra, arka, lodhra, śiṃśapā, and aparājitā.
Atimuktaka, vakra, vandhaka, and likewise madana;
surabhī, śallakī, droṇa, yūthikā, and the nine-fold mallikā.
Mālatī, Mādhavī, Vajra, Punnāga, Nāgakeśara,
Jhiṃṭhī, Sairayaka, Kuruvaka, and Kuraṇṭaka.
Mārgī, arjuna, mallī, vaka, daṃva, śatapatrikā,
vicakila, kusumbha, marupatra, and javāvuka.
The śaśara, the kadalī flower, the bright and very abundant puṣpaka,
the kaśuka, the paribhadra, the śephālikā, and the śālmala.
[He saw] the Varvara, the Navanīla, and the Sevantī as well as the Vahula; the Sarja, the Vikaṭaśīrṣa, the Madantī, and likewise the Tulasī.
Śilīṣa, pomegranate flower, vanamālā, maruvaka, clove, white mandāra, and again red mandāra.
Kṣuraka, māṃvuka, jayantī, hemapuṣpikā, kumārī, bhūtakeśī, amlā, and navamālikā.
Madhurikā, Kubjikā, and Girikarṇā were defeated;
likewise Bhṛṅgarāja, Mati, Chatra, and Agnijvālā.
Betel leaf, as well as the sprouts of the aśvattha tree,
sinduvāra, the leaf of the palāśa, and likewise the tips of dūrvā grass.
One should worship the Mother of the Universe with these water-born and land-born flowers, as well as other special blossoms and flowers of five colors.
One should worship with self-manifested flowers, those produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa* [semen and blood], and with *tulasī* flowers and leaves; thus one’s own self increases.
The two *jātī* flowers, the two kinds of *ketakī*, the *kahlāra*, the *campaka*, and others; the *kunda*, *mandāra*, *punnāga*, *pāṭalā*, and *nāgacampaka*.
The *āvakadha*, *karṇikāra*, *pāvaṃtī*, *navamālikā*,
*saugaṃdhika*, *sakoraṇa*, *palāśa*, *śoka*, and *mallikā*.
O Pārvatī, these flowers— the dhūstūra, sarjaka, bilva, arjuna,
and munipuṣpaka— are fragrant even when mixed with one another.
One should always worship Kālikā with flowers that bloom in their respective seasons;
the wise declare that those [flowers] specifically prescribed for worship are what one should offer.
With flowers produced from the Aśoka, Bandhūka, Pāribhadra, and Javā,
as well as those from the Palāśa, Pāṭalā, Padma, Kiṃśuka, and Karavīra;
With *jātī*, *ketaka*, *kahlāra*, *nāgakeśara*, and *campaka* flowers,
as well as other beautiful, numerous, and fragrant blossoms.
One should worship with fragrant flowers and auspicious leaf-stalks;
[the flowers] are vakula, śara, vajra, mārgya, kunda, and śālmala.
Karīra, arka flower, bandhūka, and likewise lotus;
mālatī, mallikā, jātī, yūthikā, and likewise māgadhī.
Nagara, Karṇikāra, Droṇa, Utpala, Campaka,
Aśoka, Kumuda, Śephālikā, and the two Kadaṃvas.
The ketakī, the forest garland (vanamālā), the kusumbha, and the kiṃśuka,
as well as the kahlāra, the vakula, the lavaṅga, and the nāgakeśara.
Indeed, Kālikā is the presiding deity over all flower garlands;
these too are dear to him, but one should not worship Śiva with leaves alone.
O wise one, among all species of flowers, the red and white Javā is pleasing to the Goddess and bestows the fruits of all desires.
O Goddess of gods, red flowers as well as those made of gold and other materials—
these twelve types of flowers, including the *mādyā* and others, should be worshipped in all the months.
The kunda, kuruba, ketakī, vaka, jhiṇṭī, nava, nīla, vikaṭa, śīrṣa, and likewise the kṣudra and bhūdhruvaja [are used].
One should worship the *vakula* and the *vakula* alone, and never any other tree in this month;
likewise, one should offer flowers that are red, black, and white, which are meritorious.
O beloved, [the flowers] are white, red, the javā flower, and likewise the karavīra;
as well as tagara, mālatī, jātī, sevaṃtī, and yūthikā.
Dhustūra, śoka, vakula, white and black aparājitā,
bakapuṣpa, bilva leaves, campaka, and nāgakeśara.
Mallikā, jhiṃṭhikā, and kāñcī are proclaimed as red;
likewise, rakta-śevantī is red and pīta-mālatī is yellow.
With *arkapuṣpa*, *javā* flowers, *varvara*, and *priyaṃvadā*,
Pārvatī becomes especially pleased on the eighth lunar day.
All the deities are satisfied by a red lotus flower;
likewise, for the goddesses, the *arka* and *mandāra* flowers, and for Āditya, the *tavaraka*.
Red flowers are very dear to Gaṇeśa and Sūrya;
Kālikā is pleased by the beautiful flower and leaf of the *āmalakī*.
The *kokanada* flower, the lotus, the *javā*, and the *bandhūka*—
among all varieties of flowers, the red lotus is preeminent.
Even by hundreds of millions of crores, all other flowers together— such as the javā, the lotus, and the pārijātaka— are not equal to it.
In the absence of *japa* and other rites, one should offer fragrant *dūrvā* grass and *śrīphala* fruits;
O Goddess, there is never any worship here without the offering of *dūrvā*.
Therefore, one should take dūrvā grass, for it consists of all flowers;
for the gods, one should offer that which is rich in all fragrances, or in its absence, a tulasī leaf.
One should worship the gods with Tulasī; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O beloved, without Tulasī, the limbs of the Śrāddha, sacrifice, and ritual worship are incomplete.
Therefore, either dūrvā grass or tulasī should be taken up by practitioners;
worship devoid of tulasī shall never be fruitful.
Whether it be Sundarī, Bhairavī, Kālī, or even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva themselves—
any worship performed without Tulasī is never complete.
With various offerings and oblations, with charming flowers of many kinds,
and with auspicious sprouts of Apāmārga leaves, excluding those of Tulasī.
She should always be worshipped with devotion by men for the swift attainment of results;
yet, upon smelling the fragrance of Tulasī, the beautiful lady becomes angry.
One should never worship beautiful goddesses with *tulasī*;
by worshipping them, one becomes a sinner, and even at the time of an auspicious union (*lagna*), one takes away one's prosperity.
He who mentally offers thousands of red lotuses for thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas [attains great merit].
Having stayed in the city, O Goddess, the glorious king shall thereafter become established in the Acchita [state];
among leaves, however, the Bilva leaf is supremely pleasing to the gods.
O Goddess, if a man here worships Kālikā with *caṃpaka* flowers,
even Brahmā is not able to fully describe his merit.
Therefore, Kālikā should always be worshipped with campaka flowers by the wise.
That man who worships Kālikā with affection using royal campaka flowers—
There is no returning for him to this essence-less cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
[One should offer] jasmine, blue lotus, red lotus, śamī, punnāga, and campaka.
The aśoka, the karṇikāra, and especially the droṇa flower,
as well as the kanavīra, the śamī flower, the kumuda, and the nāgakeśara.
The excellent man who, endowed with supreme devotion, offers these flowers to Kālikā for the sake of merit, becomes a spiritual practitioner (sādhaka).
He who offers even a single flower of the *arka* tree to Śiva shall become a superior man who attains all desires through the difficult path of liberation.
One shall obtain that same fruit which is gained by giving ten pieces of gold:
the *punnāga*, the *campaka*, the *kunda*, the *yūthikā*, and the *navamallikā*.
Tagara, arjuna, mallī, vṛhatī, and śatapatrikā; likewise kumuda, kahlāra, bilva, pāṭala, and mālatī.
Javā, bilva buds, śoka, red and blue lotuses,
damana, and marupatra increase great merit.
The ketakī, atimukta, bandhūka, kumuda, kadamba,
and karṇikāra flowers lead to the attainment of perfected heroes and prosperity.
The *śamī* flower is said to be equal to the flower of *vṛhatī*; the *karavīra*, *jātī*, *vijayā*, and *pāṭalā* are likewise to be known as such.
The white mandāra flower, the white lotus, the vatsaka,
the nāgacaṃpaka, the punnāga, the dhūstūra, and the kasamā bring prosperity.
The man who, filled with love, worships the Goddess with maruvaka flowers,
shall attain supreme good fortune and reach the world of Pārvatī.
Flowers such as the *kanaka* and others should always be offered at night;
all other flowers [should be offered] during the day, and *mallikā* flowers at midnight.
One should worship the Goddess once with unbroken bilva leaves, while standing during the watches of the day and night with jāti and karavīra flowers.
That man who worships the Goddess even once with single datura flowers is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva.
He who worships the Goddess even once with devotion using *vṛhatī* flowers attains the fruit of a hundred thousand cow-gifts and reaches the supreme state.
Having obtained the fruit of ten thousand cows, one shall go to the supreme world of Śiva.
[One should offer] mallikā, utpala, padma, jātī, punnāga, and campaka.
Aśoka, white mandāra, karṇikāra, and bukā;
karavīra, arka, mandāra, śamī, tagara, and keśara.
That man who worships Śivā with these flowers— kuśa, apāmārga, kumuda, kadamba, and droṇaja— even if he possesses only a small amount of wealth, shall obtain his desired goal.
Listen now with a one-pointed mind as to what merit one obtains:
[one travels] in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires and resemble ten million suns.
Encircled by garlands of flowers, with the sounds of singing and musical instruments, and the sweet playing of lutes, they moved at will through the abode of the sky.
Surrounded by Rudra-maidens, difficult for even gods and demons to attain,
he was fanned with yak-tail whisks and praised by both gods and asuras.
He goes to the supreme divine realm, or wherever it may please him;
or with whatever flowers, whether born in water or on land, he has offered here to Śiva.
Having worshipped with devotion using sprinkled *mālatī* flowers, that man who sacrifices with supreme affection goes to the presence of Śiva.
All success arises for one who, like Kuvera at present,
joins auspicious *mālatī* flowers with *kālikā*.

That man who, with supreme devotion, worships the beautiful Kālī— [omitting the missing syllables]— shall undoubtedly obtain incomparable majesty in person; there is no doubt in this matter regarding the attainment of the siddhis.
The man who worships the Goddess with *maruṇa* and *karavīraka* flowers obtains all accomplishments (*siddhi*) without delay; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, that man who worships Sundarī with red oleanders (karavīra) attains perfection within a year; of this there is no doubt.
The gift of one's own caste, the gift of a cow, and likewise the gift of a horse,
do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of the worship of Karavīra.
The man who, filled with devotion, worships Pārvatī with white oleanders (karavīra), his feet will become beautiful; of this there is no doubt.
The prosperity that never departs from the home of that man who worships the beautiful Kālī, the bestower of supernatural powers, with bandhūka flowers.
The man who joyfully worships the Goddess with *vaṃdhūka* flowers finds that Lakṣmī herself takes up residence in his home.
Whosoever worships the Goddess with hibiscus flowers with undivided mind,
by the command of Śrī Śaṅkara, Lakṣmī shall dwell in his home.
That man who worships Bhavānī especially with Java flowers attains incomparable perfection of speech at the end of the year.
That man who worships Śrī Bhavānī with great devotion using pomegranate flowers shall attain supreme and most excellent spiritual perfection.
Whatever man worships Kālī with most beautiful jasmine flowers, success comes under his control; of this there is no doubt.
The man of vast intellect who worships the Goddess with *yūthikā* flowers obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
The man who worships the beautiful goddesses with red lotuses shall attain the supernatural powers that bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Endowed with devotion, he worships the Goddess with white lotuses;
he attains supreme perfection of speech within a year—of this there is no doubt.
The man who, with undistracted mind, worships the Goddess with white lotuses,
becomes the recipient of boons from Śrī Kālī, who is filled with affection for him.
The man who joyfully worships Śrī Kālī with blue lotuses will find that kings become subject to his will; of this there is no doubt.
Of all flowers, the blue lotus is the most excellent;
he who offers a garland made of a thousand blue lotuses [attains great merit].
Listen to the fruit of his merit for having offered [this] to Śivā according to the rules and with devotion:
for thousands of crores of kalpas and hundreds of crores of kalpas.
He shall dwell eternally in the city of Śiva, equal to Śiva in prowess;
O high-minded ones, he shall also perform other meritorious deeds.
One should worship the goddess Śrī Kālī with whatever leaf, fruit, or flower the practitioner finds pleasing, for the sake of attaining the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should offer that very same [flower] with a devout mind to the Goddess by the command of Śaṅkara;
as for the fruit that has been proclaimed for the remaining varieties of flowers, [it shall be obtained].
In accordance with this fruit, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
even items such as kuśa grass that are devoid of fragrance are to be accepted as sacred.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess with flowers, or even with leaves, out of a state of devotion; but in the absence of leaves, one may worship with the fruits and so forth of trees and shrubs.
But if those fruits are not available, one should worship with the fruit of that [tree].
Among leaves, *tulasī* is best, as are the auspicious *bilva* and *āmalaka*.
Maruka, deva-kahlārī, viṣṇukrāntā,
as well as apāmārga, gāndhārī, patrī, and the one known as yuvati.
The leaf of the betel vine (nāgavallī), dūrvā grass, and likewise the kuśa blade are considered suitable;
so too are the leaf of the agasti tree and the holy leaf of the dhātrī.
Among fruits, the āmalaka is best, as are the leaves of the tamarind,
the pomegranate, the citron, the citron-variety (jaṃvīra), and the jackfruit.
One should always worship the Goddess with the leaves, petals, flowers, and fruits produced from plantains, mangoes, and likewise excellent rose-apples (jambū).
Indeed, worship should be performed at night with flowers produced during the month of Vaiśākha;
in the absence of flowers, one should worship with young shoots, but not with buds.
That which is brought for another purpose is defiled, as is that which has already been tasted by another;
likewise, among leaves, the bilva leaf and the very tender sprouts of dūrvā grass [are forbidden].
But in the absence of these, one should always worship with their fruit;
or else with water from the limbs [of the deity], or even with mustard seeds in the absence of that.
If even those are not obtained, one should perform mental devotion;
one should not worship the Goddess with unopened buds, nor should one offer anything that is unripe.
Having recognized that the fruit is pure, the wise should always avoid the *vālaka*, the unripe fruit, the *unmatta*, the *arka* flower, and the *viṣṇukrāntā*.
For Śiva, one should offer kunda, madantī, yūthī, bandhūka, and ketaka;
however, one should never take red sandalwood or red flowers.
One should not worship the Son of Devakī with bilva leaves or its flowers;
nor should one worship Viṣṇu with withered flowers, leaves, or even fruits.
With flowers brought after bathing, or those that have been stale, or those obtained by begging, or black-colored ones,
or those blossomed spontaneously, or those fallen of their own accord upon the earth;
One should avoid the *vṛhatī* flower, especially if it is scentless;
one should never worship with flowers that have fewer than three petals.
One should avoid the kumuda, the pāṭali, and the śirīṣa;
one should also avoid flowers that have fallen to the ground, with the exception of the sephālī and the vakula.
A wise man should not offer to Śivā a flower that has been carried away while wrapped in garments; likewise, buds should be discarded, except for those of the *campaka* and the *padmaka*.
One should avoid red hibiscus at the three junctions of the day, as well as two types of jasmine, ketaki,
saffron, white water-lily, and red oleander.
Guñjā, parājita, unmatta, along with varāhakrāntā and this āmrātaka flower— these are forbidden in the worship of the Sun.
The sun has ordained the prohibition against *tagara*, *kaṇṭakārikā*,
*mandāra*, *arka*, *dhustūra*, *śāla*, *ālī*, *kāñcana*, and *arjuna*.
One should avoid the ketakī, the atiyukta, the kunda, the yūthī, the madantikā, as well as the flowers of the śirīṣa, arka, and bandhūka.
One should avoid the leaves and flowers of the *aṅkola*, the *karañja* produced from the earth, *vibhītaka*, and the flowers of the *dhanvana*.
The *śirīṣa*, the white *puṇḍarīka*,
and the two types of *ketakī* are prohibited for the worship of Viṣṇu and Narasiṃha.

The flowers of the śirīṣa, bandhūka, vibhītaka, madantikā, ketakī, and puṇḍraka, as well as those of the karañja, sarja, and great lordly trees, and the kunda flower— none of these are auspicious for Śivā.

O Lord, worship these flowers—whose faces have been washed within the water, which have naturally withered and dissolved upon the ground; for the two-fold ritual of worship consists of no other actions.
For the worship of Durgā, the mandāra and arka flowers are not recommended;
however, for Mahālakṣmī, tulasī, jhiṇṭhikā, and likewise the kāñcana are suitable.
One should not worship the Sun with *kuṇḍa* flowers, nor Vināyaka with *tulasī*; one should never worship Kamalā with lotuses, nor Śambhu with water from a conch shell.
A flower requested [from someone] is fruitless, and one purchased for a price is likewise fruitless;
it is also fruitless if smelled, touched by the ground, or defiled by worms, insects, and the like.
One should discard stale offerings, with the exception of the excellent bilva, lotus, and tulasī;
there is no fault in water, blue lotuses, or campaka flowers becoming stale.
On *tulasī*, *agastya*, *vakula*, and *bilva* leaves, as well as in the waters of the Gaṅgā,
a floral offering (*nirmālya*)— whether fresh or even stale— is never defiled.
Likewise,
no other things please Hari as much as Tulasī does;
even worms, foodstuffs, broken items, forbidden objects, and what has fallen upon the ground [become pure when touched by it].
O Dear One, one should discard that which is dirty, touched by the ground, defiled by worms, insects, and the like,
touched by the body, smelled, or stale.
O Goddess, one should not worship with flowers that have been stale, even if they are made of gold;
nor, O Supreme Goddess, with flowers that have become *nirmālya* (remnants of an offering) or are defiled by food scraps.
One should avoid all stale offerings, that which is blameworthy, a *tulasī* leaf that has been smelled by another, as well as one that has been stolen, crushed, or trampled.
O Goddess of gods, by smelling flowers, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), or other ritual offerings, a man shall fall into hell.
O Maheśvarī, O Supreme Goddess, one should not worship Mahākālī and Sundarī with flowers or leaves that have been stale.
One should avoid flowers that have been stale for a night, and one should avoid water that has stood overnight;
however, the water of the Ganges is not to be avoided, nor is a leaf of tulasī.
Worship with all flowers, whether prescribed or not, should always be performed for all the gods; here, the yoga of devotion is the cause.
The worship of the Goddess is always praised, whether performed with aquatic or terrestrial flowers, and whether using those prescribed or prohibited, provided the mind is endowed with devotion.
In all *lakṣapūjās*, one should offer flowers;
however, if the worship is performed as a collective assembly, that is not considered the offering of a hundred thousand flowers.
The wise practitioner should offer a flower upon the Śrī-maṇḍala from the source of delusion;
whatever falls upon the ground, no fault exists therein.
Joined with the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā), one should perform the ritual of casting [the seed-syllable] again.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the section on Nirvāṇa within the Dakṣiṇāmnāya of the venerable Vārāhī Tantra.
The Goddess said:
p. 45a) Now, O Mother of the Gaṇas, you have heard all this in its entirety— the essence, the reality, and the conduct— concerning the Lord of the Rasanā, without exception.
And for those who are unfortunate, that [mantra] shall never become their lord or their disciple;
rather, it is for the sake of the cause of good fortune and with the desire for the welfare of men.
Therefore, she is Mahātripurasundarī, who has attained freedom from attachment;
you have clearly indicated something of her mantra, meditation, and so forth.
O Lord, O Master of living beings, please tell me out of compassion how that Goddess is worshipped separately in various temples by people seeking different fortunes.
As is the wheel, so is the worship; as is the limb-worship as it stands, so is the Goddess, the Root-Vidyā, accompanied by her retinue.
Likewise, O God, you have fully explained everything to Śāstra-ve; yet, O Supreme Lord, why has nothing been made manifest to the people?
"Therefore, let that most wonderful thing which reveals it be told.
Having heard this, O Lord of Gods, Pārvatī spoke thus to you.
He replied with these great words for the sake of pacifying all doubts.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret, the supreme heart of the Yoginīs,
which circulates upon the surface of the earth through the transmission from ear to ear.
Having recited this, O lady of excellent hips, one is not oppressed by any obstacles;
such is the mantra of the wheel-convention, as well as the mudrā of the convention.
The Supreme Goddess Tripurā possesses three kinds of conventions; as long as the Lord does not know these three supreme conventions, [he cannot attain liberation].
One who has bowed before Tripurā in the wheel [of the heart] shall become a bearer of the supreme command.
Listen to the secret explanation of the Krama, which has come down through the lineage of succession.
By knowing which, the gurus are never concealed anywhere:
the meaning of the inner essence (bhāvārtha), the meaning of the tradition (saṃpradāyārtha), the meaning of the secret core (nigarbhārtha), and the Kaula meaning.
Likewise, all secret meanings as well as the meaning of the Great Reality (mahātattva) are thus, O Great Goddess;
such is the sixfold nature of the Supreme Goddess.
This has been explained according to the tradition of all the Tantras in the *Lakṣaṇa* [treatise]. Indeed,
the very same essential meaning is found even in the external scriptures.

The meaning of the literal sense, the meaning of the intended sentiment, and the meaning of the traditional lineage— consisting of refined expression, the essence of verbal ornaments, and stylistic composition— are thus declared in the treatises on poetics.
O Gaurī, that which is endowed with the meaning of the essential nature, the meaning of the tradition, and the innermost secret meaning— this threefold [teaching] is explained in the Trika Tantras.
The auspicious [meaning] corresponds to external objects; it resides in the mouth of the Great Guru.
The meaning of the inner state (bhāvārtha), the meaning of the tradition (saṃpradāyārtha), the meaning of the innermost core (nigarbhartha), and the Kaula meaning [are likewise established there].
In the Mahācatuṣka Tantras, it is explained as being fourfold:
the meaning of the essence (bhāvārtha), the meaning of the tradition (saṃpradāyārtha), the meaning of the inner core (nigarbhārtha), and the Kaula meaning (kaulika).
Likewise, O Pārvatī, the meaning of all secrets has been seen here in this Tantra of five forms, in the great ocean of knowledge, and within the six Tantras.
The meaning of the syllables is indeed the meaning of existence, which is the absolute Supreme Goddess;
the oral tradition of great awakening resides in the mouth of the Guru, Ruru.
For the Nigarbha, O Great Goddess, illuminates the meaning through form;
it is free from waves and free from appearances, preceded by the state of conceptualization.
The secret meaning is greatly guarded; the divine meaning is preceded by its abiding state. The secret meaning is greatly guarded; the divine meaning is preceded by its abiding state.
The secret meaning is greatly guarded, established upon the foundation of the divine meaning;
it resides within the treatises on the seats of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) and bestows the perfection of the piṇḍa.
Thus, O Goddess, this supreme Brahman, which is the domain of both direct realization and scriptural tradition,
has been explained by the Lord in fourfold ways according to its various manifestations.
Thus, through this awakening taught by the Great Goddess Mahāsaṃkaṭakāmvikā, one becomes a Lord of the Circle of Heroes (Vīracakreśvara).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme convention of the wheel;
for that purpose, O Goddess, one should construct an excellent mandala measuring three cubits.
One should fashion its pericarp with one-third [of the diameter], marked with the sign of a wheel;
two lotuses with half of that, and the gate-guardians equal to those.
Having first laid down the Brahma-thread at the center of the pericarp, one should lay out the southern and northern threads of equal length; the seventh thread is situated therein.
Then, having omitted the middle portion of the equal sūtra, it is manifested by the intermediate share;
having made the third and fifth shoulders [the base], they are devoid of the final share.
Furthermore, one should increase those [lines] by that same amount in the middle of the path;
and at the two ends of the third and second adyasūtras.
One should extend two lines downward and upward;
there, at the seventh line in the *bhrama* and at the station of Brahmā (*brahmasthāna*), they meet.
From the fifth downward, one should lead three [lines] from that point;
on the first line of the circle, one should place the third [mark].
Two sūtras should be avoided, and one should remain within the six nyatras;
beginning from the fourteen-spoked [wheel] up to the ten-spoked, it is accomplished.
From the second thread, two threads each should be extended horizontally and vertically from both sides of the desired Brahma-thread.
Then, after reaching its extremity, two threads are stretched out;
thus is described this third wheel, which possesses ten spokes.
From the fifth sūtra upwards, one should lead two other sūtras:
one facing upwards and one facing downwards, reaching as far as the two copper-marmas situated in the middle.
One should place the third thread at the mutual junction of those two;
thus, the fourth is the letter *ra*, and the fifth is the letter *ca*.
Thus the wheel is perfectly established, equal and situated within the pericarp;
it consists of the five powers of emanation and the four fires of dissolution.
The emergence of the cakras occurs from the union of the five powers (śaktis) and the four fires (vahnis).
Within that very [system], there is the practice of austerity (kaṣṭakarman), [consisting of] twelve at the end and fourteen [at the beginning].
O Maheśvarī, there are fourteen [places] consisting of ten pairs and eight wheels;
these are the stations of Śakti in successive order according to the yoga of creation and dissolution.
The three cities (Tripura) are situated within the wheel; the mind shall be the support of the wheel.
One should fashion two lotuses on the outside, with eight and sixteen petals respectively.
Then, having made it square, one should provide four doors;
endowed with four corners, this is the supreme maṇḍala.
This [practice] with red menstrual blood is meritorious, while that with white [blood] is purgative;
O Goddess, by the mere sight of this, good fortune arises.
All vidyās perish, and that which is desired is attained;
now, O lady of excellent vows, hear the names of the cakras.
The wheel that deludes the three worlds, as well as that which fulfills all hopes,
O Goddess, the one that agitates everything, and the one that brings about all good fortune.
The wheel accomplishes all aims, is the supreme provider of all protection,
removes all diseases, and likewise consists of all spiritual attainments.
And the ninth [wheel] consists of all-bliss, O beautiful goddess;
it is the perfect Great Wheel that brings about freedom from old age and death.
Thus is this Great Wheel, which brings about freedom from old age and death;
thus is the Supreme Lord perpetually present within this Great Wheel.
The secret convention of mantras that brings about liberation while living was spoken by the goddess Tripurā; now I shall explain it to you with honeyed words.
O heroic hero among immortals, by piercing [the center], one becomes the Lord of the Heroic Wheel;
having first drawn a square, auspiciously measuring twenty-four finger-breadths.
Having first established Īśāna as the western thread and Agni as the eastern thread,
one should fix the eastern thread and then eliminate the remaining three.
The female organ is traditionally said to have three rods;
the wise man, regarding each rod as a staff, should cause six threads to fall for each.
The wombs (yonis) from which all beings are born possess equal joints;
indeed, there are forty-nine compartments, and these take the form of the female organ (bhaga).
Starting from the letter *ai* in the northeast and ending with Vināyaka in the west,
one should place all the Mātṛkās, from Viṣṇu to Śiva, in the western direction.
"Draw a single wheel upon a firm, auspicious wooden base,
triangular and three-legged, marked with the characteristics of the inscribed syllables."
Within six months, one becomes a perfected master (siddha) through worship dedicated to the Supreme Victory;
therefore, O Goddess, listen to how the mantra is to be extracted.
The essence is situated in the middle of the *ojas*, with the golden head and the nectar of the moon;
the seed-syllable is located in the middle of the body, established in the center of the excellent [lotus].
This second [syllable] is said to have the letter *ma* in its middle with a bindu;
it has the letter *va* in its middle, with the letter *ā* situated below, marked by the middle of the letter *sa*.
The first three-syllabled vidyā is known as that which effects the purification of the hands;
it is formed by reversing the order of the two [syllables], indeed without the first seed-syllable.
O slender-waisted one, know that this second [vow] is the rule for the placement within the self (ātmanyāsa);
it consists of the syllable *ṣo*—difficult to perceive—adorned with the nasal bindu (*māyā*).
Today, in the place of Vāgbhava,
she whose form is the supreme self (ātman) has taken up the first letter of both the first and the third [syllables].
The Vidyā situated on the Cakra-seat is to be known as that which is preceded by the middle, the end, and the head-syllable, joined with the six limbs and the weapon.
The one situated on the Mantra-seat is to be known as that which is preceded by the same [syllables] joined with the weapon.
In the reverse position, the two ends are at the top, not as they were in the previous position;
having placed the third [syllable] of the Vidyā at the end of the Kāmabīja according to its location.
The sixty-fold Vidyā, seated upon the Sādhyasiddha posture, has been revealed; having bestowed the three seed-syllables above, they are situated at the end of the excellent half-form.
The first letters of the *gāntastha* (semivowels and sibilants) and the first letters of the *ādyādya* (vowels) constitute the supreme *āvāhana-vidyā*.
Thus, O beautiful goddess, these great *vidyās* have been previously described.
[This is] the deity of the weapons along with the limbs and sub-limbs of Mahātripurasundarī.
Now, therefore, O fair-faced one, I shall fully explain the root-mantra (mūlavidyā).
When this is correctly understood, everything indeed becomes established. Having grasped the middle of *aḥ* and *kha*, make the middle of *aiṃ* the lowest.
In its center, one should place the letter 'A', situated above;
below it, ending with 'Ra'; and from that, ending with 'Ya', joined with the nasal dot (bindu) and the nirodhi.
That which is proclaimed as Vāgbhava begins with the letter *ya*;
one should place the sixth letter of each of the three [groups] at the beginning of each name.
The first part consists of a single syllable ending in *ya*, preceded by the letter *la* and marked with the *āḍa* vowel;
it is not traversed by the *āḍa* in its middle, and is joined with *au* and *aḥ* at its center and head.
O Maheśānī, this Kāmarāja is the revealer of secrets;
by its mere utterance, the agitation of the universe is produced.
I shall now fully declare the third, the most wonderful seed-syllable of Śakti;
it is joined with the base of Vadhū and the beginning of Phāṇṭa, having the nature of Hara.
AḤ: one should extract the seed-syllable of Śakti joined with the back of the letter Ūrddhva (Ū).
By the mere knowledge of this, one shall effect the destruction of all poisons.
This supreme knowledge has been fully explained, which bestows all sovereignty;
when correctly understood through this, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the noose, the goad, the bow, and the arrows,
by the mere application of which the God of gods becomes pleased.
The first pair of letters previously described, with the head not offered at the beginning, is declared to be the two nooses: the Śākta and the Mādana.
The first is joined with the supreme *jaṃbha* and the excellent single *aṅkuśa*;
the second is at the end of the *koṭi-yoni*, ending with the letter *ma*.
Of those [mantras], the first is said to begin with *sa*, and the second with *ca*;
they should be joined to that seed-syllable (*vīja*) in accordance with the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*).
The syllable *pā* below, then *dhonā*, and there *dho* conjoined with *lāṃ*; with the seed-syllables *au* and *aḥ* in the middle, there is the striking upon the head of all.
Those who are endowed with the oral tradition should not be employed for the sake of mere ritual offerings;
thus has been described the supreme five-fold arrow of Kāmadeva.
Having extracted the lower and middle [parts] in two ways, sow [the seed] marked by the middle;
[place] *au* and *aḥ* joined with the back, together with *ka* preceding and joined with the head.
*Gādyaṃ*, *vāṃtaṃ*, and *ca*, with *sorddhasthau* and *ā ī anta* combined;
joined with *kadya*, ending with *vaṣaṃ*, and ending with *khādyaṃ*—these are the deities and the arrows.
Endowed with the traditional transmission, he should employ those seeds;
the seeds previously extracted belong to the group of eight beginning with Vaśinī.
In the worship of the first cakra, the seed-syllables consist of *māyā* (the letter *i*) and *lakṣmī* (the letter *ī*).
For the second [cakra], those same syllables are joined with each of the sixteen vowels individually.
The secret convention of mantras has been declared, which bestows the fruits of all desires;
O Goddess, I shall now also tell you the secret convention of worship.
In the first wheel is Tripurā, in the second is Tripureśvarī;
in the third is the goddess Tripurā, and in the fourth is Tripuravāsinī.
In the fifth [cakra] is Tripurāśrī, in the sixth Tripuramālinī,
in the seventh Tripurāsiddhi, and in the eighth Tripuravikā.
But in the ninth [chapter], O Maheśānī, Mahātripurasundarī is fully described as the root-vidyā that brings the three worlds under her control.
O Pārvatī, thus, by the mere performance of these nine kinds of worship,
the power (śakti) becomes uniform in form and brings about the state of being immortal and free from disease.
Therefore, the symbolic conventions of mantra are established in various forms;
they are obtained through the lineage of various mantra sequences alone.

Then there is the Guptā (Secret), more secret than the Manifest and so forth; another is the Guptodguptatarā (Extremely Secret from the Secret), which has come down through the lineage of tradition; and likewise there is another, the Kulakaulinī.
The Yoginīs of the Great Womb are established in the secret; they are the supreme and the non-supreme.
Established in the three secrets, the Supreme One, the Mistress of the Three Worlds, is to be worshipped.
In the great seats (mahāpīṭha) and secondary seats (upapīṭha), which arise from the mouths of the Yoginīs,
[the teaching] circulates upon the surface of the earth through oral instruction from ear to ear.
Then the manifest Yoginīs appeared in the Cakra that deludes the three worlds,
as did the secret Yoginīs, for the sake of the complete fulfillment of all.
O Goddess, you who cause the agitation of all, who are both hidden and more hidden,
and who bestow all good fortune, you have come down through the lineage of the oral tradition.
The Kulakaulika Yoginīs are in the wheel that accomplishes all aims;
the Nigarbha deities are in the supreme wheel that provides all protection.
O Lord who removes all diseases, there are other secret deities within the wheel consisting of all accomplishments, who abide in the supreme secret.

All the deities, who bestow the fruits of all spiritual accomplishments, abide in that supreme state which consists of universal bliss— the ultimate secret, beyond both the transcendent and the immanent.
There, in the Trailokyamohana-cakra, the Yoginīs are manifest;
O Great Goddess, they are the eight Siddhis, beginning with Aṇimā, who are adorned with eight garlands.
In the same way, the Guptayoginīs, who effect the fulfillment of all [desires],
are proclaimed as the eternal Kalās beginning with Kāmākarṣaṇī and Rūpā.
O Goddess, in the [wheel] that causes the agitation of all, which is both concealed and more concealed,
all [the goddesses] beginning with Anaṅgakusumā are established within the wheel.
In the *Cakrasaubhāgyakāraka*, which has come down through the lineage of oral tradition,
the goddess Surasundarī stands at the forefront as the one who agitates all.
The Yoginīs of Kulakaula are the bestowers of all accomplishments;
they are the foremost givers of all siddhis within the Cakra that accomplishes all aims.
O Great Goddess, praised by heroes, all the deities of the Nigarbha, beginning with Sarvajñā, reside within the supreme wheel that provides all protection.
O Dear One, this secret of the deity removes all diseases;
in the ultimate sense, the great goddesses beginning with Vaśinī are established therein.
In the wheel consisting of all accomplishments, the supreme secret resides;
there abide Kāmeśvarī and the four deities of the seats in the east.
In the wheel consisting of all-bliss, the Great Tripurasundarī— who is full, who consists of all things, and who is the primordial secret of the supreme and the subordinate— abides.
Her nature transcends the world; she is endowed with the ultimate stages of practice; she abides in the state of supreme non-duality; she is the sphere of all that is most excellent.
Having relinquished all things and being free from all dualities,
this supreme worship— abiding in the non-conceptual— effects the destruction of evil.
Established within this great sacrificial feast (*mahāpūjā*) in the mandala of the sixty-four Bhairava-yoginīs, one becomes a subduer through awakening.
One should worship by relying on a single desire for the propitiation of the deity;
one who has renounced all desires shall attain all desires.
O Goddess, if this attainment of all desired fruits through the fulfillment of all wishes were seen by anyone, anywhere, at any time, [then it would be true].
O Goddess, listen as I briefly describe the binding of the mudrās;
both the prāṇa and apāna breaths are restrained and established therein.
Therein, the supreme middle reality arises from the states of existence and non-existence;
one should make that the knower of the middle—this is considered the Khecarī Mudrā.
The form of the Goddess, which consists of all bliss and is beyond the range of words, is established in all scriptures as being grasped by the hand of intuition alone.
He has one face and is deep red in color, seated upon a red lotus throne, and is endowed with four weapons: a noose, a goad, a bow, and an arrow.
The Goddess, in the form of rays, should contemplate the host of pure powers;
beyond that, O lady of excellent complexion, no further meditation exists.
By performing the ritual of worship in this manner, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas),
as well as the fruit of all sacrifices and the fruit of all yogas.
This secret has been declared by you in response to your inquiry; it must never be given to those who are not devoted. What else shall I tell you?
That single Śrī Vidyā, known as Tripurā, possesses manifold forms; through the realization of her essential nature, one proceeds as liberated while living.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Dakṣiṇāmnāya section of the Nirvāṇapada within the Śrī Vārāhī Tantra. || 10 ||
The auspicious Goddess said:
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—
within these five elements throughout all creations, the constellations are dissolved.
The illustrious Śiva said:
First is the unmanifest void; second is smoke itself;
in the third, fire arises; in the fourth, water is produced.
In the fifth [element], earth is born, and the five principles (pañcatattva) come into being;
this is the domain of the five, and the Supreme Lord is composed of the three qualities (triguṇa).
Brahmādharādhipa, Viṣṇujarādhipa,
Teja, Vāyu, Ākāśa, Maheśa, and Vyāvṛtteśvara.
I shall describe the birth and dissolution of these; listen, O Pārvatī.
One should contemplate them through both sequential and reverse orders with a state of pure being.
Earth dissolves into water; water dissolves into fire;
fire dissolves into air; and air dissolves into space.
These five presiding deities give rise to five times five;
O Pārvatī, the all-pervading Brahmāṇḍa should be known as consisting of the five elements.
Impurity, the elements, the channels, nails, and likewise hair—
these are the five qualities of the earth belonging to the deceased, as declared by the Knower through his knowledge.
Desire, anger, greed, dispute, and likewise contention—
these are declared to be the five qualities of worldly existence (āpapañca-guṇa), as spoken by the Knower through his wisdom.
Hunger, thirst, sleep, laziness, and dullness—these are declared to be the five qualities of *tejas*; thus it was spoken by the Knower through his wisdom.
Inhalation, retention, restraint, contraction,
and exhalation— these are described by the knowledge of the wise in terms of the nature of the vital breath (vāyu).
Fear, delusion, as well as shame, passion, and hatred—these are declared to be the five qualities of greed; thus it has been spoken by the knowledge of the wise.
O Goddess, the infinite world-system of the cosmic egg exists according to its sequential enumeration;
I shall declare their ultimate dissolution—listen with all devotion.
One should know that Vitala is at the soles of the two feet,
Sutala is at the region of the ankles, and Tarātala is above that, in the region of the shanks.
Mahātala is in the region of the thighs, Rasātala in the region of the genitals,
and Pātāla is proclaimed as the seventh, located in the cavity of the waist.
One should place the Bhūrloka at the region of the navel, the Bhuvarloka in the belly,
the Svargaloka on the left side, and the Maharloka upon the chest.
The world of Tejas is in the throat, and from there, the world [of Satya] is on the forehead;
Satyaloka is between the eyebrows, containing the fourteen worlds.
Meru shall be situated at the bottom, Mandara in the upper corner,
Kailāsa in the northern corner, and Himālaya in the southern corner.
Mālyavat is on the western boundary, Gandhamādana is on the south, and Niṣadha is on the northern part; these six mountains surround the periphery.
Jambu is situated in the bones, Plakṣa is situated in the marrow; Kuśadvīpa is situated in the flesh, and Krauñcadvīpa is the blood.
Śālmaladvīpa is in the marrow, and the collection of hair is Sālmalī;
Puṣkaradvīpa is in the nails—thus the seven islands are proclaimed.
Likewise, salt water is in urine; the ocean of milk is at the summit of the ocean of milk; wine is in curdled milk; and the ocean of spirituous liquor is in whey.
In the Śukra [ocean] there is the Sarpir-sāgara, and therein also the Jala-sāgara;
in the Śleṣmā [ocean] there is the Dadhi-sāgara—these seven oceans are thus proclaimed.
The Sun is situated in the place of the navel, and the Moon is in the place of vital energy;
Mars is said to be in the eyes, and Mercury is established in the heart.
One should know Jupiter to be in the region of the navel; Venus is situated in the semen.
Saturn is stationed in the region of the navel, and Rahu is situated in the mouth.
Rāhu is situated at the head and Ketu in the body within the circle of planets;
together with thirty-five million others, he is said to reside in the body as Śeṣa.
One should clearly visualize the ninefold fever with a pure disposition:
the linga of molasses, the eyes, the mouth, the ears, and the nose.
These nine apertures are called the nine gates.
The Goddess said:
Where should one meditate on the moon, or where should one meditate on the sun? Or in what place, O God of gods, should one meditate on the mind? Tell me this.
Śiva said:
The Moon resides at the root of the palate, and the Sun at the root of the navel;
the Fire dwells in your breath, and the Mind dwells in the Moon.
The Goddess said:
How is the vital breath produced? How is the mind produced?
Tell me all of this: how is speech produced?
Śiva said:
From the unmanifest arise the vital breaths; from the vital breath arises the mind;
and from the mind arise all modifications and all speech through all the elements.
The Goddess said:
Who performs actions, or who is stained by sins?
Tell me that, O Mahādeva, O omniscient Supreme Lord.
Śiva said:
The mind performs actions; the mind is smeared by sins. But when the mind itself becomes liberated, it is no longer stained by either merit or demerit.
The Goddess said:
In what place does Śakti reside? In what place does Śiva reside?
In what place does Kāla reside? By what is water produced?
The illustrious Śiva said:
Śakti resides in the Ādhāra; Śiva resides in the place of Nāda.
Kālī should be known as all-pervading; she is the moving consciousness and becomes like water.
The Goddess said:
Speech, movement, sleep, and the throat of the vital breath (prāṇa),
as well as hunger, thirst, and virility— from what do these ten arise?
The illustrious Śiva said:
And the wind alone is perceived through its subtle modification;
when one's state of being becomes composed of that, one is liberated from it at that very moment.
The illustrious Goddess said:
O God, how are Śiva and Śakti? And what is the nature of the ten vital winds? What is the supreme deity like? O God of gods, please explain this to me.
The illustrious Śiva said:
Śiva, Śakti, and Vāyu—indeed, everything exists according to this sequence.
O Goddess, listen as I tell you the cause; I shall explain it to you.
The wind situated in the heart is prāṇa; apāna is said to be heavy. Samāna is in the region of the navel, while udāna is said to be in the throat.
O Goddess, vyāna is omnipresent and arises from the fivefold movement of prāṇa;
thus, prāṇa is established within the body in these five modes.
Nāga, Kūrma, Devadatta, Dhanañjaya,
and Udāna— these five winds are known through their sequential application.
The *nāga* wind produces consciousness in all embodied beings,
and by the application of the *kūrma* wind, the blinking of the eyes occurs.
The *kḷika*-wind, when hunger arises, is Devadatta; it extends infinitely.
O Dhanañjaya, with sound, it fills all embodied beings.
When the serpent (Nāga) and the wind (Vāyu) are in the house together with the tortoise (Kūrma) and the intellect (Matin),
Devadatta goes forth and performs his actions.
The quality of the intellect (buddhi-dharma) is said to be the tenth [type of perception], which is immediate, free from all delay, and characterized by non-erroneousness.
The reality situated at the remaining door is obtained through the word of the Guru;
it is the form of Kuṇḍalinī Śakti, consisting of thirteen channels (nāḍīs).
It is known for certain that there are seventy-two [channels] in the body of Śrī;
among them, the thirteenth channel is the most principal.
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, as well as Suṣumnā, the upward-tending channel;
Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā, and likewise Puṣā and Prāṇalatā.
Yasā and Alambuṣā are suspended on the path of the right (dakṣamārga),
while Kuraṅgī, Śaṅkhinī, and Nityā are suspended on the path of the left (vāmamārga).
O Goddess of Knowledge, that yogi by whom these are pierced possesses the defining characteristic of yoga; he becomes equal to me—of this there is no doubt.
The Goddess said:
O Bhūtanātha, O Mahādeva, O Supreme Lord, tell me:
how are the three gods designated as "three," and what is the nature of these three states?
Śiva said:
Brahmā abides in the state of rajas, Hari abides in the state of sattva, and Rudra abides in the state of tamas; these are the three gods and the three qualities.
Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha are three deities who are one single form;
for him whose mind possesses various dispositions, liberation is not found.
I am the Veda, I am the ego, I am the omnipresent Śiva;
I am Brahmā, I am Viṣṇu, I am the void, the stainless.
The Goddess said:
O Omniscient One, Lord of all beings and Great Sovereign of all worlds,
you have spoken; O God, how is one a mother, and how is one a father?
Śiva said:
The nine gates are directly perceived; there are the three voids, the five deities, the five sense organs, and the vital breaths, where the house is situated.
The four Vedas and likewise all the scriptures are like buttermilk;
the wise drink that which has been extracted as the essence by the yogis.
All scriptures and all branches of knowledge are but remnants left behind at every turn;
O Brahmin, the knowledge of Brahman—which consists of the manifest and the unmanifest and is composed of mind—is not a remnant.
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord, O Śaṅkara, as for that which was told by you, I shall certainly not go;
tell me, O Lord, where my mind may find dissolution."
Śiva said:
O Goddess, listen with certainty: where mind, action, and speech are all dissolved, there resides the Supreme Power.
One who is like sleep without dreaming is called a knower of Brahman;
one who knows the sky within his own body is like a bird moving through the path of the sky.
Likewise, one who offers everything through the sequence of the five elements as being identical with the Self—
he who possesses the sleep of the deceased is called a knower of Brahman.
O bird, as is the true nature of a child, so is yoga in liberation;
he who is concentrated upon this knowledge of Brahman is the Supreme Self.
The union of Śiva and Śakti is like the meeting of a hundred suns;
even a single instance of knowledge of Brahman there brings peace to the mind without anxiety.
This knowledge has been told to you in its true essence, O Knower of Brahman;
and this is the complete satisfaction wherein the mind is free from anxiety.
Those yogins who do not know the six wheels, the sixteen supports, the three tufts of hair, and that cycle within their own bodies— how can they meditate?
Having made space his seat and having known the mind with perfect certainty, he sees all this as "I am thus" through his accomplishment; he beholds bliss.
In Kāśī, there is attachment for living beings; the water of the Gaṅgā is the worship of Śambhu.
No other dharma is ordained that is equal to the knowledge of Brahman.
Now, O beloved of my life, hear the *āhlādinī* mantra,
by the mere utterance of which Kālikā becomes well-pleased.
One should extract the five seed-syllables: the seed of desire (KĀM), the seed of the tongue (KŪRC), the seed of fatness (MEDYA), followed by the temple (PRĀSĀDA), and the seed of sound (RĀVA).
One should recite the mantra seven times, with the seed-syllable enclosed within five layers;
when this is done, O Maheśānī, the unsurpassed perfection of the mantra is attained.
O Goddess, one should not recite the Kullukā, nor the Nirvāṇa, nor the Setuka;
for the accomplishment of the mantra arises through the recitation of a single mantra alone.
O beloved, if one worships Kālī without knowing the Hlādinī mantra, everything becomes fruitless; such is the word of Bhairava.
Indistinctly and sweetly humming like a cricket, constantly rising and moving through the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), it enters its own abode.
Then, by means of the very process of going and returning, one should effect the dissolution of the mind;
O Goddess, one should meditate on the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) in the beautiful Mūlādhāra.
One should meditate on Khecarī in the heart and Sākinī above the head;
by that, the Śikhā-mantra becomes the illuminator of all mantras.
Salutation! Just as nothing at all is articulated in a house where the full [vowels] are absent,
so too mantras devoid of the *śikhā* (crest-syllable) never attain success.
O Queen of the Gods, this instruction on the Śikhā is concealed in all the Tantras;
its body is pervaded by the fifty distinct letters.
May this Mātṛkā, the mother of the universe, serve to clarify my speech;
having consulted the *Varṇanighaṇṭu* and extracted [the material] from other Āgamas.
The venerable Vināyaka composed this exposition of the phonemes, protected by his own wisdom.
The syllable Oṃ is eternal, transcendent, consisting of three morae, circular, and threefold;
it is the beginning of the Vedas, the Praṇava, possessing five deities and three gods.
The initial seed-syllable is the power of the bindu; it is the first mantra and the seed of the qualities.
Sāvitrī is in the middle, and the other is the quality at the beginning; such is the established order.
Oṃ.
AḤ is Keśava, Śrīkaṇṭha, Viṣṇu, and the primordial vowel;
he is declared to be Pūrṇodarī, and he is likewise celebrated as Kīrti.
The first of the letters (A) is born from the beginning; the short vowel (A) is the Lord of the Gods (Indra).
The first of the vowels (A) is Brahmā; Vāgīśvara (the Lord of Speech) is Kāla (Time), born from the forehead.
The first is Nivṛtti, named Mālā, born from the forehead of Sarasvatī.
A.
The infinite one, the self-established, the soul of the universe, the leader of the mute;
Nārāyaṇa, whose course is through the mouth, the ordainer of long shadows.
The second vowel is *ā*, born from water, and it is long;
it is milk, curd, and water, and it is considered to be like a diamond, possessing luster and weight.
I is Sūkṣma, Mādhava, Candra, Dakṣanetra, and Suguhyaka;
the one called Netra is Koṭara, Vidya, and the nose of the third vowel.
The letter *i* is Śālmalī, and Tvaṣṭṛ is Rudra, the right eye.
The fourth vowel is Śānti, Trimūrti, and Bindumālinī;
Māyā, Govinda, and the letter Ī belong to Vāmana and Caṇḍaśekhara.
Śakti is Viṣṇu, Lolākṣī is known by the name Tuṣṭi,
and Vāgviśuddha is remembered as a synonym for the name Lakṣmī.
Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Immortals, the one whose ears are terrifying to his enemies,
Dakṣakarṇa, Karṇadakṣa, and the letter *U*, which is the fifth vowel.
Vartulākṣī, Ṣaḍvaktra, Indhikā, Mohinī,
Dhṛti, Ugra, Śruti, Srava, Srota, Mohaka, and Mohana.
U.
Ūkānti, Vāmakarṇākhya, Arghī, Madhusūdana, the sixth vowel (ū), likewise Ukāra, Prajeśa, and Navabhairava.
Dīpikā, Dīrghaghoṇā, Śūdra, and Savyaśravas.
Ṛbhārabhūti, Bhīru, Dakṣanāsā, Trivikrama, Hriyā, Nirvṛtti, and the one named Nāsā— these are the letter Ṛ, the seventh vowel.
Śiromālā, Dīrghamukhī, Recikā, Rudra, and Ekapād.
Ṛtithīśa is Gomukhī, while Vāmana is Vāmanāsikā;
Māyāgni is Ūrdhvamūrti, and he who is named Vāmanāsāpuṭa is [the deity] Sthira.

The letter Ḷ is Śrīdhara; the letter Ļ is Dīrghajihva; the letter E is Asthūla; the letter AI is Medhā; the letter O is Pārthiva; the letter AU is Dakṣagaṇḍa; the letter AṂ is Māsa; and the letter AḤ is Arka, the ninth vowel.

Chapter 9: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī’s Questions Regarding the Profound Meaning of the Dharma and the Attainment of the Seal of Non-arising. Part One. The Great Vehicle Sutra of the Flower Adornment, Volume 57. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śikṣānanda of the Great Tang. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, having heard the Buddha’s teaching on the profound meaning of the Dharma, rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying: “World-Honored One, what is the name of this dharma-gate? How should one uphold it? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “This dharma-gate is named ‘The Seal of Non-arising. You should uphold it by this name. Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, what is the meaning of ‘non-arising’? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “It means that all dharmas are ultimately unarisen; they do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from others, nor do they arise from both, nor do they arise without cause. They are neither produced nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Because they are thus, they are called non-arising. Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if all dharmas are ultimately unarisen, how can there be the distinctions of the three vehicles—namely, the śrāvaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the buddha vehicle? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “All dharmas are indeed ultimately unarisen. Why? Because the nature of all dharmas is eternally quiescent and originally unborn. However, because sentient beings give rise to various afflictions, they perceive differences among dharmas. If one can sever these afflictions, then all dharmas are equal and without distinction. It is like the great ocean: although it contains immeasurable waters, they are all of one taste. So too is the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas: although it manifests various teachings according to the capacities of sentient beings, its ultimate essence is one and the same. Therefore, Mañjuśrī, you should know that all dharmas are ultimately unarisen. Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if all dharmas are ultimately unarisen, why do sentient beings still experience birth and death? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “Sentient beings are deluded regarding the nature of dharmas, giving rise to false thoughts and attachments. Because of these false thoughts and attachments, they undergo birth and death. If one can realize the true nature of dharmas, there will be no birth or death. Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if all dharmas are ultimately unarisen, how can there be the distinctions of good and evil karma, and the retributions of suffering and pleasure? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “These are all manifestations of the mind. Because the mind gives rise to delusion, it perceives the distinctions of good and evil. If one realizes that the nature of the mind is fundamentally empty and unarisen, then there will be no karma or retribution. Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen, how can there be the distinctions of the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “All these are merely provisional names established by the mind. If one examines their true nature, they are all unarisen and empty. It is like a magician who conjures illusions; though many forms appear, they have no real substance. So too are the aggregates, bases, and elements: though they manifest before us, they are ultimately unarisen. Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if all dharmas are ultimately unarisen, why do sentient beings still seek liberation and cultivate the path? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “Because sentient beings are bound by ignorance and craving, they falsely conceive of self and phenomena. To break through these bonds, they seek liberation and cultivate the path. Once they realize that there is no self and no phenomena, they attain liberation. It is like a person dreaming of being imprisoned; upon waking, they find there was never any prison. So too is the path of liberation: it is established only for those in bondage, but in the ultimate truth, there is neither bondage nor liberation. Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if all dharmas are ultimately unarisen, how can there be the distinctions of the three realms of existence? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “The three realms are all produced by the mind. Because the mind gives rise to deluded thoughts, it manifests the three realms. If one realizes that the nature of the mind is fundamentally empty and unarisen, then the three realms are also unarisen. It is like a person in a feverish dream who sees mountains, rivers, and lands; though they appear vast, they are all produced by the heat of the fever. So too are the three realms: they are all manifested by the delusions of the mind. Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if all dharmas are ultimately unarisen, how can there be the distinctions of the six sense organs and their objects? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “The six organs and their objects are all like illusions. Because of past habits and conditions, they manifest before us. If one realizes that their nature is fundamentally empty and unarisen, then there will be no organs or objects. It is like a person with cataracts seeing flowers in the sky; though they appear, they have no reality. So too are the organs and objects: they are all produced by the delusions of ignorance. Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if all dharmas are ultimately unarisen, how can there be the distinctions of the four noble truths? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “The four noble truths are established only for the sake of those who are deluded. If one realizes the true nature of dharmas, there are no truths. It is like a person with a headache who perceives the world as spinning; once the headache is cured, the world is no longer spinning. So too are the four truths: they are medicines for the delusions of sentient beings, but in the ultimate truth, there are no truths. Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if all dharmas are ultimately unarisen, how can there be the distinctions of the ten stages of a bodhisattva? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “The ten stages are all expedient teachings. Because sentient beings have various capacities and roots, the Buddhas establish these stages to guide them. If one realizes that the nature of the stages is fundamentally unarisen, then there are no stages. It is like a traveler who sees a mountain range and sets up milestones to mark the way; though the milestones are distinct, the mountain itself has no beginning or end. So too are the ten stages: they are markers for the path of practice, but in the ultimate truth, there are no stages. Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if all dharmas are ultimately unarisen, how can there be the distinctions of the three bodies of a Buddha? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “The three bodies are all manifestations of the Dharma-body. Because sentient beings have different perceptions, the Buddha manifests three bodies. If one realizes that the Dharma-body is fundamentally unarisen, then there are no three bodies. It is like the moon reflected in water: though there are many moons, they are all one moon. So too are the three bodies: though they appear differently, they are all the one Dharma-body. Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if all dharmas are ultimately unarisen, how can there be the distinctions of the various vehicles and the paths of practice? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “All vehicles and paths are established based on the mind. Because the mind gives rise to various thoughts, it manifests various paths. If one realizes that the nature of the mind is fundamentally empty and unarisen, then there will be no vehicles or paths. It is like a painter who paints various figures; though the figures are distinct, they are all produced by the brush and ink. So too are the vehicles and paths: they are all painted by the mind. Mañjuśrī said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if all dharmas are ultimately unarisen, how can there be the distinctions of the various heavens and hells? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “Heaven and hell are all produced by the mind. Because of good and evil karma, one experiences various realms. Bhairava said:
Now I shall describe meditation; listen, O lotus-eyed one!
[Visualize her] resembling the fire of universal destruction, with a form as red as vermilion.
Her complexion was like that of a pomegranate flower or a dark bandhūka blossom;
her limbs were bound together by skin and bone, and she was equipped with the organs of a serpent.
The Supreme Goddess has beautiful eyes, is endowed with three eyes, is adorned with all ornaments,
possesses six arms, and is mounted upon a bull.
Wearing a mass of matted hair, fierce, with the crescent moon as her crest-ornament,
she is endowed with a skull and a chisel, and holds a sword and a shield.
The goddess, holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, bestows the fruit of all spiritual accomplishments;
she has large breasts, is most formidable, possesses fangs, and has a wide-open mouth.
Clad in human skin and adorned with ornaments of bone,
she wears divine garments and bestows all sovereignty.
The goddess Trailokyavijayā is eternally the Mistress of the Kula;
when she is conceived as having eight arms, she should be depicted holding a noose and a goad.
Then one should meditate upon the Goddess Maheśvarī, the deity of deities, who was previously described as being engaged in battle,
possessing three eyes and having the moon as her crest-ornament.
A lotus in the right hand and a rosary in the left;
by the grace of this mantra, even a woman shall then be brought under one's control.
Resembling the fire of cosmic destruction at the end of an eon, intent on devouring the entire universe,
she has fashioned her wings like those of Garuda and wears a great serpent as her crest-ornament.
It resounded with the terrible cries of jackals and vultures, it cast a long-reaching shadow,
it had a vulture upon its banner, it was inhabited by spirits, and it was surrounded by the tracks of cattle.
One should contemplate the entire [weapon] as having its mouth filled with human missiles, possessing a luster joined with millions of sparks, and having the faces of lions and boars at both ends.
Her own sister, with eyes like hollows, who was not terrifying even in her fear,
resembling the throat of Śiva, dark as a swarm of black bees and warbling like a cuckoo.
She has long hair, long fangs, and long intestines;
she is well-born and disciplined, possessing eighteen formidable arms, five faces, and a great roar.
One should contemplate her as bearing all weapons, radiant, and possessing a universal form;
she holds a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and is adorned with human skulls.
The fierce Raudrī holds a heart and a vajra; she has fangs, long entrails hanging from her, eighteen formidable arms, five faces, and a great roar.
One should meditate upon her as bearing all weapons, blazing, and possessing a universal form;
she holds a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and is adorned with human skulls.
Hṛdā is Vajradharā, Raudrī is raised with a sword and a cloth-belt,
Tuṃburī is devoted to playing musical instruments, and Kara is raised with an elephant hide.
Having meditated upon her as terrifying with the sounds of *śūla* and *ṭaṅkāra*, and having performed the ritual actions, one should destroy [the obstacles].
Having meditated thus, one should install the slender-waisted Goddess of gods in the center.
Thereafter, one should worship her with all heroic offerings—
she who possesses five faces and great splendor, blazing with fifteen eyes.
Ten-armed and most formidable, adorned with various garlands and wreaths,
endowed with diverse jewels, and decorated with necklaces and armlets.
Wearing a divine mass of matted hair, with the moon as his crest-jewel,
he is divine, white as cow’s milk, with a luster like foam and pure white radiance.
O Dear One, by means of which the twilight at the eastern face possesses supreme great radiance,
having the appearance of a pomegranate flower and resembling the bandhūka blossom.
One should meditate upon him who resembles the rising sun, with a beautiful face,
possessing a yellow luster, appearing like turmeric, having the hue of saffron, and being three-eyed.
O beautiful one, that divine [face] on the western side produces great radiance;
it is fierce with terrible fangs and appears somewhat terrifying for a moment.
Dark blue, resembling the color of a cloud, with a luster like black collyrium;
adorned with a crest made of jewels and snakes, with tawny hair, and most terrifying.
This meditation, renowned as Ayyorām, bestows the accomplishment of all goals;
it is the face of the Lord upon the head, the form of creation, both supreme and non-supreme.
Resembling a snow-white lotus or the moon, as pure and stainless as clear crystal,
he nourishes the entire world with his lunar rays.
One who contemplates Īśāna’s face on the head, which pours forth a great flood of streams resembling nectar, shall obtain the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*.
O lady of excellent hips, the trident, the curved knife, the sword, the serpent-king, and the rosary shine as my weapons in my right hand.
Holding a skull-cup, a hand-drum, a spear, and a noose with a goad in her hands, she stands upon a corpse;
with a nose on the left, she shines brilliantly and is most beautiful.
[He holds] a mirror, a serpent-noose, the seed-syllable Śrīṃ, and a citron.
In her left hand she brandishes a weapon, adorned with a garland of rubies that destroys enemies; in her right hand, held like a knife, is a branch of the Pārijāta creeper standing amidst heroes.
O Lord, your speech is beautiful with ornaments, refined by camphor, effective for the practitioner,
possessing fifty petals and ten hands, and resembling a necklace of camphor.
Śiva, whose broad cheeks were rubbed by his earrings and who wore a serpent as a sacred thread.

With a mind desiring liberation, one should meditate upon the God who has been established in the fifteenth [digit], whose form is all-knowing, whose branches are fully understood, and who is the Lord of the lineage of noble women.
The Great Goddess has a form resembling blue collyrium, possesses two arms, and is the mistress of the eyes; she has one face, three eyes, and the moon as her crest-jewel.
This [form] has been described as gross, consisting of all its constituent parts;
O Great Goddess, I shall now describe its subtle form to you.
The yogi, seated in the lotus posture, with body steady, pure, and properly clad,
having performed the sixteen nyāsas and recollected the sandals of the venerable guru;
The coiled power (Kuṇḍalinī-śakti), whose nature is subtle and whose intellect is withdrawn,
is like a sleeping serpent, bearing the knowledge of the Khaṭvāṅga and the Vaidinī.
Having brought her there by means of the root mantra, through breath-retention (kuṃbhaka), and meditative absorption (samādhi),
she was united with Śiva while staying in the midst of a kadamba forest.
One should contemplate the body of the Goddess as pervaded by a mass of its petals;
O Goddess, with a serene mind, one should not conceptualize anything at all.
I am Bhairavāsana in form; one should contemplate the void-like state of the earth and meditate upon the Great Goddess Kuṇḍalinī, who consists of a single syllable.
The goddess Sarvarūpadharā possesses a universal form and is most brilliantly radiant;
she sits upon five corpses, is ablaze with light, and is graced by the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The goddess who assumes the form of a woman is adorned with various weapons;
she has a vajra face, many arms, many forms, and a great roar.
O Maheśānī, one should meditate upon her who possesses a universal form, with dark, curly hair,
whose appearance fulfills all desires according to one's prosperity, and who resembles Mahālakṣmī.
Resembling a mass of cool moonlight, she has five faces and three eyes;
she is endowed with ten mighty arms, with various weapons raised in her hands.
One should remember that goddess with blood-red, slightly crimson eyes, the bestower of all happiness.
