Mounted upon a lotus-pretā, resembling a crystal gem, five-faced and three-eyed, she gladdens the three worlds; worship her, whose limbs are draped in divine garments and who is surrounded by ten attendants.

May Siddhilakṣmī purify [us]— she who carries in her left hands a skull-cup, a trident, a noose, and a severed head, and who is honored by holding a bell, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a sword, a lotus, and a goad.
In all the ritual sequences, she is common to all: the three-faced, nine-eyed, exceedingly secret Mahākālī, who possesses eight arms and the nine-syllable mantra.
One should meditate on the goddess whose right face is yellow and whose left face is all-black;
she wears a red upper garment and is adorned with all ornaments.
In his right hands, he holds a trident, a goad, and a mallet;
in his left hands, a skull-cup, a noose, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and the head of a corpse.
Bearing the form of the Sovereign of the King of Steps, she resembles a thousand suns;
situated in the center, she consists of the sixty-four [squares], while the eighty-one squares are extracted from her.

One should meditate upon Bhairava, who is the form of light situated in the center of Kula as the digit of consciousness (citkalā), holding the bindu of the letter Ka in his hand; when one meditates thus, that [state] arises.
Then the goddess Sthūlanarā, wearing a garland of a thousand syllables, mounted upon ten corpses as her vehicle, and possessing a radiant form and hands adorned with bracelets.
She possesses a thousand faces and eyes, shines with a thousand arms,
has a thousand [heads] beginning with ten necks, and is covered by a thousand feet.
Holding a thousand weapons in her left hand, she is the liberator from great sins;
she has been practiced for a thousand kalpas and devours a thousand Yamas.
She resembles the *kākolī* and *gṛdhraśṛṅgālī* herbs, as well as the autumnal sky;
one should meditate upon her, whose face is the dissolution of Bhaṭṭa, who devours the entire cosmic manifestation.
Resounding with terrifying roars, the sound *hūṃ*, and the cry of *saṃ*,
she thunders like a mass of clouds at the dissolution of the world, her voice intent upon the falling of thunderbolts.

In an instant, O Bhairavī, the fierce fire of the *kalpa* burnt away the moon, sun, and stars from before her; with a terrifying radiance, she was filled with masses of flames that appeared like the very embodiment of sin.
The Yakṣiṇī Taṭāvaṭā, who casts a thousand glances, has been described;
she possesses ten red [eyes], her lips are parched, and she is like the fire at the end of an aeon.

With eyes like the fire at the end of an aeon, she was most terrifying, resembling the conflagration that consumes the universe; for a moment, she held in her hand a skull-bowl filled with the blood of those who had offered oblations during the dissolution of the world.
The Indra-Brahmā pavilion,
with its expansive ramparts of lion-claws, is adorned with the lotuses of the heads of the world-protectors and blazes with the planets.
O highly fortunate one with the wings of a Garuda, she has a skull as her crest-ornament;
she is adorned by a garland of skulls held upon her head by the hundred Rudras.
She is the sprout of Brahman, black, holding a skull and the staff of death;
she possesses bells upon her hands, is the cause of all, resplendent with the single fold of skin produced by her own deeds.
Her body is smeared with blood from the intense crushing of the universe;
she is terrifying with a wide-open mouth and the sound of her laughter like a thunderbolt.
The pavilion of the cosmic egg was shattered by the impact of the vast multitude;
its great banks and hollows were strewn with the scattered blossoms from the expansive garlands of the Brahmāṇḍa-Śakra.
O Sadāśiva, she has a girdle of bones around her hips that is most formidable;
its touch is like a diamond needle, and it is radiant with folds and lines.
It was filled with *lakṣa* trees and inhabited by those dwelling in the scorched forest;
its hair was as rough to the touch as the fierce strike of a thunderbolt or a sharp thorn.
She belongs to a family of great enjoyments, yet she is terrible; she wears the sacred thread, is the destroyer of all, the command of all, initiated, and has the face of Bhairava.
She is naked, with her body blazing like a conflagration at the end of an eon,
and she is adorned with a vajra, a bell, and other implements, while her hands are beautified by a fierce, original khaṭvāṅga.
Holding a chisel, a bow, a bull’s horn, a spear, and a javelin,
she has terrified everyone here with the fierce sound of her great drum.
She protects the skull-lotus, her hand adorned with a severed head;
she wields a terrible lute, a javelin, and an axe as her great weapons.
She who brings down the bow of the Time that destroys the entire universe, and whose soles of the feet are worshipped by ten million Rudras of the Fire of Time; p. 62a) [she is the Goddess].
The multitude of jars [of the worlds] was shattered by the flood of water from all the births,
while the terrifying and formidable *ṭaṃkāra* sound destroyed the entire continuity of the paths.
She who has made Nṛsiṃha and Bhairava her beloved ear-ornaments,
and whose hair is adorned by a multitude of a hundred thousand suns and severed heads.
O Mahāmaṅgala, perform that task for the great king:
[assume] a form that is withered, devoid of flesh, terrible in appearance, and fearsome.
The seat was a mass of splendor, with the brilliance arising from the bursting cloth;
it filled the faces of all directions with a multitude of rows of shattered silk bands.
Having become a lion, a boar, a rhinoceros, a snake, a tiger, a man,
a forest-dweller, a bear, a wolf, a lion, and one with the face of a horse or a boar.
With its reality established by the terrifying flames arising from the mouth-cavity, it is filled with human-eaters, crows, owls, great vultures, cats, and jackals.
One should meditate upon the Goddess of the Ritual, who is exalted like Mount Meru, amidst a mass of arrows and a fire falling from the peak,
who is the universal form and consists of the universe.
The lover of Saramā should meditate upon her who possesses a form according to his desire and vehicles according to his wish, she who bestows the fruit of all desires.
The solitary heroine, the great leader, dancing upon a white seat—
eight-faced, O Great God, red-colored and most terrifying.
With his body richly embraced by the Goddess, Śiva is just as the Goddess is;
thus has this supreme meditation been described, according to its gross and subtle divisions.
Through this meditation, one attains all desires; there is nothing higher than this. What else do you ask concerning this universal equality?
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with fleshless,
sinew-bound limbs, with hair standing erect, terrifying at the waist, and bearing a sword and a shield.
The Lord is adorned with a khaṭvāṅga, a ḍamaru, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons; the Goddess holds a noose, a goad, a boon-granting gesture, and an excellent trident and bell.
The Great Goddess holds a skull-bowl in her hand, beautifully adorned with a mace and a discus;
she holds a vajra in her hand and is graced by a severed head.
The goddess holds a sugarcane bow and is adorned with ornaments of serpents;
she is clothed in human skin and stands upon a tiger skin at her waist.
Wearing a garland of severed heads, she is fierce and adorned with every ornament;
her face is formidable with protruding fangs, and she is terrifying with her lolling tongue.

I shall describe the meditations on the Intermediate Goddesses; by remembering them, one attains the state of Śiva. [One should visualize her] with a formidable face, terrible, with disheveled hair, and four-armed.
Kālikā is divine, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
and holds in her lower left lotus-hand a sword with a freshly severed head.
Her right hands display the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons;
she possesses the luster of a great cloud, is dark-complexioned, and likewise wears only the directions as her garment.
The circle of shaven-headed ascetics was drenched at their throats and smeared with trickling blood;
it was terrifying, made so by pairs of corpses fashioned into their ear-ornaments.
With terrible, formidable fangs, and full, uplifted breasts,
she had a girdle fashioned from heaps of corpses and possessed many mouths.
Her face was made radiant by streams of blood trickling from her two corners of the mouth;
she possessed a terrible roar, was exceedingly fierce, and dwelt in the abode of the charnel ground.

I bow to her whose three eyes are as radiant as ten thousand rising suns, whose face shines with a gentle smile, who bears the crescent moon, who is adorned with clusters of beautiful rows of flowers,
who wears a musk tilaka, whose heavy breasts are anointed with sandalwood paste, and who holds a noose, a goad, a lotus, and a bow.
I worship her who holds a flower-arrowed bow in her lotus-like hands.
Having the luster of a bandhūka flower, with three eyes, and adorned with a crescent moon as her crest-jewel;
holding a jewel-vessel in her left hand, and a lotus in her right, with her breasts uplifted.
Seated upon a corpse on the pericarp of a red lotus,
she has a garland of severed heads around her neck, is blue in luster, and holds [implements] with her hands.
She holds the gesture of fearlessness, a pestle, and likewise a choice fruit;
she has the face of a boar, is exceedingly beautiful, possesses three eyes, and is of a most excellent ruddy hue.
Then one should meditate upon her who is dark as a rain-cloud, three-eyed, with uplifted breasts,
having the face of a boar, with the moon upon her brow, and supporting the earth with her tusks.
She holds a sword and two blades of kuśa grass in her right hands, and a shield and a noose in her left;
she is mounted upon a horse, has the face of a boar, and is adorned with various ornaments.
With flaming hair and faces, possessing fearsome fangs and terrifying forms,
these deities born from the sense-faculties are said to have their gaze directed upwards.
The deities arising from the feet of Bhūta are proclaimed to have faces turned sideways;
I shall now describe their meditation as they abide within a nest of various jewels.
A wish-fulfilling tree made of gold stood upon a floor of jeweled pavement;
beneath it, she sat upon a lion throne composed of gems.
Seated upon a white lotus, adorned with jeweled earrings,
and endowed with armlets, necklaces, a crown, a girdle, and anklets.
She holds with her sprout-like hands two lotuses, a noose, a goad,
a bow of sugarcane, and the arrow of flowers, as well as the gesture of fearlessness.
She was golden-hued, surrounded by seven youthful female messengers,
who held mirrors, betel leaves, and other items in their hands.

Beholding the practitioner with a gracious gaze, one should meditate [on her] as having hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, holding a rosary of beads and a lotus, and resembling the bandhūka flower in color.
She has a peacock as her banner, stands upon a *udumbara* tree, wears garments with the luster of red cloth,
is clad in a green bodice, and is adorned with various ornaments.
Five-faced and most fierce, with three eyes in each face,
she holds a spear, a trident, a bow, an arrow, a shield, a sword, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The goddess, adorned with ornaments of serpents,
seated upon a corpse, and decorated with snakes, holds in her right hands a curved knife and a skull-cup.
One should worship Nīlavārāhikā, who holds a bell and a trident in her four hands, wears a garland of severed heads, and possesses three eyes.
Seated in the lotus posture, ruddy in hue and wearing ruddy garments,
her limbs smeared with saffron paste, she has eyes like full-blown lotuses.
With a face of gentle smile, the eldest [sister] holds with her sprout-like arms a new pitcher filled with nectar and a goad together with a noose, both full of wealth.
One should worship the beautiful Kālikā, who has the luster of the orb of the rising sun, possesses three eyes and four arms, and holds a noose, a goad, and a bow.
Formerly, O Goddess, this Lalitā was worshipped by me with the desire for subjugation; she was then recited as a mantra, and thus Lalitā became submissive to me.
Lalitā is indeed the leader of the thirty-three crores of goddesses.

May she protect us— she who is the moon of the lord of birds, who proclaims Śiva, whose limbs are flooded with the nectar of immortality, who has three eyes, who drinks the blood flowing from the skull in her left hand,
whose hair is disheveled, who wears a girdle, a jeweled crown shining aloft, and whose tongue is blazing.
She who bears a load of blue lotuses from evil, whose feet are licked by the moon shimmering as an earring.
She has four arms and is black in complexion, adorned with a garland of severed heads;
she holds a sword in her right side and two excellent elephants in her left.
Holding a skull and a begging bowl in her left hands in succession,
she wears a single matted lock upon her head, from which two ascetic's staffs emerge.
Wearing a supreme garland of severed heads upon her head and another around her neck,
she bore a necklace of serpents upon her breast, with blood-red eyes.
Wearing black garments and clad in a tiger skin around her waist,
she places her left foot upon the heart of a corpse and her right foot—
Having dissolved [the deity] upon the back of a lion, one should visualize the self-form of the corpse as Lelihānā,
most terrifying, joined with loud, terrible laughter and a roar.
The goddess Mahāmeghaprabhā, wearing black garments,
with a lolling tongue, terrible fangs, sunken eyes, and a laughing face.
Adorned with a necklace of serpents and crowned with the crescent moon,
she brandishes a single matted lock of hair and repeatedly licks the tip of her tongue.

Her limbs were adorned with serpent-sacrificial threads; she sat reclining upon a serpent-couch; she was endowed with five faces and a shaven head; she wore a garland of human heads and possessed a massive belly.
One should visualize Guhyakālikā, endowed with a thousand names, with an infinite [form] above her head,
and encircled by the hoods of serpents in the four directions.
Takṣaka, the king of serpents, adorned his left wrist with a bracelet,
while Ananta, the king of nāgas, fashioned a bracelet for his right wrist.
One should meditate upon the goddess who has two arms, whose jeweled anklets are fashioned from the weight of a serpent’s tongues, and who wears a serpent as her sacred thread.
Anointed with human body-unguents, adorned with earrings and sacred scriptures,
she has a serene face, is gentle in appearance, and is embellished with the nine precious gems.
She who is served by hosts of sages such as Nārada, the consort of Śiva,
the one with the great laugh, the most formidable, and the bestower of the desired objects upon practitioners.
One should meditate upon the divine Kālikā of the South, who has a terrifying face, is formidable, has loose hair, possesses four arms,
and is adorned with a garland of severed heads.

She holds a sword with its blade recently severed in her upper left hand, and a lotus bud in her lower left; her upper right hand displays the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), and her lower right hand the gesture of granting boons (varada).
She possesses the luster of a great cloud, is dark-complexioned, and likewise naked;
she has a garland of severed heads around her neck, and her throat is adorned with ornaments.
She had ears adorned with a pair of corpses brought by the dead, which was terrifying with the two carcasses;
she possessed fierce fangs, a gaping mouth, and full, elevated breasts.
Her waist was bound by the gathered hooves of cows, her face was smiling,
and her mouth quivered as streams of blood flowed from the pair of corners of her lips.
Worship the protruding right [tooth] that pervades all, which is released,
radiant, and situated upon the heart of Mahādeva in the form of a corpse.
It is surrounded on the four sides by jackals with most terrible howls;
she has a face that is blissful and serene, and her lotus-like countenance is smiling.
Thus should the Goddess, who dwells in the abode of the cremation ground, be meditated upon.
She has limbs as dark as a rain-cloud, very large teeth, a flickering tongue, and matted hair; she holds a severed head in her left hand and a crescent moon in the palm of her right lotus-hand.

I bow to Kālī Karālī, whose face bears two streams of blood from her pair of cheeks, who wears a garland of skulls as a girdle, whose eyes are intoxicated by wine, and who rests upon the heart of a corpse.
The placement (nyāsa) of mantras and so forth belongs to one who has mastered the mantra;
[this is done] with black water when it is full, or with ghee at the time of the fire-oblation (homa).
Having worshipped with devotion the Goddess who is joined by the female messengers (dūtīs) beginning with Brāhmī,
one should again meditate upon the Goddess Caṇḍikā at home while reciting the Aṣṭamī Caṇḍikā Stotra.
She has five faces, each with three eyes, and is exceedingly fierce; she holds a spear, a trident, a bow, arrows, a shield, a sword, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

The practitioner, following the left-hand path (vāmācāra), should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while visualizing the Goddess holding [the weapons] with her right and left hands and adorned with serpent ornaments.
Then one should offer fuel-sticks of *picumarda* smeared with clarified butter;
or else, once the fire is fully kindled, one should perform the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and subsequent rites.
In this way, the practitioner of the mantra who has attained accomplishment shall slay the enemy, the foe,
and the adversary by performing one thousand and eight oblations of wood from a funeral pyre into a fire, while maintaining a disciplined mind.
If one performs the fire-oblation with seven substances during the twilight for a period of seven days,
death will inevitably occur, even for one whose life-span is fully extended.
In the collection of funeral-pyre bones, soot, borax, and likewise poison,
along with *vibhītaka*, black mustard, and parched grain— these are the seven substances.
Standing in the southern direction, one should perform the fire oblation while facing south.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the section on Nirvāṇa within the Dakṣiṇāmnāya of the venerable Vārāhī Tantra. || 12 ||
Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the determination of the mantra and the yantra,
by the mere knowledge of which Vārāhī becomes well-pleased.
I shall declare this which is established and hidden in all tantras;
it should be given to a devoted and excellent disciple, and never elsewhere.

One should recite the name preceded by the seed-syllables *tāra* (om), *māyā* (hṛm), *ramā* (śrīm), and *kāma* (klīm), followed by the word for the [recipient] such as "brāhmaṇa" and so forth, in the dative case and ending with "namaḥ."
For this should first be received from an elder, and once given, it should satisfy him alone;
this mantra is declared to be perfected, like the secret [mantra] of Mātali and Nārada.
If that which is without teacher, without beginning, without end, and without the division of middle or seat (pīṭha) could be obtained at all, O Lord of the Gods, then it would indeed be primordial.
This mantra, which consists of an island-syllable, likewise a hair-syllable, joined with lunar days and asterisms,
and conjoined with the initial syllables of the practitioner, is very difficult to obtain.
The hair-threads, the ghaṭikās, and the days follow in succession, and thereafter the years, months, and yugas, as well as the cycle of return.
And by the rule "a e ca taya," the *ghaṭikā* is enumerated.
He is luminosity and wonder, bliss and knowledge itself;
his nature is truth and fullness, and he is likewise the Lord, the Auspicious One.
Those devoted to the complete recitation (pārāyaṇa) speak of nine times;
the days beginning with the day of the truth (tattva) are indeed counted as the days.
The sequence beginning with Citrā belongs to Kāmeśvarī, while that beginning with Kāmeśvarī belongs to Citrā;
this is said to be the sequence of days according to the direction of the hair and against the direction of the hair.
One should not draw a triangle, a hexagon, or a yoni;
rather, one should draw a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, and a twelve-petaled lotus.
Afterwards, one should draw sixteen spokes, and then draw a perimeter circle;
and one should draw a trident in the four directions at the four gates, making it very beautiful.
The *suṃdarī* is proclaimed as the *kālikā*-yantra and as *vārāhī*; having uttered the *tāra*, one should then say "vajranakhadaṃṣṭrāyai" and "mahā".
"Siṃhāya huṃ phaṭ" is the seventeen-syllable heart mantra. After "Tāraṃ" (Oṃ), then two "Ciṭis," and after that, "Caṇḍāli."
One should utter "mahat" at the beginning and "padādyāntām" [at the end], followed by "amukaṃ me padaṃ tataḥ vaśamānaya" and the pair of "ṭha"s; this is the twenty-four-syllable mantra.
One should utter "Tāraḥ" (Oṃ), "namo bhagavate varāhāya," followed by the syllable ending in "ṅe" (the dative case),
then the Vyāhṛtis, and then the word "pataye."
"O Lord of the Earth, bestow upon me this [kingdom]," thus saying, the wife caused the fire to be given;
this Vārāha-mantra is said to consist of thirty-three syllables.
Oṃ! O Pārthivī, or you who move upon the surface of the earth, O woman, bestow youthfulness upon this couple; Cadha Cadha!
The mantra of Pārthivī is remembered as consisting of thirty syllables beginning with *svāhā*.
One should utter *ekā*, *kālī*, *mahākālī*, and *kelikālā*.
This mantra, ending with "svāhā" and consisting of the syllables of the lunar day (tithi), is considered to have one hundred thousand recitations as its requirement;
she who is Śivā wears white garments and a red bodice.
O Citrakaṇṭhī, O you of variegated cry, grant me a pair of voices!
*Bhīṃ Rīṃ Svāhā*— this is proclaimed as the mantra consisting of these syllables.

Oṃ hrīṃ namaśca vārāhi ghore svapnaṃ visargayuk | Ṭhadvayaṃ vahnijāyānto mantraḥ pañcadaśākṣaraḥ || Oṃ hrīṃ namo vārāhi ghore svapna visarga ṭha ṭha svāhā. This fifteen-syllable mantra ends with the two syllables ṭha and the wife of fire (svāhā).
Then one should worship the human skull and recite the fourfold mantra:
"O Kālī, salutation to the Skull-bearer (Kapālāya); Hrīṃ Hrīṃ," preceded by the syllable *Kaṃ*.
The eleven-syllable mantra is considered for worship and other rites by reciting:
*strīṃ strīṃ strū tāriṇī* followed by *kapālāya namaḥ*.
The second half of the skull [mantra] consists of twelve syllables less than this;
having uttered "hāṃ hrīṃ hūṃ," one says "namaḥ to the blue-skulled one."
The third worship of the skull is said to consist of eleven syllables:
*Māyā* (Hrīṃ), *strīṃ*, *hūṃ*, followed by "to the heavenly skull" (*svargakapālāya*) and "all calamities" (*sarvāpadam*).
Then, [one should worship] with "Obeisance to the All-King," likewise to the Source of All,
to Him who consists of total purity, and to the Destroyer of all Asuras.
"To Rācāruṇa and to Śubhra, and to Surābhājana;
salutation to the Goddess Kapālā—thus the fourth mantra is proclaimed."
This [mantra] consists of fifty-six syllables for the worship of the skull;
thereafter, one should worship the solar disc within that very skull.
"Oṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya namaḥ"—
this nine-syllable mantra is intended for worship of the solar disc (sūryamaṇḍala) upon a human skull.
Reciting the root mantra, one should pour wine into it with the understanding that it is nectar;
having cast in perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), one should display the triple-segmented gesture (trikhaṇḍā).
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim for the sake of Tāraka the twelve-syllable Tārā-mantra, which is worshipped by Brahmins and is very difficult to obtain.
Having [worshipped] Speech, Modesty, Lakṣmī, and Desire, who inspire confidence through the king of swans;
now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the great mantra of Mahākālī.
Oṃ kṣre& kṣre& kre& ataḥ kreṃca paśuṃ gṛhāṇa, and then one should utter hūṃ phaṭ svāhā; this mantra, consisting of the color of Indra, is declared to be perfected.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the seven-syllabled mantra of Ramā:
having uttered "aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ rājyalate" from the Self-born One (Brahmā).
Having uttered "Hrīṃ Jyeṣṭhāyai Namaḥ," this seventeen-syllable mantra is proclaimed.
Now I shall describe the great vidyās of Kālikā, which are very difficult to obtain.
By the mere knowledge of which a man becomes liberated while living,
there is no need for ritual worship, nor is there any distinction between enemies, friends, and so forth.
One should not concern oneself with the abundance of new efforts, nor with the rules regarding time and so forth;
for such abundance always causes physical exhaustion.
Whoever thus contemplates this mantra, which bestows the fulfillment of all undertakings—in his hand and at his feet resides every accomplishment; of this there is no doubt.
In his assembly, speech consisting of both prose and verse arises;
by the mere sight of him, the splendor of disputants is eclipsed.
Even kings and common people alike shall become submissive;
one will be able to bring under control both day and night.
At the end, a man attains the state of being a Gaṇa of the Goddess, which is difficult to obtain;
he who possesses the three Kāmas situated in the fire along with the Bindu.
Then, one should extract the pair of *kūrca* mantras, followed by the pair of *lajjā* mantras; and on the right, the words "kālike ca," along with the seeds of *dūrvā*.
At the end, Vahni-vadhū, Ādyā, Vidyā, and Śakti are proclaimed.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the auspicious Dakṣiṇa-Kālikā.
One should write this triad of seed-syllables: the syllable of desire (KĀM), situated in fire (R) and adorned with the left eye (I), joined with the bindu (M).
Likewise, O Goddess, there are two *kūrca*s, followed by *lajjā* (the seed-syllable of modesty) and *yoga*,
and on the right, *Kālikā* accompanied by a vocative case ending.
He spoke again regarding the seed-syllable; one should extract the mantra ending with *svāhā*, having made the *mātṛkā* alone, and the *mātṛkā* encapsulated by the *tāra*.
The best of practitioners should place the *tāra* (om) encased within the *mātṛkā*;
likewise, one should place the *mātṛkā* encased within the *śrī-bīja*.

One should place the Goddess encapsulated by *kāma* (the letter *ka*) and the *śakti* (the letter *ha*) encapsulating it; having again placed the pair *hrīṃ*, one should likewise place *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ* as before.
Having encircled the Goddess with the root mantra and likewise the enclosure of that [mantra],
one should install the mantra according to the rule, in both direct and reverse order.
One should perform one hundred and eight recitations at the base, and thereafter the pervasive [recitation].
Thus is proclaimed the sixfold limb-ritual of Guhyadurgā.
Tārā, Kālikā, Unmukhā, and likewise Parā—
by this mere placement [of mantras], all sin is destroyed.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the root-vidyā with the three mantras beginning with Oṃ according to the rules,
as well as the placement of the Self-vidyā and Śiva-tattva.
One should sequentially place the seven seed-syllables in the aperture of Brahma, between the eyebrows, on the forehead, at the region of the navel, in the secret wheel, and in all the limbs.
First, I shall explain the yantra, by knowing which one attains immortality.
Having first laid down a triangle, one should lay down another triangle outside of it.
Then the mantra-practitioner should indeed draw three excellent triangles;
having drawn a circle according to the rule, he should then draw a lotus endowed with auspicious characteristics.

Thereafter, one should perform the worship of the *pīṭha*, beginning with the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*), followed by primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the lotus of the womb (*kamaru*), and likewise Śeṣa and the earth (*pṛthvī*).
The ocean of nectar, the island of jewels, the house of wish-fulfilling gems,
the cremation ground, the Pārijāta tree, and the jeweled altar at its base.
Upon that jewel, the best of practitioners should place a pedestal;
in the four directions, he should place the sages, the gods, and the Śivas with human skulls.
O Queen of the Gods, fragrant with devotion, together with your retinue:
for as long as I worship you, may you remain steadfast.
One should perform the ritual services with the mantra revealed by the Guru.
One should worship with the ringing of the bell while reciting: *Oṃ jaya dhvani mantramātaḥ svāhā*.
Then, one should worship Mahākāla on the right side of the Goddess.
HŪṂ KṢĀṂ YĀṂ VĀṂ LĀṂ ĀṂ KROṂ MAHĀKĀRA BHAIRAVA, DESTROY ALL OBSTACLES!
HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ.
One should worship Mahākāla with effort, and afterwards one should worship the Goddess;
having dismissed them with supreme devotion by means of the *sannidhāyana* mudrā.

O Goddess, when one is absorbed in that [mantra] within the heart and the head, one certainly becomes identical with it; all perfections (siddhis) shall arise from the earth in one year for one who is devoted to Bhairava.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) during the day with purity;
at night, the practitioner, with a mouthful of betel leaf, should recite it one hundred thousand times while lying on his bed.

Having recited the mantra while observing the sequence, the knower of mantras, O Goddess, should perform ten thousand burnt offerings (homa) with one-tenth of that number, distinguishing between day and night.
Having become pure during the day and eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), a man should perform japa;
thereafter, O beloved, he should offer oblations with sacrificial food ten times the number of those recitations.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) and remaining pure during the day;
likewise, one hundred thousand times at night while remaining impure.
The practitioner of mantra should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with one-tenth of that number, offer libations (tarpaṇa), and perform the ritual consecration (abhiṣecana).
Eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), pure and observing the rules during the day, he should recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times.

At night, with his mouth full of betel-leaf, sleeping on his bed while reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times; having thus chanted two hundred thousand times, the knower of mantras should perform the ten-fold subsidiary rites (daśāṃśa).
O Goddess, one should offer oblations of aśvattha wood throughout the day and night,
from the passing of the first watch until the third watch.

And at night, it should be recited; a person should chant for the remainder of the night [the mantra] beginning with the first letter of the class, situated in the middle of fire (RA), and endowed with Rati and the Bindu (HRĪḤ).
The single-syllable great mantra bestows the fruits of all desires; indeed, when recited three times, it specifically awakens one to all the scriptures.

One should not perform the assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) of this mantra beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ), preceded by the long *kha*, the *ṣaṭyuta* (six-consonant) group, and the first [vowel]. By employing these correctly, the preceptor attains success.
The two *māyās*, the pair of *kūrca*s, ending with *aindra*, the three *mādanas*,
the two *māyās* joined with *aścara*, and the word "O Kālikā" in the south.
By means of the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhāra-krama), one should extract the seven seed-syllables;
this mantra of twenty-one syllables is the foremost mantra of Kālikā.
This king of mantras consists of twenty-three syllables ending with *svāhā*.
The *Mahāvidyā* consists of twenty leaves [syllables] and ends with *svāhā*, being devoid of the *praṇava*.
One should perform all activities such as meditation and worship with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) at their conclusion;
having first extracted the *praṇava*, one should then extract the seed-syllable of *kullukā*.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Rati (the letter *ra*) and joined it with the *prapañca* (the letter *ha*),
and further conjoined with two instances of the letter *ṭha*, this is proclaimed as the Vidyārājñī.
Bhairava is proclaimed as the seer (ṛṣi) of the mantra, Virāṭ as its meter (chanda),
and Siddhikālī, whose nature is Brahman, is proclaimed as its application (viniyoga).
The knower of mantras should perform twenty-one thousand recitations and offer oblations with clarified butter in the form of a liquid, using one-tenth of that number.
Then the root-seed, then the Māyā, and after that the seed-syllable of Lañjā;
this Great Vidyā was spoken by Mahākāla to Kālī.
The first letter of the [first] group joined with fire (ra), conjoined with Rati (ī) and the bindu (ṃ)—
these three, along with the wife of fire (svāhā), constitute the three root-mantras of fire.
One's own seed-syllable, the primordial seed-syllable, the syllable of modesty (hrīṃ), and the beloved of fire (svāhā);
then the vāgbhava-syllable, followed by the root-mantra of Kālikā and the beloved of fire (svāhā).
O Goddess, for this mantra, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is proclaimed as the seer;
Paṅkti is declared to be the meter, and Kālikā is remembered as the deity.
The two *lakṣmīs*, the *kūrca*, the *lajjā*, and "O Kālikā," followed by *phaṭ*;
then the two root seeds (*mūlabīja*), the *lajjā*, and as before, the beloved of fire (*vahni-vallabhā*).
One's own seed-syllable, the *kūrca* (huṃ), and the *lajjā* (hrīṃ)—these two [are placed] for Dakṣiṇakālikā;
then the root-seed, the *kūrca*-seed, one's own seed, and the beloved of Fire (svāhā).
One's own seed-syllable, the pair, the *kūrca*, the *lajjā*, or the beloved of fire (*svāhā*);
the root-seed, the *kūrca*, the *lajjā*, and the wife of fire (*svāhā*)—this is the beautiful [mantra].
The root seed-syllable, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), O Kālikā, and the beloved of fire;
the heart, the vāgbhava, the root, "to Kālikā," and the two *ṭha*s.
Then, the mantra of Kālikā is proclaimed with the wife of Vahni (the syllable *svāhā*).
Now, O lady of stainless face, listen to the five-syllabled vidyā.
Then, O Dear One, having extracted Prajāpati (the letter *p*), placed it within the group (*varga*),
joined with the fourth vowel, and endowed with all the *tantras*.
The three seed-syllables in their proper sequence, followed at the end by Vahnisundarī— this five-syllabled Mahāvidyā was proclaimed by Padmayoni.
O Pārvatī, listen as I shall explain the six-syllabled Mahākālī:
the wise one [should recite] three seed-syllables in sequence, and then again three seed-syllables.
This Vidyā, ending with "svāhā," is said to bestow the fruits of the four aims of life.
O Pārvatī, listen as the eleven-syllable Vidyā is now described.
The Vāgbhava seed-syllable is the heart; thereafter is Prajāpati mounted upon Brahmā, conjoined with the fourth vowel and adorned with the Nāda and Bindu.
Then, having doubled that [syllable] and adding the word *kālikā* ending in the dative case (*ṅe*),
the mantra ending in *svāhā* is declared, O Dear One, to be the eleven-syllabled *vidyā*.
The seer is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the meter is declared to be Pakti,
and the deity is remembered as Kālikā, the power higher than the highest.
The eleven-syllable mantra of Kālikā is very difficult to obtain;
it is [to be recited] two hundred thousand times in the rite of preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa).
But for others, a hundred thousand syllables were proclaimed by the Lotus-born One;
first the root seed-syllable, then Māyā, and after that the seed-syllable of Lañjā.
"Kālike" at the end of the south is proclaimed as ending with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Now, I shall further explain the twenty-syllable Vidyā.
By the mere grace of whom Indra became the conqueror of cities in this world;
one should utter the two root-seeds, and thereafter, one should speak the two *kūrca* mantras.
Having extracted the two *lajjās* (the seed-syllables of the Goddess of Modesty) and awakened the two words, one should place the sixfold seed-syllable as before and at the end [place] Vahnisundarī.
The seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra] is Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the meter (chandas) is declared to be Paṅkti;
and the deity (devatā), as stated by the wise, is Kālī preceded by Dakṣiṇā.
Now I shall further proclaim the Vidyā known as Tribhuvaneśvarī: having extracted her own seed-syllable (bīja), at its end is Vahnisundarī.
The seer of this is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and it is endowed with the Paṅkti meter;
this eight-syllable mantra, which is hidden in all the Tantras, has been proclaimed by me.
The seed-syllable of Nijā, two Kūrcas, two Lañjās,
followed by Svāhā— this is declared to be Kālī, the bestower of the fruits of all actions.
One's own seed-syllable, as well as the syllable of modesty (hrīṃ), followed by "tava sundarī" at the end—this is known as the five-syllabled great vidyā; its seer is remembered as Pañcavaktra.
O lotus-faced one, listen to the nine-syllable Great Vidyā:
[it consists of] one's own three seed-syllables, followed by a pair of *kūrca* syllables, and then a pair of *lajjā* syllables.
This Vidyā, ending with "svāhā," is declared to bestow all prosperity. Now I shall proclaim another Vidyā, which consists of nine syllables.
Having extracted the root seed-syllable and the two words ending with "saṃbudhyantaṃ," this Vidyā, ending in "svāhā," is said to cause the destruction of all enemies.
Now, O lotus-faced one, listen to the eight-syllable vidyā:
one should extract one's own seed-syllable, then the *kūrca* (the "tuft"), and then *māyā*.
Having again recited those [mantras] ending in *svāhā*, she is the bestower of liberation.
Now I shall proclaim another [mantra] endowed with the ten principles (*daśatattva*).
The two roots, the pair of *kūrca* mantras, and then the two *lajjā* mantras;
having recited these again, ending with *svāhā*, it is the bestower of liberation.
Now I shall proclaim another [mantra] endowed with the ten principles:
first the two roots, then the pair of *kūrca* mantras, and after that the two *lajjā* mantras.
Furthermore, at the end of those very seed-syllables (bījas), O beautiful one,
is the fourteen-syllable vidyā which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life (caturvarga).
One should extract the three Brahmās accompanied by fire (Ra), joined with Nāda and Bindu;
then follow the two Lañjās (Hrīṃ) and the two Kūrcas (Hūṃ).
Again, having extracted [the syllables] in sequence, the mantra ends with the wife of fire (svāhā).
This is the sixteen-syllable [mantra], joined with the two: lajjā (hrīṃ) and kūrcam (hūṃ).
Again, having extracted [the syllables] in sequence up to the wife of fire (svāhā),
this mantra is declared to be the Sixteenth, a science comparable to the wish-fulfilling tree.
O Goddess, the Heart-mantra is Vāgbhava, followed by one's own two seed-syllables;
then the word "Kālikāyai" is uttered, at the end of which follows Vahnisundarī.
*Namaḥ pāśāṅkuśau dvedhā phaṭ svāhā kālikālike*.
This fifteen-syllable mantra of Kālī has "dīrgha" as its tattva and "chada" as its covering.
O Goddess of the Suras, the worship of these [deities] should be performed with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the Vidyā that bestows all fruits.
It directly bestows the fourfold aims of life, destroys great sins,
eternally grants all perfections, and yields both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Guhyakālī is the great vidyā, exceedingly difficult to obtain even in the three worlds;
she is Kālī, Dakṣiṇā, and likewise Guhyakālī.
Having attained even the three glorious Vidyās, they are remembered by name as being preceded by the consonant groups beginning with the letter 'I',
mounted upon the vowels starting with 'A', and joined with the *rativindu* (the nasal bindu).
Then, having tripled that [letter], one should extract the vowel *ī*,
joined with the sixth vowel and adorned with the *nāda* and *bindu*.
That secret [seed-syllable] is called Kālikā; alternatively, one may recite it in the Dakṣiṇa [tradition].
Then, one should subsequently join the seven seed-syllables in their proper order.
The Vidyā that deludes the three worlds is said to end with the wife of Fire (Svāhā).
Likewise, [it consists of] the Kāma-bīja, the Kūrca, and at its end, Bhuvaneśvarī.
The secret and the Kālikā, as well as the two seed-syllables, constitute this mantra ending in svāhā; it has been declared in all tantras and remains concealed.
This is declared to be the sixteenth [chapter], which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
furthermore, O Kālikā, the secret "seven-seed" mantra was previously proclaimed.
This Vidyā, ending with *svāhā*, is declared to be hidden in all Tantras;
having omitted its name and so forth, it then consists of fifteen syllables.
Either omitting the seed-syllable of desire (kāmabīja), or else [using] the sixteen-syllable mantra;
having extracted the seed-syllable of desire, one should take the two words ending with "saṃvudhya."
Furthermore, at the end of that, one should offer the beautiful consort to the Fire;
this is the nine-syllable Vidyā, endowed with Guhyakālī.
Having addressed the right foot, one should extract "bhave" (bha-va-e).
The left eye (ī) joined with fire (ra) and adorned with nāda and bindu [is the syllable *rī*].
That secret [mantra] is called Kālikā, or else one should recite it in the Dakṣiṇa [tradition];
thereafter, one should join the seven seed-syllables in the preceding order.
The Vidyā known as Trailokyamohinī is said to end with the wife of Vahni (the *svāhā* mantra). Likewise, the Kāmabīja and the Kūrca [mantras] are placed at its end, followed by Bhuvaneśvarī.
The two seed-syllables *guhya* and *kālike*,
ending with *svāhā*, constitute the vidyā that has been taught and kept secret in all tantras.
This is declared to be the sixteenth [kalā], which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
and previously, the seven seeds were taught in the Guhya and again in the Kālikā.
This Vidyā, ending with *svāhā*, is declared to be hidden in all Tantras;
having omitted its name and so forth, it then consists of fifteen syllables.
Either omitting the seed-syllable of desire (kāmabīja), or else [reciting] the sixteen-syllable mantra;
having extracted the seed-syllable of desire, one should recite the two words ending with "saṃvudhya."
Furthermore, at the end of that, one should offer a beautiful woman to the Fire;
this is the nine-syllable mantra (vidyā) endowed with Guhyakālī.
Having addressed the foot on the right, there is the ten-syllable Vidyā in existence;
as before, one should worship Śivā with the group of months as previously described.
One should recite the vidyā as before; indeed, everything is exactly as previously described.
Likewise, the mantra-practitioner should arrange the offering of the bali-oblation as before.
The mantras of Bhadrakālī and others are now being told; listen, O beautiful one!
One should worship all the preceding and subsequent [deities] with the seed-syllable beginning with Kāma (Klīm).
One should likewise join "Bhadrakālī" with "Ṅeṃtām" in the middle of the seed-syllable;
this supreme Vidyā, ending with "Svāhā," consists of twenty syllables.
O fair-faced one, Bhadrakālī is the knowledge that bestows the four aims of life;
likewise, having extracted the seven seed-syllables, there is Śmaśānakālikā.
The seed-syllable again, in due order, ending with *svāhā*, bestows all accomplishments;
this Vidyā of twenty-one syllables is considered to be Śmaśānakālikā.
One should first utter the seed-syllables, then the word "Mahākālī," and at the end of that, the seven seed-syllables ending in "svāhā"; this bestows all accomplishments.
The Mahāvidyā of Mahākālī is proclaimed to have twenty petals;
the world-protectors (lokapālas) should be in the bhūpura, and their weapons outside of that.
The wise practitioner should worship in sequence within the four directions of the Bhūpura;
thereafter, he should worship Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sūrya, and Gaṇeśa.
A triangle, a hexagon, and a beautiful nine-cornered figure;
three circles, and an eight-petaled lotus endowed with beautiful white filaments.
This seat (pīṭha), which consists of three five-spoked [lotuses] and is adorned with a circle of the womb (yonimaṇḍala) mounted upon three city-gates (bhūpura), is endowed with all the tantras.
I shall proclaim the *vali* mantra, which is concealed within all the tantras.
Come, come, O Mother of the World, Mother of the Worlds, O Birth-giver of the Worlds! Accept, accept my offering; grant, grant me success;
destroy, destroy my enemies! Hūṃ 2 Hrīṃ 2 Hūṃ Phaṭ! Oṃ, obeisance to Kālikā, Phaṭ Svāhā!
Come, come! O Guhyakālī, seize, seize! Destroy, destroy my enemies! Devour, devour! Move, move! Flash, flash! Grant success! Huṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! Oṃ Hūṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva Mahāpreta, to Guhyakālī;
salutation to Guhyakālī! I shall now proclaim the garland-mantra of Vārāhī, which bestows all accomplishments: Hrīṃ.
Śrīṃ Aiṃ Glauṃ Aiṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, O Vārtāri, O Vārāhamukhī! Homage to Aṃdhā, O Aṃdhinī; homage to Ruṃdhā, O Ruṃdhinī; homage to Jaṃbhā, O Jaṃbhinī; homage to Mohā, O Mohinī;
homage to Staṃbhā, O Staṃbhinī! [Homage] to all those who are wicked and extremely wicked.
Paralyze all speech, mind, eyes, faces, movements, and tongues! Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! Vārāhī Ratneśvarī Svāhā!
Thus have these [teachings] been declared by the Goddess, revealing the mantras and yantras;
by the mere knowledge of which Vārāhī becomes well-pleased.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Dakṣiṇāmnāya section of the Nirvāṇapada within the venerable Vārāhītantra. || 13 ||
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, listen as I speak of the fruit of reciting the Caṇḍī;
I shall describe to you exactly the results of recitations performed once, and so forth.
Having first performed the ritual worship with a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) upon their limbs once with the mantra,
a human being obtains the supreme fruit, whether it be the offering of a bali-oblation or the attainment of the result.
The wise person should recite the two prefixes ten times;
O fair-faced one, for the affliction caused by the planets, one should recite it five times.
When great fear has arisen, a wise person should recite it seven times;
by reciting it nine times, one attains peace and obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
The conduct of Rudra has been declared for the sake of bringing kings under one's influence and for prosperity;
through the conduct of Arka, the fulfillment of desires and the destruction of enmity arise.
By the previous fifteen-fold repetition beginning with *manu-vṛtta*, a person likewise attains mastery over women;
by the fifteen-fold repetition of *mokṣa*, a human being attains prosperity (*śrī*).
They know that by this ritual, one obtains sons, grandsons, wealth, and grain;
and it serves for release from the king's fear and for the eradication of enmity.
O Dear One, one should perform it seventeen times for the twelve [syllables];
for the release from a major wound, the wise person should recite it thirty times.
Indeed, by twenty-five recitations, there is liberation from the bonds of existence;
even when one has fallen into a great crisis or a sea of distress, as well as when afflicted by diseases difficult to cure.
When there is the destruction of castes, the severing of lineages, the arrival of the ruin of life and food,
the increase of thieves, the increase of disease, the loss of wealth, and the decay of the people.
Likewise, in the event of the threefold portents, as well as sins and transgressions, one should diligently perform the Śata-vṛtta; thereby, auspiciousness is attained.
His misfortunes perish, and at the end he attains the supreme goal;
his prosperity increases a hundredfold, and likewise there is the highest growth of his kingdom.
O Goddess, O lady of noble vows, that which is meditated upon in the mind shall be accomplished as one hundred and eight times;
one attains the fruit of a hundred horse-sacrifices.
Lakṣmī herself, remaining steadfast, enters him who performs a thousand circumambulations;
having abandoned desires and mental longings, he shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Just as the Aśvamedha sacrifice is among sacrifices, and just as Hari is among the gods,
so too is the Saptashatī hymn among all hymns of praise.
Or rather, O fair-faced one, what is the use of saying much?
O beloved, through a hundred recitations of Caṇḍī, everything is accomplished.
Having placed the book upon its support, one should recite it clearly;
by holding it in the hand, O Goddess, the fruit is endowed with half [the merit].
As long as [the deity] is not worshipped, one should meditate; one should recite this for no long time.
Then one should recite the *krama*; O Goddess, one should abandon shaking the head and other such gestures.
O dear one, if there is a loss due to negligence during the recitation, one should begin the recitation again from the beginning; thus it is prescribed in every respect.
O fair-faced one, there is no hymn superior to this;
it is meritorious, the means to both worldly enjoyment and liberation, the destroyer of sins, and purifying.
One who knows that substance, having first bowed to the deities he has beheld,
and then having seen the Praṇava, should recite the hymn or the Saṃhitā.
One should place the *praṇava* at the end, preceded by "Dhiti uvāca" and so forth;
it should be recited with effort, with pure and unwavering devotion.
One should recite the *namāma* [mantra] or the hymn; indeed, the oral recitation is praised. If one reads from a book, it is a weapon [an obstacle], even if it be the *Sahasrābhidhāna*.
In cases where the oral recitation would otherwise be deficient without a book,
the wise practitioner should place the book upon a support and perform the recitation.
O Goddess, because the fruit would be meager due to the mere physical placement [of the hand],
that which is not written by oneself should instead be written by a skilled scribe.
If it is not written for a Brahmin, all of that becomes fruitless;
nor is a hymn effective if composed by oneself, nor even by one who is not another.
Since it has not reached the ears of the sages, one should read what has been written by them;
having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers, meters, and so forth, the wise person should recite the hymn.
Wherever the origin [of this] is practiced through hymns of praise,
it is considered highly lauded in the Kali age, as taught in the Bhīṣma Parvan.
The hymn known as the Thousand Names of Viṣṇu, which destroys all sins; the account of the liberation of Gajendra; and likewise the Hymn of Compassion.
The *Narasiṃha-sahasranāma*, the one known as the *Śrīrāma-sahasranāma*,
the *Divya-saptaśatī-stotra*, and likewise the *Sahasranāma*.
The hymn called *Prasāda* of Tripurā, the king of praises (*stavarāja*) of the Sun,
and also the *Indrākṣī* hymn, which was [revealed] by Ruci, the grandson of that [Sūrya].
And in the Vaiṣṇava [Purāṇa], the hymn to Mahālakṣmī was spoken by Indra;
it was composed in seven hundred verses by the sage named Bhārgava for a specific purpose.
Having spoken thus, O Lord of Pārvatī, these seven truths yield great fruit;
by the mere hearing of them, all diseases are pacified.
Sweetness, clarity of syllables, proper division of words, melodiousness, steadiness, and the correct use of short and long vowels— these six are the qualities of a reciter.

One who sings, one who recites too quickly, one who recites with the head or throat, one who recites exactly as written, and one who lacks understanding of the meaning and possesses little intelligence— these six are the lowest of reciters.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the great mantra of Cāmuṇḍā, which consists of the nine Durgās; by the mere remembrance of which, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are attained.
By whose grace Suratha, having obtained the kingdom, became Manu;
and by whom, through meditative absorption (samādhi), the bonds of worldly existence were severed upon the attainment of knowledge.
I shall now declare that mantra which bestows the fruit of reciting, and so forth, the triad of narratives concerning you as told in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
One should utter the syllables *vāglajjā kāma* followed by the word *cāmuṇḍāyai*.
This nine-syllable mantra, beginning with *vicce*, is the most excellent among all Śakti mantras.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa are proclaimed as its sages;
Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, and Anuṣṭubh are declared to be its three meters.
Of this [deity], Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Sarasvatī are the divine [powers];
Nandā, Śākaṃbharī, and Bhīmā are declared to be the triad of Śaktis.
His three powers are Durgā, Bhrāmarī, and Raktadaṃtikā;
one should assign the principles of fire, wind, and sun, as well as the seer and so forth, as previously described.
Having performed that by which a human being becomes worthy of the deity's favor,
one should then perform the second placement known as the Sārasvata.

The three seed-syllables (vīja) at the beginning of the mantra, starting with *Tārā* and ending with the heart-mantra, constitute the six-syllabled mantra; one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon nine locations.
On the little finger, the ring finger, the middle finger, the index finger, and the pair of thumbs; on the center of the hand, the back of the hand, the wrist, and the elbow.
One should again place [the mantras] endowed with their seed-syllables (*jāti*) upon the six limbs, beginning with the heart;
when this Sārasvata ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed, dullness is destroyed.
The seven true nyāsas should be performed according to the specific desire during the recitation;
thereafter, one should perform the third nyāsa, beginning with the Mātṛgaṇa.
May Brāhmī, whose seed-syllable is Māyā (M), protect me always from the east;
likewise, may Māheśvarī protect me from the southeast, and Kaumārī from the south.
May Vaiṣṇavī protect in the northeast, Vārāhī in the west,
Indrāṇī in the southwest corner, and Cāmuṇḍā in the north.
In the northeast is Mahālakṣmī; likewise, Vyomeśvarī is above;
Saptadvīpeśvarī is on the earth; and Kāmeśvarī protects the foundation.
When the third assignment has been performed, one becomes a conqueror of the three worlds;
one should then perform the fourth assignment, accompanied by Nandajā and the others.
May Nandajā protect the eastern quarter; may Raktadaṃtikā, adorned with a lotus and a goad, and holding a sword and a bowl in her hands, protect the southern quarter.
May Śākaṃbharī protect my back; may Durgā, holding a bow and arrows and adorned with sprouts, always protect me on the left side.
May her terrifying hands protect my head from the feet up to the crown;
may she who bears a whirling radiance protect from the feet up to the head.
A man performing the fourth assignment (nyāsa) wards off death by water;
thereafter, he should perform the fivefold supreme assignment beginning with Brahmā.
May the eternal Brahmā protect from the feet up to the navel;
may Janārdana protect constantly from the navel up to the point of purity.
May the three-eyed Rudra protect [me] up to the pure Brahma-randhra;
may Haṃsa protect my pair of feet, and Vainateya my two hands.
May the Bull protect my two eyes, and may the Elephant-faced One protect all my limbs; may Hari, who is composed of bliss, protect the upper and lower portions of my body.
When this fifth placement has been performed, one shall obtain all desires;
thereafter, one should perform the sixth placement, conjoined with Mahālakṣmī and the others.
May Mahālakṣmī, endowed with eighteen arms, protect the middle;
may Sarasvatī, resplendent with eight arms, protect the upper part.
May Mahākālī, endowed with ten arms, protect [me] from below;
may the lion protect the two hands, and the pair of eyes of the supreme swan.
May Yama, mounted upon a buffalo and other beasts, protect the two feet;
and may the buffalo joined with Caṇḍikā protect all the limbs, O Maheśvarī.
When this sixth placement (nyāsa) has been performed, a person shall attain the supreme goal;
thereafter, one should perform the seventh, which consists of the placement of the root-syllables (mūlākṣara).
In the aperture of Brahma, the pair of eyes, the two ears, the nostrils, the mouth, the anus,
the genitals, and the mind— one should place the phonemes beginning with *tāra* (oṃ), conjoined with the syllable *namaḥ*.

One should perform the placement during the seventh nyāsa; by doing so, there shall be no destruction. One should again place those very same [mantras] from the feet up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Yet, when that [mantra] has vanished from the earth, all suffering perishes;
one should perform the ninth placement (nyāsa), which is the mantra whose nature is pervasiveness (vyāpti).
One should place the desired [mantras] from the head to the feet, and from the feet up to the head;
in front, on the right, at the back, and on the left side.
The ninth [stage] consists of the ritual placement (nyāsa) performed with the root mantra, which effects the attainment of the deity;
thereafter, one should perform the supreme six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) in the tenth.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the root mantra, joined with the seed-syllables, upon the heart and other limbs;
when this tenth nyāsa is performed, one shall bring the three worlds under control.
Even during the recitation of the Caṇḍī, the ritual placements (nyāsas) that bestow one's desired goals should be performed;
one should then perform the eleventh [chapter], which grants the fruits mentioned for the nyāsas.
Having recited the five verses beginning with "Khaḍginī" and "Śūlinī," one should meditate upon the first seed-syllable as being intensely black and perform the placement (nyāsa) over all the limbs.
Having recited the four verses beginning with "O Goddess, protect us with your trident," one should place a second [image] resembling the sun upon the back.
Then one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using the divided root-syllables:
with one, one, one, four, and two respectively.
One should perform the six-fold assignment of the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa) using the entire mantra alone, in due order:
one should place it on the crest-lock, the two eyes, the two ears, the nose, the mouth, and the anus.
One should practice the mantra-text as a whole, which is all-pervasive and most excellent.
Then one should meditate on the Goddess; this is called the meditation on Kālikā.
She has ten faces and ten feet, with ten arms praised by the Creator;
she possesses the luster of sapphire and holds a sword, a discus, a conch, a severed head, and arrows.
Holding a mace, a trident, and a club in her right hands,
and holding a bludgeon, a bow, and an arrow— she who is praised by Brahmā.
Then, for the sake of destroying Madhu and Kaiṭabha, one should meditate upon Mahālakṣmī, who is adorned with ornaments, possesses three eyes, and is the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
Born from the radiant splendor of all the deities, she is seated upon a lotus throne;
she has eighteen arms, holding a rosary, a lotus, and an arrow.
Holding a sword, a vajra, a mace, and a discus in her right hands,
and a water-pot, a conch, a spear, an axe, and a bow in her left.
One should then meditate upon Sarasvatī, who holds a leather whip, a vessel for liquor, a bell, a noose, and a trident, and whose radiance is equal to that of an arrow and the moon.
She holds a conch, a mace, two discs,
and arrows in her right hands, and a bell, a trident, a plow, and a bow in her left hands.
Born from the body of Gaurī, she bestows bliss upon men,
serves as the foundation of the universe, and destroys inauspiciousness and the like.
One should always remember the presiding deity of the third [mantra], whose conduct is threefold;
having meditated thus, one should recite it four hundred thousand times, followed by a tenth part of that for the fire-oblation.
One should offer oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) after the [deity] has been worshipped with gold and jewels;
one should worship the Goddess upon a pedestal (pīṭha) joined with the powers (śaktis) such as Jayā and the others.
Having consulted thus, for one who has desisted [from worldly activity], there is a [mandala] endowed with a hexagon and eight petals;
with Śrī in the southwest, Viṣṇu in the northwest, and Śiva with Bhūmi.
One should worship the deer-faced goddess in the hexagon of Mahiṣa as she tears him apart; and in the six corners, starting from the east, one should worship Nandā and Raktadantikā.
One should worship Śākaṃbharī, Durgā, Bhīmā, and Bhrāmarī;
these [names] are preceded by the Tāra (Om) and their respective seed-syllables, end in the feminine suffix -ī, and are joined with the word "hṛdaya" (heart).
All the powers of every hope are considered to reside within the victory of the name-mantras;
therefore, on the eight petals [one should worship] Brāhmī, Māheśī, and Kumārikā.
One should worship Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, Surendrajā,
and Cāmuṇḍā on the twenty-five petals outside of that.
Viṣṇu’s Māyā, consciousness, intellect, sleep, hunger,
as well as the supreme power of shadow, thirst, patience, and birth— each more prominent than the last.
Modesty, peace, as well as faith, fame, fortune, and fortitude;
conduct, sacred revelation, and tradition, as well as compassion and contentment thereafter.
One should worship Puṣṭi and Mātṛbhrama within the Bhūpura (the outer square enclosure),
and likewise Gaṇapa, Kṣetreśa, and Vaṭuka in the four corners.
One should also worship the Yoginīs, Sureśānī and the others, and their weapons outside;
and one should daily recite the Caṇḍī-stava as declared in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
If one recites [the mantra] encased by the root-mantra, one attains the desired goal;
in the Kali age, there is nothing equal to Caṇḍī as a bestower of perfection within the three worlds.
Through the left and right paths, she bestows authority and fruit;
therein, one should employ the first conduct for the destruction of disease.
A wise man should employ the middle [course] for the sake of attaining heaven while avoiding destruction;
however, one who desires the objects of the lowest realm should cultivate the conduct of others.
For one whose conduct possesses the two-fold virtue, the lineage is never severed anywhere;
if one recites or gives the three-fold conduct, his misfortune perishes.
Whoever recites this beginningless [mantra] shall slay his enemies before long;
one should join it with the lotus accompanied by the anusvāra and the seven truths.
He who recites the Caṇḍī, encased within those mantras and according to the prescribed number, at both the beginning and the end, his desire shall be fulfilled.
One should contemplate one's own enemy as a demon and one's own friends as deities,
and thus meditate upon Caṇḍī, performing this practice at the three junctions of the day for a period of one month.
Whether dead or as good as dead, the enemies will undoubtedly perish,
starting from the beginning of the bright fortnight until the eighth day.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with edible offerings soaked in the three sweets;
one should worship the goddess Caṇḍī daily and recite the hymn from beginning to end.
By propitiating the Brahmins and the Guru, one quickly obtains what is desired;
thus, in the first chapter on the conduct of truth, the sage Padmabhū [declares].
The meter is declared to be Gāyatrī, Mahākālī is the deity,
Vāgbīja is the seed-syllable, Fire is the principle (tattva), and its application is for the sake of dharma and artha.
But for the middle conduct, the Sage has declared that there is no such [application] of rites as killing; rather, it is through delusion. Viṣṇu is thus cited as the authority.
The meter is Uṣṇik, the deity is Mahālakṣmī, the seed-syllable is Adrijā (the Mountain-born), the principle is Vāyu, and the application is for the attainment of wealth; this is the heart-mantra.
In this [chapter], there are two hundred applications for the rites of eradication and immobilization;
the sage Śaṅkara is said to be the author of the Uttara-caritra.
The goddess Mahāsarasvatī is proclaimed to have the Triṣṭubh meter;
the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) and the sun (R) are its essence, and its application is for the attainment of desires.
The yogas for causing enmity and subjugation are measured by the applications and so forth performed;
thus, seven hundred applications have been proclaimed here.
Therefore, it was proclaimed by the wise Vyāsa that there are seven hundred [verses];
likewise, in the Kalpa and in the day, there are seven Mahāvidyās and so forth.
They are the deities to be worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, Bṛhaspati, Śakra, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the enemies of the gods; they were praised here by Brahmā.
Therefore, it was proclaimed by Vyāsa as the "Saptashatī" (Seven Hundred),
even though gentle forms [of the Goddess] are also proclaimed therein.
On the southern path, the seven powers beginning with Lakṣmī are to be worshipped:
Lakṣmī, Lalitā, Kālī, Durgā, Gāyatrī, and Arundhatī.
And Sarasvatī—these seven are to be worshipped according to the path of the Left (Vāmamārga):
Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, Sumukhī, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
Vālā, Kubjeti, and Navamā are proclaimed as the three types of Sucitā;
she who is known by the name Saptasatī is of two kinds in the middle conduct.
The manifestation of the mantra occurs through the conventions (saṃketa) stated in its respective mantra;
thus, beginning with the words "those engaged in praise," it continues into the third [chapter].
In the Carita-sapta, those ending with Cāmuṇḍā are proclaimed;
they are proclaimed beginning from "in front of the swan-yoked celestial chariot" (haṃsayukta-vimānāgre).
The seven Satyas, beginning with Brahmāṇī, were present there;
and when the Vaivasvata Manvantara had arrived, the [seven] Manus likewise appeared.
Because they were spoken by the Goddess herself as truths, they are considered the *Saptasatī*.
Indeed, through these seven truths, I am the Brahman who is everything.
Śrī Haridvartī receives a crore-fold share, while other people receive only a single part;
just as mantras are applied and performed in a particular way for the sake of attaining success.
Likewise, seeds and so forth are sometimes used by the wise according to their desire;
thus, the manifestation of letters and their respective sounds has been explained in detail.
One who is well-versed in the science of grammar (śabdaśāstra) is suitable for the recitation of inauspicious rites;
however, one who is contrary to the science of grammar is suitable for the recitation of propitiatory (śāntika) and nourishing (pauṣṭika) rites.

On the day of the full moon, he should recite the Caṇḍī-stava, which consists of the syllables of his own chosen mantra. At the conclusion, having meditated upon Mahālakṣmī and performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*), [he should proceed].
One should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times and offer it to the deity;
he who acts in this manner never comes to grief at any time.
O beloved, I shall now describe the procedure for the Śatacaṇḍī rite for men when they encounter royal oppression, famine, or earthquakes.
In cases of excessive rain, drought, fear of an enemy army,
or destruction, all obstacles perish when the Śatacaṇḍī rite is performed.
For the destruction of diseases and enemies, and for the abundance of wealth and sons,
[one should build] an auspicious [shrine] near the temple of Śaṅkara or Bhavānī.
One should construct a pavilion with door-altars and so forth, provided with banners and arches;
there, one should fashion a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) either to the west or in the center.
Having bathed and performed the ritual purification,
he should appoint local Brahmins who have conquered their senses, are of good conduct, of noble birth, and speakers of truth.
And to those who are learned, devoted to the recitation of the Caṇḍikā, and possessed of modesty and compassion,
[one should offer honor] according to the ritual for the madhuparka, through the giving of garments, gold, and other gifts.
For the purpose of recitation, one should provide them with a seat and a rosary, and also give them food;
they, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), should keep their minds fixed on the meaning of the mantra.
Sleeping on the ground, each person should recite the Caṇḍikā-stava ten times with a focused mind, as declared in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
In the Navārṇa Caṇḍikā Tantra, they should each recite the mantra ten thousand times;
they should worship the patron and [honour] a group of ten auspicious maidens.
One should worship a maiden who is between two and ten years of age;
she should not have extra limbs, nor be deficient in limbs, nor be afflicted with leprosy or marked by ulcers.
One should not worship a girl who is blind, one-eyed, or ugly, whose body is afflicted by disease, or who is a slave-girl, even if she is endowed with beauty; nor should one worship a wicked girl.

A Brahmin should sacrifice to all the deities for the attainment of perfection; for fame, he should sacrifice to those born of the Kṣatriya class; for the acquisition of wealth, to those born of the Vaiśya class; and for the obtainment of a son, he should sacrifice to those born of the Śūdra class.
A two-year-old girl is called Kumārī; one of three years is Trimūrti;
a four-year-old is Kalyāṇī; and a five-year-old is Rohiṇī.
Kālikā is said to be six years old, Caṇḍikā seven years,
Śāmbhavī eight years, and Durgā nine years.
Subhadrā is said to be ten years old; one should worship her with mantras.
A one-year-old girl lacks the requisite affection, while a eleven-year-old is to be avoided.
The mantra for their invocation is declared in the form of a verse:
[I invoke] Lakṣmī, who consists of the syllables of the mantra and who assumes the forms of the Mothers.
I directly invoke the maiden who is the very embodiment of the Nine Durgās;
now I shall declare the worship mantras for maidens such as the Kumārikā and others.
O one worshipful to the world, O one worthy of the world’s salutation, O you whose very nature is all-powerful! Accept this worship, O Kaumārī; salutations to you, the Mother of the World.
I worship the Goddess Tripurā, the support of the three cities, whose essential nature is the triple knowledge, who is adored by the three worlds, and who is the embodiment of the three forms.
I worship the auspicious one, who consists of the creative powers and yet transcends them, whose heart is compassion, the eternal mother of all well-being, and the source of all auspiciousness.
I worship Kālikā, who acts according to her will, who is auspicious and beloved, whose very form is the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra), who grants all desires, and who is noble in her compassion.
I constantly worship the goddess Caṇḍikā, whose seed-syllable is *caṇḍi*, who consists of ferocity, who is the destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, and who possesses fierce valor.
I worship Lakṣmī, the consort of Śambhu, who bestows eternal bliss, who is peaceful, who is saluted by all the gods, and who is the self of all beings.
In difficult and insurmountable undertakings,
I always worship with devotion Durgā, the destroyer of suffering and the dispeller of miserable states.
I worship Subhadrā, the goddess who is beautiful, possessing a golden luster, and the bestower of happiness and good fortune;
I worship my mother, the divine Subhadrā.
With these mantras, one should worship each such maiden endowed with auspicious marks:
"We know Mahāmāyā; we meditate upon Caṇḍikā; may that Goddess inspire us."
With perfumes, flowers, incense, food offerings, garments, and ornaments,
[one should worship] in a beautiful *sarvatobhadra* pavilion constructed upon the altar.
Having placed a water-pot according to the rules, one should invoke Śivā there and worship her;
furthermore, one should feed young girls and Brahmins in front of it.
Having performed the previously mentioned offerings and the ritual selections (varaṇas) with various services,
and having done so for four days, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) on the fifth day.
With milk-rice mixed with the three sweets, as well as grapes, plantains, citrons,
sugarcane pieces, coconuts, dates, and sesame seeds;
One should perform the oblation by offering nutmegs, mangoes, and other sweet substances,
reciting each verse seventeen times.
And having performed ten thousand oblations with the nine-syllable mantra according to the prescribed rite in the established fire,
one should perform the worship of the feet of the deities with that same mantra.
Having properly performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and having bid farewell to the divine fire,
he should have the consecrator sprinkled with water from the ritual jars by the brahmins.
One should give a gold coin (*niṣka*) or a piece of gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for each [deity],
or else one should feed the Brahmins with various kinds of foods and delicacies.

Having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) even to them, one should then take up [the mantra] up to the end of the hair-tuft (āśikha). When this is done, the world becomes submissive and all calamities perish.
One may obtain a kingdom, wealth, fame, sons, and other desired things;
however, the ritual procedure for a thousand recitations of Caṇḍī produces these tenfold.
One should select one hundred Brāhmaṇas who possess learning and follow virtuous conduct;
and for the destruction of obstacles, one should have ten perform the recitation of the Caṇḍikā [stotra] every day.
One should recite ten thousand times for each of the nine syllables during battle;
the previously mentioned auspicious maidens [should be invoked] with the hundred mantras as before.
Having thus completed [the recitation] for ten days, they should diligently perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rule,
with seven hundred and fifty repetitions for each verse.
Having offered the nine-syllable mantra one hundred thousand times into the previously mentioned collection of substances,
one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests and feed the twice-born as previously described.
O King, when this rite for Caṇḍī has been performed by men in this manner a thousand times, it brings about auspicious results for those who are devoted to the worship of the Goddess.
Everything desired is accomplished, and suffering is destroyed;
plagues, misfortune, diseases, and other such calamities perish.

I do not declare this method to the wicked, the malicious, the thief, or the betrayer of the guru; one should declare this supreme method only to the virtuous, the self-controlled, and the disciplined.
Thus, when Caṇḍikā is pleased, she protects those who recite [her mantra] from the three-fold suffering.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Dakṣiṇāmnāya section of the Nirvāṇapada of the Śrī Vārāhī Tantra.
Bhairava said:
There is no distinction among Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Cāṇḍālas, and others;
in the Kaulika rites, the mantra is most efficacious for attaining success.
That great void is its flow, adorned by the three powers;
from that comes the bindu, then the moon, and again the eighth, the womb.
O Maheśvarī, the wise one should join that below the womb (yoni) from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
O auspicious lady, it is situated as the twenty-eighth [letter] from the Nāda and the seventh.
O highly fortunate one, bow your head to that abode, which is devoid of the syllable Om;
this is the supreme Piṇḍa, the source of all mantras.
O highly fortunate one, this is the supreme essence, the fire-drill for all mantras;
it brings about all peace, performs all duties eternally, and bestows all accomplishments while warding off fear.
The supreme *piṇḍa* of the Goddess is the essence that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Hskhphreṃ.
Starting from the end of the end (sa) and proceeding to the beginning (a), one should extract the twenty-sixth letter;
it is mounted upon fire (ra) below and joined to the head (m) above.
The Goddess Ekākṣarā is known as that which is divided up to the end of the sixth group.
kṣrjhrīṃ &
Oṃ krīṃ! Kaṅkāli Devī, the slayer of the wicked, the goddess who accomplishes my purpose, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Everything has arisen from the letter *ka*; therefore, she is the very nature of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
The letter *ra* is Kārāgni Rudra; by him she is of the nature of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
And in the letter *ī* is Mahālakṣmī, the illuminator of the three worlds.
Thus, this power of the *pālikā* and its equilibrium with the *bindu*,
in the form of an enclosure, constitutes Ambikā as creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Thus, in the form of the universal aggregate, she is the nature of the fourth Brahman;
she is composed of consciousness and bliss, manifest as the very essence of the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti).
She is the very nature of the Brahman of sound, whose essence is eternal bliss;
she is the embodiment of all the Vedas, manifest, and the bestower of eternal bliss.
The Supreme Power (Parāśakti), who is to be accomplished through recitation (japa) and is established upon the path of sound (nāda),
bestows [her grace] while assuming the form of Bhairavī, mounted upon the pedestal of the temple of speech.
Then one should remember the Mahāvidyā, who dwells in the midst of the Siddhakāmas;
having recited her twenty-seven lakhs of times, she becomes perfected.
The womb (yonirūpa), heat (uṣman), likewise the fireless (anaṣka), the hexagon (ṣaṭkoṇa), Kuṇḍalinī, Kula, Māyā, Nārāyaṇa, and Haṃsa— thus the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] is remembered as eightfold.
Situated in the midst of the eight syllables of Vāgbhava, according to the differentiation of these groups [of consonants],
the eastern face is Siddhilakṣmī and the southern is Guhyakālī.
Kālaśaṅkarṣaṇī is declared to be the northern face;
Kujā is the western face, and the one named Pratyaṅgirā is the head.
This should be known as the embodiment of meditation, which enables one to cross the ocean of saṃsāra,
bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and increases happiness and good fortune.
In a place such as a cremation ground, or in a most terrible location, or even at the site of a battle,
he should eat light food, remain absorbed in meditation, and be adorned with black garments.
One should meditate upon her who is fierce, most terrifying, black and red, and fearsome;
whose limbs are emaciated, who is mounted upon a corpse, naked, and has a distorted face.
And here, one should visualize the goddess Pretapremā, with hair standing on end, with ears hanging down like those of a child,
holding a skull in her hand, deformed, filled with blood, and ever ready for action.
Adorned with ornaments of serpents and wearing a sacred thread of snakes.
She has eighteen arms, is fierce, possesses five faces and three eyes;
bearing all weapons, the formidable goddess bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should recite the mantra of the goddess named Pratyamgirā, who destroys all transgressions:
*oṃ aṃ kaṃ caṃ ḍhaṃ taṃ yaṃ hmaṃ bhāṃ hrīṃ*.
Having uttered "Hūṃ Sa Hūṃ Tathā Straṃ Svāhā," this sixteen-syllable mantra has the sage Vidhātṛ, the Gāyatrī meter,
and six deities as its proclaimed components.
Mahāvāyu, Mahāpṛthvī, and likewise Mahākāla;
