I shall now proclaim another [teaching]: the characteristics of the Lord of Trees (Vṛkṣanātha), the secret of all scriptures, the sequence concealed within the Tantras.
O Goddess, one should avoid association with the fettered (paśu), whether it be concealed or more concealed;
I shall now proclaim the supreme, divine [teaching] regarding the vessel of the ninefold auspiciousness (navasaubhāgya).
The divine Mahākaulārṇava is infinite and possesses pure waters;
in its very center, O Goddess of Gods, is the origin of Candradvīpa.
The stone of the five jewels is the island of the moon, the remainder of bliss;
there, in its center, is the triangular-eyed place, beloved by the Yoginīs.
O Lord of Cintāmaṇi, [I bow to] that which resides within the interior of the Śṛṅgāṭaka-maṇḍala, within the heart of its womb, which has arisen and bestows the fruits of all desires.
With its roots and branches extensively spread, it is the source of the divine stream of fruits;
it is Kaula and Akula, the uprooting of the Kula, arising within the mandala of Śiva.
Meditate upon her, who is the essence of one's own true nature, the source of the nectar of bliss,
and who possesses the threefold Sāṅkhya as her expansive branches and the Vedas and Vedāṅgas as her leaves.
Filled with flowers and sense-faculties, that supreme realm is free from objects of attachment;
therein lies the ultimate repose, devoid of both pleasure and pain.

O Goddess, thus has been declared the determination of the tree, which is the divine fruit of the fragrance of consciousness, possessing supreme and infinite glory, and transmitted through the lineage.
O beloved, I shall further explain another [subject], the Convention of Flowers (*puṣpasaṃketaka*).
Flower is known as the fourth stage of mind, while the fifth is considered to be both.
The five sense-faculties, the five elements, and the five gates—
this is the supreme, divine flower, O beloved, which is common to all.
Because they cause the ancient beings, such as Puṃgala and others, to unite with one another and sustain the entire world, they are therefore proclaimed as "Puṣpas."
Thus, O Goddess, has the characteristic of Puṣpa itself been described;
now I shall further proclaim another, the supreme triad of Guha’s lineages.
O fair-faced one, there are three renowned cavities situated within the body;
I shall tell you of that divine, secret, most hidden, and unspeakable [reality].
Kadaṃba is the first goddess, Siddhā is the second, and the third goddess is Guhā; she is honored among all spiritual accomplishments.
O Goddess with the face of the best of Siddhas, when [the syllable] *kadaṃ* is situated in the middle of the mouth at the navel, it is called the *bhaga*; O Goddess, it is declared in the *Guhādevī*.
Thus has it been told to you, O fair-faced one,
regarding the cave and the divine nectar called "Go," which arises from the five jewels.
Therein, O Great Goddess, in the center is the supreme Aparikā lineage. Furthermore, I shall explain another characteristic of the secret convention (saṃketa).
One should gaze upward and behold the divine celestial mandala;
this is known as the convention of Jyeṣṭhanātha, O lady of excellent vows.
O Dear One, fixing the mind upon the heart, one should gaze with downward vision at that which resides within the circle at the tip of the nose, emitting divine splendor.
O lady of excellent vows, this is the well-known convention of Vālanātha:
[the thumb] with the middle finger and the little finger, O fair-faced one.
The threefold convention of mudrās has been proclaimed as the teaching of Siddhanātha;
O Goddess of the Gods, at the time of worship, it bestows liberation through its mere sight.
I shall further proclaim the characteristics of the secret convention of the sacred seats (pīṭha):
O Dear One, having placed [the breath] at the opening of the whirlwind of space, one arrives at the state of the blink of an eye.
Oṃ! The secret convention of the sacred seat (pīṭha) is most dear to the Yoginīs.
O Goddess, one should cast the supreme gaze toward the right ear.
The secret sign of Jālapīṭha, beloved by the accomplished yoginīs, is to fix one's gaze upon the left ear; this is the dear arising of Pūrṇapīṭha.
This is the well-known convention in the Siddhayogeśvarī-mata:
O Dear One, one should place the gaze there at the end of the nose, which is the form of desire.
For him who knows the secret convention, all desires bear fruit;
O blessed one, the secret convention of the seats (pīṭhasaṃketaka), which is difficult to obtain, has been told to you.
O Goddess, it bestows all accomplishments and is the supreme producer of good fortune;
it must be guarded with effort—this is the command of the Supreme Lord therein.
I shall further proclaim another, O fair-faced one: the seat-mudrā.
Having formed a fist with both hands, O Goddess, O beloved, extend the thumbs.
This is the Oṃkāra-pīṭha-mudrā, practiced by the Siddhayoginīs;
O Goddess of Gods, having extended both hands, the fingers are made sparse [and spread apart].
This is the mudrā of Jālapīṭha; by binding it, the Yoginī shall be pleased. O Beloved, having formed the two hands like a water-pot together with the fingers.
This is the mudrā of Pūrṇapīṭha; by binding it, one burns away all impurity. Having formed both hands like a triangle, with the two index fingers level [and joined].
This is the Kāmarūpiṭha mudrā; by it, one becomes dear to amorous women.
The index finger should be directed upward, slightly curved at the back.
O Goddess, this is the secret sign and mudrā of Khecarī, the vision of equanimity. Furthermore, O fair-faced one, I shall explain another [topic]: the abode and the state of existence.
That which rests within the womb of the triple-womb, arising from the wheel of passion (raticakra),
and is cultivated as that which is called Kulakaula— that is proclaimed to be the "House" (gṛha).
Having established themselves through the mind in that realization, which is free from the duality of existence and non-existence,
they sport within the Kula tradition, the undecaying abode of consciousness.
I shall further proclaim the characteristics of birth itself:
the various distinct descents within the fourfold noble expanse of space.
O Goddess, [I shall describe] the power within our lineage, as well as the eastern, western, southern, and northern [directions], O Goddess, which have attained the form of desire.
O fair-faced one, because of my affection for you, I shall explain in brief this secret question— more secret than the secret— which must be guarded with great effort.
The secret of all scriptures, the supreme heart of the sacred tradition,
this knowledge passed from mouth to mouth resides in the mouths of the Yoginīs.
This *Sārasamuccaya* is eternally protective of the conduct of the *khecarī*, possesses the unsurpassed conduct of the *kalā*, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Goddess of gods, O fair-faced one, this is the command of the Western Tradition (paścimāmnāya) and its sequence;
though it must be guarded with great effort, I shall nevertheless tell it to you.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the excellent teaching in its former full detail— the essence of the Yoginī doctrine, the tradition, and the Kula scripture.
I shall explain in brief the deity born of its own nature,
which resides within the Kulakaula and is the saffron-colored dawn of the white water-lily.
The goddess, whose nature is the bliss of self-awareness, has arisen there as that very locus;
she is divine, following the Kula conduct, and is the emergence of the Kula from within the womb of the Kula.
Therefore, the goddess Kuleśvarī is the maiden who consumes the *kula*;
wherever she is, the perfected ones (*siddhas*) desire the excellent hero again and again.
O Goddess, having established the descent of that place within the hermitage at the end of the sky, the deity [resides] there according to the sequence of the ancient lineage.
That Goddess, the sovereign of the three worlds, exists in three modes:
she is Candrinī and Bhāskarī, O fair-faced one, possessing intense radiance.
Caṇḍriṇī resides within the womb of the Moon, Bhāskarī from the midst of the Sun;
Tejotkaṭā and Vahnigarbhā are proclaimed as the three Maṭhikās.
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, Candriṇī emerged as Mīnanātha,
and Bhāskarī made her descent as Meṣapāda.
O beloved, Tejotkaṭā gave birth to Kūrmanātha as her own vessel;
O Goddess, she is Khageṃdranātha, the monastery of the half of space.
At that time, Madhyā emerged there before Paramānandabhairava;
by him, the entire universe was instructed in the supreme knowledge of the divine current.
The Maṭhikā is the lineage of the Siddhas, and the Vṛddha is said to be the Valli;
thus, O Goddess, has the Maṭhikā been described as the supreme root.
I shall explain in brief, O large-eyed one, the Lord Siddhanātha established by tradition, together with the sequence of his incarnations; listen.
In the first age, the supreme sovereign Kaulinī desires that humans attain perfection by practicing the union with the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) who has descended from the Tuṃvija.
While he was engaged in play there, giving rise to a continuous lineage,
Visala and Suśubha then performed their consecration.
Having gone to the state of the wheel-turner (cakravartin), having made their own lineage resplendent like the sky,
they indeed rejoice in the world, remaining within the sphere of their noble family.
The second was Kūrmanātha, and Maṅgalā was Jyoti;
by means of the Kulāmnāya of the Krīḍānātha lineage, two sons were born to them.
Ajita and Vijiteśa likewise established their lineage;
the third was Meṣapāda, together with Kāmamadgu.
The playground was closed for both of those who had attained perfection;
their lineage, consisting of two hundred descendants, was wonderfully united with the crescent moon of Brahmā.
Having established the extent and lineage of these within the three worlds,
the Lord of his own family [proclaimed] a family consisting of sixty-four [families].
O Goddess of the Suras, I shall explain in detail to you the accomplishment, the authority, the lineage, the union, and likewise the creeper (vallī).
In this most terrible age of Kali, that Lord named Piṅgala, who possesses four feet of authority, is the one who brings about this scripture.
He who grasped the entire essence of knowledge— the cause of liberation for all things moving and stationary—
and likewise deposited that knowledge within the ocean during the month of Kārtika.
Then, O Siddheśvara, worshipped with excellent offerings, that Krodha [shall deliver] sixty-four crores [of beings] from the ocean of existence to liberation.
First, O Goddess, there is no doubt that Kṣatrādhipa and Vaṭuka [should be worshipped];
and another has been mentioned by me in brief, but not in detail.
O illustrious one, the princess was worshipped by him with saffron;
though she was pure in her essence, she was rendered impure, and he indeed dallied with her.
Twelve sons, princes, were born, O most beloved;
I shall declare their names to you exactly as they are, O my Great Goddess.
Bhaṭṭasvāmarapāpa, Maheṃdravaradevaka,
Āheṃdra, Khageṃdra, and likewise Mahīdhara.
Guḍikānātha and Pāda—these twelve are proclaimed; as well as Amara, Varadeva, and likewise Citranātha.
The six types of pills (guṭikā) are proclaimed to consist of mercury, mica, and the three-footed [mercury];
O lady of excellent vows, their practice has been rendered continuous by those who possess authority.
I shall declare to you, O lady of excellent vows, each of those very knowledges individually;
they know that to be the place of accomplishment, the secret convention of Tripurottara.
O lady of beautiful hips, [the Liṅga] that grants desires belongs to Amaradeva;
Aṭṭahāsa belongs to Citra; Vaidavikoṭa belongs to Ali.
To the south of the Vindhya mountains is Kolāgirya, where Goḍika resides;
this is proclaimed as the place of assembly for all of them, intended for the purpose of milking [the earth].
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, I shall proclaim the six [observances];
I shall now describe separately the vow, the practice of begging, and the specific locations.
O beloved, that vow, which is the realization of the Lord of the Vallī lineage, is practiced there;
likewise, it is at Dubhāla-nagara in the southern direction of Śrīśaila.
O beloved, the Lord of Siddhas, remaining there, performs his conduct;
having bestowed the vow upon him, he is celebrated by the sages as "Vanannara."
O fair-faced one, O beloved, within that Śrāṃvilpā garden, a disease was seized;
by that very means, the vow was performed there by the sages.
Furthermore, O Great Goddess, having gone to Kaumārikukuṇḍa twelve years later, one should perform the practice there, O fair-faced one.
O beloved, she performed that vow in the city of Valī, which possesses the splendor of Śrīvaradeva;
likewise, there is the city of Kuṇḍina in the western direction of Śrīśaila.
Established there, the great sage performs his conduct and practices yoga;
having granted that place for his vow, she is the boon-bestower of Vidyānanda.
O Goddess, the one who observes the conduct of heroes attains the supreme divine siddhi,
and he sports wherever he may be together with the assembly of yoginīs.
O Great Goddess, Śrī Citranātha is proclaimed as Pādovallī;
likewise, there is Śrīśaila in the northern direction and Candanannagara.
O Great Beloved, Citranātha performs his ritual practice (caryā) while stationed in the thunderbolt (vajra);
where there is a bilva tree and its fruit, there is a garden in the center.
O Great Goddess, having bestowed the vow, the sage Kaulasiṃha likewise performed the practice of that vow in his own abode for the sake of the Great-Souled One.
O Great Goddess, in that mandala, Śrī Alinātha, together with Ānanda and Vallī, attains perfection in exactly twelve years.
O beloved, to the east of Śrīśaila is the village of Vālaka;
there is a *puṅgava* tree with fruit there, and in the middle of that place is a garden.
O lady of excellent hips, having bestowed that supreme vow,
Śṛṅgālamuni went to that supreme seat of Kāmarūpa, O great goddess.
O fair-faced one, one should perform the practice in its southern region,
having taken recourse to the site of Trikhaṇḍī, where the Siddha manifests his power.
O lady of virtuous vows, having observed a vow in that place for seven years,
the great sage, engaged in meditation, attains supreme bliss.
The great Māyā of Vindhyanātha is proclaimed as Yogavallī;
it is located at the great site of Śrīśaila, situated between the east, south, and center.
O Goddess, O fair-faced one, Piṇḍā performs her vow-practice in the midst of the Khaira grove within the city.
O lady of beautiful hips, having given the vow to the great sage Sāṇḍilya,
she followed him and performed the practice of the vow along with him.
O beloved, O dear one, Khecarī is joined with Bhūcarī and Sākiṇī;
she is celebrated as Oṃvallī in the lineage of Śrī Guḍikānātha.
O Great Goddess, on Śrīśaila, from the east, north, and center, there is the city of Goḍikā; there the ascetic performs his conduct.
Where there is a coconut fruit, there is a grove in its midst;
O beautiful woman, having performed the vow, the sage likewise beheld the lunar orb.
Thereupon, O Goddess, O lady of excellent vows, that great sage, the lord of yogis, remained engaged in his practice for eight years, steadfast in his observance.
Thus, O Goddess, has the sequence of the Ṣaḍovallī vow been told;
it is proclaimed as the Pūrvāmnāya according to its division within the lineage.
I shall now proclaim another [mantra], the southern, which is formidable and supreme;
it bestows great siddhi, is divine, and grants the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O fair-faced one, I shall now describe the incarnation of Kāmeśvarī;
she arises from the three seats, abides in the center, and conforms to the nature of reality.
Constantly dull-witted like the sun at dawn, yet possessing a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning,
they— driven by lust and desiring women— devour their own beloveds.
Therefore, O Goddess Kāmeśvarī, you are the Virgin (Kumārī), the consumer of the Kula,
the divine and supreme seat of desire (Kāmapīṭha), and the maṇḍala of the Lord of the Supreme Abode.
Having manifested as Kāmeśvarī and assuming the form of Kaumārī,
he, by his own nature and splendor, dissolved the circle of births.
By that [means], the family yoginī, possessing her own vigor and resolve,
proceeds; she bears a divine form, is peaceful, and is as pure as clear crystal.
She radiates with supreme splendor, a divine stream of flowing wisdom;
she has two arms, one face, and three eyes, with a slender waist.
The Yoginī Kaumārī, in the form of a maiden, is worshipped by the Siddhas;
having gone to the supreme site of the great pīṭha, Mount Mālinī.
The Goddess stands on his left side, while behind him is the cave,
the divine and most enchanting great place known as Kokila.
It was crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks and graced by *cakravāka* birds;
there were sky-faring and earth-dwelling *siddhas*, as well as *sākinīs* of divine form.
O Great Goddess, they dwell there in that most delightful place, within the divine mandala of the triangle, devoted to yoga and meditation.
In a cave within the orb of the moon, possessing a luster equal to the radiance of the moon,
that goddess Kumārī, who carries the semen, resides there.
O Great Goddess, you were established from of old for the sake of sages and ascetics;
O beloved, you are the sage, free from anger, grief, and fickleness, yet supremely fierce.
For a thousand divine years, ascetic penance was performed and perfected;
O great elder, your limbs were withered as you subsisted on air alone, having restrained the mind.
O beloved, having stood with her face turned inward, she should gaze upward;
O Goddess of the Lord of Gods, O Śukradevī of great asceticism, having thus beheld [the deity].
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, when you had reached the state of intoxication, the sages, through their divine splendor,
performed a divine transmission of knowledge for you, O Goddess.
Having gone to the realm of Kāmadeva, they bear divine forms as witnesses;
then, by the power of Kāmeśvarī, they become liquefied.
O Goddess, having combined these two seeds into one, it arises from the Rudrayāmala;
it is intensely radiant with divine splendor and bestows the fruit of divine desires.
O fair-faced goddess, having established the excellence of the power of the yoga of knowledge, O Goddess,
the Rudrayāmala was condensed by him [into] more than one hundred thousand verses.
O Great Goddess, O fair-faced one, through his own nature and by his own yoga, he is the powerful one within Vāgīśvarī; his son, O Great Goddess, is Kaulīśa.
Therefore, O beloved, that divine knowledge, which is extremely difficult to attain, has been brought down and taught for the sake of men bound by the cycle of karma and worldly existence.
I shall further proclaim another [teaching], the unsurpassed [mandala] of the deities,
which consists of the descent of Kāmeśvarī together with her retinue.
Hṛllekhā, Kledanī, Kaṇṭhī, and Manāturā would cause agitation; likewise Nirañjanā, Rāgavatī, and another, Madanāvatī.
Khecarā, Drāvaṇī, and likewise Vegavatī are recorded;
Ekāvasā is the goddess, while Madana is recorded as the twelfth.
O Great Goddess, having worshipped the six-cornered wheel pervading the fire-mandala with its closely set spokes, O fair-faced one.
On the eastern side, one should worship the divine Madana situated at the edge of the enclosure,
and in the center, one should worship the goddess Kāmeśvarī within the divine maṇḍala.
The eleven-syllable vidyā has been extracted from the Vajraprastāra;
O beloved, it consists of Madana joined with Sara, as received from the mouth of the Guru.
O Goddess, O fair-faced one, O lady of excellent vows, having worshipped the gatekeepers Kāma, Vaṃtakaka, Rati, Śukra, Vāma, and Dakṣiṇaka.
The Goddess said:
And tell us, O Great Lord, the supreme characteristics of the deities,
their ultimate resting places, and their respective individual designations.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the secret convention of the deities; I shall explain to you their names, designations, essential natures, and origins from the perspective of the inner self.
From the heart, one should contemplate the orb of the Sun, Moon, and Soma situated within the interior;
there the supreme Goddess arises, who is to be inscribed in the heart and consists of the imperishable consciousness.
Śiva-śakti as well as Rudrā constitute the threefold moistening essence;
flowing with the quintessential nectar of supreme immortality, she is considered to be Kledanī.
She dwells within the hollow of the hexagon, within the circle of the *śṛṅgāṭaka*,
delighting in the sound of bliss, while the excellent resonance of rest resounds there.
Within the center of the wheel of desire (icchā-cakra), one should awaken the interior of space;
there, the eternal Kāmakalā, known as the "Arouser," should cause arousal.
When, through the immersion into the two voids,
she flows forth as the nectar of bliss, then, like the full moon on the day of the full moon, she becomes afflicted with passion.
Within the great womb is the wheel of three syllables, born from the essence;
there, in the center, the stainless sun of awakening has arisen.
O Dear One, having placed the lunar disc between the fire and the sun within the cave,
and having made it the seat of passion for the beloved, she then flows from that [disc].
O Madanāvati, [this] is filled with incomparable joy and crowded with desire, having entered into one desire after another and situated in the midst of the circle of desires.
The goddess who is the stream of bliss, the essence that pervades all,
she should be known as the digit of space (khakalā), who bears the embryo of the moon within her womb.
The solar disc is rested within the midst of the threefold arising;
one should bind the lunar digit of consciousness (citkalā), which is known as the "melting" [state] when it has been liquefied.
When the sign of fear in the Moon was churned forth by the risen god of love,
then, according to its power, the divine flood was known as Vegavatī.
The differentiation of Śiva’s crescent moon has dissolved, giving rise to the awakening of passion;
by that, he pierces and delights [the heart], causing the divine sprout to emerge.
But the sprouts, diverse and distinguished by their differences, arise from Prakṛti;
at that time, he is the pervasive, eternal one, whose nature consists of the essence of passion.
The Goddess said:
How does the divine Vāgīśvarī become Tripurā? How is the Goddess called Vāgbhavī? And how indeed is she Nityā, the possessor of all enjoyments?
O Bhagamālinī, O Lord, how does she pierce through the triad of liṅgas?
Out of your grace, please tell me the power of Kāmeśvarī.
Bhairava said:
O beloved, I shall tell you this most secret question concerning the origin of all that is eternal— the fierce, southern Self.
One should create a mandala of throbbing *śṛṅgāṭas* (triangular diagrams) within the three divisions;
O Dear One, therein arises the emergence of the essence-less, born from debate.
Viśvamālinī is said to have four divisions beginning with Parā;
therefore, Vāgīśvarī is eightfold, piercing through the Kula.
She is the supreme power of the three natures, untainted by poison or desire;
she is without marks yet possesses marks, and is proclaimed to have three divisions.
Tripurā is to be known as peaceful, she who is the Bhairavī of one's own bliss;
she resides within the cave of the universe of the moon and showers the nectar of the flow of semen.
Self-blissful and her own eternal Nityā, she dissolves the distinctions of the *liṅga*s;
abiding within the *śṛṅgāṭa* maṇḍala, she is the enjoyer of the *bhaga* and the dawning of the *bhaga*.
Bhagamālinī, along with Sasanityā, is the consumer of the five causes;
anything else is said to be poison, proclaimed as the arrow of desire.
One should perform the recitation (japa) three times, characterized by the seed-syllable of one's own origin;
according to the distinction of facing westward, whatever [form] belongs to whichever linga.
Resorting to that state, it sets in motion the sovereignty of desires;
thus, O Goddess, has been described the supreme Ghoradakṣiṇa.
I shall further proclaim another supreme oral tradition (āmnāya),
the tranquil state of Svarodaya, which is the foundation of birth and the shatterer of [karmic] bonds.
There, O Goddess, the Kalā Kālī has arisen, the devourer of the Kaulikas;
she is the Kaulācāra, the womb of the Kaulas, the source of the Kaulas, and the Trikaula.
Therefore, the goddess Kāmeśvarī, the maiden who consumes the *kula*,
having made her descent there, [remains] at that place where you, O sage, are situated.
The supreme station Khaṇḍinī, the highest knowledge free from activity, has been declared; the transition of the Creator into the King of Wrath has been performed.
The supreme oral tradition, the divine stream, established in the lineage transmitted from ear to ear,
is clearly elucidated here through the two verses of the *Saṃpradāya*.
O Goddess, that which has come from the mouth of the Guru is characterized solely by one's own direct experience;
it is Kālī, the transmission of the skull-cup, the supreme state beyond words.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Dakṣiṇāmnāya section of the Nirvāṇapada within the venerable Vārāhī Tantra.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, how is the division of Kālī [explained], and how are there remembered as exactly twelve?
O Lord, what is the oral tradition (mukhāmnāya), and by what means is its transmission [attained]?
"Tell me, O Lord, out of your grace, so that I may be satisfied.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme Kālikā-krama;
O auspicious one, I shall now declare the tradition consisting of exactly twelve [parts].

Yoganidrā, whose supreme pervasiveness is never lost and who, though divided by differentiation, is self-luminous and beyond the reach of words— she enters into [the heart] through the mouth of the Guru.
And one obtains great knowledge through the King of Vidyās, O observer of good vows;
once the renowned King of Wrath has been mastered, one may subsequently abandon the vidyā.
I shall speak of the great gnosis; listen, O observer of good vows, for it is beyond action.
It is the lamp of the sun in the world, emerged from the very center of the sun.
Just as the sun, having entered within the orb of the sun, illumines the entire world, so too does that Kaulinī who is of the nature of light; the entire world is surrounded by her mass.
Therein arose the great mantras, the eight Bhairavas and their eight sources; the goddess Ravibhānumayī, the mistress of Kaula, who dwells in the abyss of Akula.
But at the cessation of the bliss of agitation, she beholds the lineage of Kula within the ocean of the great void of Śiva, in the solar orb, from the center of the sacrificial pit.
There, all those Bhairavas, numbering sixty-four, were dissolved;
for within the solar *kuṇḍa*, the wheel of dissolution exists by its very nature.
When that [state] has dissolved, there arises from it the nature known as one's own true nature;
then, for the embodied being who perceives, there is the destruction of both existence and non-existence, and he becomes the exhausted one.
She is both conscious and non-conscious because she possesses existence; she is pure and has a belly as vast as the earth.
The wheel arisen from her essential nature stands fixed in the movement of the sun of consciousness.
It appears like the morning sun, solely intent upon swallowing the orb [of the night].
The Nakula is the Kaulinī Śakti; therefore, it is not an arising from its own nature.
It is neither the dissolution of dissolution; divine and the enjoyer of all pleasures is she.
Will, which exists as non-different from the attribute of pure consciousness, is the emanation of that which is omnipresent; I shall now speak to you of its dissolution.
When the form born of bliss is not grasped by the flavor,
and when that [bliss] has subsided therein, it becomes the object of that mental modification.
With its functions exhausted, it becomes supremely wonderful due to its dissolution;
it is a triangle situated within a triangle, possessing a beautiful aperture and extending toward a beautiful aperture.
The mind, dissolved in the bliss of the void-of-voids, is accumulated within another state of consciousness;
in the invocation of beginningless consciousness, it experiences kissing and other such acts within the abode of the tongue.
When consciousness, having withdrawn the senses from their mutual engagement according to their sequence,
abandons one state and does not grasp another state, [that is the moment of transition].
Then that supreme Brahman proceeds according to its own inherent nature;
this is the perfected Kaula nectar proclaimed by the Yoginīs.
And it has been fully revealed upon the earth by the feet of Niṣkriyānanda. The Goddess said:
To whom indeed was it told, O Lord, on the ground of actionless bliss?
To whom was the divine Mahākālikrama transmitted, and through what transmission?
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the lineage of him whose lineage it was:
the son of that best of sages Śilācita, who was rich in asceticism.
O Goddess, devoted to the practice of yoga, bearing the excellent form of a Siddha,
he is renowned as Vidyānanda, the most eminent among the great-souled, O Beloved.
O dweller of the cremation ground, ever-abiding, supremely devoted to devouring;
O lord of perfected yoga, O heroes, you who delight in the movement of the wheel!
O Great Goddess, Śrīśaila is the beloved deity and the seat of Śiva;
to its northern direction lies a mountain with various peaks.
There, in that divine cave honored by siddhas and gods, she made an offering of gold and silver;
having performed that propitiation there, she attained the most excellent knowledge.
The lord of yogis, desiring actionless knowledge, performs devotion;
having assumed a form with excellent limbs, he manifests an exceedingly intense and divine devotion.
He [pleased] that best of sages, the supreme Śrī Niṣkriyānanda;
his own infallible speech transmitted the Kālikākrama.
The left-hand path (vāmamārga) has been described as having a sequence of five or six stages;
O Pārvatī, listen as I explain their distinctions in their entirety.
O Bhavā, from the differentiated [reality] up to the end of the wheel of existence, the sky has arisen from the sky;
she is the twelve-fold digit of light-time, whose form is space and who is the devourer.
Vibrating with a faint sound, that [state] is diminished and belongs to the divine sphere;
it is the sequence of the dissolution of dissolution, following the lineage of the traditional transmission.
Having touched one's own family, that which transcends one's own family, one's own state, and that which is beyond one's own state,
the divine Kālikrama has arisen as the Oṃgha-maṇḍala.
The sphere of the rising sun of consciousness, situated at the end of the *umanmana* [state],
flashes forth as a stream of nectar (*rasa*) that permeates all directions in a gradual sequence.
Having pierced the divine state of awakening, which is beheld by the sun of awakening,
and having dissolved it with the rays of consciousness, one drinks its supreme essence.
The supreme space, whose nature is consciousness, is devoid of both existence and non-existence;
within it, the supreme space, which is the essence of bliss, unfolds.

Therefore, O Kālī, you who arise from the splendor of the Supreme Lover, you are painted with the manifold variety of objects that delight your own self-expansion, and you are intent upon the indestructible.
The infinite, sevenfold, resting, and self-arisen consciousness, rising from the sky as a flood of radiant, expanding light, forcibly impels the bound soul.
The thought that transcends the states of *bhaga* and *bhaga-pada* is the supreme doctrine;
it is the sequence (*krama*) of the *Kula-kula-āmnāya*, the sphere of the application of the Yoginīs.
Desire for one object of desire after another, passion for one form of brilliance after another,
and enjoyment of one pleasure after another— this is proclaimed as the application of the intellect.
Rudra and Rudra-śakti together, through devotion, [attain] that;
he is Rudra, the dissolver, Kha in Khe, Kaṃ in Kā, Ke in Kulakaulika.
Situated within the liquid of the Śakti-maṇḍala during the yoga of contemplation at the end of Śiva,
that embodied *piṇḍa* becomes perfected, the abode of form, which brings about the state beyond all forms.
With the *āla*, *mūla*, *uttarāsaṅga*, and *vottara* as his upper garments, and with the intervals [between them] filled,
he sits upon the mind-throne, having attained the immersion (*samāveśa*) into the power of Rudra, as taught by the Siddhas.
In the tradition of our own school, the gnosis residing in the mouth of the Guru is attained;
the realization of the Sun of Awakening is transmitted from ear to ear in the lineage.
The Kaulinī, who rejoices in the bliss of consciousness within the expanse of the inner sky,
flashes forth as the blossoming of the supreme radiance of that very nature.
Through the power of the Kaula-skeleton, she whose form devours all that is consumed;
she is Kālī, dark as collyrium, formidable, and risen like the twelve suns.
Transcending both sequence and non-sequence, traverse the transition that is the Kālikākrama;
the supreme vibration, the unnameable heat, flashes forth within.
Situated in the midst of the wheel of consciousness and insentient matter, experienced through yogic sleep,
and having entered the void within the void, he does not perceive that which is of the nature of the Kula.
The expansion of the wheel of Kālī is an incomparable, supreme radiance, the consciousness of the state of the essential nature in which the leftward flow of consciousness has been dissolved within.
All the deities beginning with Brahmā and ending with Bhairava are proclaimed [to dissolve];
and they merge into the supreme radiance, condensed by the fire of time.
The supreme secret of the space of consciousness, proclaimed as the Sun of the Family,
richly endowed with twelve spokes and possessing a radiance equal to many suns.
That mind reveals the life-sustaining vitality of the living being;
by means of various applications of that very [vitality], it forcibly slays the animal.
O Goddess, having forcefully transcended the state of blissful union between Śiva and Vāmā, one should worship the formless Supreme Power (Parāśakti).
Beyond the sky is the arisen state of space, the solar sequence,
rich with the splendor of a thousand flames, which devours the three worlds as its prey.
Having meditated upon the fire of consciousness within the center of the three abodes,
he overcame the poison with its lack of poison and consumed the Kālakūṭa.
The lineage, the lineage, the tradition of the lineage; the essence, that which arises from the essence; the state, that which transcends word and the object of words; the supreme station of Kaula.
Abiding in the womb, the pregnant one, the womb, the progenitor of the five wombs;
the single perfection, the three base ones, effort, and the Mālinī sequence.
The stainless locus of the vowels and other phonemes is divided by passion;
that is the supreme ground of rest, illuminated by the fire of time.
O Awakening, awakening awakens itself through its own awakening, which is awakened by nothing else;
through the differentiation of the movement of the wheel, they pass into one another.
Just as one who has ascended to the summit of the sky traverses the highest void by means of his own level,
so too, through the force of his vigor, he moves from one subtle essence to another even more subtle essence.
Having abandoned right time, wrong time, and their own specific time, resting happily,
the yogi sports in that bliss upon touching the mandala of the fire of consciousness within the mind.
Form is both form and non-form; its own nature is devoid of form.
It is liberated from existence and non-existence, arisen from all things, and partless.
There, the supreme goddess Kālī, the devourer of skeletons, has arisen;
having drunk from the vessel of the skeleton-stalk the nectar born of the sky.

Those who have been whirled around and made to vomit by him [the poison]— the yogi, established in the nature of his own abode and enveloped by the power of yoga, [renders them free from] the origin of all things.
Having extracted the essence of the root-caves, he who investigates the Great Sequence (Mahākrama),
having tasted the supreme, drunk the supreme, seen the supreme, and arisen from the supreme;
Having thus become of equal flavor, the investigator of the Kālikrama [perceives] the eon imagined at the end of an eon,
and the eon imagined by the Kula-eon.
The wheel of time is indivisible, and the manifest mandala has arisen;
it consists of the gross, the subtle, and likewise the void, wherein the three consciousnesses have dissolved.

There, a certain woman named Viśvā, who delights in the supreme bliss and is intent on the attainment of the All, [abides] in the station of the imperishable Bindu and Nāda, within the circle of the plane of consciousness where all has subsided.
One should meditate upon her of divine origin, the fivefold womb of the Siddhas,
who dwells within the digit of Mahākāla, the digit that brings about the wheel of time.
Therefore she is renowned as Kālī, the devourer of skeletons and time;
she is the consciousness that has consumed the wheel of existence and non-existence, which is the true nature of all things.
The arising of the Kālikrama, throbbing with the joy of the awakening to its own flavor,
dissolves into the supreme state, resonating like the humming of wandering bees.
Therein, the lord of yogis, having attained the state of *udgalita* (the outflowing), becomes dear to the yoginīs;
with his stainless awakening fully rested, he pierces the circle of the sky.
Based on the division of the Kula and Kālī, it relies upon the Niśrīṇa-krama; based on the division of the Kula and Kālī, it relies upon the Niśrīṇa-krama.
Like the womb and so forth, the word *garbha* is the destroyer of worldly existence (*bhaga*) and the liquefier of worldly existence;
it is the bliss of the great consciousness-lotus and the blossoming sun of awakening.
Laughing, playful, and graceful, moving here and there while splashing the water, the Heroine draws [the devotee] from afar; O Kālī, perform the worship of the feet of the Krama.
When the abandonment of what is to be discarded and the grasping of what is to be adopted have both ceased through their respective distinctions,
the knower of reality, observing this state, shall illuminate it with the sun of wisdom.
The wheel arisen from the universal form illuminates the entire world through its maintenance;
it is the splendor that withdraws the universe, and its brilliance devours all other light.
Violently transgressing the gradual sequence by various wrong paths,
the Kramika yogi acts as a Sadyogi, beloved by the Yoginīs.
The devourer of its own side, whose eyes are unimpaired as they range over the objects of perception,
it is the ever-arisen, manifest expansion of bliss, vibrating with the delight of the whirling dance.
When one has reached the supreme realization of one's own awakening through the reversal of existence and non-existence,
and is firmly established in that state of rest, it is attained swiftly from the mouth of the Guru.
Neither below nor above, neither in the middle, nor outside, nor even inside.
Wherever there is the forgetting of pride, O Kālī, there arises the sequence;
this has been taught on earth by the venerable Niṣkriyānandanātha along with his consort.
The fifty-day [practice] has been taught, O Goddess; it is the supreme Kālikākrama.
The Goddess said:
I have heard from the Lord the entire manual of the Kālikākrama,
the knowledge of the assembly of Siddhas, which has come down through the lineage of oral tradition.
Even now, O Lord, I remain in doubt regarding what was stated by you in the form of a question:
"How can the name and designation 'Dvādaśārkaprabhākālī' come to be?"
"O Lord, this indeed is my narrative, accompanied by the mantra-worship.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the secret of the Kālikāgama;
it is to be kept hidden, O most auspicious one, yet nevertheless I shall tell it to you.
Sṛṣṭikālī, Sthitikālī, and Saṃhārakālī as the third;
Raktakālī is the fourth, and Sūkālī is remembered as the fifth.
Yamakālī is the sixth, Mṛtyukālī is the seventh,
Bhadrakālī is the eighth, and Paramārka is remembered as the ninth.
Mahāmārtaṇḍakālī is proclaimed as the tenth;
Rudrakālī is the eleventh, and Mahākālī is the twelfth.
O Goddess, this sequence of divisions is proclaimed as the designations of the names:
she who is by nature her own essential form, and she who devours the void at the end of the void.
Having worshipped with the mantra *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, she who is eternally manifest in the twelve-spoked [wheel] is the supreme Goddess in the center, the maiden who devours the *kula*.
O Beloved, having worshipped up to the twelve [finger-breadths] according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should likewise worship the lineage of gurus (gurupañkti) that has descended through the traditional succession.
On the exterior, however, one should likewise place the sequence on the middle and the back.
Bhairava said:
I shall further proclaim another, the supreme lineage of the West—
born from the family-festival of the family, yet beyond family and devoid of family.
O Goddess, the place where she has arisen there is clearly *pida*, *cicci*, and *cinī*;
it is the flood (*ogha*) of floods, the bliss of the digits (*kalānanda*), and that which has emerged from the womb.
Therefore, O Goddess Kubjeśvarī, the Virgin who consumes the *kula*,
having taken an incarnation for the sake of bestowing grace, O Queen of Gods, O fair-faced one!
The Supreme Goddess has emerged from the descent at Candradvīpa;
O Queen of the Gods, this has been told in brief and not in detail.
This essence of the Śrīkubjikāmata has been explained by you in detail,
including the secret tradition of the lineage (*janmāmnāya*) endowed with the four *gharas*.
O fair-faced one, out of great affection for you, I have related this supreme and divine [teaching]. Now I shall further proclaim another unsurpassed account of the fame of the Siddhas.
Listen as I proclaim the glory of the Lord Trigarbhodayanātha,
by whom the *ciñciṇī* tree was split at the great sacred site of Mātrīvana.
Furthermore, one should perform the rite of raising [the deity], following the sequence for the renown and fame of the second Lord Kīrti, whose *bilva* tree was split asunder.
Furthermore, O lady of excellent vows, one should perform the rite of raising [the deceased] by means of the divine Kaula;
this is the third [rite], well-expounded by Kīrtinātha, the Vidyādhara.
O Goddess, having cast the pill into the great heat [of the fire], one should cause it to be swallowed;
by bathing in the lake named Ciñcinī, one shall attain the power of moving through the air.
O lady of excellent vows, having subsequently favored that Vidyādhara right there, she grants him the power of moving through the sky; by means of this, O Supreme Goddess, he shall attain fame.
And having constructed other ponds, O beloved,
you favored that best of nāgas named Vitaṅkaṭanu.
The power of command (ājñāsiddhi) is proclaimed to have the form of an unbroken circle;
O Goddess, it pierces a bound soul (paśu) for a hundred yojanas in an instant.
Thus, O Goddess, has the sequence of the *Siddhakīrti* been told;
now, O Beloved, I shall further explain another matter, the threefold authority (*adhikāra*).
O Goddess with long eyes, listen to the triad of *ovallis*;
they are declared to be of six types: *trimūrti* and *trigarbha*.
O Goddess, I have explained the lineage of succession as being superior, middling, and inferior;
now I shall further declare another characteristic of the six streams (ṣaṭśrotas).
One should know sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth; the mind is to be understood as the sixth, and that is proclaimed as the object of hearing.
But by me, the pervasive power (śakti) residing within the interior of all bodies is described as having six modes and piercing the sixteen supports (ādhāras).
O Goddess, she resides within the midst of the path of three hundred thousand [yojanas] inside the five voids;
pervading the six cakras, she is remembered as the speech of all beings.
The wind is situated within the channel; the ether is situated within the wind;
power is situated within the ether; and Śiva is situated within power.
"There is nothing higher than Śiva"—this is the command of the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, I shall explain another [matter]: the determination of the five questions.
O Goddess, [I shall explain] the emergence from the mandala, the mandala of the goddess, the sequence of the mandala,
the affliction of the mandala, and likewise the twenty-seven mandalas.
I shall explain in brief; listen, O lady with long eyes!
That which is called the "Progression of the Maṇḍala" is the crossing over to the supreme essential nature, my dear.
The maṇḍala of rest is to be known as the arising of the sequence of bliss;
one should apply the light of manifesting consciousness through the successive stages.
By means of such a procedure, one becomes worthy of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
In the western part of the mandala, one should worship the accomplishment named Madana.
In the north, preceded by the maṇḍala of existence named Sahaja,
one should worship the maṇḍala of non-existence in the southern direction.
In the center of the Krama-maṇḍala, one should likewise worship the pentad:
Ananta, Mahat, Vyoman, Śūnya, and Akhaṇḍamaṇḍala.
The three worlds, full as a jar and likewise inexhaustible;
the solar mandala of radiance, and the lunar and fiery mandalas.
O Dear One, there is the five jewels, the triangle,
and again the five principles (pañcatattva), the five voids, the triple emptiness, and the maṇḍala of the Self.
O Goddess, [there are] the Vyāptimaṇḍalaka, as well as the Ajapavijaya;
O Beloved, [there are] the Kulakaula, the Siddhaguru, and the Yoginīmaṇḍala.

O lady of good vows, although there is indeed a distinction in name due to such consideration of ritual procedure, one should worship according to the Krama-vākya; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
One should fashion the altars (*vedi*) from slightly cooked, well-ground flour, raised to the height of a cubit;
the lamps, however, should be shaped like a *maruka* flower, triangular, and very beautiful.
One should perform [this] nine, seven, or five times for those who grasp the clarified butter of the extraction;
having unified the internal radiance with the external radiance, they become of measured luster.
Having circumambulated three times, O Goddess, one should offer the lamp of the Kula.
O Goddess, Sovereign of all the wheels, endowed with [all powers], O Ambika!
O Goddess, accept this *ārātrika* for my spiritual accomplishment.
Having displayed the family lamps, one should then perform the worship of Śakti;
furthermore, I shall explain again [the rite] preceded by the consumption of the lamp.
O Goddess of excellent vows, listen as I describe the sequence of the *arghapātra* vessel:
it is the lamp situated between the rising of the moon and the sun, the source of the manifestation of the universe.

O Goddess, in the circle of the support (dhāramaṇḍala), concentration (dhāraṇā) is the wick of bliss, casting a shadow that is the illuminating oil, nectar, and the arising of the essence of supreme bliss.
One should kindle that light— the lamp of knowledge, inherently pure, which speaks through the illumination of the *bindu*—
and one should illuminate the external lamp with that radiance.
Having prepared it with rice flour, one should cause it to be offered in the presence of the ritual sequence—
well-mixed, stainless, pure, filled with oil, and most beautiful.
And one should worship according to the rule and in sequence, O beloved of the Krama;
then the Khecarīs, Siddhas, Mahābhairava, and Bhairavī shall be pleased.
O Goddess of the Gods, by lighting a lamp, they indeed become present;
likewise, through song, instrumental music, dance, and devotion dedicated to hymns of praise.
O Dear One, one should pray for the sacrificial oblation (caru) with a prostration of eight limbs;
furthermore, O Goddess, one should receive it and worship it again and again.
O fair-faced one, he should cause [the disciple] to consume the divine *caru*, which bestows supreme good fortune and destroys the sins committed in previous births.
Afterwards, one should explain the lamp while observing the perspective of others;
by concentrating the two fires into one, the performed karma will certainly be consumed.
Having covered it with a cloth so that it may remain free from obstacles,
one should then consume that lamp which illuminates the path.
It should be made with rice flour mixed with jaggery;
it should be shaped like a whirlwind or a triangle, and four finger-breadths in height.
Alternatively, O Goddess, O Beloved, one should fashion a triangle measuring three finger-breadths;
it pacifies all obstacles and wards off all suffering.
One should extract the Kramadīpa, which pacifies all afflictions;
it is the goddess Kumārī, worshipped, dark-complexioned, and fair-eyed.
One should worship him, seated upon the throne of space, with eyes rolling in intoxication, drenched by the drinking of heroes, adorned with garlands of flowers, according to the prescribed ritual.
O Goddess, one should meditate upon her in the sphere of the sky as possessing such a form: four-armed, single-faced, three-eyed, and of divine appearance.
One should entreat the Kumārī and Sukumārī, who have descended through the lineage of the Kula and Kaula traditions,
with various hymns of praise, and prostrate before them with the eight limbs of devotion.
Afterwards, having lit a lamp, one should offer the beautiful woman;
the splendor arising from her face—that very splendor—one should cause to issue forth as the lamp.
The presence of the deity should be bestowed within the sequential maṇḍala;
she manifests in various forms, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Vāmālāmā is indeed Sākinī; Khecarī is known as Bhairavī.
O Goddess, she who is dancing is the mandala of the sequence of manifestation (prakāśakrama).
Thus has been described the characteristic of the lamp, which has come down through the sequence of ritual injunctions;
it should be guarded with effort and not given to just anyone.
Through the observance of the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*), eternal accomplishment (*siddhi*) comes to be.
First, the vessel should be filled with wine (*ali*) and provided with the *śiva* flower.
"O Goddess, if she were worthy, she would have become happy from the joy born of both.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, what kind of light (*jyotis*) should be employed by the practitioner?
Please explain with favor so that [the practitioner] may become free from doubt.
Bhairava said:
And Jyoti, Subhagākāyā, Śīlaśuddhā, Tapasvinī,
Svabhāvaratā, Nandā, Sukrādyā, Śubhagā, and Priyā.
She whose nature is security, who has subdued anger, who speaks the truth, and who utters pleasant words;
she who delights in the sequence of worship, who is devoted to the sequence, whose piercing is the sequence, and whose arising is the sequence.
O Goddess, she who delights in the sequential practice, who moves according to the sequence with beautiful movement,
and who is well-guarded during the time of sacrifice— if she is in her menses, she is the Samayā.
"Then one attains perfection; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Furthermore, O Dear One, I shall explain another [method] regarding restraint and grace."
The support of the body, the womb of the body, the end of the body, and that which has emerged from the body—
the entire universe, all-pervading and omnipresent, he knows as pervading that very body.
Through the various sequences of movement,
they transmit to one another the oral tradition and the secret teaching of the Yoginī lineage.
Churned by the great churning-stick, it is pierced by the Wheel of Time;
its own vowels and the essence of fire flash forth in the sequence of Ciñciṇī.
The Supreme Self, which is the stainless flood of the throbbing mind and free from all seeking,
should touch the mandala of the divine flood by means of its own nature, devoid of any external entry.
O auspicious one, that face which is born is the face of supreme grace;
O lady of excellent vows, I shall now fully explain the suppression according to the distinctions of the mantras.
And the first letter of the name of the Goddess has been extracted, O Supreme Goddess.
O Dear One, the Ulaka and Sahavarṇa mantras consist of twenty-five syllables each;
they are mounted upon fire, joined with wind, and endowed with the power of Rudra.
The supreme seed-syllable of withdrawal (saṃhāra), joined with the half-moon and the bindu,
consisting of three syllables of the color of nectar— O woman of excellent complexion, [this is] for all.
The mantra is very long, consisting of thirty-three syllables, excellent,
and composed of all the initial letters of the Goddess's names, joined with the letter following 'Pa'.
O Great Goddess, joined with that [mantra] and accompanied by the eleven,
one should utter the collection of the names of the goddesses as conjoined with the *Śrīpūrva*.
This is the supreme, divine mantra, the sovereign lord of all mantras;
it is the goddess Tribhuvaneśvarī, the destroyer of even the Great Destruction.
The group of six known as Nigraha has been described as being solely intent upon devouring the universe;
O lady of excellent vows, I shall now tell you of the group of six consisting of the Seed-syllable and Bhaya.
The ascetic Śakti, residing within the twelve [fingers], exists in the form of seed-syllables;
through the distinction between creation and withdrawal, she arises in the sequence of short and long vowels.
O Dear One, through the division of the twelve vowels, there is the short, the long, and the protracted;
the six short vowels follow the sequence of the Moon, while the long vowels belong to the Sun.
"O lady of virtuous vows, both [the mantras] and the six seed-syllables have been explained to you.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the *Śrīvārāhītantra*, within the section on Nirvāṇa in the Dakṣiṇāmnāya. 19.
Bhairava said:
I shall further proclaim another [rite], the beloved *caru-mudrā*, as well as the divine casting of the gaze; listen, O lady of virtuous vows, for I shall speak.
Having thoroughly cleaned the small area and smeared it with cow dung,
one should offer water for honor (*argha*) and flowers, burn incense, and spread sesame and mustard seeds.
Having washed the divine sacrificial porridge (caru), it is offered into the consecrated fire.
Taking a tawny-eyed cow, one should cast beautiful rice [into the fire];
or else, O Dear One, one should prepare the *caru* oblation with whatever substance is available.
O Dear One, the practitioner should prepare the divine caru with the highest, lowest, and middle [ingredients] in a state free from conceptual construction; then it is to be washed again.
Having applied a beautiful ointment, one should worship with flowers, incense, and water offerings;
then, having carefully covered it with cloth, it should be brought into the sacrificial pavilion.
O Dear One, sprinkle [the area] with the Astra-mantra and salute your own mudrā;
by the casting of the supreme gaze (parā-dṛṣṭi), all obstacles are warded off.

O Dear One, after the practitioners have offered the oblation for the sequential mandala with the root mantra, they should then cause them to receive the *caru* which has been received with [the Guru’s] command.
Having covered the head with a cloth, one should then take the sacrificial porridge (caru);
this leads to the destruction of all obstacles and the exhaustion of all sins.
"One attains perfection without delay; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Furthermore, I shall explain another [topic], characterized by the constant and the occasional."
O beloved, you are eternally adorned with the wheel of consciousness, you delight in consuming the sacrificial pap,
and you are proclaimed as that whose movement is the eternal arising of the state of rest.
One should meditate upon one's own maṇḍala as the complete manifestation of consciousness,
until that which is to be known becomes nothing other than the form of the Bhallī deity.
The omen situated upon the Sun of Enlightenment has been described;
now I shall further declare another, which is remembered as the fourfold inquiry.
Initiation is the eldest, the station is the eldest, the command is the third eldest, and the lineage is indeed the fourth eldest; what more could be said here of its preeminence?
Within the womb of initiation and purification, through the constant radiance of the Command (ājñā),
they enter the supreme abode and attain the stage of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
Thus, O Goddess, one who maintains the order of seniority should reflect;
therefore, with every effort, the Krama is indeed worshipped as the most senior.
I shall further proclaim another [section]; listen, O you with long eyes:
the lamp, the sacrificial oblation, the flower, and the sequence of the ritual for the vessel of honor (arghapātra).
And for what kind of practitioner, O fair-faced one, is that [mantra] to be recited?
For a disciple who is well-disciplined, devoted to the guru, and wise.
For the hero who possesses faith, has conquered anger, and is free from desire;
for the speaker of truth and pleasant words, there is fearlessness even when surrounded by fear.
Experiencing the power [of the practice] through gradual devotion, he is a renunciant devoted to Dharma,
whose knowledge has entered into the interior of Bindu and Nāda, and who is ever intent on Yoga.
The disciplined one is devoted to the deities and prostrates with the eight limbs;
he is a performer of sacrifices, constant in his duties, a student of the Vedas, and an ascetic.
One who is endowed with the conduct of the samaya, devoted to the words of the guru,
knowing the nature of eternal bliss, steadfast, and following the path of the heroes;
One who is disciplined and delights in discipline is a vessel for the divine *cakra*;
one who knows the further shore of the lineage of the Siddhas is a vessel for the Western Tradition (*paścimāmnāya*).
Secure, supreme, and radiant, he is steadfast, a sun of awakening,
free from honor and dishonor, and desirous of the substance of a hero.
O fair-faced one, the sacrificial pap and the lamp should be given to such a person who is devoted to the conventions of moral conduct and who investigates the divine Kaula tradition.
By means of which the teacher may become worthy of success through the prescribed method of the Puṣpa-rite, he who desires accomplishment should then examine his qualities.
If that which is to be given is [bestowed] upon one devoid of qualities, there will be a loss of accomplishment;
therefore, the teacher should deliberate with every effort.
I shall explain its meaning again; listen attentively as I speak.
You have previously asked eleven questions, beginning with the question concerning the *praśna*.
O Queen of the Gods, I shall declare to you the supreme Western Tradition (paścimānvaya):
the knowledge of the Transmission (kramajñāna), this Knower of the Transmission, the Ornament of the Transmission, and the Arising of the Transmission (kramodaya).
One who has transcended the wheel is drawn away from the division of sequence and the emergence of sequence;
likewise, there is the attainment of sequence, the practice of sequence, the non-clan (akula), and the clan (kula).
O blessed lady, O lovely-faced one, I shall tell you this:
whatever is perceived between the two, the prāṇa and the apāna.
One should understand that sequential knowledge is a characteristic mark of abiding in one's own true nature;
therefore, through the state of direct experience, one should make one's very form dissolved into that.
When one finds nothing whatsoever to be known through sequential stages,
that vision which perceives the reality of things is devoid of the threefold division.
Having seen that, the yogi who marks the stages with his all-pervading song perceives one entity as empty of another entity, grasping at existence as arising from existence.
The conduct of existence, eternal, the conduct of reality, arising through the sequence;
the sixfold sequence, the pure division, that which arises everywhere.
Viśuddhi is divided into sixteen parts, while Anāhata has twelve;
Svādhisthāna consists of six, distinguished by ten sages.

There are four divisions of the support (ādhāra) and likewise two divisions of the command (ājñā). This most excellent and supreme division is declared to be the division of the sequence (krama-bheda).
Listen, O Goddess of Gods, to the sequence of the flood [of teachings] as I shall fully explain it:
the mandala situated within the womb of the supreme Vidyadhara.
The pervasive, the unmanifest family of pervasion, Ciñcinī whose form is radiant,
the flood of transmission, the lineage of transmission, arising from Śiva and Śakti.
By the command of the king of mantras, one should cause [the energy] to vibrate and pierce the circle of the Mothers;
the heart, the lotus of the Yoginī, and the throbbing circle of life-force.
The power of consciousness should gladden [the practitioner] and reveal the supreme reality;
having dissolved the five principles into that reality, the sphere of space is liquefied.
Upon attaining heart-bliss, five states arise:
bliss, the emergence of intense joy, trembling, sleep, and finally, the whirl.
"O Goddess of the gods, five states arise for one who knows reality.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, what is the nature of this state, and how does one's own experience come to be?
Please explain it out of your grace, so that I may be satisfied with you.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the auspicious characteristics of the states,
which first produce bliss and subsequently bestow supreme joy and inner happiness.
The divine stream with upward-pointing hairs proceeds as the power of command is accomplished;
the wheel of rays is melted and expanded through the aperture of the navel.
The yogi who is constantly immersed in the *dhvani* (resonance) is liberated from laughter and sound;
when this state arises, the accomplishment of the *ājñā* (command) proceeds.
One should fill the seventy-two thousand channels and apertures with one's own divine,
solid bliss, and cause the great body to tremble.
Moving upon the earth like the sky, one should crush the bonds of worldly existence;
this is the state of trembling, wherein the attainment of the Command (ājñāsiddhi) proceeds.
Having completely renounced all phenomena, one should enter the ground of peace.
The supreme grasping of the graspable and the grasper resides within the interior of space, like space itself.
Then there is the bliss of supreme joy, which awakens the self-consciousness within yogic sleep.
This indeed is the state of sleep; the perfection of the command proceeds.
Satisfied by these four states, the yogi is the shatterer of the cosmic egg.
Though eternally measuring [the world] as full of the essence of supreme bliss,
he performs the divine transmission of the command (*ājñā-saṃkramaṇa*), which is the highest cause of eternal joy.
This is the state of the rising of the *aghora*; the perfection of the *ājñā* proceeds. O Goddess, this state is said to be the power of Rudra by virtue of its majesty.
Through immersion in the power of Rudra, one's own mandala is perfected—
the ineffable, the unmanifest, the threefold reality that is without support.
Having opened the eyes, one's vision gazes upon that which resides within the unmanifest mandala, which transcends sequence yet arises from sequence.
In that state, when existence has been completely exhausted, the gradual practice is said to proceed;
even when all conceptual constructions have perished, eternal bliss continues to manifest.
The nature of consciousness turns back and the glory of liberation is accomplished;
the unmanifest mandala is to be known, for it is not obtained by one born of the manifest.
That which is liberated from the five elements is proclaimed as *makula*;
its shadow is the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), who is pure and possesses the attributes of that [Reality].
She is celebrated as Kula, from which arises the fruit of supreme bliss. Furthermore, I shall now declare another characteristic concerning the distinction of its designations.
The incomparable, the new convention, and the triad of *ku* syllables;
favor is to be known from the sixfold [set], while the designation of the Goddess consists of five.
The Trimūrti, the Trikasaṃjñā, that which is known as the Pāraṃparyaka,
and the Saptaviṃśati-saṃjñā— these, O fair-faced one, are its divisions.
I shall further proclaim the four characteristics of the festivals:
one should joyfully perform worship on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Phālguna.
The name of Jyeṣṭhanātha’s [disciple] Varyānātha is Saṃjñikā;
O Goddess, that is his festival day, which should be worshipped with great effort.
O Goddess, this festival of his bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, grants the fruit of the perfection of the command (ājñāsiddhi),
and wards off all defects.
He too becomes free from debt, dear to the gods, and a source of joy;
one should worship him on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Caitra.
The Khecarī [mantra] belongs to Padmānanda, the Lord of the Madhyamā-vallī;
this festival of his, O Goddess, wards off all deficiencies.
One who has attained supreme consciousness shall become dear to the deities;
for mortals who have accomplished their practice, the preliminary worship must be offered.
O beloved, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship the lineage of Vālovallī;
O beautiful one, he is named Kamala, a perfected master (siddha).
This festival generates great fortune and should be observed with diligent effort.
O lady of virtuous vows, listen as I describe the majesty of that festival.
Among the Siddhas, Khecarīs, and Mātṛs, she is Vāmā, Lā, and Sākinī;
she is known as Śikhā, Raudrī, Gaurī, and Kāmasukhā within the Vīramukta.
O Dear One, she may have one eye, three eyes, or four faces, appearing in many other ways; she may be a female cat or have the face of a lion, assuming various forms.
O fair-faced one, they become pleased and desire the accomplishment of the practitioner;
the command of the heroes of the single lineage shall become manifest.
One should worship [the deity] during the Caitra festival; it liberates one from suffering and grief, bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation, and pacifies faults and poverty.
O beloved, the entire divine sequence of the three lineages has been told;
now I shall further proclaim the characteristics of a disciple who possesses the [divine] command.
O fair-faced one, O Goddess of the gods, the preceptor must bestow the empowerment of command (ājñābhiṣeka) upon the practitioner; listen, for I shall describe its characteristics.
O Dear One, there is the threefold consecration and the lineage therein;
first, the teacher shall explain the sequence and the consecration.
O Pārvatī, I shall tell you what must be given to the best of practitioners;
having thoroughly purified the most beautiful portion of ground for the sacrificial circle (yāgamaṇḍala).
O lady of excellent vows, having performed the sacrifice and laid out the *sarvatobhadra* mandala with the lord of preceptors,
one should perform the worship there for the sake of auspiciousness.
O fair-faced one, having worshipped the water-filled pitcher with the five [offerings],
it should be endowed with all medicinal herbs and accompanied by the seven grains.
Vacā, kuṣṭha, gold, mustard seeds, and sesame seeds,
combined with sahadevī and accompanied by parched grain, a bull, and a plowshare.
Having smeared red sandalwood paste and offered water for honor, flowers, and other articles of worship,
and having likewise worshipped the mantra-form, O beloved, [one should place] five jars.
O Goddess, one should worship with gold, silver, copper, crystal, and clay-made [images], being single-mindedly concentrated on the essential points.
Having fashioned a svastika mandala provided with the five jewels and the sense organs,
O Goddess of Gods, the practitioner should sit there facing the east.
Today, O Goddess, [I offer] the arghya with five [ingredients], together with five water-pots,
accompanied by song and instrumental music, as well as conch shells and kettledrums.
O fair-faced one, auspicious verses are sung for the sake of auspiciousness;
thereafter, one should cause the consecration to be bestowed upon the preceptor who is facing westward.
O beloved, the sacred thread, sandals, a svastika,
a rosary, and likewise a vessel for the fire-oblation are given to you.
After making the pledge, he should cause [the disciple] to hear it, saying: "Go, become a guide!
Having performed the deliverance of the beasts, move through the path of beings, both mobile and immobile."
The initiation for that tantra has been described; now the family preceptor (kulācārya) is being discussed.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the most auspicious practice of the essential reality (vastuyoga).
It should be four-cornered with four gates and provided with a guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla);
having made it circular in the center, one should cause it to be reddish-brown.
O you of excellent vows, having taken that back-plate and covered it with a cloth,
one should again worship the Kula upon its surface with a red cloth.
In the center, one should worship the goddess Kuleśvarī united with Kulanātha;
thereafter, O Goddess, one of serene mind should worship the eight Kulas.
Then, having worshipped the eight groups of eight, one should worship the lineage of the Siddhas;
and [worship] Kṣetrapāla, Vaṭuka, and Vighneśa, O fair-faced one.
Thus, one should perform the family worship (kulapūjā) by means of sequential deliberation;
thereafter, O Goddess, one should worship with eight rows of water-pots (kalaśa).
O fair-faced one, during the asterism of Maghā and others, one should worship with heroic substances:
jātī fruit, puṅgaphala, bilva, and hiraṇyaka.
Sahadeva, [prepare] vacā, kuṣṭha, along with all medicinal herbs,
as well as white mustard seeds, rice, and adorned with mango sprouts.
O Goddess, one should worship according to the prescribed rite with sandalwood and saffron unguents, along with offerings of water (argha), incense, and various kinds of fragrant flowers.
O Dear One, one should worship the eight deities beginning with Brahmā in the water-pot;
having worshipped them with the mantra *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, one should recite it one hundred and eight times.
One should worship the eight deities with food consisting of honey and *phalgu* fruits;
O lady of excellent hips, when they are thus satisfied, it is as if they have been fed various kinds of food.
Dancing with joy and adorned with all ornaments,
O lady of beautiful countenance, whose hair is disheveled and who utters the sounds "a" and "ra."

O beloved, O lady of excellent complexion, having caused the two hands to grasp the water-pot and having bestowed the initiation upon the practitioner, [the teacher should act] with the supreme [mudrā].
O son of the Gaṇas, O family preceptor, wander upon the surface of the earth;
as a guide, bestow your grace upon mortals according to your will.
The Yoginīs of the Devatā-kula, who eternally bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, grant these very things to the practitioner; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
The family initiation has been explained as the supreme secret state;
now I shall further proclaim another, the initiation of the ritual master.
O fair-faced one, out of affection for you, I shall describe that which eternally bestows the perfection of command and whose nature is divine touch; of this there is no doubt.
With a conch or a water-pot filled with wine mixed with living fish, or completely filled with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), he [should perform the rite].
When worshipped by virgins, the lineage of those who uphold the tradition consists of Kuleśvarī,
Kubjikā, Kālī, and the renowned Kāmeśvarī.
O beloved, he was honored with flowers, incense, fragrances, sandalwood, and saffron;
his mouth was refreshed with betel-leaf, and he was fed various divine foods.
O Dear One, a maiden with loose hair should place the water-pot;
O Lady of Excellent Gait, for the practitioner, it bestows the accomplishment of the Command.
Go, my son, O one of great wisdom; let your command be fulfilled.

O Goddess of excellent vows, by means of sacrifices involving even a hundred animals, one may be destroyed in an instant; that which has been described is the external [practice], but now hear the internal [practice].
The fish is the goddess Laṃbikā, and Rudra is called Kalaśa;
one should consecrate the disciple by sprinkling [the water] from the bee-vessel, which is filled with nectar.
That [initiation] is called Mīna, with the feet of Mīna; therefore, by means of it, there is the consecration.
This, however, is the consecration of the Siddhas, through which the accomplishment of the Command proceeds.
Thus, O Goddess, has been described the characteristic of the consecration for one's own initiated disciple,
marked by the tilaka of the Yoginīs.
O lady of excellent hips, one should fashion a name joined with the syllables of the original name;
I shall now declare the supreme classification of the Mātṛkā for the [mantra] strings.
