Bhā is radiant bliss; Ma is the bliss of the winds; Ya is the bliss of yoga; Ra is the bliss of the funeral pyre; La is the bliss of form; Va is the bliss of the dark one; Śa is the bliss of enjoyment; Ṣa is the bliss of night; Sa is the bliss of rays; Ha is the bliss of knowledge.
Kṣa, the one who blazes with bliss.
Having thus established the name of the family, one should cause the family substance to be offered;
thereafter, the consecration of the family should be performed without conceptual construction.

This is declared to be the gradual initiation (kramadīkṣā), which sets in motion the attainment of the Command (ājñāsiddhi) and brings about the supreme state that destroys the flood of sins of the great cycle of existence.
Thus, O Goddess, I have described to you the characteristics of a disciple who possesses the command.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the section on Nirvāṇa within the Dakṣiṇāmnāya of the glorious Vārāhī Tantra. || 20 ||
Bhairava said:
I shall further proclaim that which consists of the six tastes abiding within the body; O Goddess, it is the supreme five jewels, the virility characterized by realization.
Blood, flesh, fat, marrow, bone-marrow, and semen,
as well as the six tastes and the joints of the body— this is the nourishment that bestows all accomplishments.
The first is the jewel of desire (icchāratna), the second is situated in the body,
the third is known as nectar (amṛta), and the fourth is remembered as the lunar (vaidava).
The fifth is supreme bliss, which causes the certainty of happiness.
This has been declared as the Jewel; listen, O beloved, to the potency of the mantra.
O Goddess, O lady with a face as beautiful as that of Indra,
[the syllable] *ga* is joined with the sixth vowel and adorned with a bindu upon its head.
These supreme mantras shall extract the lineage of the immortals;
now listen, O large-eyed one, to the ritual procedure for the worship of heroic power.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Phreṃ Yrūṃ Kroṃ Āṃ Klīṃ Aiṃ Plūṃ! O eternally intoxicating flow, Hūṃ Haṃ Hīṃ! To Nīlapatākā, Nīravārāhī, and the Eternal One (Nityā), Svāhā!
O virtuous lady, the procedure for the mantra-worship of the five jewels has been declared;
now I shall further explain the external means as well as the internal conviction.
O you of virtuous vows, wherever a particular jewel is to be brought and placed, there prosperity arises; indeed, at that time, its pervasive power proceeds forth.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, tell me the linguistic convention and the defining characteristics,
so that I may correctly understand both the external and internal [aspects].
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the characteristics of the linguistic conventions,
the locations, the various sequences, and the physical form assumed by Khecarī.
Kuvākuṣī, kuvaiḥ, kuryā, kubhe, kukṣe, kuli, kṣamaḥ—
these eight, O auspicious lady, are the secret signs of the lineage transmitted through succession.
Pākahā, Bhākahā, O Goddess, Ākahā, and likewise Gukahā;
Makahā, Maṃkahā, O Goddess, Nokahā, and likewise Taṃkahā.
O blessed one, the eightfold convention resides in the mouth of the Yoginī.
O Goddess, listen; I shall explain the external and internal locations.
In the syllable *kukāra*, O Goddess Kubjikā, in the presence of the eight conventions (*aṣṭasaṃketa*),
your external and internal stations are worshipped.
The goddess Vāmā constantly vomits forth the Word (śabda), which is worshipped by her own attendants;
and Antaramālinī, remaining right there, [supports] that very foundation.
O Goddess of gods, listen to the word *ṣī*, which is worshipped by Kukkura and Śighara.

O Goddess, having remained within that which is perceived at the end of the fourth state (turya), Antaramālinī utters the sound "vai," while Mātaṅgī, who is worshipped by the Ghaṭas, utters the sound "mā."
Having entered between the navel and the wheel and remaining within the interior,
that place of the Yoginīs in the sound is declared to be Oṃvīghara.
For the Antarāmalinī, situated at the beginning and middle within the heart,
is to be known as enjoyment (bhukti) in the sound "tu," worshipped by Ghaṇṭhakīghara.
O Goddess, having reached the location of the throat and remaining there as Antaramālinī,
she is the supreme field (kṣetra) at Kṣeśabda, the well-honored Veśyāghara.
O Goddess of gods, having stood there at the support of the Command (ājñādhāra), Antaramālinī hears the perfectly pure Trailīghara in the soundless state.
Having remained within the interior of Brahmā’s abode, she is the Mālinī residing in the interval;
she is the station of forgiveness at the end of the twelve, worshipped by Kaṇḍakīghara.
O Goddess, having stood in that divine and excellent left-hand position, Antaramālinī spoke thus; indeed, these eight signs are difficult to obtain.
Having resolved the doubts regarding the Khecarī doctrine as it has come down through the lineage of tradition,
I shall now further proclaim another [teaching] residing in the mouth of the Yoginīs.
O beloved, Pāruṣā and Pārumūla possess their own support and origin;
there stands Kalpapālīghara, where Āntaramālinī resides.
Having touched the auspicious sequence of her own limbs at the root of the navel,
she resorted to the abode of speech and remained within the Mālinī.
The goddess Āhākā has arrived as the support for the birth of all principles;
having stood within the divine power of the Mlecchī house, she is Antaramālinī.
But the fisherwoman is the support for birth, to be known as protected by the lower abdomen.
The house is supreme nirvāṇa; having stood within it, one reaches Aṃtaramālinī.
Makahā is the convention of all things, the supreme heart of the cremation ground.
O Goddess, having stayed there in union with the Yoginīs, one reaches Antaramālinī,
Maṅkahā, Maṅgala, Kaṇṭhakūpa, and Catuṣpatha.
Having abandoned hunger and thirst and remaining within the inner impurity,
the tip of the nose is proclaimed as the single tree that spans the sky.
O Goddess, having established herself in the state of the bliss of rest within the Antarmālinī,
she moves upward from there to the Twelve-finger Space (dvādaśānta), which is the magnet for the iron of Suṃkā.
O Goddess, Kumārī, Kulabhoktrī, and Antaramālinī abide there;
this secret oral tradition (āmnāya) has been told to you in the Kaulika scripture.
O beloved, I shall further proclaim the assembly of the vital breaths (chūṣmāmelāpaka),
the sequence of the perfected ones of the sacred seats (pīṭhasiddhakrama), and the supreme locus of the circle of the Mothers (mātṛmaṇḍala).
One should touch the tip of the index finger with that which is divine, more secret than the secret;
from that, one should recognize the *śūṣma*, as it is taught in the Kula scripture.
When movement, vibration, and friction have come to rest within the interior of the sky,
one becomes filled with bliss after drinking the divine nectar of immortality that has been attained.
Then, O Goddess, when resting in the surging waves of bliss, there occurs the union (melāpaka); that is the external and internal inquiry, the compendium of the essence.
"O beloved of the Goddess, the hundred-and-twentieth [chapter] has been told to you.
The Goddess said:
O Goddess of the gods, the seat is the *Matasārasamuccaya*;
within the Great Void are the Lord of the Five [Finger] Gestures (*pañcamudrānātha*) and the Wheel of the Unperishing (*akṣayacakram*).
"O Great Hero, Guardian of the Field, speak, O Maheśvara!
Bhairava said:
O Parameśānī, O lady of excellent vows, listen as I shall describe the most excellent and divine supreme seat, which arises from the Ciñcinīmata.
O Goddess, [one should likewise meditate upon] Ādhāraśakti, Ananta, and Kālāgni; and similarly Bījākula and Mahārṇava.
O Goddess, the Pretapadmāsana is here, and from it comes the fruit of the Siṃhāsana;
likewise Siddheśvara is the secret [seat] at the navel, as is Vīreśvara.
One should place Kuleśvara in the heart, Kulakha at the throat, and Narkanātha on the forehead; these constitute the supreme seat.
The lotus of the heart, the lamp of the lineage, she who has the form of Varvara and Avakuru,
the great savior and the fifth [vow], bestows purity upon all.
O Great Goddess of beautiful countenance, you are to be worshipped at the further shore of the gateway;
you have four arms, one face, and three eyes, and possess a formidable form.
The goddess Gānāsābharaṇā is adorned with all the family ornaments;
she is surrounded by great flames, has hair standing on end, and lets out loud, boisterous laughter.
With a sword and trident in her hands, she holds a spear and a mallet;
her face is terrifying with bared fangs, and she wears an elephant hide as an upper garment.
O beloved Amalaka, you have worn a garland of human skulls and severed heads;
O fair-faced one, the great sacred site of Candradvīpa must be protected.
The temple is a place of worship for the Siddhas, the supreme abode of Kubjikā;
it is proclaimed as the Vidyā consisting of the groups of letters: a-ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa-ya-śa.

The eight goddesses of the eight groups are to be worshipped according to the prescribed rite; likewise, O Goddess, O beautiful one among the Asuras, the eight directions beginning with the East are to be honored.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, as well as Aindrī and Cāmuṇḍā, are remembered as the supreme;
these goddesses have been described by me, O fair-faced one, and they are imperishable.
O Pārvatī, they should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite on the exterior of the maṇḍala;
they are the bestowers of worldly enjoyment and liberation, as well as of the family deity (kuladevī).
O Vīranātha, O Goddess Valirā, the supreme mantra has been declared:
[one should visualize him] as dark-skinned, with tawny hair and tawny, reddish-brown eyes.
O Vaka-Kṣetrapāla, Lord of the Great Ḍāmaras, who are terrifying with fangs, exceedingly fierce, and radiant with ornaments of skulls— accept this offering!

"May flowers, incense, food offerings, and all that is auspicious become [available]!
The Goddess said:"
O Lord, I have heard all that which is the most supreme among the supreme teachings concerning me.
O Lord of Ciñciṇī, this essence of the Mata has been heard by me through your grace;
yet even now, O Protector, a doubt clearly persists within my heart.
O Lord, what is the vow of the heroic conduct, and likewise the vow of the maiden?
O Lord, tell that to me; show me your favor and grant me your grace.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the determination of the vow of the Kumārī;
O Supreme Sovereign, she bears the divine chowrie and the skull-bowl.
Having performed this unsurpassed vow with the spokes held in the right and left hands,
the Goddess said:
O Lord, what is the *camara* like, and what is the *khaṭpara* said to be?
"O Lord, tell me this: how should one perform the vow in the sacred place? Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain it to you in brief, and not in detail.
O lady of excellent vows, listen now to the description of Khaṭpara as previously mentioned;
O Goddess, the supreme *kalā* is Kakaṃdarā, proclaimed as the support of all.
By means of the flow of the wheel of movement, one should pierce the supreme state;
the nectar of the digit of consciousness, melted and situated in the center of the arising of the threefold bliss.
Therefore, O beloved of Cāmara,
the supreme Kumārī, a celibate maiden, has maintained the Carcikāmnāya which was proclaimed by him, O Goddess.
O beloved, within the Kāmākhyā-pīṭha, a vow was observed by two [goddesses]:
the supreme goddess Parā, who is dear to the Supreme Lord, and her companion.
The maiden Divyarūpā is beautiful with the jewel of form; Ratnarūpasundarī should hold a chowrie, while Rūpasundarī holds a fly-whisk.
In the center, however, is the goddess Khecarī, blazing like a streak of lightning;
having uttered Caryācārya, [one enters] the mandala of the Divine Current (divyogha-krama).
The divine word *acaleti*, the pair of words *caṃcaleti*,
*pavaneti* for great speed, and *nirmāṃse vyomabhakṣaṇī*.
Caruka and Disiṃhī spoke again and again:
"One should go to various places, to that unsurpassed assembly of play."
O Goddess, this determination of the vow of the maiden has been declared by me;
now I shall further proclaim another, the unsurpassed Vīra-vow.
Holding a whetstone and a vessel filled with cooked meat in her hand,
the Goddess spoke:
O Lord, it has been told in brief, but not in detail.
It shall be the secret of all accomplishments for the destruction of delusive cognition.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the characteristics of the hero’s drink (vīrapāna).
When this world, which is permeated by the movement of the vital breaths, is awakened through self-luminous realization, it becomes the supreme state of rest within the supreme effulgence.

Through the supreme reasoning that transcends the void and by means of the Kaula method, one should remember the divine state of consciousness, which is both manifest and unmanifest, as being there, born of maturation.
O Dear One, the form of consciousness is in the center of the *bhaga*, and Rati is in the center of the sun;
between these two is Śiva himself—therein one should contemplate the essence of the ripened fruit.
O Goddess, one should remember the solar pitcher situated within the garment,
wherein that which has arisen from the vital breaths (jīva) and so forth is located.
Having gone there and seen his own form, his anger was aroused; and having drunk that most terrible ocean of Bhaga along with Bhairava, it was made to flow away.
O hero, O best among the foremost of heroes, the world of the moving and the unmoving moves within you;
there is no fear for him who possesses liberation through his own self-knowledge.
The supreme deity, the supreme state, whose nature is all-pervading and inexhaustible— O Hero, Lord of the Kula and Kola, they call him the infinite Master.
"The characteristics of the vīrapāka have been described, O Goddess of the lords of gods.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, I have heard all of the *Matasārasamuccaya* from you;
yet even now, O Protector, I have a doubt—please explain the science of mantras to me."
O Lord of the Eightfold Wheel, tell me the five seed-syllables of Vatrī, as well as the chalk and the expansion of existence (bhavaprastāra), O Śaṅkara.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the extraction of the mantra-vidyā.
O Dear One, one should smear a pure, level area of ground with beeswax (alī).
O Goddess, having become serene-faced, one should offer flowers, incense, oblations, and the supreme offering of wine, and then extract the five seed-syllables.

The fifth is Pañcakāminī, the Vidyā-Śrī Kāmarājaka;
this sixteen-syllable Mahāvidyā is indeed the venerable, supreme, and transcendent Parā.
The palace is declared to be *sāṃbhava* when it is joined with the supreme;
the great siddhis, beginning with *aṇimā*, are proclaimed to be obstacles.
On the fivefold lion-throne sits the Goddess Mahātripurasundarī,
the supreme deity Vaiṣṇavī, who is the manifest embodiment of wakefulness.
The Supreme Goddess is the true primordial nature, possessing all forms;
she is the essence of all living beings and remains pervading everywhere.
There is no Śiva, no Śakti, no male, no female, and no neuter;
she is the very nature of all living beings and has the form of the self-liṅga.
That which is the cause of all arising is designated as the "womb" (yoni);
this has been declared by me as the nature of the Lion Throne according to the Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya).
O Great Goddess, she who is the very embodiment of waking consciousness possesses even a mere fraction [of that form];
first, her form is with the eastern face, which is Tatpuruṣa.
He spoke thus regarding the exceedingly exalted eastern lion-throne:
"The Heroines who are the powers of Rudra [worship] Śiva, the supreme Tatpuruṣa."
Pūrṇeśvarī is the great cow; she is proclaimed as the Pūrvāmnāya.
I shall indeed describe the meditation upon Cakreśvarī for the benefit of practitioners;
having established it within the mind, the Supreme Goddess is to be meditated upon.
Resembling a sapphire in luster, she possesses ten staff-like arms,
holding a beautiful trident and skull-cup, with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
In her lotus-like hands, she holds a hand-drum, a rosary, and a spear;
she is most beautiful, with a sword in her hand and a crescent moon, a bow, and an arrow.
Seated upon sun and moon thrones above a great assembly of pretas,
she stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, possesses three eyes, and is adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla became her earrings;
she was adorned with the necklace of Ananta and decorated with ornaments of bones.
With wide, moving eyes and adorned with a crescent moon as her crest,
this is the goddess Pūrṇeśvarī, who is fond of the "hā hā" cry.
She is renowned as Pūrṇeśvarī, endowed with ego and the quality of rajas;
she resides on the head at the seat of Pūrṇālaya, in the Lakṣmīvana cremation ground.
She is eternally worshipped by Indra, multiform, and the one who descends in various incarnations;
she is renowned in the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya) and honored by the ancient gods and sages.
She is the sovereign of all sciences, bringing forth a weight of great fortune;
she assumes various forms, is eternal, and descends in many manifestations.
Jayā, Ajayantī, Vijayā, Ajitā,
Nārasiṃhikā, Vyāghreśvarī, Karālā, Rājeśī, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
Raktadantā, Viśālākṣī, Kāmeśī, Caṇḍamālinī,
Vidyujjihvā, Ḍāmareśī, Nāṭeśrī, and Nṛtyanāyikā.
Nandī, Mahākāla, Bhaṅginī, Kulālikā,
and Navanāṭeśvarī are there, endowed with the four and five aesthetic sentiments (rasas).
O God, the Goddess has many divisions, as do the eight Bhairavas and the Mātṛkās;
she is renowned as Nāṭeśvarī, while Bhairava is the protector of the wheel.
The Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati), Vighneśa, Vaṭuka, the Yāginīs, and the eight Mothers (Mātṛkāṣṭaka), beginning with Brahmāṇī, are worshipped; the maiden (Kumārī) always grants all desires.
In former times, while the Lord was dancing, Bhairava was surrounded by the Mothers;
he who is named Nṛtyabhairava was established in the eastern wheel.
The Gaṇeśas, Kṣetrapālas, and Ḍākinīs are the attendants (gaṇas) who reside in the Tatpuruṣa [face];
they are to be propitiated through the left-hand paths (vāmamārga), for their rites are not performed by the right-hand path (dakṣiṇataḥ).
In Plakṣadvīpa and Kuśadvīpa, she is present in many ways;
through her, subjugation, attraction, immobilization, and other such powers are accomplished.
Having propitiated Marīci, he bestowed [this] upon Śakra;
such is the ancient tradition (pūrvāmnāya) established on the eastern throne.
Now listen to the tradition: she is the Mother Mātṛkā, the conqueror of the powerful;
she is the creator of all actions and bestows swift fruit in the Kali age.
On the Buddhist path, she who possesses a brilliance like that of a leaping fire, traversing without hesitation,
and who is renowned for the essential points of other traditions, is known as Vajrayoginī.
She has three faces and is red in color; her feet are in a dancing posture and she is possessed of latent impressions (vāsanā).
She has three eyes, is free from the maṇḍala, and is adorned with ornaments of human skulls.
The Goddess has her limbs adorned with a garland of shaven heads, wears a serpent as a sacred thread,
is clothed in a tiger skin, and has a lion skin as an upper garment.
Vairocanī, preceded by Vajra, is the beloved of Vajraghaṇṭā;
she has four arms, stands upon a corpse, and her hair is matted and rises upward from her head.
Holding a skull-bowl, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a hand-drum in her hands,
she follows the Sugata and directly bestows swift results in the Kali age.
In this very world, she bestows fruits; she is the eternal radiance whose fruit is liberation.
Following the Sugata’s teaching, she is entirely one, though she rests upon various distinctions.
Kālacakra, Saṃvara, Hayagrīva, Bhairava,
Yogāmbara, and Kāleśa— Śāvarī has taken refuge in the Sugata.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the section on Nirvāṇa within the Dakṣiṇāmnāya of the Śrī Vārāhī Tantra.
The Goddess said:
O God, Lord of the World, O Śaṅkara, please explain how the practitioner may accomplish the ritual applications and so forth through the distribution [of the mantra].
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which indicates success,
by means of which a hero may accomplish his goal within the lineage of the Vīrācāra.
But he who desires to perform the ritual application without having first completed the preliminary service (puraścaryā) will become a vessel for ten million great sins.
O Goddess, there is nothing higher than this [sin] for those who defile the path of the Kula;
therefore, even at the cost of all one's possessions, and even unto the end of one's life, one must never [do so].
Through action, mind, and speech, one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa);
the practitioner of mantra, subsisting on sacrificial food and with senses subdued, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its syllables.
During the day one should practice celibacy, and at night one may act as one desires;
one should worship the Goddess according to the prescribed rule, preceded by the *pañcaka*.
One should certainly not cause that [image] to be made there, together with its limbs and its retinue.
One should perform a fire sacrifice (havana) consisting of one-tenth [of the total recitations], using bilva leaves soaked in ghee,
and goat meat smeared with honey, for the sake of pleasing the Goddess.
One should satisfy the Goddess with nectar ten times the amount of the oblation;
indeed, the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) is declared to be ten times the amount of that satisfaction.
One should indeed provide a grand feast for young maidens with a tenth part of that [number];
however, in the Kali age, the practitioner should perform the *puraścaraṇa* four times over.
Having received initiation, the practitioner must indeed perform the preparatory rite (puraścaryā);
having received initiation, one must certainly not cause a delay in the puraścaryā.
Having realized the fickleness of life, one should contemplate one's own spiritual welfare;
for if one dies after receiving initiation without having performed the *puraścaryā* rites, [the goal remains unattained].
One will surely become one with Brahman after fasting for a hundred years;
or else, one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* rite during an eclipse of the moon or sun.
Having worshipped Sparśā and Mukti, the *puraścaraṇa* is said to be performed;
one should carry out all rites as previously enjoined, with a tenth part [of the recitation].
Therefore, listen now as I shall describe the ritual applications;
the initiation of a hero (*vīradīkṣā*) is not for one who lacks power, having first worshipped according to the rules.
Whether situated in a cremation ground, to the right of Śiva, or in the house for invocation,
she is eternally present through the three kinds of lamps and other offerings on great mountains and during festivals.
Truthful in speech, endowed with fortitude, and free from desire and anger;
accompanied by capable assistants, he is a hero, or else his assistants are heroes.
O companion, when one is destitute of wealth and subsists on alms at the onset of night,
one should first recite the mantra one thousand times for the purpose of purifying the body.
The Goddess is pleased when one performs the *homa* exactly as previously instructed by me;
thereafter, the practitioner of mantras should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, avoiding daytime activities.

When one is unable to perform the meditation after the meal, one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred times during the twilight; having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (nyāsa), one should recite it in pairs.
Then, at night, one should perform recitation according to one's ability and in the proper sequence;
subsequently, for the sake of attaining perfection in the mantra, one should perform oblations amounting to one-tenth of that number.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice (homa), the maiden should be worshipped; success will certainly be achieved.
Alternatively, one should perform the recitation (japa) twice as much for up to seven days.
In Kuru and other such regions, at the eighth [stage], after the service and the fire-oblation,
there is the pacification of the planets (grahaśāntika) during the three junctions of the day and at midnight, for one, two, three, or four days.
When there is affliction by wind and other humors, one is liberated from disease through pacificatory fire-offerings (homa).
Having commenced the Śivāvali on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, [one attains success].
Bhairava said:
Now, I shall correctly set forth the characteristics of the six rites as they exist in the tantras,
according to all the tantras, which bestow the accomplishment of the fruits of their application.

The wise recognize that pacification (*śānti*), subjugation (*vaśya*), immobilization (*staṃbhana*), as well as inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), expulsion (*uccāṭana*), and killing (*māraṇa*) constitute the six rites (*ṣatkarma*).
The destruction of afflictions such as diseases and malevolent planets is declared to be *śānti* (pacification);
the subjugation of all people is declared to be *vaśya* (subjugation), which is under one's own control.
That which indicates the cause of cessation is declared to be *staṃbhanam* (paralysis);
that which causes mutual hatred among people is declared to be *vidveṣaṇam* (inciting enmity).
Uccāṭana is declared to be the expulsion from one's own country,
while maraṇa is declared to be the destruction of the life-force of living beings.
Having understood one's own deity, as well as the directions, time, and so forth, one should accomplish the ritual acts: Rati, Vāṇī, Ramā, Jyeṣṭhā, Durgā, and Kālī, in their respective order.
The deities of the six rites have been declared; one should worship them at the beginning of the ritual in the respective directions of Īśāna, Candra, Indra, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Agni in sequence.
The seasons beginning with spring, as well as the groups of spring, summer, autumn, winter, and the dewy season, dwell day after day throughout the cycle of day and night.
It is prescribed for the rite of pacification during the winter, for the rite of subjugation during the spring,
for the rite of immobilization during the cool season, and for the rite of causing enmity during the summer.

It should be known that for the rites of inciting, driving away, and summoning, the autumn season is appropriate; and for the rite of killing, one should use a lotus, a svastika, or a distorted cock, respectively.
The wise call the seats "Vajra" and "Bhadra";
the six mudrās should be known in sequence as the lotus, the noose, and the mace, and so forth.
Mortars, Saturn, and swords are used in rites such as those for pacification (śānti);
water is prescribed for the rite of pacification, while fire is declared for the rite of subjugation (vaśya).
Earth is declared for the rite of immobilization (staṃbhaṇa), and space is proclaimed for the rite of causing enmity (vidveṣa);
wind is considered for the rite of expulsion (uccāṭana), and fire is held to be for the rite of killing (māraṇa).
The practitioner, with a resolute mind, should perform each respective rite in conjunction with the emergence of the breath (bhūtodaya) and the corresponding mandala.
The earth of the nectar of the cool-rayed moon, the wind of the sky, and the oblation for those suffering from disease—
these are the seed-syllables of the mantras for the six rites in their respective order.
Granthana, vidarbha, sampuṭa, virodhana, yoga, and pallava— these are to be employed in the six types of ritual acts.
One should interpose the syllables of the name between the mantras according to the rule;
one should know that this "stringing together" (grathana) is highly recommended for rites of pacification (śānti).
One should write the middle syllable of the name situated between two mantra-syllables.
Vidarbha alone is to be understood by the ministers in the rite of subjugation;
when the name is placed at the beginning and the end of the mantra, it is known as "encased" (saṃpuṭa).
This very [mantra] is declared by those who know the mantras to be recommended for the purpose of paralyzing;
the "obstructing" of a mantra is traditionally held to consist in placing the name [of the target] at its beginning, end, and middle.
This is declared to be the most excellent among the rites for inciting enmity;
at the end of the mantra, the name [of the target] should be placed—this is known as the yoga of eradication (uccāṭana).
At the end of the name, the mantra should have the syllable *pallava*; this is considered for the rite of killing (*māraṇa*).
White, red, white, black, black, and smoky are proclaimed [as the colors].
The deities prescribed for the six types of rites according to their color [should be visualized]; furthermore, the substances for writing mantras include sandalwood, ox-gall, and so forth.
House-soot, charcoal from a funeral pyre, poisons used for killing, the horn of a rhinoceros,
the fire of a hawk, clods of earth, bile, the juice of *dhūrtūra*, and mercury.
House-soot, a woman, and a cock are declared to be the eight poisons;
having correctly understood the deity, the time, the mudrās, and so forth, the wise practitioner [should proceed].
One should employ the six rites for the sake of attaining the results as described:
for the rite of pacification (śānti), sheepskin is used, while woolen skin is excellent for [the rite of] prosperity (ūrṇā).
Then the deity should be worshipped with white flowers upon a surface smeared with white sandalwood paste and the like, and adorned with the seed-syllable of the Moon.
The excellent practitioner, possessing pure vision and radiating a splendor like ten million moons,
clearly perceives the object of accomplishment along with the mantras during rites for pacification.
The skin of either a tiger or a rhinoceros is highly praised for use on a yantra that is joined with sandalwood and other substances and adorned with the seed-syllables of nectar (sudhā).
O Goddess, the deity should then be worshipped with red flowers and other offerings;
and by visualizing [the deity] as red in color, the practitioner achieves subjugation and attraction.
O Goddess, as the rite of subjugation is described, so too is the rite of attraction;
for the purpose of paralyzing, the elephant hide is always the primary material for practitioners of mantra.
O Goddess, the deity should then be worshipped with white flowers and other offerings in a vessel joined with sandalwood and the like, and adorned with the seed-syllable of the Earth (Bhū-bīja).
A woolen blanket (kaṃvala) is for one who is praiseworthy, while a seat made of funeral pyre charcoal, adorned with the seed-syllable of space (vyomabīja), is for the rite of aversion.
O Goddess, the deity should be worshipped with black flowers and other offerings;
likewise, when joined with the seed-syllable of Vāyu, it is used for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana).
For the killing of a horse, however, the use of its hide is recommended;
it should be joined with the eight points of a horn and the like, conjoined with the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ).
Thereafter, the crest-jewel among the foremost of practitioners— the best of adepts— should worship the deity for the purposes of pacification, subjugation, attraction, and immobilization.
One should recite the mantras at the appropriate time using the thumb and the ring finger;
for the rites of causing enmity and expulsion, one should use the combination of the index finger and the thumb.
One should recite the mantra at the appropriate time, meditating with a steady mind;
for the purpose of killing, the excellent recitation is performed by joining the little finger and the thumb.
Thereafter, one should worship the designated deity according to the procedure prescribed in the Kalpa,
with various kinds of flowers, garments, ornaments, and decorations.
With ointments such as camphor, agallochum, musk, and sandalwood;
with incense, lamps, and musical instruments, accompanied by the sounds of the *bherī* drum.
Having offered the five foods, beginning with *caryā*, to that goddess, he [should present them].
O Pārvatī, one should offer oblations of goats, buffaloes, and so forth, according to the prescribed rule,
during the performance of preliminary rites (puraścaryā) and in ceremonies such as those for peace (śāntika).
Thereafter, with a steady mind, he should perform one hundred thousand recitations according to the prescribed rite;
a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of cows, land, a bull, and so forth, should be given to the preceptor.
For the sake of accomplishing the king of mantras,
one who performs the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) should perform the purification (*śānti*) and the *puraścaryā*, followed by thirty days of fasting (*lāṅghana*).
Having prostrated before the Guru, the excellent practitioner should offer wealth preceded by devotion;
or else, he should give twenty *tulās*.
Thirty gold *tulās* are recommended for the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*);
forty gold *tulās* are prescribed for the rite of attraction (*ākarṣa*).
Fifty gold *tulās* are highly recommended for the rite of immobilization (*staṃbhanam*);
sixty gold *tulās* are prescribed for the eradication of enemies (*uccāṭanam*).
Seventy *tulās* of gold are prescribed for the slaying of enemies;
likewise, pacification (*śānti*), subjugation (*vaśya*), and immobilization (*stambhana*) are achieved with one *karṣa*.
The wise know the six rites to be: eradication and killing;
O God, for the elders, the ten-fold dakṣiṇā is superior to the most superior.
O Lord of Gods, if one has not properly offered the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and has failed to remember the sandals of the Guru,
that which was performed through the power of the mantra shall become fruitless.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
I have related that procedure for the six rites which is difficult to obtain;
by the mere hearing of which the great darkness at the root of one's own heart is dispelled.
p.
136a) O Mother, if you have ever had affection for me,
then quickly and joyfully tell me the ritual procedure for the offering of the *bali*.
The illustrious Goddess said:
Listen, my son, I shall explain the auspicious ritual for the offering of bali:
whether on a riverbank, in a wilderness, or at a crossroads.
The practitioner should offer an oblation (bali) consisting of fish, meat, and other such items;
the offering for Vaṭuka should be made with the mantra "Ehyehi" (Come, come).
O child, one should cause an offering (bali) to be given to him with the Gaṇapati mantra; then, the offering for those Yoginīs should be made with the Yoginī mantra.
One should cause the offering to the Kṣetrapāla to be presented with the mantra;
one should give four offerings in the four directions, beginning with the northwest.
Nirṛti and Varuṇa are in the middle; there should be an offering for all beings.
Having given the offering at the dead of night, one should then perform the ritual action.
Then, having worshipped the chosen deity with most beautiful offerings,
O Lord, [one should worship] again with gold and other materials, flowers, silken garments, and so forth.
O son, according to the distinctions of stringing [the rosary] and so forth, and according to the distinction of the ritual action,
one should recite the mantra of the chosen goddess and then perform the sequence beginning with the left hand (vāma) and so on.
Then, having performed the fire-sacrifice (homa), one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa);
then, having performed the ritual ablution (abhiṣeka), one should feed the most excellent of the twice-born.
When the Brahmins have been well-fed, everything indeed becomes fruitful;
if there were no food for the Brahmins, then it would be fruitless.
Bhairava said:
Just as one should bring a corpse that appears distinct from milk and nectar according to what has been seen, so too should it be performed; one must not take the nectar by one's own whim.
One should carry away the corpse of a man who was under the control of a woman, one who has fallen from his caste,
one who is untouchable, one afflicted by disease, one who is indistinct in gender, one with leprosy, or one who has been killed while worshipping the Lord of the Dead (Pretarāja).
One should entirely avoid food that has increased due to famine, food that is stale,
and the sight of women.
In an empty house or a forest, one should adorn a corpse with blue garments;
having placed upon the bed of the dead a man of divine form, [one should proceed].
Then, having washed the corpse, one should bathe it with great care;
if it remains stained with blood, there will be fear from Bhairava.
Having placed cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg,
and the heartwood of *khadira* into the four corners of the betel leaf, one should place the corpse with its face turned downward.
Having bathed [the image], one should smear it with sandalwood paste on its back;
having fashioned a square area extending from the base of the arms to the waist.
In the center, there is a lotus with four doors and endowed with eight petals; then one should place Ajita and Caileya, separated by a lotus.
Having placed the articles of worship nearby and the superior practitioner at a distance,
and having worshipped the corpse, he should enter upon it.
Having spread kuśa grass upon the ground and having spread out the hair of the corpse,
he firmly tied it into a topknot (juṭikā) in the form of that deity.
Having touched that deity well, one should recite [the mantra] in its presence for protection;
O Goddess of Devas, all success regarding the corpse will be attained in this supreme [practice].
One should not firmly bind the feet with a cloth even when washing them:
*Oṃ bhīmabhīru bhayābhāva bhāvyalocanabhāvuke*.
"Save me, O Lord of the gods of gods, O Sovereign of the lords of the Śavāśara!"—
thus one should draw a triangle upon the soles of his feet.
Because of that, the corpse is unable to rise and remains motionless.
Then, sitting there again, one should extend the feet with the arms.
Having spread kusha grass upon his hands, he should place his feet there;
with lips closed like a bud, his mind steady and his senses firm.
Always meditating on the Lord in the heart, one should perform the recitation while observing silence;
there is no fear arising from moving or sitting, but if fear arises, one should then speak.
Whatever you request as a gift, such as an elephant and so forth, that shall be given to you on another day; meanwhile, tell me your own name.
Having spoken thus in Sanskrit, one who is fearless should not offer worship;
rather, men should then speak sweet words with playful ease.
Then, having caused [the deity] to swear an oath, the man should request a boon;
however, if he does not cause [the deity] to swear an oath or does not grant the boon, [he incurs sin].
Then, the wise one, with a one-pointed and restrained mind, should recite again;
once truth has been established and the boon obtained, he may then cease the recitation and other practices.
Knowing that the fruit has been produced, one should then loosen the topknot;
having washed and positioned the corpse, one should release the binding of the feet.
Having untied the foot-ropes, one should cast the ritual offerings into the water;
then, having placed the corpse either in the water or in a pit, one should perform the ritual bath.
Then, having gone to his own home, on another day the patron should offer an oblation, saying:
"May he accept this oblation given by me."
Having given away those who are requested for wealth— whether they be one's own sons, elephants, or pigs—
one should perform the fast prescribed by me.
On the following day, one should always drink the *pañcagavya* under the guidance of the teacher;
then, one should feed twenty-five Brāhmaṇas there.
Or, one may proceed in order up to ten [days], omitting five at a time.
Having bathed there and eaten, one should dwell in that supreme place;
however, if no food for Brahmins is provided, one shall fall into poverty.
If its end is reached by that [means], the God becomes enraged;
therefore, one should protect it for three nights, or six nights, or even nine nights.
If one hears "triśarya," then one should predict disease;
by hearing "śīta" one becomes deaf, and by seeing a dance, one becomes blind.
If one speaks a word on that day, one's mouth shall become mute;
for fifteen days, the deity remains established within the body.
From what remains, one should offer incense and flowers whenever the time comes;
however, one should never at any time engage in the censure of cows or Brahmins.
Being pure, one should touch the gods, cows, Brahmins, and others every day;
and at dawn, after completing the daily obligatory rites, one should drink water infused with bilva leaves.
Then, when the final day has arrived, one should perform the bath in the Gaṅgā;
having uttered the mantra ending with "svāhā," the word "tārā" followed by "namaḥ" should be recited.
In this manner, one should satisfy the gods with water three hundred times from the top of the head;
for one who is devoid of bathing and libation, there can be no satisfaction of the deity.
By this method, the practitioner attains accomplishment;
having enjoyed worldly pleasures here, they go at the end to the abode of Hari.
Bhairava said:
I shall tell you, without doubt, of the auspicious worship of Kumārī;
by the mere worship of her, the worship of the three worlds is accomplished.
O Lord, the worship of the maiden is established as the threefold form:
the Supreme (Parā), the Lower (Aparā), and the third, which is the Supreme-Beyond-Supreme (Parāparā).
At that time, when the gods, asuras, and great serpents were somewhat subdued by you, and the three worlds had been conquered, then Kumārikā was born.
She who is the primordial creator of the universe is directly perceived as being threefold;
she has become the digit Umā, appearing in the form of creation within the oceans of existence.
Cāṇḍī is one year old; Sarasvatī is two years old;
Tridhāmūrti is three years old; and Kālikā is four years old.
At five years she is Śubhagā, at six years she becomes Umā;
at seven she is Mālinī in person, and at eight years she is Kubjikā.
In the ninth year she is Kālasaṃkarṣā, in the tenth Aparājitā;
in the eleventh she is Rudrāṇī, and in the twelfth year Bhairavī.
In the thirteenth [chapter], Mahālakṣmī is the leader of the two-times-seven [fourteen] seats;
Kṣatrajñā is [the leader] with fifteen, and Caṇḍikā is considered [the leader] in the sixteenth.
Having thus worshipped in sequence until no more flowers are available,
one should worship from the first lunar day (pratipad) until the full moon, according to the divisions of the increasing fortnight.
O Goddess of gods, one should worship the Kumārī especially on the great festival days, on other festivals, and particularly during the Pavitraka rite and on the Mahānavamī.
He who, full of devotion, worships Piṅgalā with the sixteen [upacāras], shall,
having worshipped her with devotion, possess all prosperity.
One should worship the Navabhairavī, who is my narrative of the Kula-vidyās;

By him who has satisfied the guru, the three worlds are protected;
O Beloved, there is nothing whatsoever superior to this or more dear than the guru.
O Śivā, you who are bodiless, colorless, and formless, pervading the entire universe;
just as the funeral rites and other sacraments are performed for one's parents, so too are they for the Guru.
Without having done so, O Goddess, one goes to hell for more than sixty hundred years;
yet the giver of the body, the giver of knowledge, and the guru are indeed [the true benefactors].
If one does not perform the funeral rites, such as the offering of the *piṇḍa*, for one's preceptor just as one would for one's parents,
one goes to hell for more than six hundred years.
O Goddess, she who bestows the body is the Guru who indeed bestows knowledge.
There is nothing more weighty than the Guru in the accomplishment of the sufferings of saṃsāra;
from whose mouth has issued the syllable that is the very body of Brahman.
One will certainly be delivered from the ocean of hell through this vow; there is no doubt in this matter.
Therefore, I shall fully proclaim this essence, which grants all goals and desires.
The single-syllable, the nine-syllable, and the sixteen-syllable Vāruṇī,
as well as the fifty-four-syllable and especially the hundred-syllable [mantras].
O Goddess of gods, the two-hundred-syllable mantra, the three-hundred-syllable mantra,
and the thousand-syllable mantra are indeed the very life-breath of Kālikā.
Space, wind, fire, water, and likewise earth—
this is the lore named Rāvaṇī, O beloved, which bestows both liberation and worldly enjoyment.
The single-syllabled supreme vidyā is remembered as the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
and here, O Pārvatī, there occurs the union of Śiva and Śakti.
The goddess Mahākuṇḍalinī is worshipped as Mahārāvā;
she consists of the syllables of fire and Śiva, ending with Kāla, Kāla, and Avāruṇa.
Śikhī (the letter *ra*), Madhuhā (the letter *ma*), and Kālī (the letter *ka*) joined together are declared to be Prāṇa. Having written the syllable *kha phreṃ*, one should write the Mahācaṇḍamatā.
Having bestowed the station of Yogeśvarī, this nine-syllabled Vidyā was given;
now hear of that sixteen-syllabled Vidyā which is the very life-breath of all.
By the mere instruction of which one is fit for becoming Brahman;
having extracted the three syllables, one should then write the sound "Hā Mā".
O Goddess worshipped by the thirty gods, it should be known that [the mantra] is conjoined with Niśāmādhava;
it is mounted upon Satya, is eternal, and is swallowed by Tuṣṭi.
Mounted upon the intellect of truth, she is swallowed by the subtle Lord;
thereafter, the wheel and the digestive fire are joined with Nārāyaṇa.
One should write [the mantra] joined with Mādhava, followed by Valānuja;
then one should write again Māyā, Caṇḍī, Kūrca, Rakṣā, and Mahārāva.
The Goddess should not employ him [elsewhere]; he should recite the Śiva-mantra.
This is declared to be the sixteen-syllabled mantra, proclaimed as the king of mantras.
Having offered five morsels of food before [the deity], it becomes the Great Saptadaśī;
the beginningless great mantra is proclaimed as the King of Syllables (Varṇarāja).
The king of mantras consisting of one hundred syllables, as well as that of five hundred syllables,
the primary mantra of five syllables, and likewise the eight-syllable mantra.
The great mantra of the Vidyā is declared to consist of twenty-nine syllables;
O lady of excellent vows, that of the Mahādevī consists of two hundred and ninety syllables.
O Vasiṣṭha, for in ancient times, the garland of a thousand syllables was [revealed];
this is the supreme rule regarding the Goddess within the sequence of the Kula tradition.
She is the supreme nature of Brahman, consisting of Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā;
she dwells in the midst of the ocean of all syllables and has the form of that very ocean of all syllables.
O Goddess, if that which has come down through the succession of the tradition is obtained by good fortune through the grace of the glorious Guru, who on earth could be more blessed than they?
He is Śiva concealed in a human body; there is no doubt about this.
One is simply unable to describe the Kula lineage of Kālikā.
The sixteen-syllable Vidyā is known as the bestower of sovereignty and the giver of life;
that peaceful Kālī, who bestows great bliss, is the giver of breath.
Vaikharī, being of a different nature, is incapable of describing its qualities;
that [Brahmavidyā], which is the very essence of the Self, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Goddess of gods, by a single utterance [of this mantra], there are ten million Vājapeya sacrifices,
as well as thousands of Aśvamedha sacrifices and circumambulations of the earth.
The merit gained from bathing at Prayāga when the sun is situated in Capricorn is said to be increased a hundredfold by performing the rite according to the Kālikā procedure.
Whatever merit is gained by sequentially practicing the duties of the four stages of life (āśramas),
and whatever merit belongs to the duty of one's social class (varṇadharma)— that merit is obtained from the worship of Kālikā.
O Goddess of Devas, the pilgrimage to holy sites such as Kāśī, accompanied by three and a half crores [of other pilgrims], is equal to the Tulānāyati; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
O Goddess of the gods, what more need be said? By reciting [this] one hundred thousand times, one shall surely attain perfection; for by her, the fourteen worlds were brought forth.
O Mistress of the Abode of Non-existence,
for those by whom the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) has been performed, the Vidyā reaches its fruition in the form of its causal source.
Without performing the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), a mantra will not yield its fruit;
it is the mother of millions of universes and the bestower of great liberation.
O Beloved, as sparks issue forth from a fire, many varieties of great mantras emerge; thus has this Vidyā been revealed.
Everything has arisen from the Praṇava, and she is composed of the Supreme Brahman;
neither the one who brings her forth nor the one who protects her is anyone other than Bhuvaneśvarī.
By means of Māyā, [He exists] through various lineages as His essential nature and in various forms.
Deluding the entire world and increasing sons and grandsons,
she is constantly bound within the thread of desire through the states of both woman and man.
Pervading everywhere and dwelling in the abode of Brahman,
she is called the Source of the Universe, who bestows good fortune and binds through her grasp.
This goddess, who is established in the fourfold branches of knowledge, who brings the three worlds under her control,
who is manifestly composed of pure consciousness, and who bestows good fortune, appears here in embodied form.
Great prosperity is impermanent by nature, yet she herself is directly of the form of the Imperishable; pervading the universe in the form of sixteen syllables, she remains established therein.
The nine-syllabled great vidyā, as well as those of five, eight, one, ten,
a hundred, and a thousand syllables.
Pervading all these groups of mantras, she remains established;
she is that which is remembered as the essence within the four Vedas and their auxiliary limbs (vedāṅgas).
Among the Purāṇas and the Smṛtisāras, that which is the most essential and great,
superior to all, the essence of essences, and the supreme— [that is this].
Just as butter is produced from curd by extracting its essence,
so too is that which is called nectar, the sustainer of the life-force of the gods.
Likewise, having extracted the essence from all the scriptures, the Vedas, and the mantras, it has been set forth for the sake of the Brahmin in this Agni[-purāṇa].
The Brāhmaṇa gave it to Vasiṣṭha, and Vasiṣṭha to Rāghava; by him, who is the soul of all, mortals were then delivered from the cycle of existence.
Having divided non-duality into two types, the Sage with his vision of knowledge revealed the power of mantra through twenty-nine [verses].
By him, the goddess named Pratyaṅgirā was made to achieve gentleness;
indeed, with Nārada’s consent, the name of the goddess was divided into two.
Like a treasure, it must be guarded with great effort from thieves;
it should not be given to just anyone, but should be given only to one who has saved one's life.
O Maheśvarī, this essence, which is established in knowledge, must be imparted to one who is stainless, tranquil, and dearer even than life itself.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the section on Nirvāṇa within the Dakṣiṇāmnāya of the Śrī Vārāhī Tantra.
The Śrī Devī said:
Salutations to the God of gods, the omniscient, the Great Soul;
salutations to You, the all-pervading creator, sustainer, and destroyer of the universe.
O Jayadeva, Lord of the World, O Master, I have something to ask;
my mind has become so agitated by fear that I do not dare to speak.
"Be gracious, O Supreme Lord; you ought to sever my doubt.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Do not harbor any doubt, O Queen of the Gods; there is no one other than you who is dear to me.
Free from fear, O Goddess, ask at your own will whatever is desired in your heart.
"O Goddess, whatever doubt you have, ask it as you wish.
Śrī Devī said:
Salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you, O Maheśvarī! When you, the supreme goddess Kālikā, who is the very form of consciousness, have departed, [then...]
Therefore, O God, by the consent of Nārada, that sage—
who was a knower of all scriptures, a hero, and the best among practitioners— departed for Vaidha.
"What did Bhadra do, and what did Kāra, Vaśiṣṭha, and Nārada do in the past?
Bhairava said:
You are blessed; you have accomplished your purpose, for you know how to hear according to reality.
Your mind is intent on hearing this again with its extremely subtle distinctions.
Supreme intelligence has been born; salutations to you, O Supreme Goddess!
You are the seventeen-syllable Vidyā, the supreme digit of all knowledge.
The shatterer of the fragment, the fragment itself, the one whose limbs are broken into pieces,
Kālī who has entered the circle of fragments— the seventeen-syllable Vidyā.
The unmanifest (akulā) who devours the bindu of Time in the form of a serpent,
possessing a beautiful triple-folded gait, is remembered as the seventeenth Vidyā, Lakṣmī.
Standing in the midst of the non-syllable and the syllable, abiding in the syllable yet devoid of both the syllable and the non-syllable;
she who is the supreme bliss beyond the letter 'A'—this is the seventeen-syllable mantra of accomplishment.
The letter *ra* situated at the end, the letter *ra* situated in the middle, joined with the sound *rāva-rāva*,
and the sequence *rā-valī-rāva*— this is to be known as the great seventeen-syllable mantra.
That which begins with *kāṃ* and ends with *chāṃ*, accompanied by the great heart-throb and the sound *huṃ*, and seized by the hand of the restless Rāva— this is the seventeenth digit (*kalā*).
Through the union of the perishable and the imperishable, O Kālī, you abide in the sound;
there is no state higher than the Mistress of Yoga, the seventeen-syllable Vidyā.
Haha-hā-ha-ha-līnā, vilīnā, hahane hasā;
hanādānā, padaillīnā— this is the seventeen-syllable Vidyā.
In this way, the Supreme Goddess describes the seventeenth letter.
The supreme goddess Nirguṇā is the intense healer of all ailments in succession;
she is proclaimed to consist of two hundred and ninety syllables.
The Vidyā devoid of the three qualities is proclaimed as Trikhaṇḍā;
herein, there exists no distinction among the nine or sixteen syllables.
By means of this vidyā, O Goddess, [beings] abandon birth and death;
so too did the foremost sages such as Nārada and the yogis such as Kapila.
Having become a conqueror of the three worlds, they indeed wander at will;
their movement is then unimpeded, and they have attained knowledge of the three periods of time.
O Goddess, in the city called Śoṇita, within the form of Hari and Śaṅkara,
the lord of sages Nārada bestowed [this] upon Kṛṣṇa.
Formerly, Vāsudeva, having been deluded by Hara, gave the Hariśājṛmbhana weapon to Pārtha for his protection, provided that it was to be employed only when one was thus deluded.
Just as a flower once enjoyed by Bhṛgu becomes fit for Śiva,
so too the reality that is beyond syllables is united with syllables.

O Goddess, one should not cause the extraction (uddhāra) to be written down; she is Parā herself, the Mistress of the Phonemes (Varṇeśvarī). Indeed, a curse will surely occur, and the destruction of the mantra will arise.
Kālī turns her face away from the sinful; let her become the refuge of one's name. O Goddess of Gods, always place [her] within the heart, from ear to ear.
Emerging from the mouth of the Guru and established in the heart via the path of the ears,
the extraction of the mantra becomes as if it were written upon water.
One should not write this Vidyā, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, in a book; rather,
having understood the auspicious and inauspicious nature of the ritual actions performed throughout the year, one should [inscribe it] upon a cloth.
If one desires auspiciousness, one should not bestow the mantra upon an unacquainted disciple on the eighth lunar day; for he who gives the mantra to such a person [incurs misfortune].
Residence in a most dreadful hell will be certain;
therefore, with every effort, this must never be disclosed.
The Goddess is pleased with one who possesses a mind of faith;
from faith arises prosperity, while from doubt one becomes a vessel for suffering.
There would be loss of the accomplishment of one's own body; therefore, one should take refuge in the non-conceptual.
One should not deliberate there at all as to what is to be done or what is not to be done.
I too, together with Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the sages,
took up a single vessel and remained free from conceptual construction, just as she had taken refuge.
It carries away gods, gandharvas, daityas, and others, as well as rakshasas, serpents, and humans;
it flows with the discharge of excrement and urine, thoroughly saturated by the seven bodily constituents.
By means of the twofold investigation of these, one should practice the non-conceptual state;
for when the sun has risen, do the darknesses remain as the world dawns?
Likewise, by the power of the Goddess, what conduct or reflection could there be?
O Queen of Gods, what need is there for much speaking? This must be guarded with great effort.
O Great Goddess, this which grants all accomplishments must be guarded with great effort;
if it is made public, one encounters death and the loss of accomplishment occurs.
In whatever mantra there is a particular practice, such is the dharma therein;
by that one becomes successful, whether attaining heaven or liberation.
Neither merit nor evil and the like arise from that [void] in succession; moreover,
even great merit does not increase from a prior heap.
Whatever has arisen in its entirety within this world is capable [of being that];
therefore, whether pure or impure, power is the very nature of Brahman.
O Brahmins, knowers of all the Vedas, practitioners of virtuous conduct and excellent vows:
even in a Cāṇḍāla or a dog-cooker, the Self indeed dwells everywhere.
Know indeed that the Self is Brahman; abandon delusive knowledge. Knowledge alone is the supreme reality; therefore, take refuge in knowledge.
One should completely abandon all conceptual construction by means of the path of knowledge;
for such conceptual construction is a great fault, and one who indulges in it certainly becomes a partaker of sin.
The body consists of Śiva and Śakti; from the union of Rajas and Śukra it is born.
O Supreme Goddess, you are merged in the Supreme Brahman, beyond expression, and supreme.
Indeed, there are various substances for the *nīrājana* rite, such as honey and *madhūmaira*;
however, O lady of excellent limbs, no fault exists in the sacrifice when it is performed by one who is all-knowing.
In the great horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha), how could the killing of a horse take place?
[The substitutes are] water, milk, ghee, as well as honey, maireya wine, and sugarcane juice.
There is that which originates from flowers, that which originates from grains, that which is prepared with buttermilk, and likewise that which originates from mangoes,
in various and many different varieties.
That which is performed out of ignorance immediately becomes a great transgression;
[it includes] the sins of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold, and so forth.
Through worship, the knower of mantras, being free from conceptual construction, brings forth all that is produced by the gods; he should bring forth a full jar of water, as fluid as water itself.
Once the seven-day period has been established, O Dear One, the water is endowed with life;
there is nothing [left] except for the ring finger, nor is there any milk or other substances whatsoever.
O beautiful one, the tree is level, the fire is level; thus it remains.
O Goddess, consciousness within all beings must be known by the best of teachers; just as fire is said to become manifest through the friction of wood and other materials.
Just as that wood is consumed by the fire it produces, so too is this world, composed of Brahman,
consumed by that very [realization] through the abandonment of both merit and demerit, both here and in the hereafter.
O beloved, whether it be feces, urine, or even the menses of a woman—whatever exists—all such things as excrement and the like should be investigated; for indeed, delusion alone is the cause.
One should know that food is Brahman; from it arises the origin of the various living beings who depend upon it. Since that [food] is indeed excrement, by what means could one suffer?
O Goddess, cow urine is life-sustaining;
even the consumption of cow urine is declared in the penances for liberation from such sins as the killing of a Brahmin.
O Supreme Goddess, there is no doubt that delusion regarding feces and urine is indeed a defect;
however, your body is never produced from the menses of women.
By that which is conceptualized and purified, the supreme state is attained;
for the seed of a person is indeed designated as "kha-du."
O Supreme Goddess, this body is indeed the *bindu*, bearing the form of Śiva;
by virtue of its nature as Śiva-tattva, there is truly no defilement from stool and the like at that time.
O beautiful one, by what means is the purifier of the body known? Everything is attained through the path of knowledge by one who is free from conceptual construction.

O Maheśānī, for one who is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) by virtue of being changeless (*nirvikālatayā*), no portion of sin arises, nor does anything become loathsome through its flavor (*rasa*).
Even that which is joined with faults may be considered entirely auspicious.
Knowledge consisting of the bliss of Brahman becomes identical with the Supreme Brahman;
having known that, O Supreme Goddess, O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall speak.
A Kṣatriya does not [attain] the Brahmanic star for the sake of Brahmanhood, nor does a Vaiśya [attain] the Vaiśya [star];
a Śūdra does not [attain it] through a Śūdra, but rather through the Supreme Goddess.
O Supreme Goddess, in the state of higher reflection (vicāra), even a Puṣkasa is not a Puṣkasa;
know for certain that he is the Supreme Self in every respect.
Water fallen from the sky flows along its downward path;
yet once it has entered the midst of a village, it becomes entirely filled with excrement, urine, and the like.
O Goddess of gods, even a dead cow, a horse, a cat, or a donkey, when accompanied by blood,
becomes as pure as if it had been joined with the entire Ganges.
That very water is the nectar of the Gaṅgā; turbidity does not remain there at all.
As for the defects found in feces and urine, they are merely the product of delusion.
Woman is declared to be pure, since she is produced from the body;
by means of the ritual involving blood and other substances, the supreme state is attained.
That which is the seed of a person is called the *bindu*; semen is the cause of all [existence]. Why, then, is that body censured?
When a man emerges from the womb due to the contact of the vulva and the phallus,
who at that time of birth would not be one who has violated the teacher’s bed?
Listen, O beloved, to this knowledge which is free from merit and sin:
I alone am the mother of millions of cosmic eggs, the very embodiment of my own true nature.
Having enjoyed the entire world for the sake of play by means of various vehicles,
[I shall do so] according to the division of the potter's wheel, just as the time of a jar is contained within the jar itself.
O Supreme Goddess, it is seen that [space] exists pervading the sky;
yet when there is a jar, a state of division arises within the space.
Just as the individual soul residing in the body pervades everywhere upon the destruction of the body, O fair-faced one, therefore the state of Brahman is great.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, one should always remain free from conceptual construction;
thus, in that which consists of pure consciousness, there is knowledge and equanimity toward all living beings.
And because it is non-existent in all castes, there is equality here; of this there is no doubt.
It proceeds with equality, just as light proceeds from the sun.
When the darkness of another has been destroyed, that which was given and was not pervasive dries up in an instant;
it dries up all urine and the like, but sandalwood never dries up mud.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, one becomes identical with all things;
yet, O Beloved Goddess, it should be understood that accomplishment (siddhi) comes through the grace of the venerable Guru.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, Master of the World, O Śaṅkara, please explain how a practitioner may accomplish the ritual applications and so forth through the distribution [of the mantras].
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which indicates success,
by means of which a hero may achieve accomplishment within the lineage of the Vīrācāra.
But he who desires to perform the ritual application without having first completed the preliminary service (puraścaryā) will become a vessel for ten million great sins.
O Goddess, there is none more wicked than those who defile the Kula path;
therefore, one must always protect it even at the cost of all possessions or even by the sacrifice of one's life.
Through action, mind, and speech, one should perform the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
The practitioner of mantra, subsisting on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) and with senses subdued, should recite the mantra one million times according to its syllables.
During the day one should observe celibacy, and at night one may act as one desires;
one should worship the Goddess according to the prescribed ritual, preceded by the five-fold offering.
One should certainly not have it performed there with its ancillaries and five-fold offerings;
rather, one should perform the fire-oblation ten times the number [of mantras recited], using bilva leaves soaked in clarified butter.
For the sake of pleasing the Goddess, one should satisfy her with goat meat smeared with the three sweets;
indeed, one should satisfy the Goddess with nectar using portions equal to one-tenth of the oblations.
The ritual sprinkling (mārjana) is declared to be one-tenth of the libation (tarpaṇa);
one should indeed perform the great feeding of virgins (kumārī-bhojana) as one-tenth of that.
In the Kali age, the practitioner should perform the *puraścaryā* fourfold;
having received initiation, one must certainly not delay the *puraścaryā*.
Having realized the fickleness of life, one should contemplate the welfare of one's own soul;
for if one dies after receiving initiation without having performed the preliminary rites (puraścaryā), [the result is lost].
One would surely become one with Brahman after a hundred years of remaining without support;
therefore, O Goddess, one should resort to *puraścaryā* with all one's soul.
Or, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, one should perform the *puraścaraṇa*;
having recited the mantra until liberation [from obstacles] is attained, it is called *puraścaraṇa*.
One should perform all rites as previously enjoined, using a tenth part [of the materials];
now listen, for I shall presently explain the ritual applications.
The Vīradīkṣā is not for those who are incapable; having first performed worship according to the rules, whether situated in a cremation ground, at a Śiva-shrine, in a house, or upon a vehicle.
One should always offer lamps and so forth in three ways; furthermore, on sacred festival days (parvan),
one who is truthful in speech, endowed with fortitude, and free from desire and anger [should do so].
A hero who is joined with power and resources, or else one who has companions.
Then, at the arrival of night, being without companions or wealth and subsisting on alms,
one should first recite the mantra one thousand times for the purpose of purifying the body.
When the Goddess is satisfied, one should offer oblations exactly as previously instructed;
thereafter, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times during the day, abstaining from food.
If one is unable to perform the subsequent meditation after eating,
one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred times during the twilight (saṃdhyā), followed by the pair [of mantras] and the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga).
Then, at night, one should perform recitation according to one's capacity and in the proper sequence;
afterwards, for the sake of the complete accomplishment of the mantra, one should perform oblations amounting to one-tenth of the recitation.
Those who perform the homa for you are worthy of worship; success will certainly be achieved.
Alternatively, the recitation should be performed twice as much for up to seven days.

When [a planet] is in a cruel sign and so forth, or in the eighth house, one should perform oblations for the pacification of the planets (grahaśāntika) at the three junctions of the day and at midnight for one, two, three, or four days.
One is liberated from disease through the sprinkling [of water] for wind and other humors, and by means of fire oblations (homa);
or, beginning on the eighth or fourteenth day, one should perform a hundred [recitations of the name of] Hara.
From performing the fire sacrifice (homa) with a tenth part [of the recitation] and from sprinkling [the water], great peace will clearly arise.
The mantra-practitioner should perform five hundred recitations and offer three hundred oblations.
At the conclusion of the oblation, one should behold the consecration and indeed attain nourishment;
having offered three hundred oblations and recited [the mantra] three hundred times on the eighth day.
By reciting [the mantra] ending with *hāṃ* while performing the sprinkling (*sekata*), a human being attains nourishment (*puṣṭi*).
Having recited it a thousand times, one should indeed offer five hundred oblations (*hunet*).
The serpents and the inhabitants of the cattle-pens obtain nourishment from that sandy bank.
Furthermore, one's own or another's water-mills will cease to function.
From performing this three times a day for three weeks, [the result] arises;
having taken sand from a cremation ground, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
O Gaurī, wherever one casts this chain, there shall be the breaking of fetters;
holding it empowered three times with the *bhūtāṅkuśa* foot-step mantra.
One should immobilize boats, carts, and machines, and release those that are stuck or obstructed;
likewise, one should pacify the agitation caused by poison and the presence of wicked creatures in evil families.
Having recited [the mantra] seven times over sand, one shall ward off a great storm;
having recited it seven times over black mustard seeds, one who has been seized by spirits and the like shall be released.

Having formed the *dhṛti-mudrā*, one should strike [the patient]; then fever, quartan fever, and others are certainly abandoned. Furthermore, by means of water over which the mantra has been recited seven times, [these ailments are likewise removed].
Various diseases, such as spider-bites, donkey-bites, and boils, as well as diverse ailments, are averted by the offering of the *citrāguggulu* incense.
Chanted seven times, it destroys [the effects of] sprinkling on the right, drinking, or eating;
water consecrated twenty-one times likewise [destroys them].
Whether stationary or moving, one may destroy [the enemy] by drinking poison;
likewise, success is achieved through flowers, food, white mustard seeds, and the ashes of a cremation ground.
On the seventh day of the mantra-repetition, for the purpose of deluding the enemy along with his followers,
[one should perform the rite] upon a great vessel, a heap of grain, and jars filled with the five products [of the cow].
And for one who is constantly devoted to worship, that [merit] shall become inexhaustible;
one should recite the *sauliṣya* mantra over a *bilva* fruit placed within a treasury of wealth upon a cloth.
p.
153a) Wealth equal to that of the Giver of Riches (Kubera) shall never perish;
one should worship [the deity] in the elephant stable with loosened reins using lotus flowers.
They never perish, and the increase of elephants occurs;
having formed a nine-cornered [figure] with the series of positions for the horse and the elephant.
When worshipped, dogs perish and auspicious prosperity increases;
likewise for white guñjā seeds, a snake’s skull, a tiger’s claw, and cowrie shells.
Chanted seven times, it should be held in the mouth; then no injury from weapons shall occur.
For children, mustard seeds should be consecrated with the mantra one hundred and eight times according to their number.
Tied around the neck, they increase [prosperity], or one becomes firm in longevity or wisdom;
a ripe bilva fruit [tied] during the Puṣya conjunction, consecrated with five hundred recitations of the mantra.
A woman sprinkled with water from the *tarjani* finger gives birth to a son even if she is childless;
furthermore, he who, having fasted for a day and night, remains unsmeared with oil, should perform the recitation (*japa*).
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, untimely death is destroyed;
for what secret remains before the blazing light of the wick of the lotus-rayed [Sun]?
One born in the forest sees a treasure with a thousand [verses];
having taken earth from a crossroads, one should place twenty-five [units] in the middle of the house.
Having recited [the mantra], one should dispel sleep; thus, an unfortunate woman becomes blessed.
Sesame seeds, rice, and white mustard seeds—each consecrated ten times with the mantra.
He who, having unified [the breaths], casts [them] down so that the enemy does not step upon his foot,
is called the "Reed-Flute" (Phalvālivaṃsika), numbering one hundred and twenty-five.

If one were to cast it at any time when it has already occurred, the person would become diseased. [The remedy is] parched grain, unbroken rice, and white mustard seeds, with that ash consecrated a hundred times with mantras.
Wherever the practitioner of mantra casts [the substance], from that place disease shall arise.
If [the affliction] has already occurred, one should stand in water reaching up to the neck and recite the mantra five hundred times.
Likewise, by means of oblations to Varuṇa, a great rain will certainly occur;
O Dear One, the practitioner of mantras should recite the mantra fifty times and perform fifty oblations.
Without a doubt, by reciting [the mantra] five hundred times, the practitioner shall bring even the Lord of Śacī under his control within seven days;
furthermore, he should perform one hundred and fifty fire-oblations (homa).
Furthermore, having recited [the mantra] five hundred times over white mustard seeds and unbroken rice grains,
if these are worn on the head, the throat, or the arm, they effect the immobilization of a divine being.
Having offered a hundred oblations of Apāmārga, that same act is performed for him;
he will constantly become unfortunate and shall suffer the destruction of his affection.
Having combined three hundred measures of *siddhārtha* and *guggulu*,
at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (*homa*), great joy arises for him and displeasure for his enemies.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of golden seeds for seven days;
[the target] will quickly become intoxicated, or [if using] round [seeds] mixed with ghee.
For seven days and nights, one should recite the mantra while remaining pure and endowed with the proper observances;
during the day, one should maintain celibacy, and at night, one may act as one desires.
O Goddess, one should offer five hundred oblations of cotton seeds mixed with husks and oil for twenty-one days; this would even take away the fortune of Indra himself.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Guru (Jyeṣṭha), one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times over the worship-vessel;
having offered the three sweets into the fire and performed the consecration, one obtains the eightfold prosperity from that splendor.
Having fashioned a figure out of flour up to the size of a thumb,
and having cut it into five hundred pieces and offered them as oblations, one shall marry a woman of his own lineage.
Having prepared vermilion mixed with unbroken rice grains consecrated one hundred and eight times,
and having placed it in the hand of the girl, she will become possessed by the deity.
Mustard seeds and alkali produced from smoke, consecrated ten times with mantras,
certainly pacify great serpents by the mere act of bathing.
Either oil or ghee, consecrated eight times with mantras,
when administered by drinking or applied to the navel, brings about the cessation of the newborn's sleep at the mouth.
Having worshipped the jar at the location of the head, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
then, regarding beneficial and harmful tasks, one shall receive encouragement from both oneself and others.
Having taken up his garments and drawn Kṛṣṇa toward him for a hundred thousand times,
he remains truly invisible as he plays upon the surface of the earth.
Holding twenty-five thousand [stalks] in one's hand, one should recite the *vacā* mantra;
at the conclusion of the recitation, the wise person should consume it, and they will become equal to Vāgīśvara.
When the hero performs fifty thousand oblations with kadamba flowers,
the Vetālas quickly emerge from the sacrificial pit and then attain accomplishment.
The Kākinī, Bhūta, and Piśācikā are satisfied by the *vīra-homa*;
by a *homa* of half of half a hundred thousand [oblations], she shall daily grant one *pala*.
Take the palm of the maiden’s hand at the cremation ground;
having recited [the mantra] fifty times, may you become the offering of the past, future, and present.
Taking two human eyeballs together with a hundred stalks of young grass,
and having applied a tilaka mark on his forehead, whoever looks [at them] shall become submissive.
Whoever applies a tilaka made from saffron, agallochum, camphor, and gorocana, well-mixed together and consecrated one hundred times with mantras;
In battle, in the royal court, in gambling, or in dispute, he shall be victorious;
[this occurs] when the Siddhārthaka armor is white at dawn within the belly of the jar.
Having performed [the rite] on the fourteenth day at dawn, having worshipped [it] with honey,
and having cast it into the mouth and recited the mantra, one shall be victorious in debate with others.
The root of the *śrapuṃkhikā* plant, consecrated one hundred and eight times,
when tied as a head-wrap, wards off the arrows of others.
There, due to the distinction between conduct and non-conduct, the Goddess does not exist;
even one who is without conduct is a Piśāca-conductor, and therefore the Goddess exists through suchness.
What is the use of saying more? I shall state the essential point:
