having made a seat of human skin, one should perform worship using a human skull as the vessel.
Just as one should accomplish [the practice] through non-conceptualization as taught from the mouth of the Guru,
it is completely filled by the very cause that resembles the juice of lac.
Having given a *phalgū* fruit there in the center when the vessel has been filled for that purpose,
especially on the eighth, the fourteenth, or the ninth lunar day.
Likewise, on Śivarātri, one should perform worship during the night;
indeed, one should carry out everything exactly as in the worship of the Śrīcakra.
One should place the great vessel within the triangle of the bindu-cakra;
in the five-spoked [wheel] of Pañcakālī, one should indeed place the caru-oblation in five [vessels] in due order.
O auspicious lady, there is nothing higher than this for the worship of the Kālikā-krama;
through it, one will certainly attain enjoyments, heaven, happiness, liberation, and the perfection of the command.
Truth, truth, O Great Goddess, this truth I speak to you:
whoever acts otherwise, it is through the logic of causes and fallacious reasoning.
He would only undergo exhaustion and would not attain accomplishment.
Thus has this Kula lineage of Kālikā been fully explained to you.
This supreme and divine ritual procedure, transmitted through the sequence of the scriptures and the three times, must be guarded with great effort; one should not give it to just anyone.
Indeed, she who is devoted to the Guru consists of the great scriptures;
seeing beautiful flowers and fruits, as well as garments and ornaments, [she is delighted].
Whatever on earth is dear to oneself and difficult to obtain,
one should first give that to the gurus and thereafter retain it for oneself.
The Goddess of the lineage of the Guru’s tradition should bestow [the teaching] upon the worshiper;
for when the Guru is satisfied, Kālikā is satisfied with the lineage.
By whomsoever this treatise is written, in whose hands it remains,
or wherever it is situated, there the Supreme Goddess is worshipped according to the prescribed rites.
Indeed, he who worships this book of the Kālikula lineage lives for six months without obstacles, and even for as long as he lives.
By whomsoever Kālikā, the destroyer of time, is worshipped in its entirety,
that person shall always reckon the whole universe, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, as being subject to time.
At that time, in every age of the *sāyuga*, the goddess Kālikā should be meditated upon;
there is no sacrifice equal to Kālī, and no austerity equal to Kālī.
There is no dharma equal to Kālī, and there is nothing like Kālī on earth;
he should be known as one liberated while living, for he is indeed a great Pāśupata.
O great yogi, know that those who have taken to the path are Kālikā;
I am the god Mṛtyuñjaya, and one becomes so through the worship of Maṅgalā.
In the Kali age, Kālī should especially be worshipped with great effort,
O Dear One, in a place that is free from obstacles and endowed with the presence of the deity.
He who is the unknown Lord Bhairava becomes equal to Rudra as a listener;
he alone, in many ways and at various times, acts for the benefit of those possessed of form.
The currents of various tantras have come to possess various lineages;
though there are differences in the tantras and differences in their names, they are a single power manifested a thousandfold.
Maṅgalā, Mahāmāyā, Caṇḍakāpālinī,
Śivā, Cāmuṇḍā, Carcikā, Caṇḍā, and Kālī, who is the end of creation and preservation.
She is the Inexpressible, the Great Being, Guhyakālī, the Supreme Jayā;
she is remembered as Siddhilakṣmī, Viśvalakṣmī, and Mahāpratyaṅgirā.
Sundarī, Tripurā, Cāru, Ugracaṇḍā, and Prakāśinī—
she has become divided in many ways, taking recourse in various distinctions.
One who, through the divine eye, should recognize her as being one yet manifold in form—
he alone is the most excellent practitioner, a vessel for the knowledge of accomplishment.
One who delights in the practice will certainly partake in all accomplishments.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the *Śrī Vārāhī Tantra*, in the section on Nirvāṇa within the Dakṣiṇāmnāya.
Bhairava said:
Therefore, one should practice that posture; from it comes health and lightness of the limbs.
[This was taught] by sages such as Vasiṣṭha and by yogis such as Matsyendra.
Certain accepted postures are now described:
having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the chest.
When the body is seated with the legs crossed, that is called the *svastika* posture.
One should place the right ankle on the left side of the back.
Likewise, the right and the left [should be] like the cow's mouth; thus it is the "cow-mouth" (gomukha) posture.
Placing one foot upon the thigh while the other leg is likewise positioned [upon the opposite thigh],
this is called the *vīrāsana* posture.
Pressing the anus with the two heels while remaining composed and free from agitation—
this, the knowers of yoga declare, is the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana).

Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) by placing the hands between the knees and the thighs, and having placed them on the ground, one remains in the sky-like position; this is the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana).
When one sits in the middle of the cock's posture (kukkuṭāsana) with the hands placed on the ground, it is called Vaṃdhya; when one lies flat on the back like a tortoise, this is called Utānakūrmaka.
Holding the two big toes with both arms up to the ears, one should perform the drawing of the bow;
this is called the bow posture (dhanurāsana).

Placing the right foot upon the root of the left thigh and wrapping the left foot around the outside of the knee, one should remain standing with the toes pointing forward; this is the posture (āsana) declared by the illustrious Matsyanātha.
The Matsyendra-pīṭha, blazing like a fire, is a fierce weapon that shatters obstacles;
through practice, it bestows upon men the awakening of the Kuṇḍalinī and stability of the body.
Like a corpse lying face up on the ground, it brings about pacification along with its latent tendencies;
it is the peace that removes latent tendencies and produces tranquility for the mind.
Eighty-four postures have indeed been taught by Śiva;
taking from among them a quartet that constitutes the essence, I shall now describe them.
The fourfold [postures] are the Siddha, the Padma, the Siṃha, and the Bhadra.
O Best One, two things should always remain there upon the lotus-throne:
having firmly placed the yoni against the root of the left foot, one should fix the other foot upon the penis, keeping the body perfectly balanced and steady.
Standing firm with the senses fully controlled, gazing at the space between the eyebrows with a steady gaze— this is called Siddhāsana, which generates the breaking open of the door to liberation.
Having placed the left ankle above the penis,
and likewise having placed the other ankle upon that, this becomes Siddhāsana.
Some call this Siddhāsana; others know it as Vajrāsana. Some call it Sukhāsana, while others call it Guptāsana.
Just as self-restraint is primary among the restraints (yamas) and non-violence among the observances (niyamas),
they know that Siddhāsana is the one foremost among all postures.
One should constantly practice that which is already accomplished in the eighty-four *pīṭhas*,
for the purification of the impurities within the seventy-two thousand channels.
Meditating on the Self for as long as twelve years,
one who steals [the essence] shall attain the presence of the Yoginī through constant practice of the Siddhāsana.
When the ever-perfect seat (sadāsiddhāsana) exists, what is the use of many other seats such as Kimādi?
When one is attentive to the eternal vital breath, the pure kumbhaka increases.
Just as the two thighs are naturally held fast within oneself through practice,
so too should one always remain firmly bound in the single Siddhāsana.
It arises spontaneously through the effortless mastery of the three bandhas;
it is neither the siddhāsana nor a posture resembling the kumbhaka.
The Khecarī-mudrā has no equal, nor is there a dissolution (laya) like that of Nāda.
Having placed the right foot upon the left thigh, and likewise the left knee [upon the right thigh].
Having firmly grasped [the feet] with both hands according to the procedure for the earth-pressing posture (bhūparipa), placing the two thumbs at the heart and the chin against the tip of the nose,
one marks [the face]; this is called the lotus posture (padmāsana) for the destruction of the ailments of those who practice self-restraint.
Having carefully placed the two feet palm-upward upon the joints of the thighs,
and likewise having placed the two hands palm-upward between the thighs, one should then fix the gaze.
One should fix the gaze on the tip of the nose and place the tongue at the root of the teeth;
having drawn up the chin toward the chest, one should stabilize [the body] very slowly.
This is declared to be the lotus posture (padmāsana), which destroys all diseases;
it is difficult for anyone to attain, yet it is found on earth by the wise.
Having joined the hands in the *saṃpuṭita* gesture, firmly assuming the *padmāsana* posture, and placing the chin tightly against the chest with a mind absorbed in meditation;

Or, when one exhales the breath that has been filled by forcefully uplifting the wind upward through the center of the essence, he attains incomparable awakening; may the grace of Śakti bestow this awakening.
The yogi, seated in the lotus posture, should fill [the body] through the gateway of the *nāḍīs*;
he who drinks the vital air (*māruta*) is liberated—of this there is no doubt.
One should place the ankle below the testicles and on both sides of the perineal seam;
the left ankle on the right side, and the right ankle on the left.
Placing both hands on the knees and extending the fingers,
one should gaze with wide-open mouth, fixing the eyes upon the tip of the nose.
This shall be the lion-throne (siṃhāsana), always honored by yogins;
it effects the union of the three bonds and is the supreme posture.
One should place the ankles below the scrotum on both sides of the perineal seam;
having firmly bound the sides of the feet with the hands, one should hold them perfectly steady.
This Bhadrasana destroys all diseases;
indeed, the Siddhas and Yogins call this Gorakṣāsana.
Thus, the lord of yogis, free from fatigue regarding the bonds of the vital breaths (prāṇa),
should then practice the purification of the channels (nāḍīśuddhi) and the yogic exercises (kriyā) involving the winds, such as the mudrās.
Success belongs to one who is engaged in practice; how could it belong to one who does not act?
The perfection of yoga is not produced by the mere recitation of scriptures.
Neither the wearing of [ascetic] dress nor talk thereof is the cause of success;
action alone is the cause of success—this is the truth, there is no doubt.
To those who delight in gluttony and the belly, and to those who merely wear the outward garb [of practitioners], awakening should not be given.
For one who is awakened and established in me, this entire world is but a hollow bubble.
For one who is impure and has [merely] arisen [in practice], how can there be an opportunity for conceptual construction?
[Such a person relies on] postures, breath-retentions, various mudrās, and other ritual instruments.
Now, through the sequence of practice according to the method of gradual acquisition, there is the stage of Haṭha;
one should be a celibate student, moderate in diet, renunciant, and devoted to yoga.
Success shall occur after one year; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
One should consume very unctuous and sweet food, omitting one-fourth of the usual quantity.
They say that meat from the shoulders, curd, buttermilk, horse gram, jujube, river fish, asafoetida, garlic, and the like are forbidden for those observing the vow of fasting.
One should know that food is unwholesome when it is made into a paste,
when it is dry, excessively salty, or when it consists of a morsel of sesame balls.
One should avoid the company of wicked people, attachment to women, the study of [secular] texts,
as well as bodily austerities such as bathing at dawn and fasting.
Wheat, rice, barley, ṣaṣṭika rice, and beautiful grains; milk, clarified butter, sugar-candy, fresh butter, white sugar, and honey.
Vegetables such as sūḍhī and paṭola fruits are prescribed, as well as mung beans and the like, along with divine water on the path of Yama and Indra.
He should partake of the yogi’s meal— desirable, sweet, unctuous, derived from cow products, nourishing to the bodily constituents, pleasing to the mind, and appropriate.
Whether young, old, very advanced in age, diseased, or weak,
one who is diligent attains perfection through practice in all yogas.
The seats (pīṭhas), the various types of breath-retention (kuṃbhaka), the hand gestures (mudrās) and other practices—
all these are for the purpose of practicing Haṭhayoga until the fruit of Rājayoga is attained.
Then, on a firm seat, the self-controlled yogi,
having mastered his posture through the sound "haṃ," should practice the path of yoga according to the method taught by the guru.
When the wind moves, water and wealth move; likewise, when it is motionless, they are steady.
A yogi attains the state of a pillar (immobility); therefore, one should restrain the vital air.
As long as the vital wind remains established in the body, so long is it said that there is life;
death is its departure from it, therefore one should not obstruct the wind.
When the channels are congested with impurities, the vital breath does not move through the central channel;
how then can the state of *ūrdhvamanī* arise, and how can there be the accomplishment of the goal?
Just as the entire network of channels, though clouded by impurities, attains purity,
at that very moment the yogi becomes capable of mastering the vital breath.
Then one should daily practice breath control (prāṇābhyāsa) with a sattvic mind,
so that while remaining in a state of ease, the impurities may reach exhaustion.
Seated in the full lotus posture, the yogi should fill the breath with the lunar current.
Having retained [the breath] according to one's capacity, one should again exhale through the Sūrya [nāḍī];
having drawn in the prāṇa through the Sūrya, one should slowly fill the abdomen.
Having performed the *kuṃbhaka* according to the rules, one should then exhale through the moon (*caṃdra*).
By whichever [nostril] one should expel, by that same one one should fill [the breath], holding it without contradiction.
Then one should inhale through the other [nāḍī] slowly and not with force;

having restrained the breath for three [counts], one should again perform [the exhalation] by means of the other. Having drunk in the air through Piṅgalā and then held it, one should release it through Vāmā.
For self-controlled practitioners who meditate upon the two orbs of the sun and the moon according to this method, the channels become purified after three months.
One should practice the kumbhakas four times a day— at dawn, midday, evening, and midnight— gradually up to eighty repetitions each time.
Sweat arises in the lowest degree, trembling occurs in the middle,
and the vital breaths rise up repeatedly in the highest degree when one is firmly established in the lotus posture.
One should perform a massage of the body with water produced from physical exertion;
by that, firmness or lightness of the body is produced.
At the very beginning of the practice, one’s food should consist of milk and ghee;
then, once the practice has become stable, one should adopt such a restrictive regimen.
Just as a lion, an elephant, or a tiger may be gradually brought under control, so too must the breath (vāyu) be practiced; otherwise, it destroys the spiritual practice.
Through properly applied breath control (prāṇāyāma), there shall be the destruction of all diseases;
through improperly practiced yoga, there arises the emergence of all diseases.
Hiccups, asthma, as well as pain in the head, ears, and eyes—
various disorders arise from the derangement of the wind (vāta).
The wind should be exhaled when it is properly joined, and it should be inhaled when it is properly joined.
One should bind [the breath] repeatedly while joined [in meditation]; in this way, one shall attain accomplishment.
When the purification of the channels occurs, then the signs will appear externally.
The beauty of the body is produced;
thus it will certainly arise, just as the retention of the wind [leads to] the kindling of the fire.
Through the purification of the channels, the manifestation of the inner sound (*nāda*) and freedom from disease arise;
for the purpose of destroying fat, phlegm, and other impurities, one should perform the six purificatory actions (*ṣaṭkarma*) and so forth.
Otherwise, a knower of reality should not practice [these], because of the equal presence of defects:
dhautī, vartī, netī, trāṭaka, and likewise naulika.
The bearer of the skull-bowl (Kapālabhāṣṭṛ) declares these six acts;
this set of six acts is to be kept secret and effects the purification of the vessel.
One who maintains manifold virtues is honored by the foremost among practitioners of yoga;
[the seat] should be four finger-breadths in width and fifteen cubits in length.
One should swallow the cloth soaked according to the path instructed by the guru;
then one should indeed draw it back out again—this is the practice of Dhauti, performed twice a day.
Dyspnea, cough, splenic disorders, skin diseases, and twenty types of phlegm-related ailments are purified by the power of the *dhautī* practice; of this there is no doubt.
Sitting in the utkaṭāsana posture with the anus smeared up to the navel, one should perform the contraction from the *ādhāra*; that is the cleansing *vasti* procedure.
Whether it be gulma, splenomegaly, or edema arising from vāta, pitta, or kapha—
all such impurities are destroyed through the power of the enema therapy (basti-karman).
The water-element action bestows clarity upon the senses and the internal organs, maintains one's own luster, possesses the brilliance of fire,
destroys the accumulation of all defects, and utterly subdues pride.
O Lord, one should insert the very smooth urine up to the nostril for a span’s length;
it is established by the Siddhas that it does not exit through the mouth.
The purifier of the skull (kapāla) should be performed, which bestows divine vision and swiftly destroys the garden of diseases that have arisen above.
With a steady gaze, concentrated upon a subtle object, he remained motionless until tears fell from his eyes; thus was the *tāṭaka* performed by the masters.
The bursting [of the eyes] causes eye disease, and the door-panel [of the eyes] causes drowsiness;
therefore, one should diligently conceal the *trāṭaka* exercise, just as one would a casket of gold.
One should rotate the abdomen with a non-slow whirling speed, moving it to the left and right;
this *naulī* is praised by those well-versed in the *gaula* [tradition].
May that Naulī, which always kindles the weak digestive fire, acts as a cooker, a unifier, and a source of bliss,
and is like a scorcher of all impurities and defects, be victorious here.
Like a blacksmith's bellows, one should perform [the breath] from left to right and right to left;
this is known as Kapālabhāti, which purifies the disorder of phlegm (kapha).
When the excess of *kapha*, fat, and strength has been removed by the six practices (*ṣaṭkarmāṇi*), one should then perform *prāṇāyāma*; it will be mastered without effort.
Through breath control (prāṇāyāma), all impurities within the seat of the body are purified;
however, some teachers do not consider any other practice to be as highly esteemed.
One who is devoted to the practice of cooking attains the yoga of the six-fold action;
even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, are intent upon breath control (prāṇāyāma).
They have attained perfection by means of that; therefore, one should practice *pavana*.
O noble-minded one, O beloved, O fortunate one, therefore one should practice *pavana*.
As long as the breath remains in the body, as long as the mind is free from affliction,
and as long as one beholds the space between the eyebrows— for that long, whence can there be fear?
When the wheel of channels has been purified through the systematic practice of breath control,
the vital air, having attained the state of *sukha-dviga*, pierces the opening of the *suṣumnā*.
When moving amidst the vital winds (māruta), steadiness of mind arises;
that state in which the mind remains perfectly steady is itself the state of Manonmanī.
To achieve that, those who know the ritual procedure perform various types of *kuṃbhaka* (breath-retentions);
from these diverse *kuṃbhakas*, one may attain manifold accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Sūryabheda, mukhyāyī, as well as āśītkāra, talī, bhastrikā, bhramarī, mūrchā, and kevala— these are the eight types of kumbhaka.
At the end of inhalation (pūraka), the bandha known as Jālandhara should be performed;
at the end of retention (kumbhaka) and at the beginning of exhalation (recaka), the Uḍḍiyānaka should be performed.
When contraction is performed below, constricting the region of the throat,
and by stretching the middle and the back, the vital breath (prāṇa) enters the central channel.
Having raised the apāna upward and led the prāṇa down from the throat,
the yogi becomes free from old age and attains the vitality of a sixteen-year-old.
Then, having comfortably assumed the vajrāsana posture upon the seat,
one should slowly draw in the external wind through the right nostril.
One should fill [the body] up to the tips of the hair and the tips of the nails, making the head the limit;
then, having performed this, one should slowly move the breath through the left channel (Iḍā).
The purification of the skull (kapāla-śodhana) destroys wind disorders (vāta-doṣa) and eliminates worms;
this is repeatedly proclaimed as "Sūryabheda."
When he slowly draws the breath through both nostrils into the mouth,
and its movement reaches as far as the throat and the cleansing reaches up to the heart-lotus;
One should perform *kumbhaka* as before and then exhale the breath through that [nostril];
this removes phlegm and other ailments, and increases bodily strength and the digestive fire.
One should always form the *kuṃbha* [posture] from the mouth, and it is manifested in the nose;
through such practice of yoga, one becomes a second Kāmadeva.
Having attained the wheel, the yogi becomes the agent of creation and dissolution;
neither hunger nor thirst, nor sleep nor even laziness arises for him.
By this method, the lord of yogis truly becomes free from all afflictions and gains a body that acts according to his will upon the circle of the earth.
He who constantly drinks the vital breath (prāṇa) with the tongue at the root of the palate shall become a vessel for all accomplishments; of this there is no doubt.
He who constantly drinks the vital breath (prāṇa) through the tongue by means of its root at the palate will,
within half a year, possess all his bodily functions in a state of perfect stability.
Having drawn the air through the tongue as before, one should perform the practice of retention (kumbhaka);
then, one should slowly exhale the breath through both nostrils by means of the vital airs.
This kumbhaka, named śītalī, destroys disorders such as gulma and phlegm, as well as fever, bile, hunger, and thirst.
Having placed both soles of the feet firmly upon the upper part of the thighs,
this becomes the perfect lotus posture (padmāsana), which destroys all sins.

Having correctly assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), with the neck and abdomen straightened, the wise one should carefully close the mouth and exhale the breath through the nostril of the right side.
Then, one should cause the vital wind to circulate within one's own body, as if on a dry land.
With effort joined with ease, one should exhale the breath through the nose;
when the air from the skull has then dissolved into the heart and throat.
Some should fill the breath with force up to the heart-lotus;
then one should exhale it again in the same manner, filling it again and again.
Just as a blacksmith’s bellows might be moved with force,
so too should one move the vital air (pavana) residing within one's own body slowly.
When the *āśrama* occurs in the body, one should then exhale through the solar channel (*sūryanāḍī*).
Then the abdomen becomes full, and likewise light through the exhalations.
One should firmly hold the middle of the nose with both fingers;
having performed the *kumbhaka* as before, one should exhale the breath through the right nostril.
The Kumbha [posture] removes wind, bile, and phlegm, nourishes the body,
awakens Kuṇḍalinī, destroys disease, bestows happiness, and is auspicious.
Situated at the mouth of the Brahma-nāḍī, he is the destroyer of the bolt of the skull;
perfectly arisen from the weapon, he is the piercer of the three knots.
Through the forceful inhalation (*pūraka*) of the *bhṛṅga* sound, and the gentle exhalation (*recaka*) of the *bhṛṅgī* sound,
by such practice of yoga, the swoon of the bliss of consciousness (*cidānanda-mūrchā*) falls upon the minds of the lords of yogis.
At the end of inhalation, having drawn [the breath] deeply through the Jālandhara [bandha], one should exhale slowly;
this is the Mūrcchanā-stha [kumbhaka], which bestows the bliss of mental absorption (manomūrchā).
With his belly filled by the stream of breath circulating within, he,
though standing in shallow water, floated like a lotus leaf.

Prāṇāyāma is said to be threefold by means of exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kuṃbhaka). Retention (kuṃbhaka) is considered to be of two kinds: "with support" (sahita) and "unaided" (kevala).
Exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and their performance together with retention (sahita-kumbhaka).
One should perform the placement accompanied by breath control until complete perfection is attained;
this is done by restraining the breath from the mouth, setting aside both exhalation and inhalation.
This is called prāṇāyāma; it is indeed the pure kumbhaka.
When pure kumbhaka is mastered, it is devoid of both exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka).
For him, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain in the three periods of time;
he can hold the breath at will with a pure and solitary *kumbhaka*.
The state of Rājayoga is indeed attained; there is no doubt about this.
Without Haṭha there is no Rājayoga, and without Rājayoga there is no Haṭha.
Since it is not accomplished otherwise because the pair is not produced, one should practice;
at the end of the exhalation of the breath, one should perform the *kumbhaka* (retention), which makes one free from disease.
Through such practice of yoga, one shall attain the state of Rājayoga;
from *kuṃbhaka* comes the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī, and from the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī [all things] arise.
The *suṣumnā* becomes permeated and the perfection of *haṭha* arises;
there is leanness of the body, serenity in the face, clarity of the internal sound (*nāda*), and the eyes become pure.
The drop (bindu) brings about health, the fire is ignited, and there is success within the channels— this is the characteristic mark of Haṭha-siddhi.
Just as Kuṇḍalinī is the support of the mountains, forests, and the earth,
so too does Kuṇḍalinī awaken through the grace of the Guru, who was previously asleep.
By that [practice], all lotuses and even their knots are split asunder;
then the path of the void becomes like a royal highway for the vital breath.
In that way the mind is without support, and in that way there is the binding of time.
Suṣumnā is the path of emptiness, the aperture of Brahmā, the great road.
The cremation ground, Śāmbhavī, and the central path—these are synonyms for one and the same thing.
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice the repetition of mudrās in order to awaken the Goddess who is asleep at the opening of the door of Brahman.

The great seal (mahāmudrā), the great lock (mahābandha), the great penetration (mahāvedha), and the sky-farer (khecarī); the upward thrust (uḍḍiyāna), the root-lock (mūlabandha), and thereafter that which is called the throat-lock (jālandhara).
Karaṇī, the one called Viparītā, Vajrolī, and Śakticālana—
this group of ten mudrās destroys death upon the earth.
Everything spoken by Ādinātha bestows the eight supernatural powers;
it is beloved by all the Siddhas and beloved by men as well.
It should be guarded with great effort, like a casket of jewels; it must never be spoken of to anyone, just as one would keep secret the amorous dalliances of a woman of noble family.
Vajrolī, Amarolī, and Sahajālī are considered the three [types].
I shall describe their characteristics and the specific manner in which they are to be practiced.
Pressing the perineum with the left foot and holding the extended right foot with both hands, one should maintain that posture comfortably.
Having placed the bindu upon the throat, one should hold the breath above;
just as a snake struck by a staff becomes straight like a staff.
When Kuṇḍalinī becomes straight and true according to its capacity, it suddenly arises;
then that state of contemplation (manana) occurs, resting upon the two cavities.
Then one should exhale very slowly and not with force;
this indeed is the Mahāmudrā praised by the great Siddhas.
The defects such as the great afflictions and so forth, as well as death and the like, arise;
yet those supreme among the wise do not speak of Mahāmudrā in that regard.
Having practiced for the duration of the moon's portion, one should practice again for the duration of the sun's portion.
One should release the mudrā when the number has reached its limit;
for all tastes, even those that are unwholesome, are indeed wholesome when they are intensely flavorful.
Even a released, terrible poison is digested like nectar;
consumption, leprosy, and insanity—preceded by indigestion—are likewise digested.
The defects go to complete destruction for one who practices Mahāmudrā;
this Mahāmudrā has been described as that which brings about great accomplishment for human beings.
It should be protected with great effort and must not be given to just anyone;
one should join the place of the womb with a quarter-part of the *ṛṣṇi*.
Having placed the right foot upon the left thigh,
one should then fill the breath and hold the heart and chin firmly.
Having released [the breath] and contracted the base, one should fix the mind in the center;
having retained it for as long as possible, one should slowly exhale the air.
Having practiced the breath-retention (saṃvyāga) equally, one should practice it on the right side;
however, according to the opinion of some, one should avoid binding the throat.
On the tongue of Śatadanta, a weapon shall become fixed;
this indeed is the Great Bond (Mahābandha), which bestows great supernatural power (mahāsiddhi).
And those best of the awakened do not speak of Mahāmudrā at all;
having practiced with the lunar portion, one should practice again with the solar portion.
One should release the mudrā when the number [of repetitions] has reached its limit;
for all tastes, even those that are unwholesome, are indeed wholesome when they are intensely flavorful.
Even a released, terrible poison is digested like nectar;
[so too are] consumption, leprosy, and *mudāvarta*, preceded by indigestion and similar ailments.
The humors (doṣas) go to total exhaustion for one who applies the Mahāmudrā;
this which is called Mahāmudrā brings about great accomplishment for human beings.
She should be guarded with great effort and must not be given to just anyone;
one should join the region of the womb with the heel portion of the foot.
Having placed the right foot upon the left thigh,
one should then fill the breath and hold the heart and chin firmly.
Having cast down the *yoni* and contracted it, one should fix the mind in the center;
having retained [the breath] according to one's capacity, one should slowly exhale the wind.
Having practiced *saṃvyāga* (the full contraction), one should practice *nara* (the human posture) on the right side;
however, according to some, one should avoid binding the throat.
A hundred-fold binding upon his tongue is prescribed for one who desires wealth;
indeed, this is a great binding that bestows supreme accomplishment.
He is skilled in liberating one from the great bond of the noose of time,
and he is the awakener of the upward movement of all the channels.
One should direct the mind toward Kedāra, which sustains the confluence of the three rivers (Triveṇī),
just as a woman endowed with beauty and charm cannot exist without a man.
The great seal (mahāmudrā) and the great bond (mahābandha) are fruitless when devoid of penetration (vedha);
the yogi, established in the great penetration, should perform the inhalation (pūraka) with one-pointed mind.
Having restrained the breath by means of the throat-lock (kaṇṭhamudrā),
one should again gently strike the buttocks with both hands held level like a yoke.
When the two cavities are drawn together, the wind vibrates rapidly;
through the conjunction of the moon, sun, and fire, the victory over death arises.
When the state of death has arisen, one should then expel the wind.
The Great Piercing (Mahāvedha), which bestows great accomplishment through practice and destroys wrinkles,
gray hair, and bondage, is cultivated by the most excellent practitioners.
This triad is Mahāmudrā, which destroys old age and death,
increases the digestive fire, and bestows qualities such as the power of becoming small (aṇimā) and so forth.
Day after day, at every watch, that which pervades all movement is divided eightfold; it is the eternal shatterer of the flood of sins.
For those who desire to know correctly, this is the first, very brief means:
one should practice the avoidance of fire, women, and the study of books at the beginning.
One should gradually raise the *kalā* by means of cutting, moving, and milking, until it reaches the center of the earth;
then, by means of the *khecarī-mudrā*.
When the tongue enters the cavity of the skull and moves in reverse,
and the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows, that becomes the Khecarī Mudrā.
Even if one remains for half a moment facing the supreme *kalā*,
the yogi is liberated in an instant from disease, death, water, and other such perils.
For him who embraces the Khecarī Mudrā, there shall be no disease, no death, no sleep, no hunger, no thirst, and no fainting.
He who knows the Khecarī Mudrā is not afflicted by disease, he is not tainted by karma, and he is not overcome by time.
Because consciousness moves in the void and the tongue moves having gone to the void,
these indeed are the Khecarī Mudrās, saluted by all the Siddhas.
For him by whom the aperture above the uvula is sealed by the Khecarī mudrā,
the bindu does not leak, nor does his linga [erect] before a passionate woman.
When the *bindu*, though moving, reaches the circle of fire,
its upward movement toward Brahman is forcibly restrained by the power [of the breath] through the *yogamudrā*.
He who, having positioned his tongue upwards, performs the drinking of the moon (soma),
undoubtedly conquers death within half a month through yoga.
The poison does not spread within that embodied being whose body is perpetually filled with the digits of the moon, even if bitten by Takṣaka.
One who constantly eats beef and drinks the wine of the immortals (amaravāruṇī)—him I recognize as one of noble birth; others are destroyers of their lineage.
The tongue is prompted by the word "cow," for its entry is indeed into the palate;
that consumption of cow-flesh is the destroyer of great sins.
The entry of the tongue is indeed the true state; it is truly brought about by much practice. That which flows perfectly from the moon is called Amaravāruṇī.

When sixteen drops have fallen from the lotus-petal at the crown of the head and the vital breath has been attained, one should turn the face upward, fix the tongue in the inverted position, and forcefully contemplate the supreme Śakti.
The yogi who drinks that pure *lākula* nectar of the stream born from its waves becomes free from defects; with a body as delicate as a lotus stalk, he becomes a stainless lord.
If one constantly gazes at the tip of the uvula with the tongue dripping saliva— which is like salt,
pungent, or like milk, or likewise like pure clarified butter— [the tongue becomes fixed].
It removes diseases, brings an end to old age, expounds the scriptures and traditions, bestows immortality, and possesses the power to attract the hosts of Siddhas.
Thus, the seed-syllable consists of emanation, and the mudrā is the single Khecarī;
the deity is the one without support, and the state is the unique Manonmanī.
For a very long time, endowed with the five streams, it generates gnosis; therein,
within that void and stainless state, the Khecarī Mudrā abides.
Just as Mount Meru remains covered and pleasant with its coating [of snow], so too does the wise man proclaim that truth;

from his mouth, which is like the moon, the river of essence flows forth from his body, and by that he wards off death for men— like fire [warding off] Varuṇa’s water— and thus there is no other way to achieve success in one's task.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the section on Nirvāṇa within the Dakṣiṇāmnāya of the Śrī Vārāhī Tantra.
Bhairava said:
Pressing with the heel, firmly contracting the vagina,
and drawing the apāna upward— this is called the mūlabandha.
By the power of the boon, one indeed causes that which has gone downward to go upward; by contracting [the breath] with that, yogis call it the *mūlabandha*.
Having firmly pressed the heel against the perineum, one should forcefully contract the wind;
thus, the vital air repeatedly ascends upward.
The *bindu* is impelled from the *prāṇa* and other [winds] by means of the *mūlabandha*;
therefore, for the complete perfection of yoga, there is no doubt that authority resides therein.
Through the constant practice of *mūlabandha*, which effects the unification of the *apāna* and *prāṇa* breaths and the retention of urine and feces, one becomes young even in old age.
The downward-moving breath (apāna) and the upward-moving vital force (māyā) [meet] in the middle at the circle of the navel;
likewise, the flame (śikhā) is made long by the wind when struck.
Then, the union of wind and fire is called *prāṇāyāma*;
when one is intensely inflamed by that, how could there be any decay of the body at that time?
By that [means], the sleeping Kuṇḍalinī is continuously awakened;
like a female serpent struck by a staff, she hisses and becomes straightened.
Then, from that foundation, one should proceed toward the interior of the Brahmāṇḍa.
Therefore, the root-lock (mūlabandha) must always be performed by yogis;
for by it, the vital breath (prāṇa), situated above the suṣumnā, is made to soar upward.
Therefore, it is called Uḍḍiyāna by the yogis,
because the great bird performs its flight there without ceasing.
That indeed is Uḍḍiyāna; it is designated as the "Kṣatra-bond.
Uḍḍiyāna is always said by the Guru to be the innate (sahaja).
He who practices this constantly, even if old, shall become young again;
and by bending forward, one should perform the contraction of the abdomen both above and below the navel.
The yogi should practice this; he will surely conquer death, there is no doubt.
Having assumed the vajrāsana, one should firmly hold the feet with both hands.
The area near the ankle-bite is called *kadaṃ*;
one should apply a posterior stretch (*paścimatāna*) to the heart and throat.
Just as one gradually attains that which has been reached, so too does one proceed toward the Gandha;
among all bonds, the Uḍḍiyānaka is indeed the most excellent.
When the firm Uḍḍiyāna band is applied, liberation becomes natural;
contracting the throat, one should firmly place [the breath] in the heart with a resolute will.
This [practice] called Dhara-bandha destroys old age and death;
it binds the network of vessels so that food does not flow downwards.
Then follows the Jālandhara-bandha, which destroys the dense suffering of the throat;
once the Jālandhara-bandha, characterized by the constriction of the throat, has been performed.
The nectar does not flow into the fire, nor does the vital breath rush forth;
by means of the characteristic of contraction, one should firmly restrain those two channels.
This middle wheel should be known as the binding of the sixteen supports.
This is the most excellent of the three bonds, practiced by the great Siddhas;
yogis know it to be the essence of all Yoga Tantras.
When the throat is quickly constricted by Kuñcarī below,
the breath shall enter the central channel through the expansion of the middle [channel].
Both the iḍā and the piṅgalā cause [the breath] to flow along the western path;
when obstructed while situated in the station of Brahmā, the wind proceeds to dissolution.
Consequently, neither birth nor death, nor old age, disease, and the like, arise.

With the navel above, the palate below, the sun above and the moon below—* (Note: *The term "urddhvanābhi" is interpreted here as "nābhi" [navel] being positioned upwards relative to the rest of the body's orientation).
The practice known as Viparītakaraṇī destroys all diseases;
for one who is constantly engaged in its practice, it increases the digestive fire.
Abundant food must be provided for that practitioner;
one who eats little or fasts entirely will become overcome by hunger and lethargy.
On the first day, one should remain for a moment with the head downward and the feet upward;
then for slightly more than a moment, and as one practices, day by day.
For six months, neither the contraction nor the expansion is seen;
he who practices this constantly for three months is a knower of time.
Even if he acts according to his own will,
that yogi who knows the Vajroli through the constant practice of yoga becomes a perfected one.
In this regard, I shall describe two things that are difficult for anyone to obtain:
milk, and secondly, a woman who is submissive.
Having properly covered the penis with garments, one should practice *kuñcana* (contraction);
whether a man or a woman, they shall attain the perfection of *vajrolī*.
With effort, one should utter the sound "phaṭ" at the crown of the head while wearing the bodice.
Gradually, for the sake of circulating the vital air (vāyu),
one should cause the falling drop to be drawn upward through practice into the wife’s womb.
Having repeatedly drawn up the bindu to the top of the head, one should protect it;
the knower of yoga who thus protects the bindu conquers death.
Death occurs through the falling of the *bindu*, while life arises from the retention of the *bindu*;
through the retention of the *bindu*, the body of the yogin becomes fragrant.
As long as the bindu remains in the body, whence can there be fear of death?
For the semen of men is dependent on the mind, and life itself is dependent on the semen.
Therefore, both the semen and the menstrual blood must be protected with great effort;
likewise, one should protect the seed within the drop and the drop itself.
The knower of yoga, through proper practice, should contract the perineum upward;
this effortless method is the vision of truth revealed for the fortunate among the meritorious.
Success is attained through the *nirmatsarā*, but not by those who are full of envy;
for the *sahajolī*, *cāmarolī*, and *vajroli* are of one and the same essence.
Having cast into water the substance produced from burnt iron,
the *vajrolī* [yoga] consists of the application of this to one's own body by both man and woman after sexual intercourse.
When the two [prāṇa and apāna] are seated comfortably, free from activity for a moment, this is called sahajolī; it should always be practiced by yogis.
This auspicious yoga bestows liberation even while enjoying worldly pleasures;
one should always sport in it, having abandoned the first stage—which is utterly devoid of essence—and having reached the final stage.

One should drink daily the cool, moderate stream [of mercury] with skull-cups, even if it is dull and impure; the immortal one should drink it constantly and perform nasal administration day after day.
One should practice *vajrolī*; among sentient beings, it is called *amarolī*.
By means of perfect proficiency in practice, one should contract the *bindu* of the male.
If a woman preserves her menses and you are a practitioner of yoga who is united with a yoginī, then that menses will not undergo destruction; of this there is no doubt.
Within her body, the sound (nāda) moves toward the bindu;
that bindu, together with the rajas produced from her own body, becomes unified.
Through the practice of the yoga of *vajrolī*, all accomplishments (*siddhi*) arise;
for by contracting the perineum upward, even through the *rajas*, one becomes a *yoginī*.
One who knows the past and the future shall surely become a sky-walker;
and through the yoga of practicing Vajrolī, one attains the perfection of the body.
Therefore, this [yoga] bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation from bondage upon practitioners;
thus, this yoga is fully realized only by those who possess merit.
Kuṭilāṅgī, Kuṇḍalinī, Bhujaṅgī, Śakti, Īśvarī,
Kuṇḍalī, and Arundhā— these are synonymous terms for the Goddess.
Just as a door that is stuck fast is forced open by a bent lever,
so too does the yogi pierce the gate of liberation by means of the Kuṇḍalinī.
The Supreme Goddess lies asleep, having covered with her mouth that gateway by which one must travel to the stainless abode of Brahmā.
The power Kuṇḍalinī resides within the root-center; shaped like a coiled serpent, she is eightfold in nature.
She is for the binding of the deluded, yet always for the liberation of yogins.
Just as Śeṣa, the coiled one (Kuṇḍalin), is the support for the oceans, mountains, and islands,
so too is Kuṇḍalin the support for all the strings of Yoga-tantras.
Kuṇḍalī is proclaimed to be curved like another serpent.
By whomsoever that power is moved, he is liberated without a doubt;
[even as] the ascetic woman Bālaraṇḍā was between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
One should seize that supreme abode of Viṣṇu with a roar of flames;
the Iḍā is the Bhṛṅgavatī Gaṅgā, and the Piṅgalā is the river Yamunā.
Between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, the serpent-like Sarasvatī, known as Vālaraṇḍā, remains asleep; grasping her by the tail, one should awaken her as if she were impure.
Having abandoned sleep, he stands upright with his body erect for a moment;
or else, remaining still like a serpent, he stays thus for half a watch (one and a half hours) in the morning and in the evening.
Having spread it out from the sun, the fringe is held loose; it should be protected from that [sunlight]. It is one span in length and four finger-breadths in width.
A soft, white garment is prescribed as the characteristic of the wrapping cloth;
the yogi, seated in the vajra posture, should protect the kuṇḍalinī.
Immediately thereafter, the practitioner should awaken Kuṇḍalinī;
by the contraction of the mind alone, one should then cause Kuṇḍalinī to move.

Even for one who has entered the mouth of death, whence can there be fear of death? For his life-force flows through the right nostril, and the moon-like [breath] is full in its long duration; likewise, the body of the deceased remains as before until the ghaṭikā.
Like the trunk of a felled tree, it performs its functions anew, though its multitude of channels— the fuel for the fire— is severed by the vast flames of Time.
Then, having moved the *kuṇḍalinī*, one should especially act as a bellows-woman (*bhastrī*).
For the self-restrained practitioner who thus practices constantly, how could there be death?
When one practices Sūryabheda, Ujjāyī, or even Śītalī,
by such application of yoga, how could there be any affliction for the self-controlled practitioner?
For a period of two muhūrtas, the ten directions become fearless;
having been drawn upward slightly, it is fully extracted from the suṣumnā.
By that [means], Kuṇḍalinī is raised up from that Suṣumnā;
therefore, this Prāṇa abandons [the body] and enters the motionless Suṣumnā.
Therefore, one should constantly move the Amarandhatī while it is sleeping comfortably;
by moving it, the yogi is swiftly liberated from disease.
The yogi by whom the power (śakti) has been set in motion becomes a vessel for spiritual accomplishments (siddhi); what is the use of much speaking on this matter? He passes his time with ease.
For one who is thus constantly devoted to celibacy and eats only in measured amounts,
accomplishment is seen from the maṇḍala through the yoga of the practice of Kuṇḍalinī.
Through practice, one should mix the expanded lunar *vibhūti* with *saham*;
one should wear it on the head, for it bestows divine vision.
The purification of the seventy-two thousand channels is considered to be achieved through the practice of Kuṇḍalinī, which is like the method of rinsing away molasses with water.
Thus have these twelve been proclaimed by Śambhu, the Primordial Lord;
even each one of them alone is capable of all accomplishments.
Without Rājayoga, the earth does not shine; without Rājayoga, the night does not shine;
and without Rājayoga, even the most wonderful mudrās do not shine.
One should practice some form of breath control (māruta) combined with mental focus; however, the wise person should not allow other mental fluctuations to arise therein.
Even without the central channel (madhyamā-nāḍī), through firm practice, the yogi’s posture,
breath control, and mudrās become straightened.
For through the practice of mudrās and the resulting meditative absorption (samādhi),
one mudrā bestows another mudrā and grants the accomplishment of auspiciousness (bhadrāsiddhi).
He who maintains the traditional instruction regarding the mudrās is indeed the venerable Guru, the Lord; he is the manifest Īśvara himself.
Constantly devoted to his word and thus composed,
he who has mastered the five times attains the sovereignty of the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
Salutations to Śiva, the Guru, whose self consists of Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā;
from whom the yogi devoted to the Supreme attains the stainless state.
Now I shall proclaim the supreme sequence of meditative absorption (samādhi),
which destroys death, is an easy means [to liberation], and brings about the highest bliss of Brahman.
The samādhi of royal yoga is like the supreme Self;
there, the flood of the hosts of immortals is void, and the void is the supreme state.
"Mindless," "dual-less," "supportless," and "stainless"—
these are synonymous terms denoting the state of one liberated while living.
Just as salt in water attains complete integration through yoga,
so too is the unification of the self and the mind designated as *samādhi*.
And that equality is the unification of the two; when the individual self is one with the supreme self and all volitional thoughts have perished, that state is designated as *samādhi*.
Concentration (samādhi) is likewise knowledge, just as camphor [dissolves] in water;
the unification of the self and the mind is designated as that concentration.
Who truly knows the greatness of Rājayoga?
Knowledge, liberation, stability, and accomplishment do not succeed through the words of a guru alone.
Renunciation of sense objects is difficult to achieve; the vision of reality is even more difficult to attain.
The innate state is difficult to attain without the compassion of a true guru;
as long as the moving vital winds do not enter the central path, and as long as the awakened life-force wind does not become firm.
As long as the mind is not born as something innate and natural, so long what is called "knowledge" is merely hypocrisy and false prattle.
When the vital air moves through its proper path, it attains all great glory;
likewise, it attains the eightfold sovereignty—this is the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-faced one.
When the primordial power (ādi-śakti) has awakened through various tastes, jars, and diverse instruments, the vital breath (prāṇa) dissolves into the void (śūnya).
For the yogin whose power of consciousness has arisen and who has abandoned all actions without exception,
the innate state shines forth of its own accord.
When the Suṣumnā carries the breath and the wind consists of twenty voids,
then the knower of yoga eradicates all karmas.
Salutations to you, O Immortal; even he, Time himself, has been struck down by you—he upon whom this entire world of moving and non-moving beings rests, like a fallen tree in the wind.
When the mind has attained equanimity, the vital breath enters the central channel;
likewise, Amarolī, Vajrolī, and Sahajolī are also realized.
Where can knowledge exist as long as the mind lives in the body? And how can even the vital breath live as long as the individual soul remains?
When both the vital breath and the individual soul have dissolved, that person attains liberation; it cannot be otherwise.
Having known the true division of the Suṣumṇā and having brought the vital air into the middle channel, one should remain constantly in the state of *ai* and obstruct the aperture of the breath.
Having made the sun and moon equal and having placed them within the cage of the *kārā*, one should [unite] the *suṣumnā* with the power of Śambhu; indeed, all others are thus useless.
Since the wind has been thoroughly mastered, the kuṇḍalinī is capable of remaining motionless;
then, through the practice of meditation, the proximity of the yoga of the individual soul is attained by the yogi.
That by which the breath is bound does not bind the mind at all;
for the two causes of the mind are latent impressions (vāsanā) and the vital air (samīraṇa).
When one of those two perishes, even the meditative cultivation perishes;
the vital air dissolves right there, and the mind dissolves right there as well.
Both of them, Mānasa and Māruta, were indeed joined together like milk and water, performing identical actions;
for wherever the censured mind proceeds, there the wind ceases its activity, and wherever the mind is, there the wind is withdrawn.
When one [of the two] is established and the other is destroyed, the activity of the other remains;
below those two is the activity of the group of senses, and for those who have understood this, there is the attainment of the state of liberation.
By their very nature, both the *rasa* and the mind possess a state of constant movement.
When the *rasa* is bound, what on this earth cannot be accomplished by the bound mind?
In its state of fainting (mūrchita), it removes disease; in death (mṛta), it restores life itself;
when bound (baddha), it bestows the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva); such is the Lord of Mercury (rasa-īśvara).
And by moving along the path of the vital breath (vāyu), one obtains great success;
from that, one attains eightfold sovereignty—thus Śaṅkara has spoken the truth.
When the vital air (vāyu) is established in mental steadiness, then the seminal point (bindu) becomes steady;
from the steadiness of the bindu, through the practice of truth, the steadiness of the physical body (piṇḍa) arises.
The mind is the lord of the senses, and the wind is the lord of the mind;
the dissolution of the wind is its lord— one should take refuge in that dissolution as the lord.
If you yourself have not been liberated, is there perhaps another mantra for the mind?
When the inward and outward breaths have been dissolved into the palate by the movement of the mind,
inhalation and exhalation are destroyed, and the grasping of sense objects ceases.
Victorious is the absorption (laya) of the yogi, which is motionless and changeless;
it has severed all volitional constructions (saṃkalpa) and is entirely free from all entanglements.
An indescribable dissolution, perceivable by oneself, arises or even becomes an object of experience;
where the vision dissolves, there lies the eternal union of the elements and the senses.
When that power, which constitutes the life-force of living beings, has reached the dissolution of the vision into the object of perception,
the Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas are like common courtesans.
The single Śāmbhavī-vidyā is like a guarded woman of noble family;
it is the inner vision of the mind with its focus within, devoid of blinking or closing.
This Śāmbhavī Mudrā is hidden within all mantras.
When the yogi’s mind and breath have dissolved into the infinite, he moves about as he pleases, looking outward with a steady gaze,
yet seeing neither what is seen nor what is not seen.
Through the grace of the venerable Guru, this mudrā becomes Khecarī; that which abides as the reality and state of Śambhu, free from both voidness and non-voidness.
One should join [the mind] with the stars and planets and slightly utter [the mantra] at the eyebrows;
on the paths traversed by the sun, this is the characteristic of the Time of Transcendence (unmanī).
Some are deluded by the practice of scriptural tradition, some in the confusion of the Vedas, and some by logic; they do not know the Savior at all.
With eyes half-closed and the mind fixed on the tip of the nose, for a moment let the moon and sun, having entered within, dissolve into the interval between the lights.
The form of light, entirely devoid of external objects, brilliantly shining— that supreme reality, the final object,
the ultimate that is to be expressed; what more could there be beyond this?
One should worship the Liṅga during the day, but one should not worship it at night;
one should constantly worship the Liṅga, neither during the day nor at night.
The Khecarī Mudrā, which produces bliss and knowledge and is endowed with the five streams, abides in that void which is free from all taint.
When the vital air, residing in the left and right channels, flows through the middle [channel], the Khecarī Mudrā remains there; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
Furthermore, that which is situated without support in the wheel of space (vyomacakra), between the moon and the sun, is the mudrā known as Khecarī.
The abode distinguished by the two *soma*s is indeed directly dear to Śiva;
one should worship the incomparable, divine Suṣumnā at the southern face.
When it is filled from the front, the Khecarī becomes certain;
when the Khecarī Mudrā is cast beyond, the Unmanī state arises.
One should practice Khecarī Mudrā until one attains the state of yogic sleep (yoganidrā);
for one who has attained yogic sleep, there is never a lapse of time.
Between the eyebrows is the abode of Śiva; there the mind is dissolved. That state should be known as the Fourth (turya); there time does not exist.
Between the moon and the sun, one should bestow the Khecarī mudrā,
which is established in the space-circle of the great void that is without support.
Having made the mind supportless, one should not think of anything at all;
he remains certainly like a pot situated within the space, both outside and inside.

Just as the external wind dissolves, so too does it dissolve within the center; there is no doubt that the vital breath (prāṇa) returns to its own place, as does the wind in the solar channel (sūryāṅgī).
For one who practices thus, constantly and day and night, the path of the vital air is mastered;
through such practice, the vital air arises and the mind dissolves therein.
There shall be freedom from aging throughout the body, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head;
and the Great Yoga, endowed with great power and prowess, is accomplished.
Drawing the mind into the midst of the Śakti, and the Śakti into the midst of the mind, one should,
by means of the mind within the mind, fix the supreme state upon that which is to be perceived.
Place yourself within the void, and place the void within yourself;
having made all things identical with the void, one should not think of anything at all.
Empty within and empty without, like an empty jar in the sky;
full within and full without, like a full jar in the ocean.
One should not engage in external thoughts, nor likewise in internal contemplation;
having abandoned all thoughts, one should not think of anything at all.
That knowledge which consists of all that is knowable is said to reside in the mind;
knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the mind alone—there is no other second path.
All this that is seen by the mind, whatever is moving or unmoving, is indeed the mind; for when the mind attains the state beyond the mind (unmanī), this very world is no longer perceived.
Through the relinquishing of the object of knowledge, the mind attains liberation;
when the mind has dissolved, even absolute isolation (kaivalya) is realized.
They say, "Laya, laya"—what is the characteristic of *laya*? It is the state where, through the cessation of mental fluctuations arising from this [state], one forgets the entire universe.
Thus, various kinds of paths to liberation, accompanied by their respective personal experiences,
have been correctly described by the great-souled former teachers.
p.
171b) It is impossible even for those who have realized reality, let alone for the deluded;
thus it has been declared by Gorakṣanātha that the worship of Nāda is now being described.
Victorious is the method taught by the illustrious Ādinātha, consisting of seventy-five million *layas*;
we consider the very practice of contemplating the *nāda* to be the grain among all these *layas*.
By closing the pair of ear-cavities, the two eyes, the nose, and the mouth, the pure sound should be heard clearly within the refuge of the stainless Suṣumnā.
In all yogas, there are four stages: commencement (ārambha), effort (ghaṭa), mastery (paricaya), and finally accomplishment (niṣpatti).
When the Brahma-granthi is pierced, the Nāda arises from the Void;
within the body, a diverse sound like that of a cricket is heard as the unstruck (anāhata) resonance.
Possessing divine fragrance and divine vision, radiant and free from disease,
one whose heart is fulfilled yet empty should become a practitioner of yoga at the commencement.
But when the second division is joined, the wind becomes situated in the middle;
the yogi becomes one who possesses *haṭha*-posture, a possessor of knowledge, and equal to a god.
Likewise, the distinctions within the Viṣṇu-grantha indicate supreme bliss;
in the state of extreme void, there arises a faint sound like that of a kettledrum.
Then, having pierced the three knots, the sound of a mṛdaṅga drum arises;
one enters the Great Void, which is the refuge of all accomplishments.
Therefore, having conquered the mind, the arising of innate bliss occurs;
likewise, the faults of duality, old age, death, hunger, sleep, and thirst [are overcome].
Then, having pierced the Rudra-knot, the vital breath (anila) reaches all the seats (pīṭhas);
the sound produced is like that of a bamboo flute, becoming a resonant ringing and a humming vibration.
When the mind has thus become unified, designated as Rājayoga,
that master of yoga becomes equal to the creator and destroyer of the universe.
Now begins the section on the Kingly Yoga (rājayoga) for those of limited intellect, concerning the breath in the mouth.
The resonance that is immediately perceived and cultivated is the dissolution of sound (*nāda-laya*);
it is bound within the hearts of the lords of yogis who possess the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of continuous contemplation upon that resonance.
Only the illustrious Guru-Natha knows that singular bliss which is ineffable by words.
The yogin, seated in the mukta posture and maintaining the Śāmbhavī mudrā,
should listen to the great internal sound within the right ear.
By practicing this sound of *māna*, the yogi hears the resonance of the *vācya*;
subsequently, having conquered all opposing factors, he becomes happy.
It is heard that at the first stage of practice, a great sound called *nāda* is perceived;
as the practice increases from there, something subtler than subtle is heard.
At first there was a sound as deep and resonant as the roar of ocean clouds;
then followed the clamor of drums, conchs, and bells.
But others heard various sounds from within, such as the tinkling of small bells, flutes, lutes, and the humming of bees.
Even when great sounds such as those of clouds and kettledrums are being heard,
one should thoroughly perceive there the subtle sound amidst the clouds on all sides.
Or, having abandoned sound, one should direct the mind toward the subtle; or, having abandoned the subtle, toward the wind;
and even when it is cast into a cremation ground, one should cause the mind to move through the eyes.
Wherever the mind first dissolves into the sound,
becoming steady right there, it dissolves along with that sound.
The fire arises in the stomach and is extinguished along with the stomach;
the mind arises in the sound and dissolves together with the sound.

Having become intent upon equanimity, through constant practice, one should firmly fixate upon the *nāda* alone, which instantly brings about the state beyond the mind (*unmanī*) and puts an end to doubt.

A single garment known to his kin, or a small tent or hut; wholesome food, whether milk or water; whatever is eaten as food, such as boiled rice, or a wooden trough, or even a vessel for eating—[these are the requisites].
Having completely abandoned all thought and all activity at all times, he who does not even direct his attention toward sound alone desires the sovereignty of yoga.
Just as a bee does not seek the fragrance of a flower once it has become devoid of sound, so too the mind, when detached from sound, no longer desires sense objects.
Through the practice of *nādagandhakārīraṇa*, the mind— increased, liberated, and rendered powerless— attains the state of mercury known as the supportless *khoṭana*.
When the wind has increased by means of its fragrance, he immediately abandons his fickleness;
and like trees whose branches have been severed, both he and his horses attain tranquility.
The serpent-like inner senses of one whose mind is bowed in devotion toward the Sound (Nāda),
having forgotten the entire universe, run toward something single-pointed somewhere.
This capable one is able to seize by force the sharp goad from the mountain-like lordly elephant of the mind as it wanders through the objects of the senses.
Indeed, a difference in attachment is said to be the internal disease of the horse that gallops about in its harness. Furthermore, it is also described as the malady of the inner steed.
When that which is known as the extremely subtle is recognized within the sound of the unstruck (*anāhata*), the mind dissolves therein; that is the supreme state of Viṣṇu.
As long as the mental construction of the space of meditation proceeds according to one's will, that is with sound; when it becomes soundless, the supreme Brahman, the Paramātman, is inferred.
Nāda is known as Śakti, while that which is named Nāda is Sadāśiva. When the knowledge of Nāda has perished, only Unmanī remains.
As long as the mind has not descended into the Nāda, it does not reach Manonmanī; that which possesses sound is called Vyoma (the ether), while that which is soundless is called Brahman.
When the arising of latent impressions has been completely exhausted through the continuous pursuit of the inner sound (nāda), the movements of the mind dissolve into the stainless, soundless state.
Thousands of millions of *nāda*s and hundreds of millions of *bindu*s all dissolve there,
where the stainless God resides.
Thus, the seed-syllable consists of emanation, and the single mudrā is khecarī;
the goddess is one, without support, and the state of consciousness is one—manonmanī.
And he never hears the sound of conchs or drums;
O God, the state of Unmanī certainly arises as something like a piece of wood.
Freed from all states and devoid of all thought, the yogi remains as if dead; he is liberated—of this there is no doubt.
Invulnerable to all weapons, invulnerable to all embodied beings,
the foremost of all mantras and tantras, the yogi is united with meditative absorption.

Whether during inhalation or exhalation, when the breath flows through the right nostril, whether upward or in the middle, it is certain that Vāyu does not flow [through the other]; there is no doubt in this matter.
The mind is neither asleep nor awake; mindfulness and its object are not otherwise. When the thought "this is mine" does not arise, he is indeed liberated.

He whose creation remains stable even without an object of sight, whose breath remains steady without effort, and whose mind is firm without a support— he alone is liberated, he is the Guru, and he is to be served.

In this world, the wise are the holy ford of knowledge, the virtuous are the holy ford of truth, the yogis with purified minds are the holy ford of the Ganges, and the enlightened are the holy ford of wisdom.
At the sacred ford of the river’s descent, at the sacred ford of charity, and at the sacred ford of modesty, noble young women wash away their transgressions through devotion.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the Dakṣiṇāmnāya section of the Nirvāṇapada within the Śrī Vārāhī Tantra.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the manifestation of the sixteen Mothers;
I shall describe Vārāhī and Nīlakālī in their proper order.
Gaurī, Padmā, Śacī, Medhā, Sāvitrī, Vijayā, Jayā, Devasenā, Svadhā, Svāhā, the Mothers, and the Mothers of the World.
Hṛṣṭi, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi, as well as the family deity of one's own lineage,
are depicted with their hair tied in braids, their faces turned downward toward the throat of the Moon.
Extremely captivating, she bore half a tilaka at the parting of her hair;
her cheeks were brushed by jeweled earrings, and she was adorned with a crown.
That Mother, the light of the ear-ornaments, having filled her ears, is united [with them],
resplendent with necklaces of gold, gems, rubies, and serpents.
Always wearing very beautiful garlands of fragrant lotuses with flavorful juices,
she bears them around her neck while wearing jeweled armlets.
With her beautiful, soft, and rounded arms as long as lotus stalks, she shone,
adorned with a bodice and possessing full, elevated breasts.
Her garments are worn thin, yellowed, and faded; she is adorned with a waist marked by three folds.
She likewise holds a spear, a thunderbolt, a bow, a sword, and a javelin.
The goddess, honored by the Sun, held with her right hands a mace,
a bell, a bow, a shield, and likewise a conch shell.
The Goddess, holding [the offerings] with her left hands in ascending order, beginning from the top;
They stand upon lions, wearing tiger skins,
possessing incomparable forms that enchant both gods and asuras.
Dark-complexioned like the petal of a blue lotus and endowed with four arms,
she holds a khaṭvāṅga and a caṇḍahāsa sword in her right hands.
Furthermore, in her left hands she holds a shield and a noose, positioned above and below;
she wears a garland of severed heads and is clothed in a tiger skin. She is a goddess.
She had emaciated limbs and long fangs; she was exceedingly tall and terrifying, with a flickering tongue and eyes that were sunken, blood-red, and utterly fearsome.
Seated upon a headless trunk as her vehicle, with ears and mouths spread wide,
she is celebrated as Kālī and is also called Cāmuṇḍā.
Victory to you, Jayantī, Maṅgalā, Kālī, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī, Durgā, Kṣamā, Śivā, Dhātrī, Svāhā, and Svadhā; salutations be to you!
With this very mantra, one should perform the recitation (japa) and the fire-oblation (homa),
as well as the offering of perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food (naivedya).
Whatever garment, ornament, or other item is given,
one should utter the name of its presiding deity, sprinkle it with water, and worship it.
One should offer [the oblation] with the root mantra followed by the individual names;
likewise, whatever perfumes, flowers, and so forth are given to the deities, [they should be offered in this manner].
Having consecrated [the image] with the waters contained in the argha vessel, one should release it;
for whoever should perform the installation or the sacrificial rite without a vessel [is at fault].
If the offerings are omitted, all wealth such as vehicles and the like becomes fruitless;
if the fragrances are omitted, there will be famine and sorrow.
In the absence of incense there is agitation, and in the absence of clothing there is loss of wealth.
If the *ratna* is missing, the wife dies; if the *vapatāka*, the leader perishes;
if the *chatra* is missing, one's umbrella is taken away; and if the *vitāna* is missing, death shall occur.
If one is devoid of the Vedas, there will be the destruction of the city and the town;
indeed, O Sage, it has been said that the destruction of the lineage occurs through the [defilement of the] water-pots.
However, due to the absence of the archway and the bull, he would slay his kinsmen and relatives;
if the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is omitted, everything becomes futile—of this there is no doubt.
But that which is devoid of mantra and vidyā perishes, even if it is complete;
however, that which is joined with the vessel and the mantra becomes the remover of all defects.
At night, one should perform the rites for the gods facing north, for that is indeed the direction of the gods;
having completed the worship of Śiva, one who is pure should likewise face north.
Pure, wearing clean garments, wise, observing silence, devoted to meditation, free from desire and fear, beyond dualities, having cast out passion, and devoid of all attachments.
Having honored oneself with fragrant white garments,
one should worship all the forms of the gods residing within one's own mind.
Among all varieties of fragrant substances, that which originates from Malaya is praised;
therefore, one should always offer sandalwood with every effort.
Ghee and sesame seeds are for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa), and liquor is for the unguent;
sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and nakha are considered excellent for incense.
The ointment named Candra, which bestows all accomplishments, should be applied;
it consists of black agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood from the Malaya mountains.
With equal parts of saffron, agallochum, and musk,
this mixture bestows delight through its fragrance upon the Goddess Durgā together with Śambhu.
The four substances— madana, camphor, saffron, and gorocanā—
one should smear the Goddess with these; thereby one shall attain all desires.
With flowers grown in the forest, or leaves produced on the mountains—
unwithered, without holes, sprinkled with water, and free from insects.
Or one should worship Śivā with flowers grown in Ansa-rāma,
or with seasonal flowers such as mallikā, jāti, and kubjaka.
With white and red lotuses, as well as blue and pale lotuses,
with *kiṃśuka*, *tagara*, *kiṃkirāta*, and *campaka* flowers;
And with *vakula*, *mandāra*, *kundapuṣpa*, and *tirīṭaka* flowers;
with *karavīra*, *arka*, *śāṃśapa*, and *aparājita* flowers.
With flowers of four kinds— white, red, yellow, and black—
and those possessing the luster of *dhuttūra*, as well as those produced from the *bandhūka* and *agasti* plants.
With *madanaiḥ*, *siṃduvāras*, and fragrant *uruvakas*,
as well as with creepers of the *brahmavṛkṣa* and tender sprouts of *dūrvā* grass.
With clusters of kuśa grass and beautiful bilva leaves,
as well as all other flowers— whether mentioned or unmentioned— growing both in water and on land.
One should worship with leaves and flowers as they are available, using all auspicious medicinal herbs,
and with all kinds of grains, leaves, and flowers.
If various kinds of flowers are not available, one should offer even leaves;
but if leaves are also unavailable, one should offer medicinal herbs.
In the absence of medicinal herbs, she becomes honored through devotion;
one should worship with kadamba flowers at night, while mallikā is prescribed for both times.
One should worship with flowers gathered during the day as they are obtained;
however, those infested by hair or insects, those that are withered, or those that have been stale [should be avoided].
One should discard flowers that have fallen on their own as well as those that are defiled.
One should not worship the Goddess with unblown buds, nor should one offer fruit that is unripe.
One should likewise discard fruit that is bruised, pierced, or overripe despite its age.
O Dear One, among all incenses, guggulu mixed with ghee is especially pleasing to Durgā and constantly increases her delight.
O King, that incense consisting of black agallochum, guggulu, and camphor, known as Mahāmāyā-priya and named Kalyāṇa, is eternally dear to the Goddess.
The fragrance of wood being burned— whether it be that which is dear or otherwise— is exceedingly captivating to the nose, providing pleasure through its subtle apertures.
Alternatively, that incense for which a fragrance arises without heat should be known as true incense, which bestows satisfaction upon the gods.
One who is full of passion should not fumigate with those substances prepared in one place,
nor should he offer incense preparations mixed with fat and marrow.
Likewise, one who steals flowers, incense, perfumes, or other ritual offerings belonging to others, having marked them as his own through theft; such a person is a thief.
If a man offers incense to the gods after smelling it, he shall fall into hell;
likewise, one should not burn incense upon the ground, nor in a place filled with food.
Having performed a hundred circumambulations in whatever manner possible, one should present that [offering];
first there should be a ghee lamp, and thereafter one produced from sesame oil.
The seven types of wicks are proclaimed as: those made from mustard seeds, resin, jaggery, curd, and food.
The first alternative for the oblation is with clarified butter (havis), and the second is with the juices of medicinal herbs;
one desiring nourishment should not perform it with fat, marrow, bone, or resinous exudations.
It brings delight to the eyes, possesses beautiful luster, and is free from distance; it has its own crest, is devoid of sound, smokeless, and neither too high nor too short.
To the right, a lamp-tree with a well-rounded wick,
oil, and a vessel should be displayed for the increase of prosperity.
One should diligently offer a lamp at the tip of a lamp-tree;
even if the heat from that lamp reaches only four finger-breadths, its merit is obtained.
In that which is known as a lamp, fire is indeed contained;
a tree-lamp should be offered, but never one placed upon the ground.
The entire earth, together with its inhabitants, was struck twice by him—
once by the blow of his own body and once by the blow of his foot— and likewise, the lamp was extinguished.
One should not offer lamp oils such as ghee and the like by mixing them together;
having mixed the oils, one shall go to the Tāmisra hell.
It may be made from lotus fibers, or from the inner fibers of *darbha* grass,
or even from the fibers of *gaṇajāva* or *darāva*, or from the fibers of the tip of a fruit.
For the purposes of a lamp, five types of wicks are always prescribed:
one made of hemp, one of coarse cloth, and those that are worn out or soiled.
One should never take what has been used for the purpose of the wick;
nor should one ever extinguish a lamp prepared for the sake of the deity.
One who steals a lamp shall become blind, and one who extinguishes it shall become one-eyed;
