therefore, a well-prepared food offering should be given to the Goddess by those endowed with good fortune.
One should avoid rice-pudding, flour-cakes, barley-gruel,
thin gruel, sweetmeats, flattened grains (pṛthuka), and the like, as well as roots and joints.
He should offer as the oblation divine rice cooked with milk, mixed with sugar,
and all the various divine side dishes.
Milk and other products from cows, as well as those from buffaloes in their entirety;
the wood-apple, the lāṅgalī, the grape, and the areca nut.
Vakula, madhuka, and likewise rasālāsrotaka,
as well as audumbara, punnāga, karuṇa, and the fruit of the karkaṭī.
Hantākī, āmalaka, the six kinds of nāgaraṅga,
mātuluṅga, kuñca, kadalī, and karamardaka.
One should offer śṛṅgāṭaka, kaśera, śālūka, mṛṇālaka, white water-lilies (kumuda), lotus stalks (paṅkajāla), and fruits.
And with offerings dear to the forest-dwellers—namely, parched grain, unbroken rice, fruits, and the like;
with stalks of sugarcane, white sugar, betel leaves, and oranges.
One should worship the Mother of the Worlds for the attainment of all desires and goals,
[offering] a five-year-old child endowed with auspicious marks and perfumed with fragrant scents and incense.
Having recited "Kālikālikāli" according to the prescribed rule, one should strike with a sword a buffalo,
a goat, or a ram that is five years old.
That blood and flesh, taken from those seized by pūtanas and other such beings,
should be offered to the Nairṛtas, consecrated with the Mahākauśika mantra.
In front of that [deity], the king should bathe, then fashion an effigy of the enemy out of flour;
having struck it with a sword, he should offer it to Skanda and Viśākhā.
Then one should bathe the Goddess with milk, ghee, water, and other liquids,
and worship her with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood.
Gold, flowers, gems, unwashed garments,
and abundant food offerings should be presented to the Goddess by those who are naturally pure.
The Goddess and her devotees, as well as maidens beginning with the first-born, are to be worshipped.
One should satisfy the twice-born, the poor, and even the outcaste dog-cookers (cāṇḍālas) with gifts of food.
But those who are devotees of Nanda and who observe the great vows are not to be driven away.
One should worship with particular distinction because that form belongs to the Āmnikas;
and at that time, during the night, the worship of the Mātṛkās and the gods must be performed.
One should raise banners, umbrellas, flags, and the like in the temple of Caṇḍikā;
one should perform the procession with colored powders, the offering of oblations, and worship Vaṭuka and the other deities.
By performing various animal sacrifices through which he is pleased,
that best of gods, out of devotion, attains the merit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
On the Mahānavamī day, one should worship her who grants all desires;
she has been proclaimed with devotion among all the classes of calves.
By performing this, one obtains fame, sovereignty, sons, victory in battle, and prosperity;
and by worshipping the Lord during the day in the dark fortnight on the day of Kanyā, one attains these same blessings.
On the ninth day, one should awaken the Goddess with the sounds of songs and musical instruments;
on the fourth day of the bright fortnight, however, is the untying of the Goddess's hair.
On the morning of the fifth day itself, one should bathe [the deity] with very pure waters;
on the seventh day, there is worship with leaf-garlands (patrikā-pūjā), and on the eighth day, the fast (cappupoṣaṇa).
On the ninth day, there shall be worship, a vigil, and the offering of the bali according to the rules;
on the tenth day, however, there is the dismissal of the deity along with festivities, amusements, and auspicious rites.
On the tenth day, however, there was a great lustration ceremony (nīrājana) that increased the strength of the army,
performed for the sake of Rama’s favor and for the destruction of Ravana.
Formerly, Mahākālī was awakened by the Brāhmaṇas during the night;
thereafter, having cast off her sleep, she rejoiced in the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina.
He joined the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa with a smile;
then, after seven nights had passed, on the ninth day, he [confronted] Rāvaṇa.
While Rāmaṇa was being caused to be slain by Mahāmāyā, who consists of the universe,
the Goddess herself watched the onset of the battle.
For seven nights she was highly honored by all the gods;
O hero, when Rāvaṇa had been slain, she was worshipped on the ninth day by all the deities.
The Grandfather of the worlds performed a special worship of Durgā;
thereafter, on the tenth day, the Goddess was sent forth with the Śāvara festivals.
In that very manner, all people should perform worship according to the prescribed rite;
the king should perform the *valanīrājana* ceremony for the increase of his own strength.
The guardian of the quarter should be set in motion by beautiful women accompanied by musical instruments;
singing, instrumental music, and other festive games and auspicious rites should be performed.
On the first day (the Pratipad), one should provide substances for the grooming of the hair;
on the second day, the "offering of the six parts" (ṣaḍgādāna) is performed for the sake of the removal of the hair.
On the third day, a mirror and likewise vermilion and collyrium;
on the fourth day, however, honey-mixture, a sectarian mark, and circular eye-ornaments.
On the fifth day, one should perform the anointing with poison and the decoration with ornaments;
on the sixth day, at the evening twilights, one should cause the awakening of the Bilva tree to take place.
On the seventh day, having brought [the image] in the morning, one should worship it within the house;
then, on the eighth day, there is fasting and the worship of the Eightfold Power (Aṣṭaśakti).
On the ninth day, one should worship Mucukundā during the daytime in the same manner;
with devotion, one should perform the worship as well as the offering of the bali-oblation.
The maiden should be worshipped and adorned with ornaments;
having performed the worship, one should dispatch her on the tenth day with festive celebrations.
The man who propitiates the Goddess according to this rite,
her shall protect like Skanda, even when he is beset by every calamity.
The number of his sons, wives, wealth, and prosperity is beyond reckoning;
having enjoyed supreme pleasures here in this world, he shall become a member of the host of gods after death.
On the sixth lunar day, one should awaken the Goddess on a bilva branch and within its fruits;
then, on the seventh lunar day, having brought that bilva branch, one should worship it thoroughly.
Furthermore, one should perform worship especially on the eighth day;
one should personally keep a vigil and offer the bali-oblation during the dead of night.
One should duly perform the offering of abundant oblations on the ninth day;
one should meditate upon the ten-armed Goddess and worship her according to the Durgā-tantra.
On the tenth day, one should indeed perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana) with the festive rites of Śāvara;
having performed that dismissal on that day, one should observe a fast during the night.
When the final quarter of the *praṇava* occurs during the daytime,
then there is the dispatching of the Goddess on the tenth day with the festivals of Śāvara.
With women, maidens, courtesans, and likewise dancers,
amidst the sounds of conchs and trumpets, as well as mṛdaṅgas and paṭahas;
With various banners and weapons, with scattered parched grain and flowers,
and with the throwing of dust and mud— these playful, curious, and auspicious activities.
With the naming of the vulva and the phallus, with songs celebrating the vulva and the phallus,
and with acts involving the vulva and the phallus, people sported with young men.
But for him who is not censured by others and who likewise does not censure another,
the Blessed Lady, becoming enraged, would bestow a most terrible curse.

Having reached the root [shrine] and performed the worship of Caṇḍikā at the first watch on the eighth day, remaining without food and abandoning sleep, one should perform worship in the morning, the ritual of animal sacrifice and offerings,

bathing, and giving gifts on the ninth day; however, the removal of the *nirmālya* (remnants of the offering) should take place on the tenth day when the moon is in the asterism of Śravaṇa or Vāsava (Dhaniṣṭhā).
One should worship the Blessed Lady Caṇḍī with the root mantra; and on the eighth day, one should propitiate her with devotion, being fully established in fasting and the practice of Pracaṇḍākṛti.
Having prepared an offering on the ninth day with various animal marrow, meat, and blood, and having reached the tenth day under the asterism Śravaṇa, one should dispatch [the messenger].
During the three constellations beginning with Mūla, on the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina,
one should worship Caṇḍikā with offerings for the increase of the kingdom.
One should keep a vigil on the eighth day and perform the ritual offering (bali) according to the rules on the ninth;
on the tenth, O beloved, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the sake of increasing strength.
One should awaken the Goddess with the root mantra, worship her with the eastern [mantra],
perform the ritual of adoration with the northern [mantra], and dismiss her with the *śravaṇa* [mantra].
The lunar day (tithi) is the arrow, the lunar day alone is the cause; the lunar day is the primary factor, and the lunar day alone is the means.
Without the lunar day, the moon is not seen at all; and without the moon, there is no accomplishment of ritual acts.
When there is a conjunction of the lunar day (tithi) and the asterism (nakṣatra), the anointing (lepana) should be performed on both;
in the absence of such a conjunction, the lunar day alone is to be taken for the rite of worshipping the Goddess.
The ninth lunar day is declared to be Umā’s, and the eighth is Hara’s;
the union of these two is the highly meritorious Umāmāheśvarī lunar day.
When the eighth lunar day is joined with the ninth, or the ninth is joined with the eighth,
that lunar day is like the Lord who is half-woman and half-man (Ardhanārīśvara) in all religious observances and the like.
On the eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina,
she should be worshipped during that night with extensive displays of great opulence.
O Bhairava, whoever out of delusion, laziness, hypocrisy, or even malice does not worship the goddess Durgā during the great festival— p. 179a).
When the Blessed Lady is enraged, she truly destroys his desires and his ultimate goals.
And in another life, having become the offering of Mahāmāyā, he is born;
therefore, for the sake of the welfare of the world and for the prosperity of all the worlds.
Both Bhadrakālī and Ugracaṇḍī, who are worshipped with the Durgātantra mantra during the great festival of Mahāmāyā.
And to the northeast of that, one should place [the vessel] provided with curd and unbroken rice,
covered with mango sprouts, and accompanied by a pair of fruits and garments.
One should place here an unblemished pitcher endowed with the five jewels and provided with petals of the five types of grain; therein, one should install the deity Varuṇa.
All rivers such as the Gaṅgā, as well as oceans and lakes,
elephants, chariot-paths, anthills, confluences, and the ten directions— [all these arise] from the lineage.
O best of Brahmins, having brought earth mixed with all medicinal herbs and water,
one who is mindful of dharma should place it there for the purpose of bathing the patron.
May all the oceans, rivers, lakes, forests,
and ponds come to the sacrificer, bringing about the destruction of his misfortunes.
One desiring prosperity should properly offer auspicious gold, ghee, wheat, and dūrvā grass along with rocanā, which brings equal increase to both one's own country and the world at large.
Agni, Brahmā, Bhavānī, the elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa), the great serpent (Śeṣa), Skanda, the Sun, the host of Mothers, the guardians of the quarters, and the nine planets.
Having worshipped each of these pitchers according to the prescribed rite, one should,
with a concentrated mind, offer a sacred thread for the deity's form (mūrtipavitra) to each of them.
The plantain, pomegranate, grain, turmeric, mānaka, kañcu,
the branch of the bilva, and jayantī are to be known as the nine-leaved plants (anavapatrikā).
Brahmāṇī is in the trunk of a plantain tree; Raktacaṇḍikā is in a pomegranate; Dhānyalakṣmī is in turmeric; and Durgā is on the mānaka leaf.
One should worship Cāmuṇḍā-Kālikā, who is established upon a Śivā-vilva tree,
free from the sorrow of the Aśoka tree, and installed on the full moon day of Kārtika during the Jayaṃtī festival.

On that [altar], the Goddess should be fashioned from gold or likewise from silver; she should have beautiful eyes and be endowed with all auspicious marks. One should worship her with bilva leaves and a sword.
There, on the eighth day, the most terrible Bhadrakālī, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
manifested together with ten million yoginīs.
On that day, for the sake of crossing over [saṃsāra], she should be worshipped by men who have observed a fast,
with garments, incense, garlands, jewels, and unguents.
Likewise, with lamps, men [should worship] with edible offerings, fruits, flowers, coriander,
various kinds of meat, incense, fire-oblations, and the gratification of Brahmins.
With bilva leaves, śrīphala fruits, sandalwood, and ghee;
with animals, pleasant drinks, and by keeping a vigil throughout the night.
In the temple of Durgā, weapons should be worshipped by the wise,
as well as musical instruments, insignia, armor, and armaments.
At night, those [images] should always be worshipped by the artisans themselves;
and when the sun is situated in Virgo (Kanyā), one should perform the worship on the eighth day of the bright fortnight.
Having fasted, one should commence the worship of the Goddess at midnight with extensive displays of great opulence, or under the constellation presided over by Varuṇa.
The slaughter of animals must be performed, as well as the killing of bulls and horses;
having offered oblations to the lords of the gods, one should complete everything for the end of the night.
O child, when the sun is situated in Virgo, one should worship on the eighth day of the bright fortnight at midnight while observing a fast,
with extensive and magnificent offerings.
One should commence the worship of the goddesses, whether under the asterisms of Rakṣa, Ṛkṣa, or Vāribha;
likewise, the slaughter of a beast should be performed, as well as the killing of a cow or a goat.
The scattering of sand should be performed for the Rākṣasas for the sake of pacifying all enemies;
it should be undertaken on the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) of the bright fortnight when the Sun is situated in Virgo.
On that night, she should be worshipped with extensive displays of great opulence;
on the ninth day, however, the offering of the bali-oblation must be performed according to the prescribed rule.
There, for the sake of prosperity, one should perform recitation and fire-offerings according to the rules;
and at that time, during the night, worship should be offered to the Mothers and the Goddesses.
O Hataghorā, O Great Hero, who causes fear to the gods and asuras!
The gods, the yakṣas, and likewise the rākṣasas are the devotees of the Goddess.
Having arrived and seen that invincible buffalo slain,
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the lords of the gods— Indra, Candra, Yama, and Anila— [approached].
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Grahas, Nāgas, and Guhyakas—
all those gods together praised the Goddess with devotion.
And she, the destroyer of fear, bestowed her favor upon all the worlds;
and Bali offered oblations to the spirits with buffaloes, goats, and rams.
Thousands of conchs resounded with piercing blasts;
there were the sounds of drums, the clashing of weapons, the rattling of armor, and the thundering of crushing impacts.
On that day, the supreme gods, devoted to the Goddess, caused it to be made covered with flags and banners, and adorned with bells and chowries.
And having performed a great and eternal worship by all the gods,
in the month of Āśvina, at the end of the month of Meṣa, [they worshipped] the peahen-like [form] of the Enemy of Mahiṣa.
Having fully worshipped the Goddess on the eighth lunar days at midnight, [one attains success].
Those who slaughter animals out of devotion become possessed of great strength,
as do those who offer a sacrifice intended for the destruction of all beings.
The Goddess is pleased with them for as long as the Kalpa of Śaṅkara;
they sport with various enjoyments in the celestial realm, which is so difficult to attain.
For them there are no mental afflictions nor physical ailments, O Śakra, and no fear shall arise;
neither gods, nor planetary spirits, nor Daityas, nor Asuras, nor Pannagas [shall cause them harm].
O Lord of the Gods, they trample upon the feet of the Goddess that have touched the earth,
as far as the wind, space, water, fire, moon, and planets extend.
And for that long, the worship of Caṇḍikā shall always exist on earth,
especially during the rainy season and on the eighth days of the month of Āśvina.
On the ninth day, you shall attain great renown throughout the world;
O Indra, Lord of the Devas, this bestows upon you the fruit of dwelling in heaven.
And the yoga of action has been proclaimed according to the division of the higher and the lower.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the Dakṣiṇāmnāya section of the Nirvāṇa-pada within the Śrī Vārāhī Tantra.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
In the place consisting of nine lotuses, the worship of Durgā is performed according to her own forms:
first in the center, then in the directions starting with Indra, in sequence by means of the syllables of the nine principles (tattvas).
O beloved, she has eighteen arms, a lovely and broad chest, and thighs;
she holds a hair-tuft, a shield, a bell, a mirror, a raised index finger, and a bow.
Then, she holds a banner, a hand-drum, and a noose in her left hands;
thereafter, a spear, a mallet, a trident, a thunderbolt, a sword, and a goad.
Equipped with these very same weapons, including the *raśara* and the *cakraloka*,
the remaining [deities] have sixteen arms and hold the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) and the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), excluding [the previous ones].
Rudracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, and Caṇḍanāyikā.
Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavatī, Caṇḍarūpā, Caṇḍikā,
and Ugracaṇḍā as the ninth— these are proclaimed to be situated in the center.
Yellowish-red, black, blue, white, and smoky;
yellow, pale-white, and reddish; these [colors] abide in the non-desired state, while the golden one abides in Hari.
Then the Mahiṣa, the Mahāśastrin, and those Graha-muṣṭikas should be stationed in a row in the enclosure; thus it is stated in the Skandayāmala.
O slayer of Mahiṣa, O you of great illusion, O Cāmuṇḍā, garlanded with severed heads;
O Goddess, grant wealth, health, and victory; salutations to you always!
Grant me form, grant me fame, grant me fortune, O Goddess;
grant me sons, grant me wealth, and grant me all my desires.
First of all, Caṇḍikā, having stood in the middle of the lotus,
repeatedly placed a flower with her hand upon Śāradāmbikā.
Come, come, O Supreme Sovereign; manifest Your presence here!
Accept this portion of worship, O Goddess Durgā; salutations to You!
O Durgā, O Durgā, come here together with your hosts and retinues;
accept this portion of worship, protect the sacrifice, and salutations to you!
We know Nārāyaṇī; we meditate upon Caṇḍikā;
may that Caṇḍī impel us in the remaining portion of the Gāyatrī.
Having offered the bath with this very Durgā-tantra,
one should then offer the sixteen items beginning with water for the feet (pādya) using the four-syllable mantra.
O Bhairava, one should perform the secondary rites as previously described; furthermore,
one should worship the limbs of the Goddess with the Durgā-tantra mantra.
By this [mantra], O Durgā, the heart is seized; by this, O supreme Durgā, the head is seized.
The wise one should worship the crest-lock, the armor, the eyes, and the arms and feet, respectively, with the five remaining syllables beginning with "vā".
In the eastern part of the mandala, one should worship the powers (śaktis) of the Goddess:
Ugracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, and Caṇḍanāyikā.
One should grasp the hands of the Goddess, as well as Caṇḍā, Davatī, Caṇḍarūpā, and Caṇḍikā, along with her weapons, missiles, and mount.
One should first worship Pañcānana and the Daitya Kāmasara;
having recited the mantra and offered praise, one should present the bali offering, bow down, and perform the veiling (avaguṇṭhana).
Having displayed the *yonimudrā* and offered the remains of the flowers (*nirmālya*) to the direction of the Trident-bearer,
one should dismiss [the deity] by saying, "Salutation to Caṇḍeśvarī."
The eight auspicious Yoginīs, beginning with Ugracaṇḍā, are to be worshipped;
likewise, the sixty-four Yoginīs and indeed the Koṭiyoginī.
Likewise, one should worship the nine auspicious Durgās who are present near the Goddess,
for Jayantī and the others are indeed the very forms of that Goddess, to be honored with perfumes and flowers.
The weapons and missiles of the Goddess,
as well as her ornaments complete with their primary and secondary parts, and her vehicle, the lion itself.
One should always worship Mahiṣāsuramardinī with devotion,
as well as the planets and the ten guardians of the directions, according to the previously mentioned sequence.
The wise one should worship Bhairava and Bhairavī as before;
he should also worship these sixty-four Yoginīs on the right.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the sixty-four forms,
which possess great fortune and are especially endowed with wealth and righteousness.
One should worship the goddess Vijayā, who bears a trident and lotus seeds,
who is intent on granting boons, who is seated upon a lion, and who bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
One should worship the auspicious goddess Maṅgalā, the bestower of all accomplishments,
who is seated upon a lion-throne and a lotus-seat, who is serene, and who wears a crown of matted locks.

One should worship the goddess Bhadrā, seated upon the auspicious throne (bhadrāsana), holding in her right hands a trident, a rosary, the gesture of granting boons (varada), and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya).
One should worship the goddess Dhṛti, who holds a blue lotus, a trident, a rosary, and the boon-granting gesture, and who is seated upon a fierce throne.
Holding a lotus and a mirror, adorned with all ornaments,
Śānti should be visualized as bestowing peace, seated upon a lotus throne.
The goddess should be depicted holding a rosary, with her left hand in the boon-granting gesture;
she is seated upon a bull, possesses three eyes, and has her hands in the boon-granting gesture.
She holds a ḍamaru drum and a serpent, and she wields a trident while bestowing fearlessness;
she wears a crown of matted hair with a crescent moon and has Vāsuki as her bracelet.
Seated upon a lotus throne of forgiveness, with a sun-disk in her hand,
she is equipped with a girdle and a trident, and wears a yogic cloth as an upper garment.
Siddhi is to be invoked as resembling Caṇḍā;
she grants boons while seated upon a lotus throne and adorned by a reflected sun.
And one should worship the goddess Tuṣṭi, seated upon a water-pot,
holding a noose and a goad, gentle in appearance, and bearing a lotus and a svastika.
Umā should be depicted seated upon a lotus throne, turned away from the deer and the lion;
she is auspicious, wearing a yogapaṭṭa as an upper garment, and holding a water-pot in her hand.
Surrounded by Varā, Dyatā, Triśūlā, Jyā, Jayā, and others,
she shines brilliantly with a garland of skulls and wears lotus earrings.
Listen now to how the goddess Puṣṭi, who is devoted to the worship of Śiva, should be visualized:
she has a sword in her hand, is mounted upon a great [vehicle], and carries a shield and a mallet.
Puṣṭi, mounted on a horse, should be of such a form as described;
Śrī should be depicted seated on a lotus, holding a lotus and a śrīphala fruit.
Being bathed by elephants with golden jars, she is most beautiful; worship Ṛddhi, who stands upon a lotus and holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in her hands.
The goddess Rati, seated upon a lotus, should be depicted with beautiful eyes, her hands raised in the act of giving, uttering auspicious words, and accompanied by the playing of the lute (vīṇā).
She should be visualized as radiant, seated upon a fierce throne, bearing a mass of blazing rays;
she may also be seated on a lion-throne, holding a mace or a lotus in her hand, and is most beautiful.
The goddess possesses a luster like that of a blue lotus, holds a lotus and a blue lotus,
is adorned with a garland of skulls, and is embellished with all ornaments.
She should be depicted seated in the paryaṅka posture, illustrious, performing her duties with great beauty;
she holds a conch and a book, and is radiant with fine garlands and ornaments.
Lakṣmī should be depicted seated upon a lotus, holding a lotus and a śrīphala fruit;
Īśvarī, however, is seated upon a bull and wears a crown of matted locks.
The goddess has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament and is adorned with a trident upon her chest;
she is established in the *kala* and holds a citron fruit.
Wearing a yogapaṭṭa as an upper garment and bearing a beautiful jewel garland,
Śākrī should be depicted seated upon an elephant, holding a vajra in her hand and appearing most resplendent.
Jayāvatī is seated upon a lion, auspicious, and holds arrows and a horn;
Brāhmī should have a swan as her seat and wear a girdle of muñja grass.
The four-faced one, Svarūpā and the others, hold a staff, a wooden water-pot,
and a rosary; she holds a sacrificial ladle in her hand and carries clarified butter.
She who holds the yogic belt and the khaṭvāṅga staff, the giver of all, whose face is that of a boar.
Jayantī, who stands upon a mongoose, is auspicious, holding a sacrificial vessel (kuṇḍa) and a trident (śūla);
she should be depicted holding a sword and a shield, with her hands granting boons and fearlessness.
The Aparājitā, however, should be depicted as mounted upon a lion and possessed of great strength;
she holds a Pināka bow and arrows in her hands, and carries a sword and a shield.
The goddess has three eyes, wears a mass of matted hair, and bears the serpent Vāsuki;
she holds a lotus and a goad in her hands, and is seated upon a makara-throne.
The goddess Mānasī, standing upon a chariot, should be visualized holding a bell and a mallet,
bearing a thunderbolt and a goad, and adorned with all ornaments.
Seated upon a white lotus, holding a staff and a rosary,
Diti should be depicted bearing a staff and adorned with all ornaments.

Māyā holds a lotus and a blue lotus as her excellent upper hands, while her lower hands hold a child on her lap; Māyā holds a noose and a goad as her excellent upper hands, while her lower hands hold a child.
The Great Māyā, mounted upon a boar, deludes all that is moving and unmoving;
she is the Enchantress, seated upon a deer, bearing a banner, a trident, and dice.
Adorned with flutes, hand-bells, wine-cups, necklaces, and armlets,
she is mounted upon a lustful elephant and holds a mirror for removing impurities.
Mounted upon the moon, the maker of stars, she is stainless and possesses a heart-pleasing luster;
she wears a rosary of pearls and holds a beautiful, auspicious water-pot.
Gaurī is seated in the lotus posture, her hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
the auspicious goddess holds a rosary and carries a water-pot.
The refuge-giver seated upon a lion, her hands bestowing boons and fearlessness,
Kauśikī mounted upon a hawk, bearing a trident and a severed head.
Holding a skull-cup and a flaying knife in her hands, of terrible form and great power,
she should be visualized as standing upon a human corpse and adorned with all ornaments.
Skilled in playing the lute and dancing most beautifully,
she wields the weapons of Durgā and others upon her back, destroying the enemies.
Wielding the Pināka bow, arrows, shield, and sword, the slayer of Mahiṣa was surrounded by his soldiers who were engaged in great tasks arising from his head.
Struck by those of great strength with blood-dripping red eyes, they were encircled by serpent-nooses; some had their lives departed at the waist.
The goddesses should be depicted as standing upon tridents, all facing forward;
each one is seated upon a lotus-throne with her feet placed upon a lion.
In this manner, Durgā should be fashioned in no other way;
she is beautifully depicted as seated upon a lotus, performing her ritual activities.
Shining with a garland of flowers, adorned with a halo of light,
wearing a single girdle, and endowed with every beauty.
One established in the vow should fashion an auspicious image of Ruṇḍhatī holding flowers and water;
one should worship the goddess Ghaṇṭā, who holds a bell in her hand and bears a trident.
Her ears should be fashioned according to her true form, and she should be made very beautiful;
she should hold a lotus and a rosary, auspicious and observing the great vow.
She should always be visualized as Kapālinī, bearing a skull and a trident;
she is of the form of Rudra, yet fierce (raudrī), seated upon a bull, and most beautiful.
One should worship Kālī, who stands upon a chariot, wearing a crown of matted locks, adorned with the serpent Vāsuki as a bracelet, and bearing a skull and a trident.
The auspicious Mayūrī should be fashioned with three eyes, adorned with all ornaments, seated upon a peacock, and holding a noose and a spear. She should be depicted as Śikhin.
One should worship the Goddess in her own form, seated upon a staff-posture (daṇḍāsana), bearing the lotus and the svastika, and adorned with necklaces and armlets.
One should worship the goddess who holds a trident and a sword, who possesses many forms, who is seated upon a man, who has three eyes, and who bears a spear and a sharp-edged axe.
Adorned with the moon upon the heads of matted serpents, she is the embodiment of Śiva;
for the sake of destroying enemies, she is the slayer of foes, bearing the thunderbolt, the discus, and the bow.
Likewise, she should be worshipped as mounted upon a horse and adorned with all ornaments;
then one should worship Ambika, who holds a trident, a thread, and a rosary.
Now hear of Carcikā, the queen of the gods, seated in the lotus posture;
the great goddess is mounted upon a corpse and adorned with serpent ornaments.
One with upward-pointing hair, formidable, bearing a severed head and a knife,
worshipped by the gods, mounted upon an elephant, and possessed of great strength— she should be so depicted.
Listen likewise to the goddess who holds a vajra-hook, as well as Vaivasvatī,
who has a skull-staff in her hand, a boar’s face, and is seated upon Yama.
The goddess Kaumārī is worshipped as having a peacock for her seat and a spear as her weapon;
she possesses the form of a young girl, wears red garlands, and holds a cock.
The consort of Maheśvara is mounted upon a bull, three-eyed, and bearing a trident;
she is devoted to playing the lute and adorned with necklaces and armlets.
The goddess Vaiṣṇavī, who bears the conch and discus, is seated upon Garuḍa;
she is the goddess Vanamālādhara, and likewise Mahālakṣmī—listen now.
Emerging from space, she holds a trident and dances as the skull-bearing goddess;
her face is gentle, she is perfectly full, possesses three eyes, and is adorned with a severed head.
Facing her, one should worship Kārttikī, who presides over the departed spirits;
she is Śivadūtī and Kartī, youthful and radiant with ornaments.
Holding a skull-topped staff and a vajra-hook, she is fleshless with a hollow interior; her lips are likewise closely set, and she has disheveled hair bound by a serpent.
Her ears are adorned with mudrās, and her left thigh rests upon her hand.
Seated upon a pedestal in the south, the goddess Cāmuṇḍā— whose face is distorted, whose hair stands erect, and who is terrifying— is likewise worshipped.
Seated upon a corpse, fleshless, bearing a garland and a khaṭvāṅga staff,
with a skull and a trident in her hands, she is radiant with earrings as her ornaments.
With her left hand placed upon her upper lip in the *mudrā* posture,
she is Raudrī, the slayer of the Asura Gajacarma, adorned with serpent ornaments.
The iconography of the sixty-four goddesses has been described to you;
now, O Lord of Nectar, I shall speak of their great fortune.
O Goddess, just as there is no end to the worship of Śiva,
likewise I see no end to the worship of the sixty-four [deities].
O Goddess, the fruit that results from the gift of gold land and the gift of a cow—
sixty-four times that fruit, it is remembered here, belongs to the recitation [of this mantra].
O highly fortunate one, when worshipped on a palace, a pavilion, a house, a painting, or a garment,
the sixty-four [Yoginīs] bestow power, sovereignty, and auspiciousness.
O Goddess, by establishing sixty-four, or thirty-two, or sixteen,
or eight [liṅgas], one overcomes all ill-deeds.
I shall describe the characteristics of the Mothers exactly as they were previously taught:
Brahmāṇī resembles Brahmā; she has four faces and four arms.
Maheśvarī should be depicted mounted upon a swan, holding a rosary and a water-pot;
she is considered to be Māheśvarī by her very nature.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, seated upon a bull, and having the moon as her crest-jewel,
she has four arms, holding a skull-bowl, a trident, and a khaṭvāṅga staff, while bestowing boons.
Kaumārī has the form of a youth; she rides upon an excellent peacock,
wears red garments, and is likewise considered to bear a trident and a spear.
Adorned with necklaces and armlets, possessing a beautiful throat and broad shoulders,
she is Vaiṣṇavī, resembling Viṣṇu, and seated upon the throne of Garuḍa.
Four-armed and granting boons, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
she may also be seated upon a lion-throne together with Cālaka.
And I shall describe Vārāhī, who stands upon a buffalo;
she is a goddess resembling a boar, holding a bell and a chowrie.
Likewise, O Lord of the Dānavas,
[worship] Indrāṇī, the destroyer of the lords of the Dānavas, who resembles Indra and holds a thunderbolt, a trident, and a mace.
Mounted upon an elephant, they praised that Goddess, who was surrounded by many eyes,
possessing the luster of molten gold, and adorned with garments and ornaments.
Likewise, one should meditate upon this auspicious Yogīśvarī, who wields a sharp khaṭvāṅga,
has a long tongue, hair standing erect, and is adorned with a mass of matted locks.
One should indeed fashion Kuśodarī with a face made terrifying by fangs;
she is the Goddess garlanded with skulls and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
In his left hand he holds a skull-bowl filled with flesh and blood, and upon it is a head with hair; likewise, he holds a knife in his right hand.
Or she may be depicted as standing on a vulture or a corpse, fleshless and devoid of affection;
likewise, she who has three eyes should be made with a gaping mouth.
Cāmuṇḍā, Dvayaṅghaṇṭā, the auspicious one wearing a leopard skin,
the naked Kālikā, and likewise Kapālinī mounted upon a donkey.
One should fashion Vināyaka with deep red flowers, ornaments, a vessel for prosperity, and a banner;
likewise,
one should do so for the Mothers and the Mantrikas.
And the Lord Vīreśvara is mounted upon a bull and wears matted locks.
Holding a lute in his hand and bearing a trident, he should stand before the Mothers;
indeed, the Mothers should be worshipped by one who desires both visible and invisible fruits.
Having likewise worshipped the host of Mothers and the Lord in the form of Bhairava with perfumes, food offerings, incense, oblations, garlands, and ornaments;
O Brahmins, women, young maidens, and Brahmin women should be honored according to one's ability;
they are known as Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī is not the seventh among the virtuous—Candrāṇī and Cāmuṇḍā [being the first and second];
Mahālakṣmī is said to be the eighth; these are declared to be the Mothers of the Universe.
In the Caṇḍikā Tantra, eight Yoginīs of the mantra are proclaimed;
Brahmaṇī is said to be the first, and thereafter Māheśvarī.
Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, and likewise the next,
Nārasiṃhī, as well as Aindrī, and Śivadūtī is the eighth.
Bhairava and Pāṇḍanātha are red and white in color, each possessing four arms;
they hold a mace, a lotus, a spear, and a discus in their hands.
O Goddess, this one who bears the form of Viṣṇu is worthy of worship in the eastern quarter;
wherever my worship proceeds, there it shall be yours as well.
O Dānava, this body, which is to be worshipped and meditated upon, is located right there;
one should place a trident in the right hand, and likewise a sword and shield above it.
Likewise, one should understand that he holds a sharp arrow and a spear even in his left hand,
as well as a shield, a full bow, a noose, and a goad.
He should place either a bell, or even an axe, or a sacrificial post (medha).
[The deities] have two arms, wear divine garments, and likewise hold a sword and a shield.
And likewise Divyasundarī, Rūpā, and those bearing nooses and tridents.
Another holds a bow and arrows, while another has a bell and discus raised in her hands;
yet another goddess holds a thunderbolt and a staff, possessing ten arms.
Holding a knife, a mallet, a water-pot, an axe, and a threatening forefinger before them,
they carry a hand-drum and a spear, possessing great strength.
The goddess holds a lotus and the gesture of fearlessness in her [first] two hands, while the act of libation (*tarpaṇa*) is performed with twenty hands;
possessing such a form, she is seated upon a lion.
Mahāmāyā should be visualized as seated upon a pair of lions,
or else seated in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), granting boons (*varadā*), and endowed with the bloom of fresh youth.
Abounding in the beauty of all her limbs, adorned with the forms of Jayā and the others,
or else engaged in combat as the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
O Goddess, when meditated upon and constantly worshipped, you bestow the fruit of all desires;
yet you are not so pleased by fire-offerings, gifts, or recitations.
In this matter, there is no [other means] for pleasing the Goddess as through the worship of a maiden;
[so too do] the ancestors, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the hosts, and the world-protectors [attain satisfaction].
On the eighth and fourteenth days of the bright fortnight, and especially on the ninth day,
one should specifically feed young girls during the dark fortnight.
O Vāsava, having washed the feet of all those maidens,
they were seated upon divine seats on the ground that had been well-smeared.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and various kinds of food;
having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should cause the meal to be offered at the palate.
Sugar-candy, jaggery, clarified butter, curd, milk,
and honey should be given to those young girls; one should cause them to break these items gently.
When water is requested, it should be given; when a mantra is requested, the auspicious one should be given.
When all of them have been satisfied, then one should give the self-consecration.
Having sipped water and offered all the unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*),
the girls should then place the unbroken rice upon the head of the giver.
Therefore, one should perform prostration preceded by devotion;
by this very method, the Goddess quickly becomes pleased.
O Lord of the Gods, he grants various desires cherished by the mind;
thereafter, having ruled his kingdom, he goes to the world of the gods.
And on the ninth day, one should perform the offering of abundant oblations according to the prescribed rite;
and those who offer the oblation effect the destruction of all malevolent spirits.
May the Goddess be satisfied and perform her ascetic penance for as long as the aeon lasts;
may there be the destruction of all malevolent beings and the slaying of Mahiṣa.
The slaughter of animals in nine ways, the killing of buffaloes and goats, and the rites for Bhūtas and Vetālas should be performed on the ninth day, never according to one's own whim.
Birds, tortoises, crocodiles, boars,
rhinoceroses, buffaloes, monitor lizards, and rams— these are the nine kinds of wild animals.
May the nine kinds of deer— the black antelope, the Sāra, the Ruru, and the others—
grant their satisfaction and offer as a sacrifice the blood from their own limbs.
A thousand [offerings] bring satisfaction; having pierced his own body with blood, Durgā is duly propitiated by [offering it from] the arm and the shanks.
The goat, the horse, and the buffalo, as well as the man, in their respective order;
these are proclaimed as Vali, Mahāvali, and Valiśva.
O hero, O King, when Durgā is worshipped according to the prescribed rites with the heads of Nara and Īśa,
she becomes the embodiment of desire for a full hundred thousand years.
Blood purified by mantra is called the nectar of the head;
therefore, during worship, one should offer strength, the head, and blood.
O Hero, O King, one should worship Cāmuṇḍasūdinī according to the rules with devotion,
as well as with blood and various kinds of heads.
From the tearing apart of buffaloes and his own body,
[he was born] with severed tail-hairs, ears, and eyes, and likewise with broken teeth.
One should never give [an animal] whose horns or other parts are broken,
nor one that is withered by *kāśa* grass, nor one that is aged, diseased, or suffering from a discharging wound.
One should not offer as a sacrificial animal to Śiva’s oblation a beast that is impotent, has emaciated limbs, or whose penis is pierced and discharging semen, nor one younger than three months.
One should certainly not give fewer than three of each kind—
be it beasts, birds, or especially men.
One should not give food to a woman after having offered the bali; one would thereby incur hell.
Likewise, one should not give what has not been prescribed, nor to Brahmins who are ignorant of the Rigveda.
One should offer a five-year-old animal endowed with auspicious marks as an oblation to Kālikā according to the rules;
having recited the mantra for Kālikāsinī according to the rules, one should strike it with a sword.
Facing north, the practitioner should likewise gaze at the bali offering facing east, and thereafter recite this mantra.
You are a man who has appeared before me in the form of Bali due to my good fortune;
therefore, I bow down to you, the one who possesses all forms, appearing in the form of Bali.
Caṇḍikā bestows prosperity upon the giver through the gift [offered];
O Cāmuṇḍā, who takes the form of the sacrificial offering—homage to you, O Baleru! Homage to you!
The serpent was created by the Self-born One himself for the sake of sacrifice;
therefore, I cause you to be slain today. Thus, though you are a serpent, you shall not be killed in this sacrifice.
With the mantra "e& hrī& śrī& mi," one should offer the bali-oblation in its true form.
Having reflected thus, O Bhairava, one should place a flower upon his head;
then, the deity, aiming for that [recipient] and aiming for one's own desire, [should bestow it].
In that manner, he consecrated Kṛṣṇa and the wielder of the Pināka bow, who was the very embodiment of the Night of Doom—
fierce, with red face and eyes, and adorned with red garlands and unguents.
Wearing a single red lower garment, holding a noose in his hand, and accompanied by his family,
he drinks blood and partakes of offerings mixed with ritual substances.
The sword is the destroyer of enemies, sharp-edged, formidable, and enduring;
it is the source of glory, victory, and the protector of dharma—salutations to you!
Then, having worshipped the sword with the mantras "ĀṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ," and having taken up the stainless sword, one should cut the excellent sacrificial offering (bali).
Oṃ e& hrī& kauśiki, may [this] blood be nourished!
One should assign the blood to the location and the head to the seven islands.
By offering the bali in this manner, the practitioner obtains the full fruit;
however, if it is offered at the wrong time, it will be deficient, and by doing the reverse, it will be fruitless.
Then one should worship other powerful beings such as the buffalo and others;
the body attains a state of middleness, and Śivā indeed takes the blood.
In the case of the propitiation of Durgā, however, this procedure is prescribed everywhere:
fish and meat for the Daityas, and meat and rice for the goddesses.
The *kuṣmāṇḍa* gourd, the sugarcane stalk, liquor, meat, and hemp—these constitute the offering; by my command, they are equal to a goat when [the deity] is not yet satiated.
Cutting with a *caṇḍahāsa* [sickle] is prescribed for the *kartari*;
cutting with a *dātra*, *asidhenu*, *krakaca*, *vaśaṭ*, or *kulā* is for the middle [size].
The cow-horn-shaped, the arrow-shaped, the wheel-shaped, the whirlpool-shaped,
the knife-shaped, the razor-shaped, and the broken-shaped are proclaimed to be the lowest.
He cannot ever be cut down by our spears, tridents, or other weapons;
no one who offers this oblation to the Goddess shall meet with death.

Having cut the offering with one's own sword at the time of the ritual, one should apply a tilaka on the forehead with all those blood-stained pieces while reciting the mantra of subjugation (*vaśya*).
Whether it be a king, a prince, women, or yakṣas and rākṣasas—
the entire fourfold assembly of beings comes under his control.
One should propitiate Durgā according to the prescribed rites by means of the slaughter of goats, buffaloes, and rams, satisfying her with offerings of flesh and blood.
He who worships Durgā day after day with blood and other offerings,
having delivered a hundred lineages, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
O King, Caṇḍikā becomes satisfied with even a single drop of blood from one's own body when she is duly propitiated here with the blood of a goat.
O hero, when the earth is thoroughly drenched with blood for a hundred years, Caṇḍikā becomes satiated by Mahiṣa.
Having pierced his own arm and thigh, Durgā was duly propitiated with the blood from his own body, which brought satisfaction to a thousand [deities].
O hero, O King, when worshipped according to the prescribed rites with one's own head,
Durgā becomes satisfied and grants a hundred thousand boons.
Having cut through and pierced the elements, and having destroyed all this that moves,
he who bows his head to the goddesses is not defiled by sins.
The sight of Durgā is meritorious; better than the sight is salutation;
better than salutation is touching her; and better than touching her is worshiping her.
Bathing is superior to worship; libation is traditionally held to be superior to bathing.
The gift of meat through satiation, and the slaying of a buffalo or a goat,
yields that same fruit which is obtained from all sacrifices, all fasts, and at all sacred pilgrimage sites.
O Hero, he who prostrates himself on the ground with his body fully extended like a staff, having bowed his head to Sī, obtains that fruit.
O hero, he who goes before Caṇḍikā attains the supreme goal,
as do those who perform austerities, give gifts at sacred fords, or offer sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees.
Neither those three nor even you, O Queen of the Gods, can attain such a state:
long life, health, happiness, prosperity, and beloved wives.
For whatever purpose he has them, that man, with a joyful heart, should worship the goddess Vāsava-bhairavī Caṇḍikā.
Having joined one's palms in reverence, one should recite this hymn:
"Oṃ! To Durgā, the auspicious one, the bestower of peace, the daughter of Brahmā, and the beloved of Brahmā."
I always bow to Śivā, the leader of all worlds,
who is auspicious, beautiful, perfected, partless, and the supreme digit.
I bow down to Caṇḍikā, the sovereign of the universe and mother of the universe,
the Goddess who embodies all the gods and who removes the fear of all diseases.
I perpetually bow to Umā, who is saluted by Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu;
she who dwells on the Vindhya mountains, whose abode is the Vindhya range, and who resides in the divine sacred place.
I bow down to the Yoginī, the Mother of Yoga, Caṇḍikā;
to the Goddess who is the Mother of Īśāna, the Sovereign, the beloved of Īśvara.
I bow forever to Durgā, the savior from the ocean of saṃsāra;
that man who recites this hymn or even hears it [attains liberation].
Released from all sins, he rejoices together with Durgā;
O Vṛttāra, one should pray to that Sovereign of the Gods with this mantra.
O Mahiṣāgni, O Mahāmāyā, O Cāmuṇḍā, wearer of a garland of severed heads;
O Goddess, grant me wealth, health, and victory—homage be to you!
O Maheśvarī, may I always be protected from ghosts, spirits, and piśācas, from rākṣasas, from gods, from humans, and from serpents.
O most auspicious of all that is auspicious, O Śivā, who accomplishes all purposes;
O Umā, Brahmāṇī, Kaumārī, you whose form is the universe, be gracious to me!
Grant me beauty, grant me fame, and grant me fortune;
grant me sons, grant me wealth, and be gracious to me for all my desires.
Anointed with sandalwood paste and smeared with saffron,
I have come to Durgā for refuge, wearing a crest-ornament fashioned from bilva leaves.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the section on Nirvāṇa within the Dakṣiṇāmnāya of the Śrī Vārāhī Tantra.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
In the house of Durgā, weapons should be worshipped by the wise,
as well as musical instruments, insignia, armor, and other implements of war.
The sword is the destroyer of enemies, possessing a sharp edge and a noble hilt;
it is the womb of prosperity, victory itself, and likewise the upholder of dharma.
Thus, these eight names of yours were first uttered by Nīladaṇḍa;
Kṛttikā is not your field, but the gods Maheśvaras are your gurus.
The Rohiṇīs are your body, and Janārdana is your deity;
the Father, the Grandfather, and the God are you—protect me always.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with sharp fangs and a lean belly,
he is pure in disposition, patient, and likewise possessed of exceeding splendor.
Salutations to that sword of yours, which is sharp-edged and pure, by which this earth was upheld and the great asuras were slain.
You were fashioned first among all weapons by the wielder of the Pināka;
having been extracted from his trident for combat, he made your auspicious hand a fit receptacle for its grip.
These [mantras], which destroy all evil beings, were bestowed upon Caṇḍikā;
she expanded them and presented them to the gods.
O Churikā, who has become the limbs of all sentient beings, who eradicates all that is inauspicious, protect us always; salutations to you who bestows peace.
Protect my limbs, protect my cattle, and protect my horses and wealth;
always protect my body, O Kaṭṭāraka—salutations to you!
O great minister of all weapons, O destroyer of all enemies of the gods,
protect my body here with this bow and these excellent arrows.
I bow to the divine bow and arrow, which was shaken by Kṛṣṇa for the sake of protection and by Hara for the sake of destruction, and which has entered the form of the Triple Veda.
Fell the lives of the enemies with your sharp-edged blade through their misconduct;
seize their life-force, O Kunta, and protect these five for me.
O armor, you who bestow protection in battle, protect me—me, who am worthy of being protected—along with my army, its fame, and its exertion; O son of Tapani, salutations to you!
O beloved chowrie-bearer, white as the moonbeams and as pale as a mass of snow,
do you dispel our misfortune!
Just as a cloud covers the auspicious earth during a sacrifice,
so do you always cover me with your umbrella when I have entered the fray of battle.
O Śakraketu, the one of great heroism, Vainateya— the king of birds and the banner of Nārāyaṇa— has himself taken refuge in you.
Kāśyapa, the remover of death, the enemy of serpents, whose vehicle is Viṣṇu;
the immeasurable, the unassailable, the slayer of the gods of battle.
O Garuḍa, whose movement is like that of the wind, you are present and stationed [there];
protect the warriors armed with swords and shields, and the enemy who is of a protective nature.
The Hutabhujas, Vasus, Rudras, Vāyu, Soma, and the great ṛṣis;
the Nāgas, Kiṃnaras, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Bhūtas, and Mahoragas.
The Pramathas, along with the Bhūtas, Śāmas, and Mātṛs, as well as Skanda— the commander-in-chief of Śakra— and Varuṇa, have taken refuge in you, O Mahādevī.
May he strike down all enemies and attain royal victory;
likewise, may whatever harmful spells have been employed by his foes be neutralized from every side.
The *sadātis* were always slain by your splendor in battle after battle during the slaying of Kālanemi, O destroyer of Tripura.
Just as you shone in battle after battle during the war between the gods and the asuras against Hiraṇyakaśipu, so too do you shine today; remember that divine splendor.
Seeing you, red, blue, and white, our enemies' hearts shall tremble;
O Dundubhi, you are the shaker who causes the roar of our adversaries to increase.
Likewise, Vijayavardhana [advanced] against the armies of King Bhavabhūti,
just as noble elephants rejoice at the thundering roar of clouds.
"Let it be so; by your voice, our joy is destroyed as victory is taken away, just as terror arises in women at the sound of a thundercloud."
Likewise, by that sound there, you are superior to all other sounds;
O Puṇya, among all meritorious things you are the merit, and among all auspicious things you are the most auspicious.
You are eternally upheld by Viṣṇu; O esteemed one, grant me peace!
You are victory, the giver of victory, the conqueror, the destroyer of enemies, and the bestower of fearlessness.
The destroyer of suffering, the bestower of bliss, the peaceful one, and the annihilator of all misfortunes—
these are your eight names, because of which you possess the prowess of a lion.
Seated upon that lion-throne, you are celebrated among the gods by name;
Śiva himself resides in you, as does Śakra, the lord of the immortals.
While you remain, the gods headed by Hari perform penance for your sake;
O lord of the earth, may you be auspicious in every way and entirely well.
O Conqueror of the Three Worlds, O Lord of all, homage be to you, the Lion Throne!
O Horse, live long, being marked by the supreme weapon.
O protector of the enemy, always eat meat; O master, always perform your duty!
You are born of a Gandharva lineage; may you not be a defiler of that family.
By means of truthful speech, the Brāhmaṇa [attains] the splendors of Soma and Varuṇa,
as well as those of the Sun and the ascetic power of the sages.
Through the celibate discipline of Rudra, the power of Pavana,
and the majesty of Hutāśana, the horse grew pure and strong.
Remember that you are a prince; remember the Kaustubha jewel [produced] from the Ocean of Milk when it was being churned by the gods and demons for the sake of nectar and other treasures.
Uccaiḥśravas was born long ago; you were born from that very source.
Whatever destiny awaits the slayer of a Brahmin, as well as the slayer of a father or a mother, that same fate shall be yours.
The liar regarding land and he who is averse to righteous conduct—
these evildoers are watched until the very end by the sun, the moon, and the wind.
O horse, you will quickly go to that destination and experience that evil if you undergo a transformation and flee from the battle.
Having conquered the enemy in battle along with his followers, he shall become happy;
likewise, the jackals, skeletons, vetālas, pūtanās, jambhakas, and other such beings [shall be auspicious].
All of them attained satisfaction, being gratified by the offering of the *bali*;
he who performs the vigil, devoted to the Daughter of the Mountain (*Girisutā*), offers a cry that drives away disease on the day of the Caitra festival and other such occasions.
O slender-waisted one, he is celebrated in song by the Kinnara maidens who speak with sweet and fragrant voices and play the lute;
through the gift of music and instrumental performance, one attains unsurpassed happiness.
By performing circumambulation, one is born endowed with beauty.
O Hero, listen to the meritorious fruit for that person who worships the Trident-Bearer on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja.
O hero, one obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices, and is honored by the hosts of gods in heaven.
By the slaughter of goats, buffaloes, and likewise rams,
one should gratify Durgā according to the prescribed rites with offerings of flesh and blood that satisfy her for a month.
Arise, O Goddess Caṇḍeśī, and having accepted this auspicious worship,
perform my welfare together with your eight Śaktis.
Go, go to the supreme abode, O Goddess Caṇḍikā, to your own place;
remain in the house like a diamond-flood for the increase of water and for prosperity.
Oṃ, O Goddess Durgā, Mother of the World, you who have been worshipped, go to your own abode;
may you indeed return once the year has passed.
O Goddess, having accepted this worship offered by me according to my ability for the sake of protection, go to your supreme and secure abode.
One should meditate upon Aparājitā, who has four arms, wears yellow garments, and is adorned with all ornaments;

who holds a sword and a shield in her palms on the upper right and left hands respectively, while her lower two hands display the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness; she is three-eyed, possesses a slightly smiling face, and is named Aparājitā.
With a lotus-face as beautiful as the dawn, she blazes with variegated gold.
O Goddess Jayā, O Śivā, you who are adorned with variegated gold and camphor, grant all my desires to me, you who are devoted to [Śiva].
May Mahāmāyā, who bestows victory and whose mind is permeated by Śiva,
grant me perpetual fortune and victory.
Adorned with a most variegated necklace and a radiant golden girdle,
may Aparājitā, who delights in Rudra, grant me victory.
Having praised her thus, one should worship Haridrā with yellow offerings, [saying]:
"Since you are always invincible (*parājitā*) among creepers, you are the mother of all plants."
O Goddess who fulfills all desires and goals, why do I entrust myself to you? O Conqueror of Existence, [I do so] for the sake of accomplishing all my aims.
When you are worshipped, may there be welfare for me; may my evil be destroyed. Oṃ, victory, O goddess who has assumed a divine form, O unconquered one on the tenth day!
I wear this bracelet on my right arm for the sake of increasing my attainment of water;
indeed, bestow strength upon me for the defeat of the enemy.
By your wearing [this], may there be an abundance of wealth and grain for me;
may the gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—be favorable toward you.
Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, as well as the all-pervading Saṃkarṣaṇa,
Pradyumna, and Aniruddha— may they grant you victory.
The Lord Ākhaṇḍala, Agni, Yama, Nirmati, Varuṇa, Pavana, Dhātṛ, Adhyakṣa, and likewise Śiva;
May the remaining guardians of the directions, together with Brahmā, protect you always— Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Medhā, Puṣṭi, Śraddhā, Jayā, and Mati.
Intellect, Modesty, Form, Peace, Contentment, and Radiance— these mothers,
the wives of the gods who have assembled here, shall consecrate you.
May the Sun, Moon, Soma, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus,
Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu— being duly propitiated— consecrate you as their abode.
The Gandharvas of the Dattādāna [class], the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas;
the Ṛṣis, Mānavas, cows, and the gods of auspiciousness (Māṅgalas).
The wives of the gods, Umā, the Nāgas, the hosts of Apsarases, all weapons, all scriptures, O King, and the mounts;
Herbs and gems, the divisions of time,
the rivers, oceans, mountains, sacred fords, clouds, and demons;
"May these indeed consecrate me for the accomplishment of all desires and goals.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the procedure for expiation to you:
a disciple who abandons his guru must certainly perform penance.
Having recited the *śrīpādukā* mantra one hundred thousand times, one is purified from that sin;
O Dear One, one who abandons the mantra should avoid association with such a person.
Being pure, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times along with fire offerings and libations;
for the pacification of defects in the daily rites and other procedures, one should recite the Vidyā one hundred times.
In the case of crossing [a boundary] due to some specific cause, one should mutter the mantra a thousand times;
just as a bee, out of greed for honey, goes from flower to another flower.
Likewise, a disciple who is greedy for his teacher may go to one even greater than his teacher;
if, by chance, knowledge is obtained from a beast by men born of noble lineage.
But having approached a Kaulika who is a twice-born, one should again seek the Vidyā;
for he may be incomplete, devoid of life-force, doubtful, or likewise censured.
If the mantras do not succeed and the guru becomes a slayer of Brahman,
then, having suddenly recognized that, one should abandon the mantra, the deity, and the guru.
Forgive that sin, O Mother; O Goddess Hari, show mercy!
For those Kaulikas who consume the jewel of the animal in manifold ways—
One should recite the *lopā* mantra three hundred thousand times, or one hundred thousand times the *japā*;
then,
by performing oblations with clarified butter at the end, one will certainly become free from sin.
If a heroic devotee of Maheśvara should drink the substance from a single vessel, he shall succeed.
If one should consume the leavings of a dog, that Kaulika must perform atonement by reciting the Gāyatrī mantra a thousand times and observing three days of fasting.
One whose mind has been thoroughly purified should offer gold to the Guru;
whether by force or spontaneously, he should restrain himself toward the mantra and the Mother.
Having recited the mantra one million times, one should perform the fire-sacrifice with parched rice for the daughter of the mantra-deity,
for one's own daughter, for a sister, and for a woman of noble family.
Through a hundred thousand recitations of the mantra during dalliance, the Kaulika becomes purified;
by means of the instruction and the naming [of the mantra], the mantra-daughter is received as a son.
Having committed the slaughter of a hero, the practitioner of mantras [should perform] futile drinking for the Guru; [then] he should recite [the mantra].
Having killed a collection of boneless living beings, one would go to hell;
therefore, one should recite the Ekādaśa [mantra].
Snakes, cats, mongooses, mice, camels, donkeys, horses,
elephants, and so forth—
[these are for] the offering of the sacrificial fee (*vali-dāna*).
For the killing of a cow, [one is purified] by ten [lakṣas];
for killing a guru, through grace, it may be accomplished by five lakṣas.

If a Brahmin falls [from his status] through negligence, the fields and other [donations] are freed from that sin by means of twenty million auspicious [recitations], according to what has been prescribed.
For the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, one hundred thousand [times the fine] is prescribed; for a Kṣatriya, it is remembered as double;
for a Vaiśya, it is declared to be triple; and for a Śūdra, it is fourfold.
For killing an Arhat or a Buddhist, the practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
for killing a ram or a pig, five thousand times.
For killing birds, the practitioner is purified by two thousand [recitations];
for the killing of snakes, cats, or fish, [one must recite] a thousand Vedic verses.
For treachery against the deity and treachery against the guru, one should recite the mantra thirty million times;
likewise for one who reviles the rules of conduct (samayas) or the yoginīs and heroes, [one should recite it thirty million times] until [the state of] Śiva is attained.

If a follower of the Śaiva vow is killed while adhering to either the Vāma or Dakṣiṇa Siddhānta, one should perform a thousand recitations (japa) of the scriptures, the mantras, and the names of women.
By reciting the mantra four times ten million times, the practitioner is purified from sin;
by reciting it one million times at dawn, the practitioner is purified.
One should first drink the nectar of the *argha* offering and then raise up the Goddess;
for him, that becomes the drinking of the bound soul (*paśu-pāna*), and its destruction shall occur by the hundreds of thousands.
The mantra-practitioner should perform penance for drinking alcohol in vain, as well as for [the transgressions of] a hero’s wife or a hero’s daughter-in-law,
by means of the worship of divine heroes and other such rites.
In the event of the lamp being extinguished, the bowl being broken, or the bowl being knocked over,
one should worship the Mahādevī and recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
This was taught out of ignorance; through knowledge, it becomes twofold.
O beloved, [the same applies if] the yantra is broken, cracked, or stolen by a thief.
One should observe a fast for one day with a focused mind and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, preceded by fire offerings (homa) and libations (tarpaṇa).
Having satisfied the Guru with true devotion, one should also feed the Brahmins.
Occasionally, if a mark is lost or an ornament is cracked and so forth, [one should restore it].
The mortal who breaks [an image] will certainly meet death;
therefore, [one should repair it] at the king of holy places (tīrtharāja) or at the foremost of rivers, such as the Gaṅgā.
Or else, O Goddess, he might throw it into the ocean; otherwise, he would encounter suffering.
O Mother, whenever a practitioner of mantra relies upon the nature of the physical body, [he falls into error].
The final rite should be performed there by his disciples and others according to the prescribed rules;
having performed the daily obligatory rites, the performer should purify [the site] with the five jewels.

Having drawn forth the deceased’s individual soul (jīvātman) from the eye or other [orifices] as it has departed for another world through the path [of the veins], one should establish it within the corpse according to the instructions of the Guru.
By means of the yoga of the five *praṇavas* consisting of ether, fire, and the dark-blue [wind],
one should utter the word "bestower of liberation" (*mokṣada*) and then recite the eyes and the other [senses].
Having pronounced the name of the *preta*, one should say, "I invoke.
With this, one should invoke the *preta* and there perform the placement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
The wise practitioner, endowed with long [vow], should fashion the limbs through illusion;
having established the jar, the mantra-master should bathe the deceased.
One should consecrate [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) using the Aghora mantra, and with the Vardhinī mantra;
having bathed it with pure water, one should bathe it again with sacred ash.
The wise practitioner should place the corpse with its head facing south upon a bed of darbha grass,
having adorned it with new garments, garlands, unguents, and ornaments.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the root mantra, the practitioner,
having properly made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), should place the deceased there upon the palanquin.
Circumambulating the village to the right amidst the sounds of conch shells, kettledrums, and other instruments,
one should enter the cremation ground, which extends from south to north.
Having sat down upon level ground, one should scatter there parched grain, sesame seeds, and unbroken rice grains mixed with mustard seeds; then, one should install the celestial chariot (*vimāna*).
Having established the funeral fire there and having strewn grass around it in the reverse order.
The practitioner of mantra should place the sacrificial vessels to the south, with Viṣṇu as the presiding deity;
having placed the *praṇītā* vessel and worshipped it with flowers and other offerings.
The practitioner, having covered it with *darbha* grass, should place it in the southeast corner;
on its right side, he should worship the deity Bhairava and the mandala in due order.
Having performed the visualization of the tongues of the fire and other elements according to the prescribed method,
one should cause the excellent caru-oblation, mixed with sesame seeds and rice, to be offered.
The wise one, having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra using pure sacrificial porridge (caru), especially with the five jewels;
One should offer oblations with the root mantra, proceeding in order up to the final enclosure;
thus, by reversing the sequence of the oblations, all mantras are offered into the body of the Guru.
Having brought [the elements] to dissolution in sequence, one should offer oblations with the Vāgbhava mantra;
then, having offered with the root mantra, one should say "O Preta, give! in reverse order.
Having brought all the principles (tattvas) to dissolution, one should unite everything with the Self;
reciting the mantra, one should offer both merit and sin as an oblation into that [Self].
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should unite [the soul] with the supreme state—
pure, consisting of the nature of Śiva and Śakti, and free from rebirth.
Thus the deceased is united by the disciple with the supreme state, which consists of truth, consciousness, and bliss, which is directly manifest, transcends all principles, and is undisturbed.
Having purified the impurities and defilements, for the sake of the intended visualization,
one should offer oblations into the fire with clarified butter, using the root mantra of Aghora-Astra.
Following the prescribed method for atonement,
the practitioner should prepare a bed according to the measurement of a deceased body.
In the southern direction from the fire, with stakes produced from the family tree (*kulavṛkṣa*), or likewise with *bilva* wood or *kuśa* grass, having their tips pointing toward the south; (p. 194b)
The practitioner, having spread out the bed with a triple-stranded thread, should perform the rite.
Having wrapped it, one should worship it with offerings such as perfumes and flowers;
or, having covered it with a cloth, the wise practitioner should draw the yantra there.
A lotus with a triangle, a hexagon, a pericarp, and eight petals, with a half-line [around it]; then, having scattered flowers there on all sides.
The practitioner should place the corpse here with its head facing south,
having consecrated it with the protection mantra and the *jvālāmālinī* vidyā.
Having ignited [the fire] with the Aghora mantra, the wise practitioner should burn [the body] starting from the feet,
using either the Aghora-astra mantra or the Pāśupata mantra.
"Let those who know the samaya, having assembled here, perform the homa until this [substance] is reduced to ashes; let them perform the recitation of hymns and mantras."
When that other [fire] has been reduced to ashes,
the practitioner of mantras should properly worship the mental fire (ciṃtyagni) and protect it when the seventh day arrives.
Extinguish [the fire] along with the bones and wrap them in a new cloth;
one should cast those ashes somewhere and dissolve them in pure water.
The practitioner of mantras should dig up a heap of bones either in a temple of the Mother Goddess or in his own home;
he should bury them and worship this [rite] at the three junctions of the day.
One should perform the initial worship on the anniversary of death every month;
at the completion of the year, one should diligently conduct a great festival.
Therefore, having extracted the *kūṭa* from there, or having fashioned an image, a pair of sandals, or a skull-bowl (*kīkasa*) of him in a river that is touched by ritual rules,
the practitioner (*mantrin*), devoted to his guru, should worship it with mantras.
For those who have died in another land, or even for those still living,
the practitioner [should perform the rite] with *darbha* grass offerings, or with *palāśa* leaves, or again with rice flour.
Having first fashioned the body [of the deity], the wise practitioner should perform the remaining rites;
or else, being a believer, he may perform them himself in solitude by means of the mind alone.
Then one should join the words *vāgbhava*, *dīpinī*, *jvālā*, and *mālinī* with the leaves of *krodha*, *haṃsa*, *indu*, and *hetu* by means of the *sampuṭa* (encasement) method.
These are the seed-syllables therein: the Praṇava (Oṃ), Jīva (Sa), Keśava (Va), Haṃsa (Ha), Indu (I), Gāṃ (Gāṃ), followed by Kuṭila (Kṣa), Vahni (Ra), and Bindu (Ṃ), resting upon Bhaga (E).
This mantra, consisting of the collection of Śiva, Śakti, Earth, Moon, Water, Fire, Wind, and Ether,
has been declared by those skilled in mantras as "Jvālāmālinī."
One should utter the seed-syllable of Māyā, followed by the pair "sphurat," and likewise the pair "prasphura";
at the end, one should speak the word "tanurūpa" preceded by "ghoraghoratara."
This great mantra, consisting of the pair "caṭa-pracaṭa," has been declared;
having uttered the pair "kaha," one should then utter "ghātaya" twice.
The weapon-mantra is taught as ending with the armor-syllable; the mantra of Aghora consists of the letters of the [Aghora] name.
One should utter the syllables of the armor and the weapon at the end of the letters of the name of Tāriṇī and the sacrificial animal (paśu).
Manu is the Pāśupata weapon that wards off minor planetary afflictions;
it consists of fifty-one syllables, joined with the letters *ya*, *ma*, *dha*, and *anta*.
A wise person should place the letter *i* (Indra) followed by *r*, then the letter *ā*, and finally the moon (*u*) upon the left ear;
this is declared to be the "Five Jewels" (*pañcaratna*), which bestows whatever the mind desires.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the section on Nirvāṇa within the Dakṣiṇāmnāya of the Śrī Vārāhī Tantra.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
At Kurukṣetra, at Prayāga, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean,
at Mahākāla, and at Kāśī, one should not even think of a place for a lamp.
The rule is to be known as applying to the man, never to women;
for women there is no depositing [of the seed], nor meditation, nor worship here.
For women, mantras are perfected through mere recitation alone;
however, during the period of *puraścaraṇa*, one should worship the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*).

Having brought the initiated one into an empty house with garments, flowers, and other offerings, as well as foods consisting of milk-rice (pāyasa), he should provide purified water for the arghya offering.
Having performed the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), one should lead the Śaktis forward;
having joined them all with the water of the *argha* offering according to the prescribed ritual.
One should perform the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) and then the rite of total integration (sakalīkaraṇa).
Now I shall describe the eight maidens who bear the form of the Goddess.
From a Śūdra, there were a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, a Vaiśyā, and Lakulabhūṣaṇā;
likewise, from a barber, a Veśyā, a daughter of a washerman, and a Rajakī Yoginī.
Indeed, all those excellent women, endowed with every auspicious limb,
having observed the eightfold varieties of maidenly forms and his display of indignation, were filled with wonder.
They are designated by the names of the eight powers beginning with Brāhmaṇī;
their forms are white, black, and so forth, and their qualities are gentleness and the like.
Having first offered a seat, one should again say "welcome";
then [offer] water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), drinking water, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and water once more.
One should bathe [the image] with perfumes and flowers and perform the grooming of the hair;
then, having fumigated the hair, one should offer a silken garment.
Then, after the bath, having spread out a seat and offered a pair of sandals,
she sat there adorned with various ornaments.
Having adorned her with ointments and offered perfumes and garlands,
one should invoke each respective power and unite them with their heads.
In the center of the dining pavilion, within a most beautiful golden vessel,
[one should place] the chewed, the sucked, the licked, the drunk, the eaten, and the crunched.
When they may be uninitiated, then one should offer the *māyā* [syllable];
thereupon, one should perform the hymn of praise (*stotra*) into their left ear.
O Mother Goddess, salutations to you; O Daughter of Brahmā, O sinless Earth!
By your grace, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra.
O Maheśī, O boon-granting goddess, whose form is supreme bliss!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra.
O Kaumāri, sovereign of all obstacles, in the forest where the youth sports,
please remove my impediments and grant me the perfection of the mantra.
O Goddess who bears the form of Viṣṇu, O carrier of the son of Vinatā,
please remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra.
O Vārāhī, O boon-granting Goddess, you who lifted the earth with your tusk;
out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the accomplishment of the mantra.
O Goddess who bears the form of Śakra, worshipped by Śakra and the other gods,
please remove my obstacles and grant me the accomplishment of the mantra.
O Cāmuṇḍā, garlanded with severed heads, smeared with blood from the corners of your mouth, destroyer of obstacles!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra.
O Mahālakṣmī, O bestower of great liberation, O destroyer of agitation and torment!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra.

O Goddess, you who consist of the Mother (Mātr̥mayī), you who are measured as the Mother, and you who are established beyond the Mother; O Goddess, you who are one, yet most manifold, and whose form is the universe—salutations be to you!
Whoever recites this hymn with devotion at the commencement of mantras,
or upon beholding a learned woman, for him no obstacle shall arise.
If they are intent on play, one should stand outside their house while eating and recite the hymn until satisfaction arises.
Having sipped water for purification, one should offer mouth-fresheners such as betel leaf;
then, one should again present a garland and auspicious sandalwood paste arranged in rows.
Having released [the breath], performed circumambulation, and requested a boon, one shall become happy;
one sees light everywhere, or the body becomes endowed with radiance.
O Goddess of the gods, having performed the rite according to the rules for cruel deeds, [one should employ] either one's own body or indeed a body consisting of the deity.
Having again bathed after being freed from the oil, the wise one should worship the remaining deity along with the limbs and the enclosures, using mantras for the sake of self-protection.
O Dear One, with a tranquil mind, one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times;
having said, "Protect me, protect me," O Śivā, one should bow and dismiss [the deity].
