O Goddess, one should have one's self protected by other very affectionate friends using the Mṛtyuñjaya and other mantras, as well as the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra).
Through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and the like, as well as by propitiating Brahmins and other such acts,
the practitioner of mantra should perform the worship of the Cakra at the conclusion of the ritual application.

The practitioner of mantra, endowed with meditation and ritual placement (nyāsa), should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for the purpose of pacifying defects in ritual application and for the sake of self-protection.
If [the mantra] does not yield fruit, the deity shall incur a curse.
A mantra preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) grants liberation; one preceded by the *śrībīja* (śrīṃ) leads to the acquisition of wealth.
The Vidyā beginning with Hṛllekhā bestows great siddhi and brings all under control;
that beginning with Vāgbhava is the moving Vidyā; and that beginning with Kāma is the one that destroys the cycle of birth.
One should recite with a gaze directed upward for pacification; for killing, the gaze should be downward;
for enchantment, the gaze should be level; and for sprinkling, one should look toward the side in due order.
In cases of conflict, for the purpose of eradication and killing, one should gaze at the sun;
for the sake of [attaining] knowledge, while standing in the midst of water, by gazing at the solar disc.
O Goddess, by gazing at the space between the eyebrows, one succeeds in all auspicious rites.
One should always perform recitation using the hand, never with a rosary during the actual ritual application;
for the rosary prescribed for ritual application is intended according to the specific nature of each rite.
The three mudrās for the fire sacrifice are said to be Śṛṅgī, Haṃsī, and Śūkarī.
Śūkarī consists of the contraction of the hands; Mṛgī is formed by releasing the little fingers.

The *haṃsī* mudrā is formed when the index fingers are released; this mudrā is proclaimed to be threefold, used for rites of pacification (*śāntika*), nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), as well as for killing (*māraṇa*) and expulsion (*uccāṭana*).
O Supreme Goddess, the Mṛgī is to be known for causing enmity, immobilization, and subjugation; and the Haṃsī is to be used in rites of pacification and nourishment.
In rites of sorcery, one should employ the Śūkarī mudrā, as well as in rites of inciting hatred, expulsion, and the like; for the gods do not accept an oblation devoid of the proper mudrās.
But that dull-witted person who, out of delusion, desires to consume [the offering] without the mudrās—
[for the rites of] subjugation and pacification, a golden vessel is prescribed, while for paralyzing, an earthen vessel is considered appropriate.
For the rite of causing enmity, a vessel made of śālmali wood is used;
for expulsion, one made of iron; for killing, it should be a hen’s egg; these are the vessels for the propitiation of the mantras.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, knower of all truths, benefactor of the world!
By what means, O Lord of Gods, is the purification of the body brought about?
"Tell me that, O Omniscient One, if you have affection for me. The Lord said:
O Goddess of gods, O you who are fragrant with devotion, I shall tell you the medicine;
this must not be revealed anywhere, for it is difficult to find even in the three worlds.
One should grind *kumārī*, *chatradharī*,
and black gram (*rājamāṣa*) with the milk of a cow of uniform color, as well as with the seed of the plantain tree (*raṃbhā*).
At dawn, one should smear the body; thus the accomplishment of subjugation (*vaśya*) arises.
One should consume the root of white *aparājitā* together with wine.
And for the destruction of white leprosy,
one should apply a plaster on a Sunday consisting of the fruit and flower of the Aśoka tree together with the fruits of the Eraṇḍa.
One should invite [the guest] on the previous day and consume [the food] on the following day;
otherwise, a disease arises in his body due to undigested wind (vāta).
Having taken up the twelve supports, one should break through that knot;
then, having brought it to the tip of the tongue, one should contemplate it in the form of a lamp.
Having recited this one hundred thousand times, one shall burn away all sins;
thereafter, having known everything moving and stationary, one shall attain omniscience.
Then one should recite the Great Vidyā;
the person becomes a master of speech, and his words become a paralyzer of the opponent in the assembly of debate.
Then that scholar, whose pride was shattered and whose luster eclipsed,
was one who knew the essence of logic, grammar, the meaning of sentences, and the ornaments of poetry.
O Lord, by placing [the mantra] upon the tongue, even a mute person becomes a skilled poet,
one who perceives the essence of expansive poetic figures of sound that are most delicate.
Then, one should arrange the forms equal to a garland;
with hidden feet, it shall become a great poem (mahākāvya) composed by a superior author.
One should write [the mantra] on the tongue of a child within three days, so that his intellect becomes unimpeded in the scriptures, just as Vijaya was for Vālmīki.
Having worshipped and recited [the mantra], one should now write the Vidyā, beginning with the syllable *Vāgbhava*, upon a golden plate using white *durvā* grass.
He alone is wise and illustrious, and never a fool;
this is the Vāgīśvarī-vidyā, which [resides] even upon the head of one who is like water-grass.
Having paid the fee, a person should recite the vidyā one hundred and eight times.
He too composes all these verses and sentences just as they are;
he who meditates on Tāriṇī, resembling a lamp, upon his tongue.
The poetic skill of Bṛhaspati was surpassed by Śukra;
having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, he brought him under control along with his retinue.
Meditating upon the Vidyā on the tongue, the wise one should then recite it in its formal form;
his speech shall then become a showerer of nectar and be effective in every way.
Having visualized at dawn the Knowledge in the form of a lamp upon the tongue,
one should drink water after reciting three times the Mātṛkā along with that Knowledge.
By the method of drinking water, even a mute becomes eloquent;
by meditating upon it on the tongue, O God, a man becomes a knower of the three periods of time.
But that best of practitioners who contemplates the Vidyā as non-dual shall certainly become liberated while living and fully liberated at the end.
This libation for the Goddess with honey bestows the fruits of all desires,
directly grants the eight supernatural powers, and destroys even the greatest of sins.
Eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya) and with hair loosened, one should recite ten thousand times with devotion;
for him, speech consisting of both prose and verse shall become perfect in every way.

By merely reciting [the mantra] one hundred times, a man who applies a mark with *rocanā* (yellow pigment) and gazes at someone while holding the mantra will bring that person under his control like a servant.
In a pond with deep water, when a wooden staff was seized by a crocodile, it was quickly pulled out with a tooth; one should therefore fashion a peg from that very wood.
On a mere lotus leaf with honey,
one should write the root mantra, which bestows success, in the center of a circle of vajras.
The best of practitioners should say, "O Kurumāyāntī, [do] such-and-such!
Having cast that into a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), he should offer oblations of curd.
One should visualize a thousand lotuses, red as blood, with a crimson luster;
having first uttered the *praṇava* (Om), one should likewise utter the pair of words "padme."
One should utter the word "mahāpadme," then the word "padmāvati," and with the mantra "huṃ huṃ svāhā," one should offer the bali oblation as before.
Thus, whoever performs this rite with diligence and certainty,
he should always offer a bali-oblation at midnight on the fourteenth lunar day.
Having first extracted the Praṇava and then Hṛllekhā thereafter,
one should utter the word "Mahā" at the end of the word "Ekajaṭe."
Having addressed the word "yakṣa" and so forth, and then the word "mama" (mine) for the intellect,
and having spoken the word "upanīta" (brought near), one says "gṛhṇa baliṃ" (take the offering) followed by two ṭha syllables.
Then, cause [the disciple] to grasp all my words, which are declared in two ways;
perform the rite of peace (śānti), and thereafter the mantra of the Supreme Knowledge (paravidyā).
Having divided [the mantra] into two parts, one should say "itiṭha," and likewise "truṭa" and "chiṃdhi.
This mantra, beginning with "māyā svāhā," bestows success in intelligence for offerings and other rites.
This mantra for the offering of oblations destroys the armies of enemies, planetary portents, misfortunes, diseases, and malevolent spells;
if one applies it according to the ritual procedure, it shall accomplish the goal through its practice.
When midnight has passed, one should always offer an oblation at a crossroads;
this destroys enemy armies, planetary portents, misfortunes, diseases, and malevolent spells.
Having first uttered the Praṇava, then [the word] Ugratāre, one should utter the two [phrases]: "O you with formidable fangs, agitate the opposing faction."
Recite "khādaya" twice, then "paṭhamattha" twice, and likewise say "dvayaṃ dvayaṃ":
"Those who indeed seek to harm me, as well as those intent on reviling me."
O Yoginīs, together with the circles [of deities], destroy them! HŪM PHAṬ SVĀHĀ!
"Draw forth the knowledge of others, cut it away, svāhā! O Kapilā, seize [it], seize it, svāhā!
Or else, one should apply honey and parched grain to the tongue of the child.
Then, after cutting the channel,
the mantra-practitioner should first write the root mantra with a golden stylus, or else with white *dūrvā* grass, upon that which is desired.
By the recitation of this mantra, even a child shall become eloquent and a swift poet;
it is praised as a rite of birth-consecration to be performed immediately upon the birth of a son.
The practitioner of mantra should write [the syllables] upon the tongue with a splinter of sacrificial wood,
having worshipped it three times with the right hand alone.
Having recited the mantra, one should form each line very beautifully;
having first performed the consecration (saṃskāra), one should write the mantra at the end.
One should worship the auspicious Tāriṇī with perfumes, sandalwood, and flowers;
then, facing north, one should establish the excellent pedestal.
One should worship the goddess Tāriṇī with various beautiful offerings of food;
[the devotee] shall become a poet through words, a son who speaks the truth and has his senses subdued.
One should diligently write the mantra with honey using the root of *kuśa* grass;
either the father’s brother, or the mother’s brother, should likewise write the mantra.
The father alone should engrave the mantra, and never anyone else;
furthermore, the elder brother is always praised as the one who may do so.
Therefore, O Goddess, one should place the mantra that grants the fruits of all desires,
having carefully spread darbha grass and established [the deity] within the lap of the Mother.
Accompanied by practitioners, one should perform a rite for the child’s peace;
first, one should recite the hymn into the mother’s left ear.
Brāhmī, bhayā, vacā, vāsā, and pippalī, combined with honey—
by the use of this for seven days, one is sung of together with the kiṃnaras.
The Goddess said:
What is the substance for cleansing the tongue, and what is the protection for oneself?
O Lord, what is the protection for a son, what is the protection for the house, and what is the medicine?
"O Lord, I wish to hear it; please tell me out of your grace.
Īśvara said:
Having smeared the tongue with black jayantī flower and the root of apāmārga on the sixth day, [one obtains] a son.
One should know the protective substances that were prepared on the day of birth:
[the wood of] the *vipra* tree, the root of the lotus, and likewise the dried skull of a cow.
One should place it at the entrance; then there will be no fear whatsoever.
One should wear the bark of the *jambu* tree, the leaf of the *śimbī*, and matted locks upon the head.
There is no fear of Rākṣasas, nor of diseases, malevolent rites, and the like,
once a Pippala tree has been planted in the four corners of the house.
One should station [the deity] outside at the door and bind a goat and a monkey;
on the sixth day at night, one should plant two roots of the *raṃbhā* plant.
In that very place, one should set down a sword and a very handsome Brahmin;
having established an elderly woman, or a brother-in-law endowed with humility.
One should not bathe the Kumāra with water alone on the Jayantī day;
rather, one should sprinkle him with water mixed with ghee on the Jayantī.
Having installed it upon an eight-petaled lotus, a wise man shall become possessed of a virtuous son;
and having carefully obtained the root and bark of the Nāgeśvara tree.
Having filled [the vessel] and prepared a wick smeared with ghee,
the knower of mantras should then light the lamp and cut the umbilical cord of the son.
The son should be well-disciplined, intelligent, and endowed with virtues;
one should place the bark of an *aśoka* tree from the south at the entrance.
These substances should be kept ready: jambu bark and salt.
For one who always places [this] at the door, there shall be the destruction of obstacles;
having worshipped Tāriṇī during the night on the thirteenth lunar day.
Holding the bark of the Arka plant in his hand, he should touch the Tāriṇī stone;
directing his intent toward his desire with diligence, he obtains it—of this there is no doubt.
He who, holding the root of a mango tree in his hand, should remember the mantra of Tāriṇī—
especially on the thirteenth lunar day— shall obtain the fruit of all desires.
O Kulluketāra, O bestower of supreme bliss,
O Supreme Goddess, protect me in this terrible and difficult-to-cross cycle of existence.
O destroyer of all sins, O you who destroy all sins,
O you whose form is consciousness, time, and ignorance, protect me, O Supreme Goddess!
Oṃ, salutations! O Goddess Caṇḍikā, salutations to you, O Mother;
you who dwell eternally at the confluence of the five rivers, ever uttering sweet sounds.
O elephant-faced one, O peak of the left, O single-tusked, three-eyed one!
Homage to you, Gaṇeśa, the destroyer of obstacles, the son of the Gaṅgā.
Having prostrated, the goddess with golden limbs, seated upon a lotus,
worthy of worship, free from sloth, the sixty-fourth [power], who moves through the fields and the dwellers of the fields;
Obeisance to you, O Rudrāṇī, who possess serpent-earrings and the trident as your weapon, who have a skull and the moon as your crest-jewel, who are three-eyed, and whose vehicle is the bull.
Kaumārī, seated upon a peacock, has a body the color of ruby, possesses a radiance equal to the rising sun,
and holds a spear in her hand.
Her playful sport is manifold and she utterly destroys all fear;
holding the conch, discus, and mace in her hands, she is Jayantī, whose vehicle is Garuḍa.
I bow to Vārāhī, who has red hair and garments, holds a sword in her hand, possesses three eyes, has a face with protruding fangs, and is seated upon a buffalo.
O you who are golden-hued, whose form is your own true nature, who possess a gentle appearance and friendliness;
salutations to you, O Lord, consort of Indra, holding a thunderbolt in hand and seated upon an elephant.
She holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, wields the vajra and the śakti, and possesses three eyes;
she has the radiance of fire, great flames, emaciated limbs, and consumes lotuses.
O Goddess, sovereign of the five elements, whose form is stainless knowledge;
salutations to you, Mahālakṣmī, the performer of auspiciousness free from obstacles!
The goddess Caṇḍicāmuṇḍikā, Carcikā, and Caṇḍeśvarī,
who bestows all perfections and destroys all obstacles.
Holding a noose, a goad, a spear, a trident, and a khaṭvāṅga staff in her hands,
she is the burner, the garlanded one, the fierce goddess, and the destroyer of the pride of the dānavas.
She whose voice is beautiful, who has red hair and a red song, adorned with red ornaments,
she resembles the twelve Ādityas and is the destroyer of the stain of misfortune.
She traverses difficult terrains, possesses a fierce form, and effects the destruction of the three worlds;
she has flames issuing from her fanged mouth and sits upon a garland of severed heads.
Victory to you, O Mother of the World! O Goddess, salutations to you, the Sovereign of the three worlds!
O Goddess, wearer of human skin, clothed in tiger skin!
Her body is adorned with the ornament of a skull-bowl, she delights in drinking wine,
and her ornaments consist of a hand-drum, a small drum, a yantra, and bells.
She is adorned with a canopy, possessed of ego, mounted upon a fierce corpse,
filled with various sounds, and uttering great roars of "phe" and "phaṭ."
She who terrifies the three worlds, the fierce one, the most violent, whose vehicle is a corpse,
who is like the fire at the end of an eon, and who is adorned with ornaments of blazing flames.
Caṇḍimuṇḍī and Cāṇḍālī bring victory and auspiciousness in battle;
she dwells in Jālandhara, Oḍiyāna, and Devīkoṭa.
Homage to the Goddess who assumes manifold forms, the protectress of the three worlds;
she whose face is ablaze, whose cheeks bear beautiful lines, and who wears vermilion upon her forehead.
The ḍākinīs, bhūtas, vetālīs, piśācas, and ayānavastanis;
the devas, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kinnaras, and puṭanas.
Her limbs were smeared with fragrant sandalwood paste, and she was adorned with flower garlands;
she was accompanied by Vaṭukanātha, Mahākāla, and Kṣetrapāla.
Śrīmacchakti is united with Yogeśvarī and is herself worshipped;
on the eighth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight, she is Aṣṭamī Vajramaṇḍalā.
The Goddess is seated upon a skull-bowl in a place crowded with human skeletons;
O Beloved, she is fond of offerings of blood, fat, marrow, fish, and meat.
I bow to Jayabhairavī, who is united with Mahābhairava;
you are the secret one, possessing meritorious impressions, in the field, the seat, and the great seat.
Kāmākṣī, who can assume any form at will, she who is delusion and illusion yet free from passion;
she who destroys suffering, grief, old age, death, fear, and sin.
The Goddess who bestows the perfection of the sword, Lakṣmī, the bestower of fortune and auspiciousness—
those men who recite this hymn with a spirit of devotion while on a journey [attain their desires].
Having attained the fruit of the fulfillment of desires, she who bestows auspiciousness and joy,
Bhairava said:
Salutations to Vīracāmuṇḍā; salutations to the Supreme Goddess, the mother of all beings and the one who provides protection to all.
The goddess is filled with Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, bestows boons, is without a seat,
assumes various forms, is free from passion, and possesses the nature of the moon.
Full-breasted and large-eyed, adorned with all ornaments,
she wears earrings and a crown set with pearls, gold, and rubies.
Your slender arms are adorned with divine armlets, beautified by necklaces of pearls and gems;
various jewels are bound as a girdle upon your waist.
Displaying all her limbs with hands adorned by various weapons,
she resembles the form of Bhairavī, with red eyes and terrifying prowess.
The goddess who is devoid of enemies, the vanquisher of foes, the destroyer of all adversaries;
she who bears various weapons and is the sovereign of the gods through manifold scriptures.
The fierce Goddess of the Suras has eighteen arms, wielding various weapons:
an axe, a noose, a mace, a discus, a javelin, and a tomara.
Śaktinānā, Gāndī, Triśūlā, Śūradhāriṇī,
Khaḍgapheṭakasaṃdhārī, Kartārī, and Kartṛdhāriṇī.
With hair and face turned upward, she is terrifying and roars with a fearsome form;
scattered like the rays of the sun, she is the destroyer of all defects.
In the four seats, in the four trees, and in the cremation ground, you alone are present;
you are the Goddess of all beings, assuming manifold forms at will.
The omniscient one, whose nature is that which is to be consumed within the self, exists in the form of the individual soul (jīva);
she is Padminī, the mistress of the wheels (cakras), seated upon the lotus posture.
You alone are the earth, the water, and the netherworld; you are the nature of the five elements, and you are the ten vital winds in the form of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*.
Established in the navel, the throat, the region of the heart, and the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra),
she resides in the place of the head as the form of the great gnosis, the nectar of immortality.
The Goddess resides in the midst of the Kula, her form being the essence of the middle of knowledge;
she is the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation, the omniscient mistress of Rudra.
He is served by Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara Śiva;
he is the lord of the Nāgas, Yakṣas, and Gandharvas, and he is enchanting to all the gods.
The four world-protectors, all the Mothers,
as well as the ṛṣis and munis who are worshipped by the Dānavas and Asuras.
Uttering most terrible cries of "hā hā" and loud bursts of boisterous laughter,
she holds a great conch shell, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a hand-drum (ḍamaru) in her left hand.
Constantly laughing with loud, piercing laughter, Aghorā and Aghorarūpiṇī always sport in the cremation ground together with Bhairava and Bhairavī.
Venerated by throngs of vultures, crows, jackals, dogs, piśācas, humans, and rākṣasas,
as well as ḍākinīs, rudras, vetālas, and yoginīs.
The Goddess Kapālamālikā, who bears the excellent skull-cup,
is eternally fond of red garments and brings about the dissolution of the world.
Possessing many names, you have been my leaders in manifold ways;
with various forms and names, O you of many aspects, homage be to you!
O Blessed Caṇḍikā, Durgā, Bhavānī, you whose form is the ether; O Kālikā, wielder of the staff of Time, Kātyāyanī—salutations be to you!
Vedamati, Viśālākṣī, Gāyatrī, Gaṃdamādinī, Sāvitrī, Śobhanī, Caṇḍī, Bhūcapadmī, and Vasuṃdharī.
Victory and Triumph, the Unconquered and the Invincible,
Nandā, Bhadrā, and likewise Pūrṇā— O Goddess Umā, salutations to you!
Gaurī, Jāmukṣagaṅgā, Śivā, Niśivarūpiṇī, Bhyaśvarī,
Caṇḍikā, Abhyaśī, Gandharvā, and Tribhuvaneśvarī.
She is the upholder of wisdom, the ordainer, and the performer of creation and dissolution;
she is the shatterer and the paralyzer, the fair-faced one who has gone beyond all fear.
Mohanī, Carcikā, Caṇḍī, Haṃsinī, Nādarūpiṇī, Kālinī—
the purifier of manifold knowledge— and Kulanāyakā.
The six-syllabled [mantra], Bhadrā, Vedanī, Nīlasarasvatī,
Mātaṅgī, Kālikā, Harā, and Lakṣmī— salutations to these eight.
Manonmanī, Indrā, Tripurā, and likewise Tripurabhairavī;
she is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the connector of existence, and the increaser of both being and non-being.
Established in the abode of manifold mantras, she whose limbs are the mantras and who possesses manifold forms,
is mounted upon four arms, has four faces, and is golden in appearance.
O Grandmother, Mother of the Vedas, O Brahmayani, salutations to you!
I bow my head to the Goddess who wields the trident and the spear.
O Goddess who deludes the three worlds, O Māheśvarī, salutations to you!
You hold a spear in your hand, possess a great body, and are seated upon the throne of a peacock.
O Kaumārī, whose limbs are entirely red on every day, salutations to you!
You have four arms, are mounted upon Garuḍa, and hold a conch, a discus, and a mace.
O fair-complexioned Mahāmāyā, O Vaiṣṇavī, salutations to you!
You who hold a staff in hand, possess a massive body, and are both terrifying and formidable.
Homage to you, Vārāhī, who has three eyes, whose gaze is fierce and terrible,
who is mounted upon the seat of an elephant, who possesses a thousand eyes, and who wields the thunderbolt.
O slayer of many enemies, O Indrāyaṇī, salutations to you!
You who sit upon a corpse, the most fierce one, adorned with a beautiful garland of skulls.
O you with upward-pointing hair, O Skeleton, O Cāmuṇḍā—salutations to you!
You whose limbs are smeared [with ashes], who destroys the moon, and who holds the excellent trident.
Obeisance to you, O Great Goddess, who has the bull as her vehicle; obeisance to Mahālakṣmī!
Likewise, [obeisance] to Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, Mahālakṣmī, and Gaṇeśvarī—
you are the Goddess who assumes the forms of many deities, yet you are Kālarūpiṇī.
Bhairavī joined with the eight; salutations to you, O Bhairavī!
Jayadhūma and Siṃha are located in the south-west and the west respectively.
And obeisance to you in the northwestern direction, in the northern part, and in the northeast.
Whether below, above, within you, O Goddess, in the stars, in the water, or on the earth—you are Power, the sustainer of power, whose very form is power; salutations to you!
Constantly bowing to the one endowed with power, the Yoginīs of the Kula perform their rites;
these Yoginīs are the axe that severs the cycle of existence.
Whoever recites this hymn with a mind concentrated on a single point, shall obtain the divine bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Whether in a cremation ground, or while traveling abroad, or in one's own home, or within a forest; in battle, in a place infested by thieves, during a conflagration, or in the midst of great terror—
The person who recites this constantly attains victory;
he obtains that divine fruit which is sought after, and reaches the auspicious state of the Radiant Abode.
And by that which has been spoken, O merit-bringer who brings happiness to all sentient beings,
she shall become a bestower of auspiciousness upon all mothers and fathers.
Bhairava said:
Vārāhī, Sundarī, Kālī, Sundarīvadana,
Śubhā, Saumyarūpā, and Saumyasthā— she who bestows all good fortune.
O Goddess, creeper of the left-hand path, you who are worshipped through the left-hand practice;
you who are auspicious when worshipped, the bestower of boons, and of gentle form—salutations to you!
Mounted upon the buffalo-seat, slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura, I do not know how to offer praise to you; O Supreme Goddess, please forgive me.
Seated upon a lion, possessing a gentle form, you bestow the fruits of the lion-throne;
O Kālī, you are my royal mother, the granter of sovereignty and royal power.
You alone are the Mother Kālī and Vārāhī; salutations to you!
O King of Gems, may there be victory everywhere in the gambling match.
Whoever recites this hymn shall obtain all their desires.
O Kālī, by reciting [the mantra] a thousand times with *japā* flowers and a thousand *nīlotpala* lotuses, and having performed worship, Caṇḍikā becomes manifest before one's eyes.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the section on Nirvāṇa within the Dakṣiṇāmnāya of the Śrī Vārāhī Tantra. || 31 ||
Bhairava said:
If the *pavitra* should be lost, there shall be a *caru* offering for one who possesses the *pavitra*;
when the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is uncooked, one should sacrifice with that very same oblation.
One should cook exactly four handfuls of rice; if it burns, there will be weeping.
One should feed four Brahmins with that remaining portion as they set out on their way.

If the thread is mostly burnt, like an oblation that has been partially consumed, then the sacrifice should be performed again with what remains; however, if it is completely destroyed, then one must begin from the very beginning.
When that [oblation] has been completely burnt, one should produce the sacrificial offering (havis) once again;
that same yoga must be performed, but a renewed sacrifice (punaryāga) is not required.
If the oblation from the middle and the eastern half should become spoiled,
one should again cut portions from the very same oblation, from the middle and the eastern half.
If a defect occurs when the fuel and other materials have been prepared, one should offer clarified butter (ājya) in place of the three primary oblations;
however, one should offer that which is not defective in its proper place.
Thus, having completed [the rite], one should cast that which is spoiled by contact into water;
however, the sacrifice beginning with the *anvādhāna* must indeed be performed again.
If a defect occurs in the primary oblation after the fire has been established but before the offering is made,
one should produce that oblation again and complete the rite as before.
If the sacrificial oblation of the limbs is spoiled, one should throw it into the water;
however, for the defect of the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, one should complete the rite with clarified butter alone.
By means of fallen nails, hair, or insects dwelling within, or by those that defile with fat, blood, semen, marrow, bone, urine, feces, and bile;

If the sacrificial oblations (havis) should be seen to be defiled by phlegm and other such loathsome substances, or if they are broken or sprinkled [with impurities], they become corrupted; one should cast them into water.
One should perform the *caru* oblation for one who has died during a *parvan*;
in that case, they perform the rite in the same manner as a *pārvaṇa* ceremony.
One who has not yet performed the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice should eat new grain only after this [rite];
for Vaiśvānara, a caru-oblation and a full-spoon offering (pūrṇāhuti) with a sruva-ladle must be performed.
When one eats the food of an enemy, even there this sacrificial porridge (caru) should be offered;
if the fire has been rekindled while the fuel is still burning, a re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya) is required.

In cases where the specific rule for an expiation has not been stated, this hundredfold offering of sesame seeds shall serve as a general substitute that is not in conflict with the stream of the sacred tradition.
Indeed, an oblation must be offered there with the mantra "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā";
following every such incident, a full expiation (prāyaścitta) shall be performed here.
If a defect should arise even before the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya),
then the expiation (prāyaścitta) must take place immediately after that consecration.

If there should be a transposition of the deities at the beginning of the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) and so forth, or likewise a transposition of the mantras at the beginning of the fire-oblation (homa) and so forth;
If there should be an inversion of this [order]— namely, [offering] from the middle and from the eastern half—
if there should likewise be an inversion of the substances during the pouring out and other such rites;
Alternatively, Brahmā should offer a spoonful of oblation with the *devārcā* verses;
he gives to the performer of the *homa* whatever principal substance is available in his own home.
The sacrificer should offer oblations with the *sruva* ladle into the *brahmāgni*;
whatever substance he gives to any Brahmin on that occasion belongs to him.
In this case, a single oblation must be offered here using the mantras known as the *vyāhṛtis* in combination;
once the expiation has been performed, even a past ritual act is indeed rectified.

"One teacher says it is a ritual act (*kārya*), but other wise ones say that these [obstacles], appearing in various forms such as demons, are merely the recitation (*japa*) and oblation (*homa*) being carried away."
For one who has performed the purification of the hands, [the obstacles] flee in the ten directions;
whether much or little, whatever rite is enjoined according to one's own Gṛhya-sūtra [is accomplished].
For him, when the purpose of the scripture has been accomplished to that extent, he becomes one who has done all;
[he is] seven cubits tall, with four horns, seven tongues, and two heads.
With a serene countenance, comfortably seated, pure, and smiling,
he has Svāhā on his right side and likewise the goddess Svadhā on his left.
He should hold in his right hands the *śakti* mantra, the *śruva* and *sruva* ladles, the *tomara* spear, and the fan; and in his left hands, he should hold a vessel of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
The sacrificial fire is of such a form, seated facing toward oneself;
by the mere recollection of it and by various utterances, [one attains success] therein, in the performance of sacrifices and other rites.
Whatever is deficient attains completeness by immediately saluting Acyuta;
the worldly fire known as Pācaka is proclaimed as the first.
The fire named Māruta is prescribed for the rite of conception (garbhādhāna);
thereafter, in the rite for ensuring a male child (puṃsavana), it should be known as Pavamāna.
In the *sīmantonnayana* rite, the fire named Maṅgala is produced; in the *jātakarma*, it is indeed Pārthiva by name; and for the *prāśana*, Śuci is prescribed.
Satya is [the fire] in the Caula ceremony; its manifestation is in the Vratādeśa;
Sūrya is the name [of the fire] in the Godāna; and Agni is considered the Yojaka in the Vivāha.

The fire of the household (āvasathya) is to be known as the twice-born; in the Vaiśvadeva rite, it is the protector of the house; in penance, it is the wise one; and in sacrifices, it is the purifier.
He is the carrier of oblations for the gods and the bearer of funeral offerings for the ancestors;
he is declared to be the bestower of peace and the increaser of strength in rites of nourishment.

In the *pūrṇāhuti* it is named *mīlana*; in the *abhicāraka* rite, it is the fire named *akrodha*; for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), it is named *kāmada*; and in the *vanadā* rite, it is the *hetudūṣaka*.
The Jāṭhara fire is to be known as being in the belly; Kravyāda is in the cremation ground;
Vahni is in the Lakṣa-homa; and Hutāśana is in the Koṭi-homa.
In the ocean is the Svāgni fire, and in the abode is the Saṃvarta fire; Brahmā is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, and Īśvara is likewise the Dakṣiṇa fire.
Viṣṇu is the Āhavanīya fire; in the Agnihotra, there are three fires for Agni. Having thus understood the names of the fires, one should commence the domestic rites (gṛhyakarma).
May all the oceans, rivers, sacred fords, clouds,
and streams come to the patron of the sacrifice, bringing about the destruction of his misfortunes.
O Kumbha, when the great ocean was being churned during the conflict between the gods and the dānavas,
you were then born and were personally held by Viṣṇu himself.
All sacred fords are your essence; all gods reside within you.
All forms abide in you, and all vital breaths are established in you.
You alone are Śiva himself; you are Viṣṇu and you are Prajāpati.
You are the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Viśvedevas together with the Pitṛs.
Since all [the gods] abide in you and grant the fruits of one's desires,
O Lotus-born One, it is through your grace that I desire to perform this sacrifice.
Be present, O Lord of Gods, and remain forever gracious;
[behold] the Goddess seated upon a shimmering lotus throne, positioned in the half-lotus posture (ardhapadmāsana).
Abounding in the splendor of all ornaments, with full and elevated breasts,
ever pouring forth nectar, and clad in yellow silk garments.
Four-armed, she holds a thick staff with her right hand,
and with her left upper hand she holds a beautiful blue lotus.
Holding various weapons with her left and right hands,
come, O boon-granting goddess renowned as Mahāṣaṣṭhī!
Protect me with your powers, O Goddess; salutations to you, O Great Ṣaṣṭhī!
Victory to you, O Goddess, Mother of the World, who brings joy to the universe!
Be gracious, O auspicious Jayā; salutations to you, O Goddess Ṣaṣṭhikā!
O Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, O being of great essence, bestower of sons upon all!
O Giver of Boons, O You who are affectionate toward Your devotees, by Your grace may this child live long,
[for the sake] of the gods, the sages, and the devotees.
And protect this son of mine, O Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī; salutations to you!
Just as the infant Skanda, the son of Gaurī, was protected by you.
Likewise, may this child protect me; O Ṣaṣṭhikā, homage to you!
O Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, homage to you, who dwell in the lying-in chamber.
O Mother of the Children, you have been worshipped with supreme devotion;
you are the mother of all beings and the increaser of wealth and prosperity.
She is the mother of all branches of knowledge and the cause of their birth;
she is the mother of all the worlds, and especially so for children.
In the form of Nārāyaṇa, protect my son from all sides;
you are the power of all the gods, acting for the welfare of children.
O Great Ṣaṣṭhī, protect my son; salutations to you!
O Rudrāṇī, who, in the form of Rudra, destroys all obstacles.
O Goddess of Life, protect the hair-tuft; be the bestower of auspiciousness at all times.
Protect this child born of my lineage here from rākṣasas,
bhūtas, and piśācas, as well as from ḍākinīs and yoginīs.
And as my mother, protect my child from beasts of prey and from serpents;
for you alone are established as both the goddess Vaiṣṇavī and Brāhmaṇī.
O you who are proclaimed as the power of Rudra, O Great Sixth, salutations to you!
You are the nurse of him who is renowned as Mahāṣaṣṭha in the month of Kārtika.
By your grace, may this boy live long without obstacle—
he by whom a mountain peak was held aloft with his hand.
"O my son, may that army be overcome by Kṛṣṇa with a single hand;
may there be peace, may there be auspiciousness, and may there be well-being and prosperity."
Therefore, let this [being] return to that very place from which it came—
from the Moon, the Sun, the Lords of the Quarters, Yama, and Bhava.
"Protect this boy for me as if he were a deposit entrusted to you;
whether I am heedful or heedless, and whether it be by day or by night."
All the gods, led by Śakra, shall provide protection on every side;
one should recite the mantra from the Āyurveda for protection near the child.
May the Nāgas, Piśācas, Gandharvas, Pitṛs, Yakṣas,
and Rākṣasas always strike down that person who approaches him with hostility.
May those night-stalkers who protect the earth and the intermediate space,
and whoever else [dwells] in the cardinal and intermediate directions, protect you and the world from that [danger].
Moreover, the sages, the gods, the chanters, and likewise the royal seers;
the mountains, the rivers, and all the oceans as well— [all these praise you].
One should place Agni on the tongue, and likewise Prāṇa and Āyu.
May Soma protect your vyāna and your drinking; may Parjanya protect you all around;
may the lightning protect your udāna, and the clouds your samāna.
May Vaimindra, Valapati, and Vācavācastathā protect your speech;
may the Gandharvas protect your desires, and may Indra protect your being.
May King Varuṇa protect your wisdom; may the ocean protect the circle of your navel; may the sun protect your eyes, the quarters of space your ears, and the moon your mind.
May Vāyu protect your nose, and likewise may the herbs protect your hair;
may Ākāśa protect your ears, and may the Earth protect your body.
Vaiśvānara is your head, Viṣṇu is your prowess;
the Supreme Puruṣa is your manliness, and Brahmā is likewise your feet and eyebrows.
Thus, by specifically identifying with the body here as "I am," one brings about the destruction of disease through these mantras declared in the Vedas.
"Since you have been protected by me in this way, may you attain a long life!
May Viṣṇu grant you well-being; may Nārada and the others grant you well-being!"
May Agni and Vāyu grant well-being, and may the gods who traverse the great paths grant well-being;
may the Grandfather (Brahmā) grant well-being, and may they always bestow long life upon you.

Nirvāṇa is non-conceptual, formless, stainless, and changeless; he bears the discus and the staff, possesses the face of a messenger, and has the nature of Rudra’s mantra; with a mouth whose brow is knit in a frown, he is the terrifying Bhairava, holding a trident and millions of *khaṭvāṅgas* along with a *ḍamaru* drum.
I bow to Kṣetrapāla.
All you Gandharvas, who are of divine origin and assume various forms,
protect my son yourself; having seen him, accept my offering.
All the planets, beginning with the Sun, dwell eternally in heaven.
May you all provide protection for me, personally accepting this offering;
likewise, may the guardians of the directions, Indra and the others who dwell in their respective abodes, do the same.
May they all grant you peace and protection; being satisfied, accept this offering:
Kṛṣṇa, Nanta, Acyuta, Cakrī, Vaikuṇṭha, and Janārdana.
Upeṃdra, Yajñapuruṣa, Vāsudeva, Hari, Yogīśa, and Puṇḍarīkākṣa— these are the names [of Viṣṇu] in successive order for each month.
O Earth, I entrust this to you for safekeeping on behalf of the Moon, the Sun, the lords of the directions, the quarters, and Varuṇa; protect it always.
Whether he is heedful or heedless, by day or even by night,
all the gods, led by Śakra, shall constantly protect him.
O Goddess Earth, O auspicious one, always protect this entire world;
O beloved of Hari, deposit the allotted measure of life within yourself.
Burn down, without delay, whatever obstacles there may be to this short life,
as well as those that stand in the way of one's vitality, health, and mind.
O Mother, you who sustain all beings, you are indeed superior;
O Mother, protect Kumāra, and may Brahmā grant his approval to that.
On their birthday, everyone who has bathed with auspicious waters should diligently worship the preceptor, the gods, the sacred fire, and the brahmins.
O God, one's own birth-star, the ancestors, and likewise Prajāpati—
every year, a great festival should be performed for these with diligence.
O Mārkaṇḍeya, salutations to you who live through the end of seven kalpas;
O venerable sage, be gracious for the sake of attaining long life and health.
O twice-born one, foremost among sages, just as you are long-lived,
O tiger among munis, act in such a way that I too may become long-lived.
O highly fortunate Mārkaṇḍeya, who lives through the end of seven kalpas,
grant us your boon for the sake of attaining long life and health.
Having obtained a boon from Mārkaṇḍeya, Vāyu drank half an añjali of milk mixed with sesame seeds and jaggery, which caused him to increase in size.
Aśvatthāman, Bali, Vyāsa, Hanumān, Vibhīṣaṇa, Kṛpa, and Paraśurāma— these seven are the long-lived ones.
O Mārkaṇḍeya, he who constantly remembers these eight [verses] shall live for more than a hundred years, free from all diseases.
From the time of conception until the tonsure ceremony (caula), when the proper time has passed, one should perform the rite by means of the ritual action;
having performed the *vyāhṛti* oblations and the purificatory consecrations (*saṃskāra*), one should offer the oblations in the prescribed order.
Among these, for even one of the minor sins (kaluṣa), one should perform a quarter-penance (pāda-kṛcchra);
for the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā), it should be half a kṛcchra; thus it has been declared in the case of distress.
But in all other cases, one should perform each rite at double the duration;
however, the purificatory rites such as the birth ceremony (jātakarman) and others should take place at their own prescribed times.

Some teachers maintain that the girdle-tying ceremony for a child should be performed before the *caula* and immediately after the expiation rites; however, other wise scholars do not agree with this. The binding of the girdle for a child should take place during the five months beginning with Māgha.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha—that is, the birth-month of Jyeṣṭha—one should perform [the rites] for all:
the father, grandfather, brother, kinsmen, those born of the same lineage (gotra), and those born of the same womb.
One who is qualified should perform the initiation; in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent one should do so.
The father himself should initiate the son, and in his absence, the father’s father.
In the absence of that [father], the paternal uncle; in his absence, the uterine brother.
For the Vasiṣṭhas, the *cūḍā* should be in the middle of the head, but for others, on the right side.
Atri holds that for both sides, the crest-lock (śikhā) of the Kāśyapas is prescribed;
one should not perform the tonsure ceremony (cūḍākarma) while the child's mother is pregnant.
One may perform [the rite] even for a pregnant woman after the fifth month;
if one performs it with the Mahāpanīya [mantras], then no fault is found.
At a time when the twilight is rumbling with rain and is defiled by the falling of hailstones, one should cook *brahmaudana* on the fire; even if it is cooked, one should not desist.
One who seeks awakening should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times in a temple of Śiva while observing celibacy and one's own duty; even if it is deficient, it shall indeed become complete.
A twice-born man should not remain even for a single day without belonging to an āśrama;
for he who remains without an āśrama must indeed perform penance.
Having given a gift to the teacher, he should bathe according to his command;
or, having undertaken the Vedic vows, he may bathe on that very day.

A celibate student who has not failed in his vows should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks— one who has belonged to no other man before, who is not a sapinda relative, and who is younger than himself.
Fifth from the mother and likewise seventh from the father;
if, for the bride and the groom, the seventh is the common ancestor (kūṭastha) from the paternal side.
The fifth [ancestor] from these two mothers ceases to receive the rice-ball offering (piṇḍa),
because he is the fixed root-ancestor (kūṭastha-mūlapuruṣa) from whom the lineages diverge.
Lineage, character, age, physical form, learning, wealth, and lordship—having examined these seven merits, a daughter should be given away by the wise; everything else is not to be considered.
In the family, shaving is not performed even for one who eats from a vessel three *darva*s in length during the three seasons;
nor should one perform the three shavings by entering and exiting [the house].
In the family, shaving does not take place until after three seasons have passed from the purpose [of the marriage], but there is no shaving [before then].
Neither the son's marriage nor the daughter's marriage should take place within three menstrual periods;
furthermore, there should be no shaving for one year, nor should two shavings occur at the same time.
In the months of Phālguna or Caitra, however, for the marriage of a son or his initiation ceremony,
they observe a delay of three seasons due to the difference in the year's reckoning.
On one's birth asterism and on the day of birth, a wise person should avoid both auspicious and inauspicious rites;
likewise, for a woman, even those performed during the first pregnancy in the month of Jyeṣṭha are to be avoided, with the exception of auspicious ones.
For two persons born of the same mother—one male and one female—within the same year, the same rite must not be performed; it is prescribed that the rites be performed separately.
One should not perform two tonsure ceremonies in a single pavilion, even if they belong to a sister's generation, a brother's generation, or both a sister and a brother.
The wise declare that one should marry off a daughter within four days;
they do not perform the wedding on the day following the daughter's [natal] asterism.
Those born from the same womb do not perform a marriage nor the tonsure ceremony atop the sacrificial pavilion on the same day.
The father himself should give the maiden away, or the brother,
or even the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, a kinsman, or a relative, as Manu has ordained.
If the state of motherhood exists in all [women] by virtue of their natural condition (*prakṛti*),
then members of one's own caste should give their daughters to those who do not abide in that natural condition.
The Brāhma, the Daiva, the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, and the Suragāndharva; as well as the Rākṣasa, the Paiśāca, and the Rākṣasa.
May the Lord who assumes the universal form be pleased with this cow, who has become the means for performing sacrifice and who today brings about the destruction of the universe.
All crops have flourished on the earth raised up by the Boar;
therefore, O giver of infinite fruit, grant me peace.
O Śrīvatsa, this maidservant is bestowed by me upon you; she is always fit for labor. May you seek what is desired; may it be well with you.
O Keśava, by the gift of this pillow, may you grant me a bed that is never empty, as well as constant fortune, prosperity, exaltation, and good luck for my lineage.
I offer this golden ring, produced from the *hiraṇyagarbha*, which bestows all things; may it please the Lord of Kamalā.
"The two earrings previously extracted during the churning of the Ocean of Milk, which arose together with Śrī—may Śrī be pleased; I give them."
"O Brahmin, accept this house, complete with all its furnishings; through your grace, may the fruit of my desire indeed be mine."
May that auspicious Mahiṣī, the supreme queen of the world-protectors beginning with Indra and the mother of the demon Mahiṣāsura, grant all my desires.
May the sin produced from slandering others, malicious speech, and the eating of forbidden food be destroyed by this gift of a copper vessel.
Whatever sins have been committed by me alone, arising from desire— may they always perish through the gift of a bronze vessel.
The lineage, the progenitor of the lineage, the most excellent, the lineage, and that which arises from the lineage— may these two,
being pleased by this gift of the lineage, grant me prosperity.
This meritorious bamboo vessel, produced from a bamboo-born species, is the most excellent gift among all bamboo objects; therefore, grant me peace.
All these bamboo vessels have indeed been prepared by me;
they are given for the sake of Umā’s rite to increase my lineage.
This gift, which increases one's lineage and is endowed with good fortune and other virtues,
is covered with cloth and accompanied by betel nuts and gold.
It causes the destruction of all sins, is filled with various substances, and is the supreme among all gifts; therefore, grant me peace.
This girl, though only seven years old, has been nurtured by me like a son;
she is now given by me out of affection to your son—may she be a source of fulfillment for you both.
During constant drinking, when a house is old, at the seven occasions following the consumption [of food],
at the auspicious entry of a bride, and during the rising of Jupiter and Venus.
During a Vyatīpāta yoga, at a solar or lunar transit, during an eclipse, and also during a Vaidhṛti yoga,
no auspicious rite whatsoever shall be undertaken by a human being, even when the time has arrived, if it is performed without a Śrāddha.

One should not perform [the rite] even when the proper time has arrived during an intercalary month (amāsaṃkrānti), on the day of Viṣṇu (the eleventh lunar day), or at other such times; nor should one do so during a gift-giving ceremony, a wedding, a sacrifice, in battle, or during a national upheaval.
Even when one falls into extreme distress, immediate purification is ordained; likewise during marriages, festivals, and sacrifices, even if an impurity due to birth or death occurs in the interval.
No fault is proclaimed regarding objects previously intended for marriage, festivals, or sacrifices, nor during the period of impurity following a death or birth.
O best of the twice-born, others should provide the jewel and one should speak [of it] during vows,
sacrifices, marriages, ancestral rites (śrāddha), fire offerings (homa), worship, and recitation (japa).
If the rite has already commenced, it may proceed despite the impurity of birth (sūtaka); however, if it has not commenced, one must wait until the impurity ceases.
In this context, "commencement" means the formal invitation (varaṇa) in a sacrifice, and the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) in a vow or a sacrificial session (sattra).
In the case of a dispute regarding the *nāndīmukha* rite or during a *śrāddha* meal preparation,
one should offer clarified butter with *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras for the sake of attaining purity that has not yet been obtained.
One who has undergone birth-impurity (sūtaka) shall be purified by giving a cow and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
this ancient rite was created by me to bring me pleasure.
Created by Brahmā from the sun, may you protect us!
Homage to you, O auspicious goddess; homage to you, daughter of the Sun!
Save me out of compassion, O Goddess; you have come here as my wife.
You were created by Brahmā as the Arka plant for the welfare of all living beings.
You are the primordial source of trees and the increaser of the gods' joy;
as the third [fire], you swiftly destroy the sin born of the marriage rite and death itself.
By those who have fallen away with their nails, hair, or insects dwelling within,
and by those who defile with fat, blood, semen, marrow, bone, urine, feces, or phlegm;
Sacrificial offerings (havir) defiled by phlegm and other such loathsome substances, as well as all those that have been broken, are considered spoiled; one should cast them into water.
If the *sruk* breaks, one should take it up with the index finger and offer the oblation;
likewise, broken wooden implements with their handles pointing eastward should be cast into the fire.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the Dakṣiṇāmnāya section of the Nirvāṇa-pada within the venerable Vārāhī-tantra.
Bhairava said:
Endowed with the art of knowing the time, it was spoken by the Lord Saṃbhūta:
"By which, within six months, the Rohiṇī of death is known beforehand."
Time brings beings into existence; Time destroys all creatures.
Time remains awake even while others sleep; indeed, Time moves through the succession of misfortunes.
In due time the gods perish, and in due time the asuras and serpents;
the lords of men perish at all times, as do all living beings.
In the middle of the day, fourteen Indras fall;
at the end of seven years, even he perishes in that time.
It was previously declared by the Divine that even a human being who has lived for seventy years will perish in a short time through the power of unwholesome actions.
Rain, cold, and heat—
these are described as Time by means of Time, appearing in his forms during the dawn, midday, and the afternoon.
Trees bear fruit in due season; a seed is sown in due season;
a woman becomes flowering in due season; yet she gives birth at all times.
Through attachment to anger and greed, time carves away the lives of living beings;
however, for one engaged in knowledge through constant practice, it acts as the destroyer of the opposite.
Once he is born within the belly of the Fire of Time (Kālāgni), a desire arises in him for four things:
food, water, sleep, and sexual intercourse as the fourth.

From a deficiency of food, the bodily elements (dhātus) are diminished; from a deficiency of water, the blood; and from a deficiency of desire, the body is consumed. Sleep, moreover, is a cause of disease.
A dish lacking salt destroys the eyes and ears;
ghee lacking milk destroys the [digestive] fire; and meat lacking fat causes the destruction of the flesh.
Food that lacks alcohol causes the loss of virility, and likewise food that lacks fish;
even if prepared with the six flavors, such food gives rise to a great disease.

For those deficient in digestive fire, even medicinal herbs act like the heat of the stomach; if clarified butter is not properly processed, it becomes unwholesome and gives rise to all manner of diseases.
Dry meat, dried fish, and the tasteless consumption of fruits and roots,
as well as being deprived of the two-fold enjoyment of betel-leaf, gives rise to diseases of the mouth.
One becomes deprived of a marriage-thread and deprived of clothing, and suffers from trembling and disease;
by rejecting water and nectar, phlegm and asthma arise.
O Goddess, a seat made of stone or clay bestows the fruit of white heat;
likewise, an uneven seat that is excessively high or low, as well as sleeping during the day and walking about at night [are obstacles].
Retention of urine and feces, as well as diseases arising from six causes—
excessive sin, excessive anger, and constant defilement by falsehood and the like— [occur].
One who betrays the gods or betrays one's master is born with the disease of leprosy.
A man who approaches those who should not be approached, eats what should not be eaten,
and hates his guru, the gods, or Brahman, is born with epilepsy.
O physician, how can he who does not know the six chakras, the sixteen supports, the three voids, the five spaces, and the winds born of the self within his own body, be called a doctor?
There is one pillar, nine gates, three voids, and five deities;
within the families of the five senses, I, whose nature is inert, have my attachment there.
The differentiated (sakala) is devoid of time, while the undifferentiated (niṣkala) is conjoined with time;
through the modifications of the senses, death and life are produced.
If the physician, the listener, and likewise the speaker are all endowed with gentle gazes, and if the patient's temples are warm, he is curable; of this there is no doubt.
If the hands and feet become warm and a slight burning sensation is felt, it is known as a mild case;
if the tongue becomes soft, that patient does not perish.
If a fever arises in a person devoid of perspiration, yet nasal discharge and respiration proceed normally,
and the throat is also free of phlegm, that patient certainly lives.
If today his sleep is at ease, his body is active,
and his senses are serene, that sick person does not perish.
He whose entire consciousness clearly perceives the fragrance and taste [of the food] shall live with his throat filled with phlegm; of this there is no doubt.
There is no modification by the senses; everything is declared to be consciousness.
Having tasted food and drunk water, he lives—of this there is no doubt.
If there is no disease of the stomach, yet one suffers from urinary disorders,
and all the sense organs are afflicted with pain, that person will live; of this there is no doubt.
One who experiences pain in the head, pain in the eyes, as well as in the ears and tongue, pain in the teeth, or pain in the throat, shall live; of this there is no doubt.
There is suffering in the arms, suffering in the heart, and indeed suffering in the three joints;
there is suffering in the knees and in the feet—he shall live, of this there is no doubt.
If there is no pain at the joints, nor wandering of the breath, nor its cessation, and if no blood flows from the wound, he will live; of this there is no doubt.
If there is pain at the penis, suffering [will come]; if at the heart or the throat, there is suffering;
if it is at the root of the ear, there is no suffering—he will live, of this there is no doubt.
Having seen flames in the eyes and smoke from the head in one's own body-reflection, and having heard sounds in the ears and seen them with the eyes, one will live; of this there is no doubt.
One who experiences no pain in the tongue, teeth, hands, or feet, and whose desires come to him spontaneously and clearly, shall live; of this there is no doubt.
If there is a melodious voice, auspicious news, or idle chatter, yet no one speaks of unprecedented news, that person will live; of this there is no doubt.
One who practices security, truth, self-control, and generosity, who restrains the five senses,
and who abandons the wives of others, shall live— of this there is no doubt.
One who has no desire for another's field or another's wealth, and who does not engage in the censure of others—that person shall live; of this there is no doubt.
One who perceives one's own self and the supreme self as equal, and views one's own body and the bodies of others with equanimity, shall live in this world without doubt.
One who is always devoted to the path to heaven, which has charity as its head and austerity as its crest, and who constantly honors cows and Brahmins, shall live long; of this there is no doubt.
Wind gives rise to bile; bile arises when there is an excess of phlegm;
and when phlegm reaches the throat, life is difficult to sustain.
He who experiences burning at night and coldness by day,
having his throat filled with phlegm, will meet his death.

One with a weak voice, a hoarse voice, a faltering voice, or one afflicted by cough and asthma, accompanied by hiccup and dyspnea, lives for a long time only through the disease of consumption (kṣaya).
If the heart, the navel, the nose, and the hands and feet become cold while there is heat in the head, death will occur for that person.
He whose *huṃ* sound is cool, yet whose *phuṭ* sound is like fire,
and for whom there is a great burning— death shall come to him.
With trembling limbs, faltering gait, discoloration of the skin, and distorted speech, he no longer perceives fragrance or taste; such a person goes to the realm of Yama.
If three fingers emerge from between his rows of teeth,
he will certainly be born in the house of a king within seven nights.
If head-sudation occurs for this person, one should cause the wind to move in the mouth;
even he who has not survived for eight nāḍīs shall live through time.
Those whose lifespan has diminished do not see Arundhatī, Dhruva, the three footsteps of the Maitrāvaruṇa, nor the circle of the Mothers in the fourth month.
Aruṇvatī becomes the tongue; Dhruva is released from the nose.
O Viṣṇu, beyond Dhruva is Tārikā in the middle, merely a circle.
If one's tongue becomes black and the face is indeed smeared with saffron,
death will come to that person born under the asterism of Udrasala.
If sparks resembling fire appear on the root or branches of a tree,
a human being will certainly die within six months.
By pressing the Kuṇḍalinī with the vital air (vāyu), the food is bound within the fiery energy (tejas).
He whose heart is set upon food does not perish during the year,
even when the falling of raindrops upon the earth becomes a torrential flood.
Death occurs within seven days, as declared by the knowledge of the time of death;
a woman [is characterized by] being joined with heedlessness, and from heedlessness comes the utterance of anger.
Within six months, O Jīva, he shall go to the abode of Yama—
unattached, pale in complexion, and afflicted by many labored breaths.
If water flows continuously for one month, he lives for a hundred thousand years;
by that pure water from the sun’s orb, he attains a hundred thousand marks of excellence.
In the south, west, north, and east, [the smoke] lasts for six, three, two, and one month respectively;
in the center, when it has entered the hollow, it remains as smoke for ten days.
In the Kula system, that day is declared by Sarvajña to be the fixed measure of the lifespan in the mind of the Jina.
Likewise, [the yogas] are described as Utkalā, Lambā, Mandā, Aśubhāntarā, Sthirā, Sūkṣmā, Mṛdhu, and Raudrī.

One should know the characteristics of the channels (nāḍī) as being fierce, such as Syāmā, Anirāmā, and others; the wise man should contemplate these three types and perform the rite of the thread (sūtakarma).
By the addition of lead and copper, and with equal parts of tin, the form of Rāma is to be known; it is filled with phlegm (kapha).
Food that is digested slowly due to the combination of kapha and vāta causes excessive acidity,
particularly by flooding the blood.
In the beginning bile flows, and likewise phlegm in the middle;
at the end, it is declared by physicians that wind and phlegm prevail here.
The wind-channel (vātanāḍī), being bold and flowing in conjunction with bile (pitta),
causes the wind to break up the phlegm (kapha); this is called vātapitta.
The bile channel is foul-smelling and flows with phlegm;
it carries feces mixed with phlegm—this should be known by wise people.
When [the disease] resides with a slight excess of wind and phlegm, it destroys both pitta and kapha;
one should recognize this as arising from pitta and kapha, and one should administer its appropriate medicinal treatment.
When the wind (vāyu) and phlegm (kapha) move within the afflicted person and are joined in the throat,
and the bile (pitta) has vanished, that state is called sannipāta.
If one constantly touches a scorpion, Skanda will always manifest [the disease];
this is declared to be incurable, yet one should not avoid a woman who is far away.
When wind, bile, and phlegm have all become equally dependent upon one another, one should recognize that as the sign of death; such is the characteristic of the pulse.
If the asterism named Ravi or Indu is established in Mṛgaśiras at the beginning, at the end, or in the middle, it shall become a single nāḍī of odd dā.
For at that time death arises, as it is declared everywhere;
at that time, those very symptoms which appear as poison are indeed the medicine for the wise.
In the first stage of fever, fasting should be observed for two days;
neither water nor medicine should be given to the patients, as it has been taught.
Neither exposure to wind nor shelter from it is beneficial, nor is fasting;
for a person afflicted by fever, the maintenance of bodily equilibrium is what must be practiced.
In the months of Pauṣa, Māgha, Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa,
and Bhādrapada, the king is proclaimed to be Citrasena.
In the months of Āśvina, Kārttika, Vaiśākha, and Jyeṣṭha,
the king is certainly proclaimed to be born from the digestive fire (pitta) through the investigation of all the scriptures.
In the months of Phālguna and Caitra, there is the greatest affliction for living beings;
cold winds arise, and the king of phlegm (śleṣmarāja) is known to be very strong.
A man of windy temperament (vātaprakṛtika) in a dream has thin thighs and chest, disheveled hair, and an unsteady mind; he stands on tiptoe, speaks with his arms raised, and moves through the sky.
One who has premature graying hair, is fair-complexioned, perspires easily when angry, and sees things like lamps in dreams—what kind of man is this? He is one of Pitta constitution.
One who is very dark-complexioned, has phlegmatic secretions, is yellowish, possesses a steady mind and patience,
dreams of water, and is fond of society— such a man is of the phlegmatic (ślaiṣmika) constitution.
One should indicate that fire is at the navel, the imperishable is abiding in the heart,
the breaking of the voice is in the throat, and [disturbance] in the channels is in the head.
O auspicious lady, when wind prevails, it produces the symptoms of wind; when bile prevails, it produces the effects of bile;
and when phlegm prevails, it produces the symptoms of phlegm; thus, when applied, it causes disease in men.

A *phūṣṇī* lives amidst ten thousand [ordinary] beings, and a *bhalodarī* lives amidst a thousand; a *mehī* lives amidst ten thousand *sahasra*’s, but a *rājamaṇḍī* does not live even among ten thousand.
The wind element (vātadhātu) arises as one-third of the *prarūḍha*;
one should likewise designate the self-expanding (*tanotmāna*) as bile (*pitta*) and phlegm (*kapha*).
Food that is wind-increasing, consumed by one who is victorious [in battle], or eaten by those who are ill due to their lifestyle, becomes indigestible;
such food is considered to cause the increase of disease.
When pitta is flowing in the stomach, whatever food is eaten with a relish,
even if taken in small morsels, will not cause sleep.
Furthermore, that physician who prescribes unwholesome food to a patient suffering from phlegm (kapha) becomes a bringer of danger to his life in that very state.
Whether suffering from fever or free from it, one who has a bilious temperament should eat light food;
whatever qualities are proclaimed for fasting, those same qualities are found in eating light food.
Water is medicine with food; water is the destroyer of strength when food is digested;
it is nectar at the midpoint of a meal, but it is poison after a meal.
If one drinks water at the beginning of a meal, it acts as fire; if in the middle, it is a rejuvenative elixir;
and if one drinks water at the end of a meal, that water becomes twice as effective.
There is no medicine for the power of action that brings success;
therefore, at the end of the night, one should drink water for the destruction of all diseases.
One may drink thousands of jars [of water] as long as the sun has not set;
once the Lord of Day has gone to his setting, even a single drop becomes like a jar.
A foul odor, a bad taste, vomiting, and pain in the abdomen—
these are the symptoms that arise in fever caused by undigested food (viṣṭabdha-ajīrṇa).
Excessive thirst, incoherent speech, intoxication, vertigo, and headache—
these are the symptoms that arise when one has consumed impure water.
Drowsiness, yawning, cracking sounds, breaking pains, and likewise a craving for food— these are the symptoms by which it is called *sveda-jvara* (fever with perspiration).
Headache, vertigo, fainting, delirium, blood in the urine,
and a burning sensation in the eyes, nose, and mouth are the symptoms of Pittaja fever.
Yawning, distension of the abdomen, flatulence, attachment to fluids, and vomiting—
these are the symptoms by which that fever is known as Dṛṣṭijvara.
In fever arising from Vāta, there is whiteness, horripilation, goosebumps, headache,
a parched throat, and a dry cough.
Fever that causes heat in the limbs and coldness in the head, hands, and feet—
these are the symptoms by which it is called *kāla-jvara*.
Breaking pain in the limbs, labored breathing, discoloration of the body, and redness of the eyes.
He who possesses these symptoms is said to have *kāra-jvara*.
[The symptoms are: sleepiness, perspiration, loss of appetite, vomiting, nausea, and frothing at the mouth.
A desire for warmth occurs in cases of *kāśa* (cough), dyspnea, phlegm, and fever;
these various afflictions caused by fever arise at intervals of one, two, or three days.
In that regard, one should recognize *popiha* by its own specific characteristics:
it is characterized by irregular onset and occurs during long nights of fever.
One should avoid treating a fever characterized by intense force like that of *gaṃbhārī* if the patient does not open their eyes and the body appears afflicted by disease.

Lassitude and loss of appetite indeed arise from the consumption of heavy food during fever; likewise, it is forbidden for pregnant women, children, the elderly, those with sexual desire, and those suffering from a recent fever.
"One should never perform fasting (laṅghana)," so say those former teachers;
for one who indulges in Nirghāta, sweating, fasting, and hot water [these are forbidden].

When the fever caused by the consumption of living beings (pāṇādāmajvara) has been cast out, how is it subsequently treated? Lethargy, wind, thirst, burning sensation, and pain in the joints are its complications.
When there is excessive urination accompanied by exhaustion, fever occurs;
its symptoms are excessive intensity of the fever, thirst, delirium, sweating, and dizziness.
Excessive perspiration and inflammation of the mouth are signs of one who has been freed from fever;
so too are a lightness in the body, the channels, and the bowels.
Discrimination, inflammation of the mouth, and fever—these are the symptoms of one released from fever;
likewise, the *saṃdhiga*, *āndrika*, and *sādhya* types, as well as *vittavibhrama*.
Kaṇṭhakubja, Karṇika, and likewise Jihvaka are difficult to cure;
Rugdāha is known to be even more difficult than the others, and it may or may not kill.
Antaka has broken eyes, spits blood, and utters incoherent ravings.
Śītāṅga—thus is the assignment (of the names); these six incurable and fatal conditions, along with the thirteen types of *sannipāta*, must be known in every way by physicians.
Accompanied by phlegm, there is first pain, coughing, and distress;
moreover, dryness is a symptom when the *sannipātika* [fever] is located in the joints.
Overcome by excessive sleep, fever, and labored breathing, she is tormented by a burning heat;
her throat has become thickened, she is dark-complexioned, and there is a throbbing pain in her throat and tongue.
In sannipātaka caused by a slight excess of kapha and citta,
there is fainting, delusion, vertigo, fever, and a burning sensation, as well as singing and incoherent speech.
Death is conceptualized suffering; it is the gaze of the side of agitation.
By these characteristics, this "sannipāta" (convergence) is to be known as a delusion of the mind.
Seizing by the throat, fever, fainting, burning sensation, trembling, distress,
delusion, heat, pain in the head, affliction from news, weeping, and sleepiness.
One should declare the combination of symptoms involving the throat and the hump (kaṇṭhakubja-sannipāta) as difficult to cure,
characterized by fever, swelling extending to the ears, labored breathing, and delirious speech.
Perspiration, constriction of the throat, fever, nausea, or even pain in the stomach—
these indeed are the symptoms that occur when the *karṇikā* is afflicted by *sannipāta*.
His tongue is constricted and stiff; he is overwhelmed by coughing and labored breathing;
he possesses the characteristics of being like one mute and deaf, suffering from the ripening of afflictions, and devoid of strength.
This is the *jihvaka* type of *sannipāta*, which is difficult to cure and causes loss of strength;
it is characterized by delusion, fever, delirium, pain in the throat, vertigo, and exhaustion.

By these symptoms— thirst, stupor, and labored breathing— one should know that this most difficult-to-cure fever arising from the derangement of all three humors (*sannipāta*), characterized by pain and burning, is curable.
One should destroy a *sannipāta* fever arising from the three *doṣas*, whether curable or incurable,
by [administering] burning sensations, delusion, trembling of the head, hiccups, cough, and shaking of the limbs.
Fever characterized by intense burning and internal heat should be known as *sannipāta*;
it is severe, accompanied by labored breathing, sunken eyes, vacant memory, and excessive fever.
Delusion, incoherent speech, trembling, vertigo, and sleepiness— by these symptoms,
one should recognize this as "Broken Eyes" (bhagnanetra), a type of *sannipāta* that causes destruction.
Spitting of blood, fainting, fever, delusion, thirst, giddiness, vomiting, hiccup, diarrhea, loss of consciousness,
pain, and dyspnea [occur].
When the body exhibits these symptoms— such as being dark greenish-blue or reddish—
one should recognize this as *sannipāta*, which destroys the patient who spits blood.
One who suffers from mental distress due to excessive talkativeness, who is tormented by the loss of wisdom,
who has pain in the feet and the limbs, and who is impaired in his ability to walk.
The *sannipāta* known as *nikṛntaka*, characterized by incoherent speech, should be recognized by these signs:
the body feels cold as snow, there is vomiting, diarrhea, and trembling.
For a moment there is a sound, then this hiccup occurs; accompanied by labored breathing, exhaustion, and cold limbs, it strikes all the limbs with looseness—this is the fatal *sannipāta* [fever].
The mouth is coated with the three doṣas, sleep is disturbed or lost,
consciousness is absent, breathing is shallow, the digestive fire is weak, and there is a loss of strength.
For a false attribution [of symptoms] is equal to death when one carefully observes the *sannipāta*;
all the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) waste away, and consequently, the person withers.
Loss of appetite, aversion to food, fever, dyspnea, cough, appearance of blood,
and hoarseness of voice— these six arise as the symptoms of pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman) when it is situated in the sixth house.
There is a burning sensation in the shoulders and sides, along with labored breathing and heat in the hands and feet.

Loss of vitality and weakness are the symptoms of royal disease (rājaroga). For one who is strong, has many morbid humors (doṣas), and has undergone oleation and sudation, purification therapy (śodhana) is indicated.

In a patient with consumption (yakṣman), when [the doshas] have been depleted, one should not perform purification (śuddhi) if it causes upward or downward movement; rather, one should avoid inducing it.
Excessive laziness, much sleep, slight burning sensation, vomiting, and dizziness [are signs of this state].
Vomiting arises from blood and pus; it is diminished when caused by pitta and kapha.
It is provoked by injury from smoke, silver [dust], sexual intercourse, physical exertion, and the consumption of dry substances.
Due to the improper digestion of food, the force of suppressed hunger,
and the upward movement of the *udāna* breath, coughing arises in men.

The five types of kāsa (cough) are known to arise from vāta, pitta, śleṣman, chest injury (kṣata), and wasting (kṣaya). Their premonitory symptom is a sensation of the throat and mouth being filled with semen.
There will be a swelling in the throat, and after eating, a sense of constriction arises;
there is wind in the heart, pain in the temples, and also in the head, the sides, and the stomach.
In *kṣāmakāsa*, the cough is emaciated, pale, and accompanied by a broken voice;
one should first treat this cough arising solely from vāta with unctuous substances (*sneha*).
When the wind, preceded by phlegm, obstructs the channels, it should be treated with wind-alleviating, unctuous, and proven preparations such as gruels, vegetable soups, and meat broths.
Then, becoming enraged, he pursues everyone and becomes one who utters harsh words;
his knowledge and discernment are lost, and his eyes are wandering.
The breath flows upward and long, yet it does not descend;
with the openings of the mouth and nostrils obstructed by phlegm, one gazes upward with a fixed stare.
"One suffering from constipation becomes intensely distressed and miserable.
Thus [it is said] in the *Śrīvārāhītantra*, in the section on Nirvāṇa within the Dakṣiṇāmnāya.
The thirty-third chapter, titled "The Determination of the Characteristics of Time, Knowledge, Life, and Death. || 33 ||
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the portents and earthquakes:
Kṛttikā, Viśākhā, and likewise Pūrvabhādrapada.
If, during the asterisms of Maghā, Ārdrā, Bharaṇī, Pūrvaphalgunī, or Revatī,
a wind should blow or a halo should appear around the moon or the sun;
If there is an earthquake, a thunderclap, or the falling of meteors,
or if there is an eclipse of the moon or sun, or even the appearance of a comet;
There was a rain of blood, excrement, and dust, as well as the falling of stones; likewise, there was the falling of stars and other great wonders.
One should recognize the *āgneya* temperament; I shall describe its characteristics:
it is characterized by eye diseases, diarrhea, and a predominance of fire and wind.
Cows yield little milk, and trees bear few flowers and fruits; when these signs appear, one should predict that the rain-bearing regions will perish due to scanty rainfall.
The people of Kapāla and Duṣṭadṛśya are seen to be greatly afflicted,
as are those of Saindhava, Yamunā, Kānyakubja, and Āthavāhnika.
Jālandhara, Nepāla, Kāśmīra, and the Northern Path; Kāva, Jāvāli, and likewise Nāgapura as well.
These regions will perish as the fruit of the fiery mandala:
Jyeṣṭhā, Rohiṇī, Anurādhā, and likewise Śravaṇa.
Dhaneṣṭhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and likewise Abhijit as the seventh—
if anything should move [within these] or if any alteration should occur;
