One should know that to be the Māhendra [type]; I shall describe its characteristics.
All the subjects will be delighted and free from disease;
they will celebrate marriages, there will be an abundance of grain, and the king shall be prosperous.
Samudra and Āmāgadha, as well as Madhyadeśa;
the entirety of Kurukṣetra and likewise Pāṇipatha.
These regions will perish when such portents are observed;
specifically, Aśleṣā, Mūla, and likewise Pūrvāṣāḍhā.
If Revatī, the asterism of Varuṇa, the Raudra (Ārdrā), or the two Uttarā-proṣṭhapadas should move even slightly at this time, or if it should become an improper hour;
One should know that to be of Varuṇa; I shall describe its characteristics:
there are many trees bearing flowers and fruits, and cows are held in abundance.
There, many groves and crops will grow upon the earth,
as well as insects, mice, locusts, and monkeys.
Fish, reptiles, and likewise *pippalīkas* appear;
there shall be rain on dry land, and the force of the waters will be terrifying.
Grains will be inexpensive, there will be an abundance of food, and the king shall be prosperous;
the earth will have excessive water, yet living beings will have no fear anywhere.
Nāgarā, Ākīra, Saurāṣṭra, as well as Siṣu and Sāgara; Auḍumbara, Chatra, and likewise Nāgapura.
These regions will perish when these portents are observed:
Hasta, Citrā, Svātī, Mṛgaśiras, and Punarvasu.
And likewise Uttaraphalgunī, as well as Aśvinī and Revatī.
If anything moves here or if it becomes untimely, one should recognize that as pertaining to Vāyu; I shall describe its characteristics.
Then, when great fear and even a supreme terror have arisen,
such that the clouds rumble but do not release their water.
Mountains, mountain peaks, archways,
and even celestial vehicles were blown away by the wind and fell to the surface of the earth.
The gods, the brahmins, as well as the king, the trees, and all that is insentient—when dharma has perished, everything becomes a scene of lamentation, crying "Alas! Alas! (hāhābhūta).
The Pañcālas, Āsuras, and Senas, along with the Ujjayinī Mlecchas,
the Varcasas, the Uddharas, Magadhas, Andhakas, and Draviḍas as well.
All the Karṇāṭakas as well as others who dwell in the Vindhya mountains—
these countries will perish when such a portentous omen appears.
I shall proclaim the chapter on dreams as it has been taught everywhere, for the sake of providing knowledge to men who do not understand the true nature of dreams.
A dream in the first watch of the night yields fruit within a year;
in the second, within eight months; and one occurring in the third watch, within three months.
It is seen on the fourth day of the fortnight; of this there is no doubt.
At the time of dawn, one shall obtain the fruit immediately in a dream.
Therefore, after such an auspicious dream, no obstacle remains;
having performed auspicious rites at dawn, one should thereafter proceed with the auspicious departure.
Henceforth, I shall explain those [states] arising from merit and demerit:
namely, mounting upon cows, bulls, elephants, palaces, mountain peaks, and trees.
Having boarded a boat, taken up a lute, and having wept and cried out, there is the certain attainment of one's goal.
In dreams, having a body full of worms, wounds on the limbs, ornaments,
smearing with excrement, much sneezing, approaching a woman who should not be approached, and traveling to a fortunate place— these are auspicious.
But he who sees at the end of a dream a king, a herd of elephants, a horse,
gold, silver, a cow, or his own family— his household shall prosper.
He who alone ascends a tree that bears both milk and fruit—
even if born into a family of slaves— he too shall become a king.
He who sees at the end of a dream a lamp, food, ripe fruit, a maiden, an umbrella, a chariot, or a banner— for him, prosperity faces every direction.
And listen now to the qualities of him who, in a dream, should eat the green and ripe fruits of human beings.
If one eats [the insect] on the foot, the gain is five hundred; if on the arm, a thousand;
and by eating it on the head, one obtains a kingdom or a hundred thousand.

He who is pierced by entrails [in a dream] regarding either a village or a city shall become a lord of the circle (maṇḍalabhogī) if it concerns a village, or a sovereign (pārthiva) if it concerns a city.
One who dreams of obtaining an umbrella and sandals should be told that he will attain mastery;
one should also point out to him a stainless, sharp sword that makes a ringing sound.
Furthermore, for one who boards a boat and crosses over it when it is broken or lost,
one should predict exile, followed by a swift return.
One who dreams of a *valīkī*, a hen, or a crane attains success;
he obtains a beloved wife and wealth that speaks kindly.
Having seen the image, which was especially and constantly worshipped.
In legal proceedings, he shall achieve victory and obtain abundant wealth,
provided that he beholds the solar disc or the moon in his dream.
A sick person is indeed freed from diseases, and one who is healthy shall attain prosperity;
whoever is bitten by this serpent on the right arm [shall have these results].
On the tenth day, he shall obtain complete wealth;
yet, bound by various fetters, he cries out again and again.
A son is born to him, and one should predict his establishment;
or he drinks blood or even liquor in a dream in some way.
A Brahmin obtains knowledge, while another likewise obtains wealth;
thus, drinking milk in a dream yields the fruit as described.
For him, there shall be the drinking of Soma; one should point to this as the unprecedented cause.
But he who, having arrived there, should eat curd and milk-rice in the middle [of the rite].
If a snake, a scorpion, or even a leech is seen in a broad lotus-leaf vessel, this person is undoubtedly a king.
Seeing curd, there shall be victory, the acquisition of wealth, and the birth of a son;
and through wheat, there will be the arrival of riches.
Through barley, one should know that sacrifices will come; through white mustard seeds, the attainment of knowledge;
when [the plant] has borne fruit, one should know there is fruit; and when it has flowered, one shall obtain prosperity.
One who controls the smoke, controls the flame, and controls the wind shall attain prosperity—
whether regarding one's seat, bed, vehicle, body, carriage, or house.
When it blazes up, his glorious fortune becomes all-pervading;
likewise, the deities, the foremost of the twice-born, the ancestors, and those who bear sectarian marks [become favorable].
Whatever one says at the moment of death in a dream, that shall come to pass exactly so.
The glory that faces in all directions belongs to him whom a woman of excellent complexion, wearing yellow garments and anointed with yellow fragrances, embraces in a dream.
If a woman dressed in white garments, adorned with white perfumes and unguents,
embraces one in a dream, one should declare that Lakṣmī belongs to him.
All things are most auspicious except for cotton, ashes, bones, and skulls; all things are inauspicious except for cows, elephants, gods, brahmins, and horses.
O twice-born one, [he dreams of] climbing mountains, palaces, elephants, bulls,
trees with white flowers, and likewise elephants.
The fire emerged from his navel, towering over the grass and trees;
likewise, he possessed many heads and the appearance of grey hair.
The embracing of Śakra’s banner, as well as the act of raising it;
the falling of Śakra to the ground, and the act of slaying the enemies.
O twice-born one, there shall be victory in disputes, in gambling, and likewise in battle;
and there shall be the eating of mango meat, fish, and milk-rice.
The sight of blood, bathing in blood, or even drinking blood; likewise, the drinking of wine, the juice of the Aruṇi plant, or even milk.
Wrapping with the intestines on the ground, as well as in the sky;
milking with the mouth, and likewise the falling [of milk] from buffaloes and cows.
Likewise, [the gift] of lionesses, female elephants, and strong [animals],
as well as a palace to Brahmins and teachers, is auspicious.
Anointing with water, as well as with the water from the horns of cows,
and with the water of the moon-encircled king (the lunar disc), is known to be highly conducive to bestowing sovereignty.
Likewise, there may be a royal consecration, or even the covering of one's head;
the acquisition of the fire of death, and the burning of houses and other dwellings by fire.
There is the attainment of royal insignia, the playing of musical instruments such as the lute and the like,
as well as the crossing of waters and the leaping over difficult terrain.
The presence of female elephants, cows, and women with offspring in the house,
as well as mounting a horse or chariot and the sound of weeping, are all bestowers of auspiciousness.
The gain of a son from another's wife,
as well as the piercing of the genitals, O blessed one, and likewise being bound with fetters and smeared with excrement.
The lives of the protectors of the earth, the sight of friends,
the sight of divine images, as well as celestial chariots and the waters;

For when a man sees these auspicious dreams, he obtains the attainment of divine wealth; for one who knows the Dharma, his life shall last until death, and likewise, there shall be liberation from disease as well as boons.
One should predict that a woman wearing red garments, adorned with red perfumes and unguents, who embraces a man,
will always bring him disease.
If a woman wearing black garments, anointed with black perfumes and ointments,
embraces one in a dream, one should predict his death.
If one's teeth fall out or appear to fall out during a dream,
there will be loss of wealth or suffering for that person’s body.
O beautiful lady, if horned animals, fanged beasts, or even monkeys attack one in a dream, there will be danger from the royal family for that person.
If, however, one is excessively smeared with oil, ghee, milk, or even fat,
or likewise with any other [substance], one should diagnose him as having a disease.
Where dancers are seen, singing, laughing,
and even celebrating a festival, one should predict death in that place.
If a man mounts a vehicle drawn by a donkey, a camel, or a buffalo,
he will quickly meet his death, overwhelmed by oil.
Where the deities dance, sing, and laugh,
and where they clap their hands and run about, that place perishes.
The navel does not arise from elsewhere on the limbs; likewise, the growth of grass and trees occurs [only] on the head, while for those of base conduct there is shorn hair and brokenness.
Wearing dirty garments, having limbs smeared with mud,
jumping from high places, and likewise climbing onto swings.
The killing of horses not yet employed by people,
the sight of trees with red flowers, and the sight of a Caṇḍāla.
Likewise, there is the act of mounting boars, bears, donkeys, and camels,
as well as the eating of the flesh of birds, oil, and *kṛsara*.
Laughing and joking with women, marriage, singing,
and the playing of musical instruments devoid of stringed accompaniment;
One may go to a flowing stream for bathing, using cow-dung water,
or likewise water from the foot-print of the Buddha, or even water from the earth.
The entry into the mother's womb, the climbing of a palm tree,
the falling of Indra’s banner, and the falling of the moon and the sun.
One should avoid gambling, the observation of portents occurring in the atmosphere or on earth, and other such dreams as these.
There is no blessing more supreme than this, nor likewise a better auspicious dream;
one should perform ritual bathing, an oblation with sesame seeds, and the protection of the Brahmins.
Mindfulness, Vāsudeva, as well as his worship,
and the hearing of the liberation of Gajendra— this should be known as the destroyer of evil dreams.
One should offer oblations of red sandalwood wood smeared with clarified butter;
by reciting the Gāyatrī mantra eight thousand times, one destroys bad dreams.
A dream experienced while afflicted by anxiety, grief, or disease,
or with a mind intoxicated by passion, does not bear fruit.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of Earthquakes and Dreams," in the *Nirvāṇapada* of the *Dakṣiṇāmnāya* within the *Śrīvārāhītantra*.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme installation of the Yoginīs,
by means of which one whose body has been thus installed becomes Bhairava himself within six months.
One should meditate upon that mantra, fully bestowed within the seven-petaled heart-lotus,
as one's own body arising from two hundred thousand suns.
Remaining in a state of oneness, one should meditate upon the goddess who is equal to ten million suns;
one should visualize Śrīnātha upon the crown of the head, and the *pādukā* and the *bali* offering to one's left.
One should duly install Gaṇapati on the right, Kṣetrapāla in the region behind,
and Kātyāyanī in front, each with their respective mantras.
One should first place the Mātṛkā for the pacification of the goddess's anger;
[the mantra is formed] with the pure vowels, including the bindu and visarga, and with the bindu and visarga at the end.
Having first performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the sages and other elements,
one who has conquered envy should meditate upon the form consisting of Śiva and Śakti, and then perform this supreme rite with focused intent.
p.

221a) One should not perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) starting from Śrīkaṇṭha for one's own accomplishment, [but rather] that which is joined with Power (śakti), which protects all beings from the nether world (nī). [The ailments: pain in the eye, pain in the ear, pain in the forehead, and pain in the foot.

It cures pain in the womb, pain in the genitals, pain in the anus, and all types of pain such as that in the joints; it is a destroyer of boils and a separator of the [disturbed] humors (*doṣas*). Indeed, it pacifies all diseases and is beneficial. It is protection for oneself and protection for others.

Protection from fire. Protection from tigers. Protection for the four castes. Protection from the terrifying Bhairava. I bind fear upon the throat of the child. Hāhā! By Kālī with her elephant-gait, among the five powers, with the hand of bliss for living beings and their mothers, [I bind] the throat of the quarrelsome Piṅgalā; Hāhā! Mātaṅgī, HŪṂ!
HŪM! Mātaṅgīśa is the Lord; the Sovereign Lady by the staff of Brahmā, and the Sovereign Lady by the staff of Viṣṇu [subdues] fever.
Subdue it with the staff of Agni; bind it with the staff of Nairṛti; pierce it with the staff of Kubera.
With the staff of Īśāna: Nṛtyā, Cakraṇī, Śūlanī, Padmanī, and Kṛṣṇākṣī.
Like a black serpent. Om, svāhā to Vāyu. Om, svāhā to the North. Om klīṃ, svāhā.

oṃ klīṃ klīṃ svāhā || oṃ bhlīṃ svāhā || oṃ bhlīṃ bhlīṃ svāhā || oṃ mlīṃ svāhā | oṃ mlīṃ mlīṃ svāhā || oṃ jvīṃ svāhā || oṃ jvīṃ jvīṃ svāhā || oṃ hrīṃ svāhā || oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā || oṃ bhūḥ svāhā || oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā || oṃ svaḥ svāhā ||
Svāhā! Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā! Oṃ, wherever the drink has gone, let it return to that very place;
svāhā!
Oṃ kratu svāhā || Oṃ sphuṭ svāhā || Oṃ brahmaṇe svāhā || Oṃ vaiṣṇave svāhā ||
Oṃ, svāhā to Prajāpati! Oṃ, svāhā to Agni! Oṃ, svāhā to Gandharva! Oṃ, svāhā to Kūṣmāṇḍa! Oṃ, [svāhā] to those bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and thieves who harm this person!
I bind the direction of those wicked ones—the Rākṣasas, Vetālas, Śākinīs, Kuṣmāṇḍas, and Vāsins.
I bind the sky; I bind the netherworld; I bind the water; I bind the land;
I bind the hands; I bind the feet; I bind the eyes; I bind their movement.

I bind my mind. I bind the mantra. Rudra binds a mandala five yojanas in extent. In the center of that mandala: Oṃ, O binder of the Rudra-mandala, bind, bind! Protect me, protect me! Do not move, do not move! Perform the meditation-act, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Rudra, in the southern direction.
In that direction, Mahisha is mounted upon his buffalo; with staff in hand, he pursues this circle.

Oṃ, protect, protect the Yama-maṇḍala! Do not waver, do not waver; do not act [otherwise], svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Rudra! In the southwestern direction (naiṛtī), he is mounted upon Skanda, holding a sword and a shield;
with his hand, he binds the maṇḍala of Nairṛti. Bind, bind the Nairṛti-maṇḍala! Protect!

2 mācala 2 mākarmi svāhā || Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Rudra, who has mounted upon the shoulder of Varuṇa, the direction of Yama, and the Maruts, with a noose in his hand; may Varuṇa bind the maṇḍala! Bind the Varuṇa-maṇḍala, bind it twice! Protect, protect! Do not move, do not move! Do not act [against me], do not act! Svāhā!

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Rudra! In the northwestern direction, [he who has] a corpse-shoulder mounted [upon him] and a foot in his hand—[homage to] Vāyu, the lord of the northwest. Bind the mandala! Bind the mandala of the northwest!

Rakṣa 2, mācala 2, mākarmi svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Rudra! In the direction of Kubera, mounted upon the shoulder of a mountain, with a mallet in hand, Kubera binds the maṇḍala; bind the Kubera-maṇḍala, bind it! Rakṣa 2, mācala 2, mākarmi svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One...

To Rudra in the northeastern direction: the Lord, mounted upon the shoulder of a bull, with a trident in his hand, worships the mandala. Worship the Īśvara-maṇḍala! Protect! Protect! Do not move! Do not act [against me]! Svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Rudra, in the eastern direction, mounted upon the shoulder of an elephant, with a thunderbolt in his hand.
Indra protects the mandala; Indra-mandala, protect, protect, guard, guard, do not move, do not move!

Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed Lord Rudra. In the upward direction, mounted upon the shoulder of a swan, with the Vedas in hand, Brahmā protects the mandala; Brahma-mandala, protect, protect, guard, guard, do not move, do not move!

*mākarmi svāhā* || *Oṃ namaḥ bhagavate rudrāya*. In the downward direction, [I invoke] Viṣṇu, mounted upon the shoulders of Garuḍa, holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands; bind the circle, bind the Viṣṇu-circle! Protect, protect! Do not move! *mākarmi svāhā* || *Oṃ glīṃ svāhā* || *Oṃ*...
Bhlīṃ Svāhā! Oṃ Stvīṃ Svāhā! Oṃ Jlīṃ Svāhā! Oṃ! Kaumārī protects the head, and likewise Māheśvarī protects the face.
May Vārāhī protect my throat, and Indrāṇī my two arms;
may Cāmuṇḍī protect my heart, and Brahmāṇī be stationed at my hips.

The goddess Vaiṣṇavī is at the feet; on all limbs, however, are two arms. Oṃ Brahmāyaṇī, protect [me] twice! With the staff in your hand, ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā! Oṃ Māheśvarī, protect [me] twice! With three hands, maṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā! Oṃ Kaumārī, protect [me] twice! With a lotus in your hand, ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ!

Svāhā! Oṃ Cāmuṇḍā, protect, protect! With a discus and the entire universe in her hand, ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā! Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, to Rudra, to the Protector of the Field (Kṣetrapāla); salutations! Protect, protect! With a sword in his hand, ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā! Having written down the eight Brahmans who are to be received, one should offer them.
If the science of architecture (vāstu-vidyā) is practiced while joined with false speech, it will not succeed;
or else, the members of the assembly (gaṇa) will fail, and Rudra himself would indeed become a slayer of a Brahmin.
He who recites [the Veda] through the hand of a disciple is indeed a slayer of a Brahmin.
I was not born in rivers; do not fight me, O mountain!
Born from the heart of the Enemy, I am Kāma in my true form;
whether a woman or a man, one should recite this mantra for protection in this world.
He attains all accomplishments; there is no need for deliberation on this point—that twice-born man who, having performed his twilight devotions, recites the Mahāvidyā daily.
One without a son obtains sons; one without wealth becomes wealthy;
one seeking a daughter obtains a daughter; and one seeking a son obtains a son.
A barren woman indeed obtains a son through this supreme practice of Maitrī;
all portents of misfortune vanish and every obstacle is destroyed.
One should write this on birch bark with the eight fragrant substances on an auspicious day;
one should recite the vidyā a hundred times and wrap it with a red thread.
One should place [the image] within gold, or silver, or even copper;
it should be worn upon the head, or on the neck, or on the right or left hand.
All success shall belong to him; he will certainly obtain his desire.
By the grace of the Great Vidyā, there shall be constant protection from all [dangers].
Thus ends the Mahāvidyā Maṃtrapālāyaṇa.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Dear One, there is the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa), the placement beginning with Niṣādyā, the primary deity and so forth,
as well as the purification of the kalās and the placement of the powers (śaktinyāsa).
The fingers are the heart-enclosure; the seat is threefold and complete; the corners are the *nāda* and the weapon-syllables; the limbs are the *vaśinī*; the pedestal is the principle (*tattva*).
The nine *yoni*s and the mantra should be placed separately,
either in the morning, at the time of worship, or during the performance of the fire sacrifice (*homa*).
Furthermore, at the time of recitation (*japa*), the specific application (*viniyoga*) is as follows:

*hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ āṃ sauḥ*. One performs the finger-assignment (*aṅguly-nyāsa*) starting from the middle finger and ending with the little finger, and starting from the thumb and ending with the palms. *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ: O Śrīman Mahātripurasundarī, protect, protect my self and enemies!*
One should place [the mantra] on the right side of the heart; such is the ritual placement (nyāsa).

*Sauṃ astrāya phaṭ*. [Perform] the binding of the directions with finger-snaps (*choṭikā*). Then, having pervaded that body of light with the three sections of the root-mantra (*mūlabīja*): with the first *kūṭa*, from the base (*mūla*) to the heart; with the second, from the heart to the space between the eyebrows; with the third, from the space between the eyebrows to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
Having pervaded [the body], one should perform the triad consisting of the three types of breath control (prāṇāyāma). This is the "arising" (utthāna) placement (nyāsa).
*Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ*, salutation to the seat of the self of the Goddess. [Thus, from the feet up to the knees.]

*Hrīṃ śrīṃ haiṃ hmlīṃ hsauḥ*, salutation to the seat of the wheel (*cakrāsana*). [This is applied] from the knees to the private parts. *Hrīṃ śrīṃ hsaiṃ hmlvīṃ hsauḥ*, salutation to the seat of all mantras (*sarvamantrāsana*). [This is applied] at the root.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Vlaṃ, salutation to the seat of the Sādhya and Siddha; [at] Svādhiṣṭhāna.
Thus ends the description of the seat and the ritual placement (nyāsa).

Based on the root-section (*mūlakhaṇḍa*), one should place [the mantras] upon the two hands at their roots, middles, and tips, and likewise upon the root, heart, and between the eyebrows, respectively. This is the "three-by-three" placement (*tristrika-nyāsa*). Then, within the *pūrṇavidyā*, one should perform the triple-pervasive placement (*trivyāpya-nyāsa*) from the head down to the feet and from the feet up to the head.
The entire [mantra] is the nyāsa.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Avikṛtanāda; [place] on the head.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the Sound of Emptiness; [place this] on the forehead.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Sparśanādā; [this is] in the middle of the eyebrows.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Bindunātha. [The Face]
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Nādanāda; [at] the throat.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the seed-syllable; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the sound of resonance—at the navel.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Aṅkuranauda. [At] Svādhiṣṭhāna.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the syllable-sound (akṣaranāda) at the mūlādhāra.
The placement of the resonance (nāda).
Then, having meditated upon a hexagon on one's own head, one should place [the syllables] within the six corners by moving clockwise from the front corner.

Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Vāmā. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Jyeṣṭhā. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Raudrī. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Ambikā. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Śāntā. Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Śāmbhavī. Thus is the assignment of the corners (koṇanyāsa).
Then: *Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Drāṃ Drīṃ Klīṃ Vlūṃ Saḥ Yāṃ Rāṃ Vāsāṃ*, obeisance to the arrows of Kāmeśvara for the purpose of paralyzing.

KĀMEŚVARĀṄKUŚĀYA 2 || 2 YĀṂ 5 DRĀṂ 5 KROṂ STAMBHANĀYA KĀMEŚVARĀṄKUŚĀYA 2 || [To the right upper hand. Thus is the placement of the weapon (astra-nyāsa).

Then, at the end of each of the three sections of the root-mantra, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the letters in the positions of the Mātṛkās, beginning with *aṃ namaḥ* and ending with *kṣaṃ namaḥ*. This is the placement of the script (*lipinyāsa*). 2 *aiṃ* to the two middle fingers for the All-knowing One (*sarvajñā*).

2 *klīṃ* to the eternally satisfied one, svāhā with the two ring fingers. 2 *sauḥ* to the beginningless awakening, vaṣaṭ with the two little fingers. 2 *aiṃ* to the independent one, hūṃ with the two thumbs. 2 *klīṃ* to the one whose power is eternally undiminished, voṣaṭ with the two index fingers. 2 *sauḥ* to the infinite power.
*Phaṭ* for the weapon (*astra*) on the backs of both hands. *Astra*. Likewise for the heart and the other limbs. Thus is the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
Then Vaśinī: 2 AṂ 16 RVLŪṂ, to Vaśinī Vāgdevatā, 2. Brahma:
2 KAṂ 5 KMPRĪṂ, to Kāmeśvarī Vāgdevatā, 2. On the forehead: 2 LVRIṂ, to Modinī Vāgdevatā, 2. On the tongue: 2 ṬAṂ 4 YLUṂ, to Vimalā Vāgdevatā, 2. On the throat: 2 TAṂ 4 KṢMRĪṂ, to Aruṇā Vāgdevatā, 2.

In the heart: 2 PAṂ 4 HMKṢMLVRYŪṂ Jayanī, bestow speech! 2 NĀBHAU (at the navel): 2 YAṂ 4 JHMRĪṂ Sarveśvarī, bestow speech! Thus is Vaśinī. Then: 2 AIṂ 1 In the fire-wheel (agnicakra), in the abode of Kāmagiri...

To Kāmeśvarī Devī, whose nature is Mitrīśanātha, [salutations] twice; to the Śakti whose nature is Rudra, [salutations] twice. Klīṃ! To Vajreśvarī Devī, whose nature is Ṣaṣṭhīśanātha, in the Sūryacakra at the cavern of Pūrṇagiri, [salutations] to the Śakti whose nature is Viṣṇu, [salutations] twice.

In the heart: 2 Sauḥ! To the goddess Bhagamālinī, who is the power of the self of Brahman, at the lunar wheel (somacakra) in the sacred seat of Jālandhara, whose essence is Uḍḍīśanātha: 2. On the tongue: 2 Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ! To the goddess Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, who is the power of the supreme Brahman, at the Brahma-wheel (brahmacakra) in the sacred seat of Oḍyāna, whose essence is Caryānātha: 2. Brahmā.

Thus is the placement of the seats (*pīṭha-nyāsa*). Then: [twice] first, to the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, the pervader of the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*), [twice]. Having pervaded as far as the heart.

2. A second [time], to the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, who pervades the *vidyā-tattva*—from the heart up to the midpoint of the eyebrows. 2. A third [time], to the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, who pervades the *śiva-tattva*—from the midpoint of the eyebrows up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). Having uttered these three [mantras], [one offers to her] who pervades all *tattvas*.

To the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī, [twice]. One should perform the placement (nyāsa) from the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head) down to the feet, and from the feet up to the aperture of Brahmā; this is the *tattva-nyāsa*. Thereafter, one should perform the *navayoni-nyāsa* and other placements using three seed-syllables (*bījas*) each: on the two ears, the chin, the two temples, and again on the face.
In the two eyes, in the nose, and in the lotus of the heart, there are two parts each.
On the two breasts, at the region of the navel, on the knees, the crown of the head,
the feet, the secret place, the two sides, and above the heart.
One should place [the syllables] beginning with the right one below the breast and in the region of the throat;
thereafter follows the placement (nyāsa) of the mantra-syllables.
On the crown of the head, in the secret place, in the heart, and likewise in the three eyes;
in the two ears, in the region of the mouth, in the two shoulders, and again on the pedestal.
In the same way, one should know everything [to be placed] from the knees up to the head.
Thus is the ritual placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa).
Then, having meditated upon oneself as consisting of mantra, from the feet to the head and from the head to the feet— thus [are described] Sundarī, Vārāhī, Kālī, and the Ṣoḍhā.
This is the ritual procedure for the fire oblation (homa) of this [deity].
The preeminent practitioner, having gathered the necessary materials, sits upon his seat, sips water (ācamana), and performs breath-control (prāṇāyāma).

Having announced the place and time, he makes the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the fire-oblation according to his specific desire, resolving: "I shall perform the installation of the fire as an ancillary part of this rite. Then, he performs the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), and the ritual placement of the phonemes (mātṛkānyāsa).

Having prepared the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should gaze at it with the root mantra (mūlamantra), sprinkle it with water using the weapon mantra (astramantra), strike it with kuśa grass using the weapon mantra, and sprinkle it again with the armor mantra (kavaca). Then, having dug it with the weapon mantra,
one should lift up that earth with the thumb and ring finger using the heart mantra (hṛdayamantra).
Having filled [the vessel] with what is called pure clay, one should level it with the Astra-mantra; sprinkle it with water using the Kavaca-mantra; rub it with the Astra-mantra;
perform the cleansing with the Kavaca-mantra; smear it with cow-dung water using the Kavaca-mantra itself;
and contemplate it as consisting of the thirty-eight kalās of Agni, Sūrya, and Soma by means of the Kavaca-mantra alone.

The three-stranded cord is prepared with the *kavaca* mantra. Worship is performed with the mantra: *oṃ amuka-kuṇḍāya namaḥ*. One should contemplate [the pit] as being made firm like a vajra by means of the *astra* mantra. The four corners are formed with *kuśa* grass using the *hṛdaya* mantra.

The covering of the entire sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with armor-mantras (kavaca) and kuśa grass is called *akṣapāṭana*. Alternatively, the letters from 'A' to 'Kṣa' may be inscribed [there]. Thus are the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*). Having inspected the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) with the root mantra, struck it with kuśa grass using the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and sprinkled it with water using the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), one should proceed therein.

Having drawn three lines each, oriented toward the east and upward, with the root of *kuśa* grass using the heart-mantra, and having sprinkled them with water while reciting the *praṇava*, [one should proceed] upon the lines directed toward the east.
Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu. Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra. Oṃ, obeisance to Indra. [These are placed] upon the prominent lines.
Oṃ to Brahmā. Oṃ to Yama. Oṃ to Candra. Having thus worshipped, and having worshipped there the Yoga-pīṭha beginning with Maṇḍūkā and ending with Paratattva: Oṃ to Jayā. Oṃ to Ajitā. Oṃ to Aparājitā.
Oṃ to Nityā. Oṃ to Vilāsinī. Oṃ to Dogdhrī. Oṃ to Aghorā. Oṃ to Maṅgalā, obeisance.

Having thus worshipped the deities of the seats (*pīṭha-devatāḥ*), one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) upon the seat of Vārāhī with the mantra: *hrīṃ sarvaśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ*. Having worshipped Vārāhī with the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), one should meditate upon Śiva there, worship Him, and contemplate the Goddess as being in her menses (*mṛtumatī*) and the God as intoxicated with sandalwood paste.

Having taken fire produced from sun-crystals (sūryakānta) and the like, or brought from the house of a Vedic scholar (śrotriya), and having discarded the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda)— the embers— with the Astra mantra toward the southwest (nairṛtya), [one should discard] the portion belonging to the deity.

Having consecrated [the water] with the four purificatory rites beginning with *vīkṣaṇa*, and contemplating the unity of the digestive fire (*audarya*), the lunar fire (*vaindava*), the terrestrial fire (*pārthiva*), and the [inner] fire (*vahni*), one should join consciousness to the fire by means of the syllable *ra*.
Then, having consecrated the navel with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), rendered it nectarine by means of the *dhenumudrā*, protected it with the *astra-mantra*, and veiled it with the *kavaca-mantra*: Oṃ.

Having worshipped with "Raṃ, obeisance to Vahni," and having gone near the fire, one should take that vessel with both hands, circumambulate it three times clockwise around the fire, and then, with the thought that it is the womb of the Goddess and the seed-syllable of the Śrī-devī,
place it facing oneself in the center of the fire-pit with "Oṃ Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ."

With the thought that [the offering] is sexual union, the gods and goddesses do not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). Having offered [the oblation] with "Oṃ citpiṅgala hana paca 2 daha 2 sarvajñāpaye svāhā," and having thus caused the fire to blaze up with wood, one should rise with palms joined in reverence and recite: "Oṃ, Agni, the blazing god, Jātavedas, the bearer of oblations..."

Having approached and sat down before [the fire] which is golden-colored, stainless, perfected, and facing in all directions, one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the mantra: "Oṃ, O Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, bring [the gods] here; O red-eyed one, accomplish all rites, svāhā! Then, one should place [the sacred syllables]: "Oṃ, salutation to the sage Bhṛgu" on the head, and "Gāyatrī" on the mouth.

Salutation to *Chanda*. Salutation to the deity Śrī-Vahni in the heart. "This is the application (*viniyoga*) for my fire-oblation (*homa*) and ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Having thus performed the placement, then [one should place] *oṃ śūṃ* to Hiraṇyā, the immortal presiding deity, in the secret place (*guhya*).

Oṃ ṣyūṃ, homage to Gaganā, the presiding deity of the Pitṛs; thus on the head. Oṃ śmrūṃ, homage to Raktā, the presiding deity of the Gandharvas and others; on the mouth. Aṃ, homage to Kṛṣṇā, the presiding deity of the Yakṣas.
Homage! At the nose: *lyūṃ*, homage to the presiding deity of the serpent, Suprāṇā. At the eyes: [lyūṃ]... homage.

*Mṛūṃ*, salutation to the goddess presiding over the Piśācas, who is exceedingly red; [this is for] all limbs. *Yyrūṃ*, salutation to the goddess presiding over the Rākṣasas, who possesses many forms; thus, having performed the placement of the seven tongues of fire: *Oṃ sahasrārciṣe* (to the thousand-rayed one), salutation to the heart; *Oṃ svasti pūrṇāya* (to the full one of well-being), *svāhā* to the head; *Oṃ uttiṣṭha puruṣāya* (arise, O Supreme Being), *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*).

"Oṃ dhūmavyāpine kavacāya hūṃ | Oṃ saptajihvāya netrāya vauṣaṭ | Oṃ dhanurdharāstrāya phaṭ. Having thus performed the internal placement (*nyāsa*) of the six-limbed mantras, one should also place them upon the heart and other parts: "Oṃ agnaye jātavedase namaḥ" on the head; "Oṃ agnaye saptajihvāya" on the left shoulder.
Homage! On the left side: Oṃ, homage to Agni Havyavāhana. On the left hip: Oṃ, homage to Agni Aśvadarāja. At the genitals: Oṃ, homage to Agni Vaiśvānara.
On the right hip: Oṃ, homage to Agni, the youthful splendor. On the right side:
Oṃ, homage to Agni, whose face is the universe. On the right limb: Oṃ, homage to Agni, whose face is the gods.
Having performed the placement [of mantras] on all limbs with the words "on all limbs," one should display the *saptajihvā-mudrā* and release [the breath]. Then,

having visualized for the fire a pedestal (*pīṭha*) in the form of a hexagon, an eight-petaled lotus, and a square, and having worshipped there [the deities] beginning with Maṇḍūka and ending with the Yoga-pīṭha;
Oṃ, homage to Pītā. Oṃ, homage to Śvetā. Oṃ, homage to Aruṇā. Oṃ, homage to Kṛṣṇā. Oṃ, homage to Dhūmrā. Oṃ, homage to Tīvrā. Oṃ, homage to Visphuliṅginī.

Oṃ, obeisance to Virājī. Oṃ, obeisance to Jvālinī. Having thus worshipped the powers of the pedestal (pīṭhaśakti), and having worshipped the pedestal with "Raṃ, obeisance to the lotus of all powers," one should meditate upon the Fire.

"I praise the Fire-god, who has three eyes, is the color of vermilion, is adorned with ornaments of refined gold, whose head is decorated with matted locks, and who holds in his hands the excellent svastika, the śakti, the gesture of fearlessness, and a lotus upon which he sits. Having thus meditated, one should recite: "Oṃ, O Vaiśvānara, Jātavedas, come here, O red-eyed one; accomplish all rites, svāhā!"

Having worshipped the fire with the mantra, beginning from the seat (āsana) and ending with flowers, one should then worship within the six corners, starting from the northeast (īśāna) and proceeding clockwise: Oṃ *m*prūṃ, salutation to Hiraṇyā; Oṃ *p*prūṃ, salutation to Gaganā;
Oṃ *g*prūṃ, salutation to Raktā; Oṃ *p*prūṃ, salutation to Kṛṣṇā; Oṃ *l*prūṃ, salutation to Suprabhā.
Homage! Oṃ yrūṃ, homage to Atiraktā. Madhya yyūṃ, homage to Bahurūpā.

Then, upon the filaments of the eight-petaled lotus: Oṃ sahasrārciṣe hṛdayāya namaḥ | Oṃ svasti pūrṇāya śirase svāhā | Oṃ uttiṣṭha puruṣāya śikhāyai vaṣaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ dhūmavyāpine kavacāya hūṃ namaḥ | Oṃ saptajihvāya netrāya vauṣaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ...
Salutation to the wielder of the bow and the weapon; phaṭ! Namaḥ!
Then, on the eight petals starting from the east: *oṃ agnaye jātavedase namaḥ* || *oṃ agnaye saptajihvāya namaḥ* || *oṃ agnaye havyavāhanāya namaḥ* || *oṃ aśvodarajāya namaḥ* || *oṃ agnaye* ||

Salutation to Vaiśvānara. Oṃ, salutation to Agni Kaumāratejas. Oṃ, salutation to Agni Viśvamukha. Having worshipped the weapons of the world-protectors (lokeśas) within the outer square, and having worshipped [the deity] with incense and other offerings, one should spread darbha grass to the north of the fire and place the vessels there. [The vessels include] the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the sprinkling water, the clarified butter vessel, the oblation-pot, the five enclosing sticks, the fuel wood, the sacrificial grass, the full vessel for the Brahman’s fee, and the materials for the offerings and worship, and having rendered them pure,
one should wash the sprinkling-vessel with the *prokṣaṇī* mantra; then, having placed the two strainers (*pavitra*) into it, one should pour [the water] into it while reciting the *astra* mantra.
Having thrice sprinkled all the vessels with their openings facing upward using the root mantra,
having seated the Brahman priest to the south, and having consecrated the praṇītā vessel like the prokṣaṇī vessel,
one should place it upon kuśa grass to the north of the fire; then, some of that water [should be poured] into the prokṣaṇī vessel.

Having prepared that water, he should sprinkle all the sacrificial materials with it; then, using the palm of his hand, he should sweep around the fire, strew grass around the fire with four blades each, excluding the eastern direction, and having laid the enclosing sticks, he should worship Brahmā at the southern enclosing stick, Viṣṇu at the western, and Rudra at the northern; thereafter, [he should worship] behind the fire.

Having spread the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with excellent *kuśa* blades, and having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, one should heat them: the tip with the tips, the middle with the middles, and the base with the bases.

Having mixed [the substances] again, heated them, and sprinkled [water] over them, one should place them upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Then, one should worship the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) at the root, middle, and tip [of the grass]. Having worshipped Māyā in the *sruc* ladle and Śiva in the *sruva* spoon, and having taken the vessel for the clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), one should wash it with the *astra-mantra* and pour the clarified butter into it while the *pavitra* strainer is present.

Having consecrated [the clarified butter] with the four [mudrās] beginning with Vīkṣaṇa, one removes the embers of the Vāyavya [quarter]; having placed the clarified butter over them while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra, one washes two *kuśa* blades, throws them into the clarified butter while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra, and casts them into the fire.
Then, having washed another pair of *darbha* blades and performed the *paryagni-karaṇa* (circling fire) around them with the Kavaca-mantra, [one places them] in the fire.
Having cast [the first two blades] and again kindling another pair of *darbha* blades with the *astra-mantra*, he should display them toward the fire and cast them into the flame. Then,
having removed the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) and placed it upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) by circling it clockwise, and having drawn out the embers,
he should hold the two *pavitra* strainers with his thumb and ring finger while reciting the *astra-mantra*, [and then pour] the clarified butter.
Having purified the ghee three times with the *utpavana* mantra while facing oneself,

having placed the *pavitra* strainer with its tips pointing eastward in the center of the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), and having divided it into two portions— conceiving the right portion as the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) and the left portion as the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*)— one should proceed.
Having visualized Iḍā on the left side, Piṅgalā on the right side, and Suṣumnā in the middle,
one should take clarified butter from the right side with the *sruva* ladle while reciting the mantra "Namo," and offer it into the right eye of the fire with "Oṃ Agnaye Svāhā.
One should then place the residue of the butter that was taken there back into its original vessel, continuing this up to four oblations.

*Oṃ agnaye idaṃ namaḥ*; thus one should perform the renunciation (*tyāga*) for the upper region. Again, taking clarified butter from the left side, one offers it into the left eye with *somāya svāhā*, and then, taking clarified butter, [offers it] with *oṃ agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā*.

Having offered oblations into the third eye of the fire, one should again take clarified butter from the southern side and offer it into the mouth of the fire with the mantra: *oṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā*. In all cases, one should perform the ritual renunciation (*tyāga*) by designating each respective deity. Then: *oṃ svāhā paramātmane idaṃ*; *oṃ bhūḥ svāhā agnaye idaṃ*. *Oṃ*.

*bhuvaḥ svāhā*—this is for Vāyu. *oṃ svaḥ svāhā*—this is for Sūrya. *oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ svāhā*—this is for Prajāpati. Having offered three oblations with the mantra: *oṃ vaiśvānara jātaveda ihāvaholohitākṣa sarvakarmāṇi sādhaya svāhā*, one then performs the *agni-garbhādhāna* (the conception of the fire).

I accomplish [this], svāhā! Thus [are performed] the *puṃsavana*, the *sīmantonnayana*, and the *jātakarman*. Then, having purified the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) by the offering of the five fuel-sticks (*pañcasamidhātyādhāna*), [there follow] the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first outing (*niṣkramaṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), the initiation (*upanayana*), the *mahānāmnī* vow, and the *mahāvrata*.

Having offered eight oblations of clarified butter with the formula "I perform the Vedic initiation (aupaniṣada), the gift of a cow, the return home, and the marriage; svāhā" for each rite, and having performed for the fire the purificatory rites beginning with Garbhādhāna and ending with Udvāha, he should dismiss the white bull and the two deities from the fire. Then, having sprinkled five fuel-sticks with clarified butter, [he should worship] Prajāpati mentally.
Meditating thus, he should place [the oblation] into the fire with the mantra "oṃ svāhā."
Then, one should offer an oblation to each of the limb-deities (*aṅgadevatā*): *stryūṃ hiraṇyāyai svāhā*;
*ṣpūṃ gaganāyai svāhā*; *śrpūṃ raktāyai svāhā*; *vyrūṃ kṛṣṇāyai namaḥ svāhā*.

*lprūṃ* svāhā to Suprabhā; *pprūṃ* svāhā to Atiraktā; *yprūṃ* svāhā to Bahurūpā. *Oṃ*, obeisance to the heart, Sahasrārcis; *oṃ* svāhā to the head, Svastipūrṇa; *oṃ* vaṣaṭ svāhā to the tuft, Uttiṣṭhapuruṣa; *oṃ* hūṃ to the armor, Dhūmravyāpin.

Svāhā! Oṃ, to the one with seven tongues, to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ svāhā! Oṃ, to the wielder of the bow, to the weapon, phaṭ svāhā! Oṃ, to Agni Jātavedas, svāhā! Oṃ, to Agni Saptajihva, svāhā! Oṃ, to Agni Havyavāhana, svāhā! Oṃ, to Agni Aśvodaraja, svāhā! Oṃ, to Agni...
Svāhā to Vaiśvānara! Om, Svāhā to Agni Kaumāra! Om, Svāhā to Agni Viśvamukha! Om, Svāhā to Agni Devamukha! Om Luṃ, Svāhā to Indra, and so forth;
then one should offer one oblation each to the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons. Then, with the *sruva* ladle, [offer] four portions of clarified butter.
Having taken up the *sruva* ladle, placed the *sruc* with its opening downward, and stood up, he offers an oblation with: "Oṃ, O Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, bring hither!
O red-eyed one, accomplish all rites, svāhā vauṣaṭ! Having offered thus, he sits down and recites:
"Oṃ svāhā; Oṃ Śrīṃ svāhā; Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ svāhā; Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ svāhā; Oṃ Śrīṃ..."

hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ svāhā || oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ svāhā || oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṇapataye varada svāhā || oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada sarvajanaṃ me vaśam ānaya svāhā || oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye ||

"O Giver of Boons, bring all people under my control, svāhā! Having offered oblations ten times with this mantra divided into ten parts, one should then offer oblations with the entire Mahāgaṇapati mantra at the four gates. Thereafter, one should prepare the sacrificial porridge (caru) for the purpose of the caru-homa.
Thus, when the fire has been consecrated: "Oṃ, Agni, you are divine splendor, for you are the supreme purifier."

"Therefore, I worship the supreme Śiva within your heart-lotus. Having thus petitioned the fire as one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadeva), and having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) along with the limbs (sāṅga) and the enclosures (sāvaraṇa), one should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter (ājyāhuti) with the root mantra (mūlamantra) for the purpose of unifying the faces. Likewise, [one should offer] with the root mantra.

For the purpose of joining the channels (nāḍī-saṃdhāna), one should offer eleven oblations of clarified butter (ājyāhuti). Then, having offered one oblation of clarified butter for each of the deities of the retinue (āvaraṇadevatā), and having completed the fire-oblation (homa) to one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) with the primary substance according to the prescribed number,
[one should likewise perform it] for the deities of the six limbs and the deities of the retinue.
As before, one should offer each oblation of clarified butter (ājyāhuti). Then, one should perform the Mahāvyāhṛti-homa:
Oṃ bhūr agnaye ca pṛthivyai ca mahate ca svāhā. Oṃ bhuvo vāyave cāntarikṣāya ca mahate ca svāhā. Oṃ suvar ādityāya ca dive ca mahate ca svāhā. Oṃ...
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaś candramase vanakṣatrebhyaś ca digbhyaś ca mahate ca svāhā. Thus, four oblations.

Having offered the fifth oblation with "oṃ svāhā," [one recites]: "Oṃ! Whatever [I have done] prior to this, through my vital breath, intellect, body, and faculties, through modification, in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, by means of mind, speech, or action..."

"Whatever has been done by my two hands, my feet, my belly, or my genitals; whatever has been remembered, spoken, or performed—may all that be an offering to Brahman, Svāhā! With this, one should offer eight oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*). Then, having worshipped the Fire as before, one should offer sesame seeds with clarified butter for the sake of rectifying any deficiencies or excesses, saying: "Oṃ Hūṃ, I give."

*Sāṅgaṃ kuru 2 svāhā*. Having thus offered one oblation with sesame seeds, [he recites]: *Oṃ sahasrārciḥ mahāretā namaste bahurūpadhṛk | sarvāśine sarvagatāya pāvakāya namo'stu te || tvaṃ raudra ghorakarmā ca ghorahā ca namāmi te*.
"O Viṣṇu, O Guardian of the World, grant me this peace.

Having thus prayed to Agni, and having filled [the vessel] with ghee taken four times, he places the *sruva* spoon upon it with its bowl facing downward; then, rising, he offers the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) in the form of the mantra of his chosen deity followed by "vauṣaṭ."
It is stated in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā: "Then, having filled the sruva-ladle with the remaining ghee..."

Having placed a flower before it, having covered it with a downward-facing *sruva* ladle together with *darbha* grass, and having stood up with his hands joined in *añjali*, he [should recite] the root mantra.

One should offer oblations ending with *vauṣaṭ*, according to the verse beginning "dhārāṃ tu vayasaṃsitām. Having offered three full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*) ending with *vauṣaṭ*, having worshipped the deity, and having dismissed [the deity] from the presence of the fire,
one should give sacrificial offerings (*bali*) to the attendants of the god, to Vaṃdeśa, and to the world-protectors (*lokapāla*).
Having released [the fire] as before, he offered oblations into the fire with the four vyāhṛtis, the [names of the] tongues, the six limbs, and so forth,
and one oblation for each of the forms; then he poured out the praṇītā water onto the sacrificial grass, except for that which was permanently remaining from the surrounding strewing.

Having cast the lower garment into the fire and sprinkled water around the fire with the *prokṣaṇī* water, he should worship it, saying: "O Fire, O you of great power, accomplisher of all rites! When another rite is about to commence, please remain present here with respect. Having thus petitioned the Fire and withdrawn it with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, [he should place] the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) of Brahmā.
Having offered [the oblation] to Brahmā, one should dismiss him.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Procedure for the Siddhānta Homa," concerning the Great Vidyā of the Yoginī Nyāsa, within the Dakṣiṇāmnāya Nirvāṇapada of the venerable Śrī Vārāhī Tantra. || 35 ||
The Goddess said:
Having heard the first section spoken by you to Vārāhī, I now desire to hear the five-limbed [text]; please tell it, O Lord.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess; I shall speak, I tell you of Vārāhī.
Listen to the five-limbed essence, O Sāraṅgī; it is being told as the very core of the essence.
Since even by the mere remembrance of it the great sins are destroyed,
I shall now describe its five-limbed ritual manual (pañcāṅga) along with the chapters (paṭala).
Homage to you, O Great Māyā, who bear the name Vārāhī;
you are Kolāsyā, the Great Fierce One, and the Goddess who holds the adamantine snout.
Resembling a thousand suns, endowed with a mass of splendor,
she has the form of Rudra— most terrible, possessing a fearsome appearance, and inspiring dread.
Resembling the *vaṃdhūka* flower, like the blossom of the *ḍāḍimī*,
resembling sharp vermilion, and similar to the *javā* flower.
She was in the prime of youth, intoxicated with passion, and possessed full, swelling breasts.
Her limbs were adorned with every kind of ornament, and she wore a dangling garland of severed heads;
she had three eyes and terrible red eyes, shining with fangs that were fearsome to behold.
The goddess Dharā may have four arms or even eight;
she holds a fruit in her right hand and a mace in her left.
The goddess Earth, the bestower of boons, adorned with various ornaments,
is seated upon a red lotus and stands atop a corpse.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and beautiful in every limb,
the Goddess is fond of wine and meat, and is saluted by the bliss of liquor.
Worshipped by all the worlds, she pervades the three realms including all that is mobile and immobile;
the Universal Yoginī is established within the great wheel situated in the triangle.
In the great five-cornered wheel are established five deities:
Andhanī, Yudhinī, Jambhanī, and likewise Mohanī.
And when joined with the *staṃbhanī* [mantra], she should always be worshipped by the wise;
she is worshipped externally within the six-cornered wheel in the midst of the *śṛṅga*.
In the center of the northeast corner, one should worship Ḍākinī,
who consumes all actions and brings about their total destruction.
In the southeast corner is Rākiṇī, who drinks the blood of enemies;
in the southwest corner is Lākinī, who devours flesh.
Kākinī is in the wind-corner, devouring the bone element;
Śākinī is in the eastern corner, seizing the fat element.
The Rākṣasī resides in the corner; Hākinī is the devourer of marrow;
Yākinī is with Kusumālinī, situated in the midst of the flood of six tears.
And they consume the seminal essence as food for the purpose of dissolving the body;
this is achieved by propitiating the Goddess through both restraint and non-restraint.
When worshipped and meditated upon, she is the supreme bestower of all accomplishments;
the goddess effects killing and expulsion through her dark complexion and intense splendor.
Standing upon the corpse, she possesses eight arms;
in her right hands, she holds a sword, a discus, a mace, and a club.
Holding a skull-topped staff and a conch in her left hands,
she brings about the death of all beings and the destruction of all enemies.
The father [is] by means of the yoga of the pillar and so forth; in the act of deluding, she is red in form, Vandanī, and Rodanī, resembling black fire.
In the Jambhaka [mantra], she has the luster of smoke-colored light for the sake of crystal-like liberation;
in one's undertakings she is red-limbed, and in battle she assumes a black form.
One should worship her in various forms through many manifestations at all times;
and in all battles, she appears in the form of one who has abandoned food.
The goddess Trailokyavaminī is fierce in form and terrifying;
she is filled with blows from her snout and utters a terrible, thundering *ghutkāra*.
Chewing upon the great enemy, adorned with bracelets and anklets,
she is drunk with blood and her eyes are rolling wildly.
The Great Goddess, who dwells eternally in the cremation ground, dances;
by remembering her during the *tāla* rhythm in every peril, she protects all sentient beings.
In battle and in the royal court, in fears of thieves and tigers,
among spirits, ghosts, and piśācas, and among gods and apsarases;
In the lineage of the eight *nāgas* as well, there is likewise fear of *rākṣasas*;
by remembering these various others, everything perishes.
And by means of swords and other weapons, as well as various other missiles in manifold ways.
By your grace, there is restraint; by your counsel, there is retention;
and it is rendered fruitful through various utterances, such as those beginning with "Sukha."
By remembering her, one is released from the noose; she is the mother Śrī Pañcamī, who bestows liberation from bondage, possesses a formidable form, and removes all fear.

With wrath, one meditates upon the Goddess; the procedure for recitation, fire-offerings, and worship, as well as the offering of oblations and the special worship during the rite of Bhairavī, is thus performed.
Through practice for seven nights, she destroys all enemies;
she brings about peace, nourishment, subjugation, accomplishment, delusion, and paralysis.
The goddess who bestows all accomplishments in the acts of subduing and slaying should likewise be worshipped in her various forms with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
Having offered wine, meat, and other such items as an oblation (naivedya) along with animals,
and having presented three handfuls of flowers, one should prostrate like a staff according to the Mata.
Having performed meditation and recitation, one should say: "Salutations to her, salutations again and again!
O Goddess Vārāhī, giver of boons, beautiful and endowed with youth."
O Goddess, bestower of boons upon your devotees, O beautiful one, salutations to you!
Buffaloes, goats, cocks, rams, and others who slaughter men [are your offerings].
Satisfied by offerings, she bestows victory in battle;
she is the beautiful Goddess Kālikā, Vārāhī, the granter of boons.
O beloved, having worshipped Mahākālī, the bestower of boons and slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura, as well as Kaumārī, one hundred and eight times.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, O Goddess, one shall attain satisfaction.
Thus, in the Śrī Vārāhī Tantra:
"Whatever may be deficient in syllables or words, and whatever may be lacking in prosodic measures (mātrā), may all that be forgiven, O Goddess; be gracious, O Supreme Sovereign."
The First Section of the Vārāhī Tantra.
The completion of the Śrīvārāhī Tantra, folio 233.
